#1404. England throw it away with defending unworthy of a top nation

There had been so much talk – first raised by Thomas Tuchel after the shocking World Cup exit to Argentina – about England’s DNA. About whether they could keep the ball, pass the ball, control the ball, the way Spain do.

The world and European champions were England’s first opponents – after the World Cup – in this Nations League campaign and came away from Wembley with a deserved win. They are now 39 games unbeaten with substitute Mikel Oyarzabal, who scored the winning goal against England in the final of the last European Championship, doing so again.

Mikel Oyarzabal SCORES against England AGAIN! 🎯Spain retake the lead after a slick finish from the Spaniard 👏#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pPT3KvRHWl

That may have been no surprise, even if the inevitable “olés” after Spain’s third goal will have hurt. But the nature of it? For the England manager this was another shocker. Not in the way his team went about the task. They were positive, fun, attacking. But in the way they conceded – goals and chances – and lost.

On this performance, DNA, for England, stands for Defensively Not Able, as they threw away what could have been a famous and restorative victory. Instead, with Croatia beating the Czech Republic in the other group game, England are under immediate pressure to win in Prague on Tuesday.

In fact, England have conceded 13 goals in their past six matches – in fairness including four in that third-place World Cup 6-4 win over France – and that is not good enough for a top-tier nation. Tuchel needs to sort it out defensively.

It could have been very different if Harry Kane had not missed from the penalty spot, slipping as he struck the ball, with England improbably 2-1 ahead. “It would have been the decisive punch,” Tuchel stated. Maybe so, even if there was always the feeling that Spain could go through the gears.

Kane MISSES from the penalty spot! 😧Harry Kane slips when he strikes the ball, let off for Spain and Luis de la Fuente#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pvg3GGa9ma

Afterwards there were claims, led by the impressive Anthony Gordon, that this was a missed opportunity for England. A bit like the World Cup. They need to shake this theme.

The irony was this was one of their best creative displays for quite some time. They took the game to Spain and could have scored more. And conceded more.

In truth it could have been Spain 4 England 0 inside half an hour and before Tuchel’s team laid a glove on their opponents.

Another let off for England 😧Ferran Torres misses another big chance one-on-one with James Trafford #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/KFkJoJUW6c

The manager had also spoken about how England should “embrace the chaos” as their best route to success. That may appear a questionable tactic – does chaos ever win a tournament? – but England certainly did that. This was as chaotic and, admittedly, entertaining as it gets.

England attacked with pace and power with the pick of their players the two based in Spain: Gordon, who scored, and Jude Bellingham. And the defenders? This was a bad night for Marc Guéhi, his Manchester City team-mate Nico O’Reilly (cue speculation about whether they were distracted by the verdict on the Premier League charges against their club) and for Jarell Quansah at right-back who is so evidently a centre-half.

A penny, once more, for the thoughts of the unused Trent Alexander-Arnold. The fourth defender, Ezri Konsa, vented his frustration at what was happening around him.

It was not just the errors but the unforced nature of them. Poor in possession with misplaced passes and defensively wide open. There is a gap between Spain and England but not as big as the gaps that were exposed in England’s back four. They endured a full house of calamities. They seemed strangely unaware – or incapable of dealing with – the danger posed by the outstanding Lamine Yamal.

Maybe because of the opposition – or the criticism – England felt the need to play out. But what an horrific start. What an inexplicable moment for Guéhi as he received the ball from O’Reilly and turned into trouble, gifting possession to Yamal who ran on and scored. Inside two minutes.

WHAT A START FROM SPAIN 🇪🇸Lamine Yamal pounces on a Marc Guéhi error to give Spain an early lead at Wembley #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/Et83EyTPlp

Spain walked out with the second star on their shirt – to mark their second World Cup triumph. That was the star Tuchel had promised for England.

Now, straight away, they were up against it. It could have turned very ugly. Ferran Torres, who had scored the winner in the World Cup Final, had one disallowed for offside, then was thwarted by James Trafford after – inexplicably again – being played onside by Quansah.

BIG SAVE from James Trafford 🧤The Leeds United goalkeeper keeps out Ferran Torres#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/nj5b8AUSQU

Then Torres was sent clear following Elliot Anderson’s poor pass, only to drag his shot wide. The third miss came from Dani Olmo, again set up by Yamal.

It could – it should – have been game over. Then England unexpectedly turned it around. They had kept attacking despite what was going on at the back and struck through a truly thrilling counter-attack, with Gordon and Bellingham combining before the Barcelona winger calmly beat goalkeeper Unai Simon.

ENGLAND ARE LEVEL! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿A brilliant finish from Anthony Gordon after a breathtaking counter attack 👏#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/z0nSfWIHVd

It was an exceptional goal and was quickly followed by a fortunate one as O’Reilly’s cross was met by Kane who stooped to steer in a header, only for it to strike Marc Cucurella, who made a mess of clearing, and it went past Simón.

I think we'll give that goal to Harry Kane 🎯England come from behind to lead Spain thanks Harry Kane, with assistance from Marc Cucurella ⚽️#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/X3qSOWUhVT

The Spain left-back hit the post with a cross, misjudged by Trafford who was given this game and the next to stake his claim ahead of Jordan Pickford who has so long been the undisputed first-choice.

England dominated for a while and Bellingham won a penalty, after a VAR intervention, only for Kane to strike the crossbar.

How Spain made them pay and worryingly so. O’Reilly passed the ball straight to Olmo who swept it inside. Substitute Álex Baena checked and beat Trafford from the edge of the area. Even worse was how Spain cut through the heart of England defence with Baena finding Oyarzabal. Why was no defender closer to him? What was Guéhi doing? And O’Reilly? Oyarzabal exquisitely dinked the ball over Trafford.

Thomas Tuchel does not think Manchester City’s guilty verdict over almost all of their Premier League charges distracted his England players in the Nations League defeat to Spain.

City players Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly were at fault for two of Spain’s goals and both Tuchel, the head coach, and England captain Harry Kane confirmed news of the verdict had been discussed among the squad.

Tuchel does not plan to address the issue with his players ahead of the remaining Nations League games against Czech Republic and Croatia.

Asked if the City verdict had been a cause of discussion ahead of the Spain game, Tuchel replied: “Not for me, but I can imagine maybe for the Man City players. I won’t comment on it as it’s an ongoing case.

“I didn’t make it a topic. It was not a topic for me. I’m just thinking about Spain and the team and meetings. The players have more time than me. So I can imagine they talk about it. It’s good they do. I don’t think it was a distraction for them.”

Kane added: “There was a discussion, but when we’re with England, we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week.”

Tuchel also refused to point the finger of blame at Guéhi, O’Reilly or Kane, who missed a penalty, for England’s defeat despite admitting his team got off to the worst possible start by conceding a goal after two minutes.

“We will focus on the positives, but also highlight the stuff we can do better,” Tuchel said. “Not even speaking about individual mistakes because this is normal. It just happens. It should not happen, and for sure not in this amount. But there is no sense in showing the individual mistakes or telling them ‘please don’t make mistakes’. That is normal, but we can do things better. We can defend the third goal better. But we will focus on the positives. There is a lot to take away from the game.

“We wanted to be the team desperately to beat them [Spain] and we think we had them. We still think we had them at half-time. That was the way the team showed up after half-time. So we will focus on that, but the reality is we lost and the reality is we need to prove it again.”

“It was a terrible start, the worst possible start, which makes it so difficult against a team like this. The reaction was very good. After 10/12 minutes, we were the better team but we gave away too many mistakes. We were the better team. If we had converted the penalty, it could have been the decisive moment. We have to keep going and learn from the mistakes. We could have created more if we had been more clinical in the final 20 metres. We showed great bravery and courage with our high-ball wins. There will always be moments you suffer against teams like this. The effort and quality were there tonight but the result does not prove it today.”

“I think there is a gap [between Spain and England]. They [Spain] are the world champions and European champions. Mikel Oyarzabal was never going to miss. He was always in control of the situation. Honestly, people talk about sexy football, that is sexy football. I would watch that all night.”

🗣️ "We went toe to toe with the European and world champions" 💪Harry Kane remains positive about England performance despite their 3-2 defeat to Spain 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿🇪🇸#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/qkhqsqmPEl

🗣️ "You have to beat them to show people we can do this" 💪@IanWright0 reflects on England's 3-2 defeat to Spain at Wembley#ITVFootball | @markpougatch pic.twitter.com/ko2FYs4VqA

Marc Guehi and Nico O’Reilly may want to look away now but Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon scored well. Our very own Mike McGrath has provided his player ratings.

Tonight: England 2 Spain 3 (H)Tuesday September 29: Czech Republic (A), kick-off 7.45pmSaturday October 3: Croatia (A), kick-off 5pmTuesday October 6: Czech Republic (H), kick-off 7.45pm

🗣️ "I think it's a bit of a missed chance" 👀Anthony Gordon says mistakes cost England the win tonight against Spain at Wembley 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @gabrielclarke05 | @England pic.twitter.com/AJBxVNjbjq

A highly entertaining game. England will probably argue the game changed on Kane’s missed penalty, but Spain missed a lot of very clear chances and will feel they deserved the victory. A losing start to the Nations League for Tuchel and his team, but there were some positives. Gordon, Bellingham and Anderson were all excellent. Some of the defending, not so excellent.

Possession: England 47%-53% SpainShots: 13-15Shots on target: 5-5Corners: 6-3Touches in opposition box: 37-15

England have one last chance with a corner out on the left. This will be it. Spain are able to deal with it and clear their lines.

Then comes the final whistle at Wembley and the world champions Spain claim a 3-2 victory in north London. It was an absorbing game, where momentum swung one way and then the other, but it is Spain who are the victors.

Baena brings down Rogers with a silly challenge to gift England a free-kick deep in the Spanish half. This could be England’s last chance.

Anderson is over it but his delivery is poor, easily caught by Unai Simon.

England are running out of time to find an equaliser.

O’Reilly appears to be suffering with cramp but England have made all five substitutions.

A late change for England as Branthwaite replaces Guehi.

Rogers delivers a dangerous cross from the right that runs through the six-yard box and forces Pubill to put it behind for a corner.

England take it short before Anderson clips it in but Laporte heads away.

Garner should have done so much better with that. His run into the Spain box on the left side is picked out by Anderson’s pass. Garner has Calvert-Lewin waiting at the back post but the former massively overhits the cross.

Double substitution from England as Calvert-Lewin and Gibbs-White replace Kane and Saka. Rare to say Kane taken off, especially when England are behind.

Saka goes down under a challenge from Cucurella inside the Spain penalty box but no penalty is forthcoming. VAR has cleared the incident. Moments later, Bellingham is then booked for stopping Spain going on the counter.

Spain make a change as Merino replaces Olmo.

The way Spain control possession and keep the ball is impressive. They toy with you pretty well and often look so composed.

Baena, who has been superb since coming on, feeds a lovely pass into the path of Oyarzabal on the right side of the box. Oyarzabal takes one touch before lifting it over Trafford into the England net. That is a lovely assist from Baena and lovely finish from Oyarzabal.

Mikel Oyarzabal SCORES against England AGAIN! 🎯Spain retake the lead after a slick finish from the Spaniard 👏#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pPT3KvRHWl

Given the quality of the opposition and the sustained threat he carried, that might have been Gordon’s best-ever performance in an England shirt. Him and Bellingham have been excellent. But now he’s been replaced by Morgan Rogers.

Guehi joins O’Reilly in the book for a cynical foul on Olmo. You can put that yellow card in the category of a professional foul.

England are making a double change as Garner and Rogers come on for Lewis-Skelly and Gordon. Garner was not in the initial squad but takes his chance now after the withdrawals.

Spain also make a substitution as Pedri replaces Ruiz.

At one end, Yamal has a shot blocked after England gave the ball away before Lewis-Skelly’s shot down the other end is easily saved.

The first booking of the night sees O’Reilly shown a yellow card for a foul on Yamal.

England come close to going back in front. After good work from Bellingham, Saka has it on the right side of the box. Saka cuts inside onto his left and looks to pick out the far corner but his effort goes narrowly wide.

Another big mistake from England is punished. It is absolutely dreadful from O’Reilly, who gives the ball away so poorly deep inside the England half. Spain capitalise and it is the man who has only just come on, Baena, who curls into the bottom corner from the edge of the box. All to play for with half an hour to go at Wembley.

SPAIN EQUALISE! 🇪🇸A brilliant finish from Alex Baena after a Nico O'Reilly mistake 🎯#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/tXygPfbPmb

Yamal and Baena exchange a lovely one-two on the right side of the box and you think the former will find the far corner but his effort goes wide.

How did Yamal MISS that! 🤯A big opportunity goes begging to pull Spain level! #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/jyzLm9VBd5

Cucurella has a real habit of making himself unpopular wherever he plays. The Wembley crowd have been booing his every touch and were not happy with him staying down after the ball hit him in the head. Spain haven’t got going at all in this second half.

Spain have made a double change as Oyarzabal and Baena replace Torres and Williams.

Kane steps up but his effort smashes into the bar. Kane slipped just as he took it. In fact, a free-kick is given to Spain as it was a double hit.

Kane MISSES from the penalty spot! 😧Harry Kane slips when he strikes the ball, let off for Spain and Luis de la Fuente#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/pvg3GGa9ma

The referee overturns the original decision and points to the spot. A foul from a Barcelona midfielder on a Real Madrid midfielder is given.

Yet more England appeals for a penalty. Bellingham goes down, believing he was fouled by Rodri, but the referee gives nothing. There is contact but is it enough for a penalty? The referee had a good view and there is a decent shout for a penalty.

The referee is being sent to the screen so we know what that usually means...

Certainly no sitting on the lead from England at the start of the second half. Tuchel was adamant that Bellingham should have been awarded a penalty after going down in the area.

And Tuchel might get his way as VAR have sent referee Davide Massa to the screen.

England want a penalty. Saka goes down under a challenge from Laporte from behind but those appeals are waved away. VAR checks and clears the incident. Laporte got the ball.

Chance for England. Bellingham’s cross from the left picks out Quansah in the centre of the box but the defender’s header from eight yards out misses the target. What an opportunity that was for Quansah to score his first international goal.

Spain are unbeaten in nearly 40 competitive matches and, as it stands, that run is set to come to an end. Still a long way to come though tonight and Spain could have been 3-0 up before England even scored one goal.

We are back under way at Wembley. No changes for either side at the break.

During half-time, Kyle Walker received a framed shirt to celebrate his 96 England caps.

What a response from our #ThreeLions! 💪 pic.twitter.com/qBoY0J79JL

2 - Lamine Yamal has scored the third quickest goal England have ever conceded at Wembley Stadium, behind only first minute goals for Scotland in 1957 and Hungary in 1953.Punch. pic.twitter.com/NxVp1qOnVi

Possession: England 45%-55% SpainShots: 6-8Shots on target: 2-2Corners: 3-3Touches in opposition box: 10-10

Tuchel will be delighted with the half-time score and England’s spirit after going behind so early. But how on earth have Spain only scored once? They’ve missed a couple of one-on-ones, hit the post and blazed over the bar. Highly entertaining and England will know they will have to defend better if they are going to hold on to their lead.

An absorbing and end-to-end first half is brought to an end. Somehow, despite the fact at one point they could have been 3-0 down, England lead 2-1 at the break.

Cucurella’s cross from the left loops all the way to the back post, where it strikes the frame of the goal. I do not think Cucurella meant that.

It is chances galore at both ends, with the latest falling to Ruiz, whose shot from the edge of the box is deflected wide for a corner. Bellingham heads away at the front post.

England gift the ball away so poorly and Yamal should punish them with his second goal of the game but he blazes high over the bar.

What on earth has happened to Spain? O’Reilly’s cross from the byline picks out Kane, who guides a header towards goal. Cucurella makes an absolute mess of things, effectively kneeing the ball past his keeper and into his own net. Kane will try and claim it but surely that has to go down as an own goal. 10 minutes ago, Spain should have been 3-0 up. Now, England are 2-1 ahead.

I think we'll give that goal to Harry Kane 🎯England come from behind to lead Spain thanks Harry Kane, with assistance from Marc Cucurella ⚽️#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/X3qSOWUhVT

England are inches away from taking the lead. Saka drives forward towards the Spain box and lays it across to Kane, whose shot goes just wide. Should Kane have scored? Maybe.

SO CLOSE FROM KANE! 🫣England nearly go in front 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/YgoRblxuiH

Somehow, England are on level terms. Spain should have been 3-0 up but England equalise with a clinical counter-attack. Anderson wins the ball back for England on the edge of their own box and plays it forward to Gordon, who flicks it brilliantly first time into the path of Bellingham, who drives into the Spain half. Gordon is on his bike and is ready to receive the forward pass from Bellingham. Gordon takes it to the Spain box before slotting home clinically past Simon.

ENGLAND ARE LEVEL! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿A brilliant finish from Anthony Gordon after a breathtaking counter attack 👏#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/z0nSfWIHVd

England have missed Declan Rice’s delivery so far this evening. Saka has floated a couple of corners straight into the hands of Spain goalkeeper Simon and there have been some promising free-kicks wasted too.

No love lost between the Real Madrid team-mates Jude Bellingham and Marc Cucurella, there. Bellingham was unhappy with a challenge from the left-back and let’s just say they exchanged words afterwards.

If Olmo had slotted that home, the assist from Yamal would have been quite incredible. A quite sensational flick from Yamal plays Olmo in behind on the right side of the box and the latter’s shot goes narrowly wide of the far post.

Saka’s shot is blocked and the ball spins behind for an England corner out on the right. Saka takes the corner he won but his inswinger is caught by Unai Simon.

England want a penalty. Lewis-Skelly goes down inside the Spain penalty area under a challenge from Cubarsi and his appeals are waved away. The referee was spot on with that call.

That is a second sitter missed of the half from Torres and Spain should be 3-0 up. Rodri times his through ball to perfection and Torres’ first touch is glorious to take him past Anderson and away. Torres is one-on-one with Trafford and should score but his effort slides by the left post. How Spain are not 3-0 up is beyond me.

Another let off for England 😧Ferran Torres misses another big chance one-on-one with James Trafford #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/KFkJoJUW6c

That is a waste from Bellingham. The Real Madrid man is found by Quansah on the edge of the box and Bellingham should get his shot off quickly but dithers for too long. Bellingham then goes down far too softly, wanting a free-kick, but those appeals are rightly waved away.

England have enjoyed more of the possession thus far but are still yet to register a shot through 25 minutes.

The Spain fans are certainly enjoying their night in north London. In general, they have a lot to be happy about currently holding the World Cup and Euros trophies as well as the fact that their team is 1-0 up this evening.

That is a big save from Trafford and a big miss from Torres. Yamal plays a through ball to pick out the run of Torres, whom many in the ground think is offside. However, he was clearly being played onside by Quansah and Torres, who is fine scoring form this season for PSG, should score with a one-on-one opportunity but is denied by Trafford. England could and perhaps should be 2-0 down.

BIG SAVE from James Trafford 🧤The Leeds United goalkeeper keeps out Ferran Torres#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/nj5b8AUSQU

Anderson plays a lovely switch from right to left to pick out Gordon in space. Gordon takes just one touch before getting it out of his feet quickly, curling a cross to the back post. He is looking for Saka but Cucurella just about deals with it, even though he did not know much about it. The ball appeared to come off Cucurella last but a goal-kick is given.

After a very shaky start, England are beginning to grow into the game, slowly, but it is gradually happening.

England are really not helping themselves at the moment, gifting the ball away in dangerous area. This time it is Lewis-Skelly who gives it away and Spain end up with a corner.

The delivery is drilled to the edge of the box, where Yamal’s powerful volley is blocked by Gordon.

Spain keep it alive and the ball comes back into the England box. Torres fires into the bottom corner but the offside flag goes up and replays show he was clearly offside.

The OFFSIDE Flag saves England's blushes 👀Ferran Torres saw his close range finish chalked off #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/unIj6NsO7z

England have their first sight of the Spain goal. Kane plays Gordon in down the left and the latter gets past his man easily. He gets to the byline before crossing but Unai Simon in the Spain goal is on hand to cut it out.

What on earth are you doing Guehi? Spain take the lead inside two minutes and it is a real gift. Guehi should pass to O’Reilly or Gordon to his left but instead comes back towards his own goal, seemingly unaware that Yamal is right behind him. What then follows is a clinical finish from Yamal, who drives into the England box before curling towards the far corner, with the ball going in off the inside of the post. That will help Yamal’s pursuit of the Ballon d’Or. Dreadful from Guehi, fantastic from Yamal.

WHAT A START FROM SPAIN 🇪🇸Lamine Yamal pounces on a Marc Guéhi error to give Spain an early lead at Wembley #ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/Et83EyTPlp

Now Tuchel is out with his arms crossed after that nightmare start from England. The Spain fans are in good voice.

We are under way at Wembley. There is VAR in use.

Tuchel was not shown on the big screens ahead of kick-off. He’s just got up off his seat for the first time and entered his technical area to complain about something.

Before we get under way at Wembley, we stop to remember the great Kevin Keegan with a minute’s applause, with a wreath being laid down on the side of the pitch. England are also wearing black armbands to remember Keegan. Wembley also pays tribute to a few other England players who have died over recent months.

As feels customary at every England game, Oasis rings around the stadium to build up the atmosphere.

Here come the two sides and it is time for the national anthems. Marcha Real followed by God Save The King. There are plenty of Spanish supporters in attendance tonight and they are making their voices heard.

Here comes the Wonderwall compilation. Harry Kane said yesterday that he wants to win the Nations League next summer and then celebrate by going to one of the Oasis gigs.

Spain have been forced into a late alteration during the warm-ups and it comes at right-back, with Eric Garcia injured so Marc Pubill comes in.

I quite like Tuchel’s idea of giving Trafford the first two Nations League games, against Spain tonight and Czech Republic in Prague, and then going back to Pickford for the final two, in Croatia and against the Czechs at home. How will we ever know if England have an alternative to Pickford if nobody ever gets a proper go?

Chelsea’s Cole Palmer was one of a number of England withdrawals. Thomas Tuchel had his say on Palmer missing too many games in his press conference and ITV’s Roy Keane has had his say:

“If you think he is going to get England to another level, forget about it. I watched him before the break against Brentford. I think he has far too many bad habits for me.”

The England players all got good receptions from the England fans inside Wembley when their names were read out. We’re yet to see head coach Thomas Tuchel on the pitch or the big screens. Will he also get a big cheer? He was booed by England fans ahead of the World Cup bronze medal match in Miami.

Thomas Tuchel has confirmed that James Trafford will start the first two games of this international break and then Jordan Pickford will start the other two. Tuchel insists that Pickford “has done nothing wrong”.

Thomas Tuchel has decided to start Leeds’ James Trafford in goal instead of Jordan Pickford. Is that the right decision? You can have your say in the comments section at the bottom of the blog.

Thomas Tuchel is limited to a 23-man matchday squad for this game, so Rio Ngumoha is not on the bench. The Liverpool forward impressed during the pre-World Cup squad in Florida when he earned his first cap. It would be harsh if he did not make the bench over the course of the international break, with two matches against Czech Republic and a clash against Croatia coming up.

Harry Kane wants England to address how they lost their identity and went “against our beliefs” at the World Cup.

In a brutally honest assessment of the tournament, the England captain admitted Thomas Tuchel’s team did not play to their full potential in several games – even before the painful semi-final exit against Argentina.

Kane, who played golf instead of watching the World Cup final, revealed the 2-1 Atlanta defeat hurt more than missing a penalty four years earlier in Qatar, when England were knocked out by France in the quarter-finals.

“This one hurt more than any other one. I would probably say even more than when I missed a penalty in Qatar because of the manner that it happened,” Kane said. “It was not us as a team.

“We trust our players and the player know very well that if you miss a camp then someone plays well in your position that the competition is always on. You have to make sure to be available and to produce top-level performances in camp and if you do so, that counts for something. Right now, it is not on my list of worries. I am not wired like this. From the moment I arrived at SGP my full focus is 100 per cent with the players who are here.

“There is no threat, distrust or threat of consequences. It will come naturally. I truly believe that we have the opposite. You will talk to our captain, Harry Kane, who has the most minutes for club and country and is happy to be here while teammates of his are enjoying a 10-day break. He is the role model and that is the vibe we have here.”

🚨 THE XI IS IN. 🇪🇸New adventure. Same hunger. 🔥Here's our starting XI to take on England.#VamosEspaña | #NationsL pic.twitter.com/jP87xd7TfJ

This is the first meeting between these two nations since the Euro 2024 final in Berlin. From that team, only Harry Kane, Marc Guehi, Bukayo Saka and Jude Bellingham are starting tonight. Most of Spain’s winners from that evening are playing here at Wembley. Dani Carvajal, Robin Le Normand and Alvaro Morata are those who are not playing from that team.

James Trafford is poised to start for England ahead of Jordan Pickford against Spain tonight.

Pickford has been England’s No1 for eight years but Thomas Tuchel is set to make a change to face the world champions in the Nations League opener at Wembley.

Trafford went to the World Cup in the summer and has started the Premier League in good form following his move to Leeds.

In the first match since the World Cup, changing his goalkeeper is a major selection decision from Tuchel.

Elsewhere, Jarell Quansah is set to play at right-back ahead of Trent Alexander-Arnold while Myles Lewis-Skelly is also in line to return to the starting XI after being recalled into the squad after missing the World Cup.

England begin their Nations League campaign with a home game against the world champions Spain. This is England’s first game since the World Cup, with their dreams of glory ended by Argentina in the semi-finals, but they did finish third after beating France in a high-scoring third/fourth play-off. The last meeting between these sides saw Spain beat England to win Euro 2024. They also faced off in the Nations League back in 2018, with Spain winning at Wembley and England taking victory over in Spain.

England’s plans for these games has been disrupted by a number of withdrawals. Cole Palmer had earned a recall having been left out of the World Cup squad but the Chelsea forward has withdrawn due to a minor injury, despite playing the full game for Chelsea against Brentford in the final game before the international beak.

“He [Palmer] plays with discomfort and pain and cannot play on the highest level with discomfort and pain,” Tuchel said. “Chelsea informed us. That is my understanding. We are not managing load. This is not an ‘international break’. It is a competitive environment, where the players love to train and be together. That is what we created. We will never compromise on that. We will never let this feeling creep in that the players do not want to come [to England camps]. We focus on the guys who absolutely want to play for England.

“For sure it is a missed opportunity. It is another missed opportunity. He misses too many opportunities. I do not blame him for it, it is just a fact. He misses way too many camps with injuries. I only want to rely on what I personally witness and see within my team. For that you have to be in camp. If you are not in camp there is a next level to impress that you cannot achieve because you can only do it with me on the pitch and with us on the pitch. It is a missed opportunity.”

Declan Rice has also withdrawn from the squad despite playing the full game in Arsenal’s defeat to Brighton as have Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento. Morgan Gibbs-White and James Garner have been called up as a result.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is back in the fold for the first time since June 2025. 18-year-old Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha made his England debut against New Zealand during the World Cup warm-ups and takes his place in this squad, although he does make the matchday squad for tonight’s game. England will also take on Czechia, Croatia and then Cezchia again during this international break.

Having been crowned world champions back in July, Spain are now champions of both Europe and the world. Back in June 2025, Spain made the Nations League final but lost on penalties to Portugal. Ahead of this international window, The Royal Spanish Federation has extended Luis de la Fuente’s contract until 2032. After tonight, Spain will host Croatia and Czechia before travelling to Croatia to cap off this international window.

This is an extended international break, with four games to take place during this window. Team news from Wembley to follow shortly.

Gary Neville has criticised Gabriel Magalhães for what he described as “absolutely embarrassing” play-acting during Arsenal’s 1-0 Premier League victory over Liverpool at Anfield.

Gabriel was involved in an early confrontation with Alexander Isak after the Liverpool striker made contact with him around the upper chest.

The Arsenal defender immediately went to ground clutching his face, prompting a frustrated reaction from Neville on commentary.

The incident did not ultimately overshadow an excellent defensive performance from Arsenal, who held on to Kai Havertz’s first-half goal to secure their first league victory at Anfield since 2012.

As reported by Metro, Neville felt Gabriel had let himself down despite otherwise being a player he greatly admires.

The former Manchester United defender said: “He does let himself down at times.”

Neville added: “I love his fire, his passion and his tenacity. But there’s a push into his upper chest and he goes down holding his face.”

He then delivered an even stronger verdict: “It’s absolutely embarrassing. He needs to stop doing that.”

Gabriel’s reaction came during a game already filled with debate over players exaggerating contact.

Liverpool’s Alexis Mac Allister was also criticised later in the match after going down theatrically following a confrontation with Noni Madueke.

The contrast was particularly striking because Gabriel otherwise played a major role in Arsenal’s defensive effort. Liverpool pushed hard for an equaliser, particularly after falling behind, but Arsenal repeatedly dealt with crosses and pressure around their penalty area.

Neville’s point is difficult to argue with.

Gabriel’s aggression and emotional intensity are important parts of what make him such an effective defender. Arsenal would not want him to lose that edge.

But exaggerating contact is different. Going down holding the face when the contact clearly came higher up the chest only invites criticism and can damage a player’s credibility when a genuinely serious incident occurs later.

The frustrating part is that Gabriel did not need to do it. He was part of a superb Arsenal defensive performance that helped secure one of their biggest results of the season. That should have been the main talking point around him.

Instead, his reaction gave Neville an easy reason to criticise him.

Gabriel remains one of Arsenal’s defensive leaders, but Neville is right that moments like this should be removed from his game.

#1402. Man United boss Michael Carrick appears to ignore Lisandro Martinez after defender sent off for deliberately elbowing Wesley Fofana

Published: 10:04 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 10:21 EDT, 31 October 2026

Michael Carrick could not even look at Lisandro Martinez after the Manchester United defender's moment of madness saw him sent off away at Chelsea.

Martinez, not looking at the ball as a corner was whipped in, went in with his elbow on Wesley Fofana's throat, only a minute or so after picking up a yellow card for pulling back Morgan Rogers.

A VAR review was recommended and Martinez, who was in the headlines earlier this month for calling out the United hierarchy for letting Carrick and the players down, was shown a second yellow card and given his marching orders.

It was a ridiculous decision by Martinez to make the challenge he did on Fofana and Carrick elected not to even acknowledge his centre back as he trudged down the tunnel.

Cole Palmer scored the resulting penalty, given away by Martinez, to make it 2-0.

Lisandro Martinez (left) got ignored by boss Michael Carrick (right) after his sending off

Martinez made a ridiculous decision to lead with his elbow, fouling Wesley Fofana in the box

Director of football Jason Wilcox, explicitly called out by Martinez after a 2-0 defeat in the Champions League to Atletico Madrid, watched on alongside CEO Omar Berrada as Martinez's dire decision making took the game away from Carrick's side, who had been the better team in the first half.

'You can't keep changing, changing, changing the manager,' Martínez said in his Madrid rant. 'What about other areas? [looks up] I can't say more.

'It is easy to say the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas [points up].

'He [Carrick] does his best. Every season is different. You can't stay with what you did last season.

'The teams knows how you play, they know every detail, if you don't change next season is a big problem.

'Last season we did everything, we created the base to create an amazing team.

'It is annoying, disappointing coming here and I am not seeing my team trying to get an amazing result here.'

But he cost his team dearly away at Chelsea, not just with his defending for the opening goal by Rogers, where Martinez and centre back partner Harry Maguire looked incredibly slow, but also for the reckless foul on Fofana that saw Chelsea awarded a result-sealing penalty.

Martinez had a lot to say in Madrid but he was the key person to blame at Stamford Bridge

Martinez was fined for his comments made in Madrid and he sat down for a pow-wow with the hierarchy to thrash out any differences and to get back on the same page.

Yet, at a time when results on the pitch needed to see huge improvement, not least after the Stretford End booed the players off after the 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth last weekend, Martinez let his team-mates down on a day where they looked the better side for 45 minutes.

The expectation is that Martinez will leave at the end of the season and it could even be as early as January with no guarantee that United trigger the additional year option they hold on a contract that expires at the end of the season.

#1401. Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers

To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The N7-methylguanosine (m7G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex1,2,3,4. The m7G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m7G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

Over 150 RNA modifications have been described to date, with transfer RNA (tRNA) being one of the most highly modified RNA species5,6. tRNA modifications are critical for the folding, stability and function of tRNA2,7,8. One of the most prevalent tRNA modifications is m7G1,2. It is deposited at position 46 of tRNA (m7G46) by the METTL1–WDR4 heterodimeric protein complex, with METTL1 functioning as the catalytically active component of the complex, and WDR4 having a scaffolding and RNA-binding role2,3,4. The m7G modification on tRNA has been shown to have an important role in stabilizing the tRNA structure, regulating the translation of mRNA and influencing a number of cellular processes, including stress response and oncogenesis9,10,11,12,13. Recent studies have shown that METTL1 may also deposit the m7G modification on mRNAs and microRNA precursors14,15,16, although at a substantially lower rate compared with the m7G levels on the tRNA fraction.

Many studies have implicated the role of the epitranscriptome in the development and regulation of cancer17,18,19. An increasing amount of evidence shows that dysregulation of tRNA modifications and their pathways contributes to the pathogenesis of human disease, including cancer6,18. Notably, upregulation of METTL1 and its catalytic activity has been linked to oncogenic transformation as well as the initiation and maintenance of aggressive haematological and solid malignancies, including acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), melanoma, glioblastoma, liver and lung cancers11,20,21,22. Moreover, the non-catalytic function of METTL1 has recently been linked to the development of sarcomas through its interaction with the multi-tRNA synthetase complex23.

To date, epitranscriptomic drug discovery efforts have largely focused on the targeting of the m6A mRNA modification and its regulators24,25,26,27. Early prototype inhibitors of METTL1 have recently been described and support the feasibility of pharmacologically inhibiting METTL128,29. However, their limited potency and selectivity render them unsuitable as tools to assess the molecular and therapeutic impact of targeting METTL1 catalytic inhibition. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a potent and highly selective first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1 that demonstrates significant anti-tumour activity across diverse cancer types through the reduction in m7G on tRNA substrates of METTL1.

We performed a high-throughput screen of 250,000 diverse drug-like compounds. After initial hit triaging, STM4529 was identified as a singleton non-S-adenosyl methionine (non-SAM)-related hit that inhibited METTL1 with a half-maximum inhibitory concentration (IC50) of around 15 μM (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis showed that STM4529 binding to METTL1 was competitive with the SAM analogue S-adenosyl homocysteine (SAH), indicating its binding to the catalytic site of METTL1 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). After extensive chemical optimization of potency, selectivity and in vitro and in vivo absorption–distribution–metabolism–excretion properties, we identified STM9005 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Note 1a).

a, The chemical structure of STM9005. b, Representative biochemical activity assay showing inhibition of the METTL1–WDR4 enzyme complex using a concentration range of STM9005 and the less active analogue STM9001. c, Representative METTL1 cellular target engagement of STM9005 and STM9001 was assessed using the InCELL Pulse assay. For b and c, the geometric mean IC50 and s.d. indicated in brackets were derived from n = 13 (STM9005) and n = 3 (STM9001) independent experiments. d, STM9005 selectively inhibits METTL1–WDR4 in a methyltransferase profiling panel of 49 methyltransferases. The asterisk indicates less than 1% activity remaining. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 2 independent samples. e, The reduction in m7G modification on small-fraction RNA after treatment with vehicle, 0.6 or 1.2 µM of STM9005 was measured using RNA MS in the MOLM-13 and OCI-AML2 cell lines. Ratio of m7G to A, C, G and U nucleosides. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 3 independent samples. P values were calculated using two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with multiple-comparison correction. f, Crystal structure of METTL1 (carbon atoms in green) in a complex with STM9005 (carbon atoms are shown in purple). The interactions between the compound and the protein or neighbouring water molecules (red spheres) are indicated (yellow dashed lines). PDB: 9RYL. g, The pharmacokinetic (PK) profile of STM9005 in vivo was measured in mouse plasma after a single i.p. dose of either 10 or 30 mg per kg. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 2 (12 h time point for 10 mg per kg cohort) and n = 3 (all other groups) mice. Compound exposure over time (area under the curve, AUC), maximal concentrations (Cmax) and half-life (t1/2) are indicated in the pharmacokinetics summary table. Pharmacokinetics values after oral dosing are shown for comparison. p.o., oral gavage.

STM9005 inhibited recombinant METTL1 enzyme activity with an IC50 < 13 nM, a value restricted by the lower detection limit of the assay (Fig. 1b). To use a more sensitive assay system and to verify binding to METTL1 in an orthogonal system, we performed SPR analysis, which demonstrated direct stoichiometric high-affinity binding of STM9005 to METTL1 with a Kd of 2 nM (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Moreover, using a cellular target engagement assay, we confirmed cell penetration and binding of STM9005 to METTL1 in cells with an IC50 of 13 nM (Fig. 1c). STM9005 was found to be highly specific to METTL1 as it had no effect on the activity of other RNA-methyltransferases (METTL3/14, METTL16, BCDIN3D, TSG1 and NSUN2) when used at comparable concentrations (Extended Data Fig. 1e), and exhibited greater than 10,000-fold selectivity for METTL1–WDR4 when tested against a broad panel of 49 RNA-, DNA- and protein-methyltransferases (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 1). Moreover, no significant off-target toxicity liabilities were identified when STM9005 was tested in a broad panel of 97 kinases (KINOMEscan, Eurofins DiscoverX; Supplementary Table 2) and over 70 assays testing a range of receptors and enzymes commonly associated with drug toxicity (SAFETYscan 47, Eurofins DiscoverX; Supplementary Table 3).

To further investigate the cellular activity of STM9005, we applied RNA mass spectrometry (MS) to assess the specific effect of STM9005 on the m7G modification level of tRNA from the previously known METTL1-dependent AML cell lines MOLM-13 and OCI-AML211,30,31. We observed a significant decrease in m7G levels (Fig. 1e), but not in the levels of the m1A and m5C RNA modifications (Extended Data Fig. 1f). To further quantify the cellular effect of STM9005 on m7G-modified tRNA, we developed an antibody-based m7G detection assay (Meso Scale Discovery (MSD)), which enabled us to measure the effect of STM9005 on tRNA-Val. This demonstrated a concentration-dependent decrease in tRNA-Val-m7G after treatment with STM9005 with an IC50 of 34 nM (Extended Data Fig. 1g), confirming potent inhibition of tRNA modification by STM9005 in cells at nanomolar concentrations. Moreover, we confirmed STM9005 acts specifically on the METTL1–m7G tRNA axis, as we observed no significant effect on m7G modification of 18S ribosomal RNA (Extended Data Fig. 1h).

To characterize the binding of STM9005 to METTL1 further, we performed X-ray crystallography, confirming unequivocally that STM9005 binds to the SAM-binding site of METTL1 (Fig. 1f, Extended Data Fig. 1i, Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1b). Notably, part of STM9005 binds in a pocket not previously observed in METTL1 crystal structures, where it forms molecular interactions such as the hydrogen bonds between Tyr184 and the central carbonyl moiety of STM9005, and a pi-carbon interaction between Phe159 and the tetrahydroisoquinoline methyl of STM9005, providing the basis for its high affinity and selectivity. In strong support of this, STM9001, a diastereomer of STM9005 in which the tetrahydroisoquinoline methyl is in an opposite orientation, is around 100-fold less active (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a,g), providing further evidence of the specificity and binding mode of STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 1i and Supplementary Table 1).

The observed binding of STM9005 to the catalytic pocket of METTL1 did not impact the RNA or protein levels of METTL1 after in vitro treatment (Extended Data Fig. 1j,k), in contrast to the significant and selective effect observed on the m7G tRNA modification levels (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). Finally, pharmacokinetic profiling of STM9005 in mice after a single intraperitoneal (i.p.) dose of either 10 or 30 mg per kg showed good bioavailability with maximal plasma exposures of 13 and 56 μM, respectively, and a half-life of around 1 h. Importantly, at the 12 h time point, STM9005 plasma levels remain above the METTL1 cellular IC50, indicating METTL1 inhibition in vivo over a period of at least 12 h (Fig. 1g).

Taken together, these data establish STM9005 as a potent, selective and bioavailable catalytic inhibitor of METTL1 that is suitable for both in vitro and in vivo investigations.

To investigate the anti-cancer potential of STM9005 in cellular models, we initially screened the impact of STM9005 treatment in three different cancer cell panels using colorimetric assays which measure metabolic activity (MTS assay). For these experiments, we used cancer cell models that were either previously reported to be sensitive to the genetic inhibition of METTL111,32,33, or their METTL1-dependency status (sensitivity or resistance) was validated here using CRISPR-based genetic disruption of METTL1/Mettl1 (human and mouse, respectively) in competitive co-culture assays (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). We observed a dose-dependent reduction in the proliferation of human leukaemic cell lines (Fig. 2a), primary mouse AML models (Fig. 2b) and human and mouse solid cancer models (Fig. 2c) from different tissue origins (skin, lung, pancreas, colorectal, oesophageal and soft tissue). Investigating the direct effect of STM9005 on cell growth using a methylene blue assay, we observed highly potent, dose-dependent effects on the fitness and growth of a subset of these cell lines (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Additional reprofiling in proliferation assays using ATP quantitation under optimized culture conditions confirmed the anti-proliferative activity of STM9005 at submicromolar concentrations in these cells (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3b). By contrast, the diastereomer control compound STM9001 was significantly less potent in these systems, consistent with its reduced activity against the catalytic activity of METTL1, providing strong evidence that the anti-proliferative effects of STM9005 are due to METTL1 catalytic inhibition (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3b). There was also a significant dose-dependent negative effect seen in the colony forming potential of MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+-driven primary mouse AML cells after ex vivo treatment with STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Notably, the cancer models that appeared to be independent of METTL1 genetic loss (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b) were also not significantly impacted after treatment with STM9005 (Fig. 2d). To confirm that the anti-proliferative effects of STM9005 are mediated specifically through METTL1, we assessed its impact in two insensitive (OE33, mPDAC2) and two sensitive (B16F10, mPDAC1) cancer cell lines with a loss of METTL1 or Mettl1 after CRISPR–Cas9 targeting. STM9005 treatment in both sensitive and insensitive cell lines resulted in no additional negative effect (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e) despite the absence of METTL1 protein (Extended Data Figs. 2a,b and 3a), consistent with the small molecule exerting its mechanism of action specifically through inhibition of METTL1’s catalytic activity.

a–c, STM9005 concentration–response curves measuring cell viability (MTS assay) in panels of human haematological cancer (a), primary mouse leukaemia (b) and human and mouse solid cancer cells (c) after 6 days of treatment. Data are mean ± s.e.m. n = 3 independent cultures. IC50 values are shown in parentheses. d, The normalized confluency was measured by quantification of methylene blue staining of sensitive (top) and insensitive (bottom) cells after 9 days of treatment with vehicle or STM9005 at the indicated concentrations. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 4 independent cultures. P values were calculated using one-way ANOVA. Representative images for each well are shown under the corresponding bars. OE, overexpression. e, Representative STM9005 and STM9001 concentration–response curves (CellTiter-Glo) in LoVo and OE21 cells under optimized culture conditions after 7 days of treatment. Geometric mean IC50 ± s.d. (parentheses) were derived from n = 25 (LoVo, STM9005) and n = 8 (OE21, STM9005) and n = 2 (STM9001) independent experiments. f,g, Myeloid differentiation of MOLM-13 (f) or primary mouse MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+ AML (g) cells after 6 days of treatment with vehicle or 1, 2.5 or 5 µM STM9005. Left, representative histogram of CD11b–APC (f) or Gr1–APC (g) staining. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 3 independent cultures. P values were calculated using one-way ANOVA. Right, the mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of CD11b–APC-stained (f) and Gr1–APC-stained (g) cells. h, Cell cycle analysis of A549 (top) or LoVo (bottom) cells after 7 days of treatment with vehicle or 1 or 2 µM STM9005. n = 3 independent cultures. i, Breakdown of h, shown as the proportion in each cell cycle stage of A549 (top) or LoVo (bottom) cells. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 3 independent cultures. P values were calculated using two-way ANOVA with multiple-comparison correction. j,k, Western blot analysis of a cell cycle protein panel in A549 (j) and LoVo (k) cells after 5 day treatment with vehicle or 0.3 or 1 µM STM9005. n = 3 (A549) and n = 2 (LoVo) independent cultures.

In the context of haematological malignancies, pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 using STM9005 caused significant and dose-dependent myeloid differentiation in both human and primary mouse models of AML (Fig. 2f,g and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Moreover, we and others have previously shown that genetic inhibition of METTL1 negatively affected various cancer models by impacting their cell cycle status11,20. To examine whether the observed effect on cell cycle is dependent on the catalytic activity of METTL1 we analysed a panel of solid cancer cell lines with different tissues of origin and mutational background and showed that treatment with STM9005 causes a significant disruption of cell cycle, with a dose-dependent increase in cells in G0/G1 phase and a significantly decreased number of cells in S phase (Fig. 2h,i and Extended Data Fig. 3g,h) as the most common changes across the cell lines tested. Moreover, western blot analysis of cell-cycle-related markers confirmed the observed cell cycle dysregulation seen in the various cancer models tested here (Fig. 2j,k). Moreover, annexin V analysis showed no significant levels of apoptosis after treatment with STM9005 (Extended Data Fig. 3i).

These data confirm the importance of METTL1’s methyltransferase activity in maintaining both haematological and solid cancers, and that pharmacological inhibition of its enzymatic activity is sufficient to elicit anti-cancer cellular effects.

To assess the molecular changes caused by treatment with STM9005, we analysed its impact across different layers of the transcriptome. We first performed modification-induced misincorporation tRNA sequencing (mim-tRNA-seq) to investigate the m7G modification status on tRNA fractions from B16F10 melanoma tumours and a primary mouse MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+-driven AML. Analysis of the mim-tRNA-seq data revealed a highly specific and significant reduction in the m7G46 mark in known m7G-modified tRNAs—a result that was highly similar between both cancer models (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 4).

a,b, mim-tRNA-seq analysis of the mean (red) and individual replicate (grey) log2-transformed fold change (log2[FC]) in misincorporation at the m7G46 site of tRNAs (a) and the log2[FC] (grey) in tRNA levels (b) in B16F10 (left) and MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+ (right) cells after 72 h treatment with vehicle or 2 µM STM9005. The purple asterisks represent a significant change (a; P < 0.01, unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests) or a significant decrease (b, Padj < 0.05, Wald test). Related to Supplementary Tables 4 and 5. n = 3 independent samples. c, Northern blot analysis of m7G-modified tRNAs and non-m7G-modified RNA controls for MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+ (left) and A549 (right) cells after 72 h treatment with vehicle or 2 µM STM9005. n = 2 independent experiments. d, Western blot analysis of CDK4, KDM1A and β-actin after treatment for 7 days with vehicle or 1, 2.5 or 5 µM STM9005 in a panel of cancer models. e,f, Rescue of phenotype in B16F10 melanoma cells after overexpression (OE) of Arg-TCT-tRNA (e) and Cdk4 (f) versus an empty vector control. The normalized confluency was measured by quantification of methylene blue staining of B16F10 cells with Arg-TCT-tRNA overexpression (e), Cdk4-overexpression (f) or an empty vector control, after treatment for 6 days with vehicle or 1.25 or 2.5 µM STM9005. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 3 independent cultures. P values were calculated using two-way ANOVA with multiple-comparison correction. Representative images are shown under the corresponding bar. g,h, Rescue of phenotype in A549 (g) or mPDAC1 (h) cells after overexpression of WT METTL1 (A549) and WT Mettl1 (mPDAC1) versus an empty control vector and METTL1MUT (A549) and Mettl1MUT (mPDAC1) overexpression. The normalized confluency was measured by quantifying methylene blue staining of cells overexpressing WT or mutant METTL1 or an empty control vector that were treated with vehicle or 313.5 nM or 625 nM STM9005, after 6 days of treatment. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 3 independent cultures. P values were calculated using two-way ANOVA with multiple-comparison correction. Representative images are shown under the corresponding bar.

Subsequent investigation of differential tRNA expression from the same two cancer models showed selective downregulation of a subset of m7G-modified tRNAs after pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 5), which was validated using northern blotting across a panel of m7G-modified tRNA substrates (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4a).

We previously showed that the catalytic function of METTL1 drives the translation of key oncogenic proteins, including CDK4 and KDM1A, by modifying and stabilizing a subset of tRNAs11. To explore the dependence of these outcomes on METTL1’s catalytic activity, we performed western blotting using a panel of cancer models from diverse tissues, confirming that CDK4 and KDM1A protein levels were reduced after STM9005 treatment in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4b), while the same was not seen with corresponding mRNA levels (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). To verify that STM9005’s mechanism of action is mediated by inhibition of the m7G–tRNA axis, we performed rescue-of-phenotype experiments by overexpressing either the established METTL1–m7G tRNA substrate Arg-TCT or the METTL1 biomarker CDK4, a known substrate of Arg-TCT11. Notably, overexpression of Arg-TCT tRNA in both a solid cancer and a leukaemia model (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 4e–g) led to a partial but significant response to STM9005 and an increase in the viability of the cancer cells. Similarly, overexpression of Cdk4 in both a solid cancer and a leukaemia model (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 4h–j) mirrored the partial rescue of phenotype seen when using Arg-TCT tRNA overexpression, supporting the conclusion that the cellular effects caused by STM9005 treatment are dependent on the m7G–tRNA molecular pathway, which is maintained by the catalytic activity of METTL1.

To further validate that STM9005 acts specifically by inhibiting the catalytic function of METTL1 we overexpressed wild-type (WT) METTL1 and mutant (MUT) METTL1 carrying two amino acid changes in the catalytic domain (L160A/D164A for human METTL1 and L154A/D157A for mouse Mettl1). Forced expression of WT METTL1/Mettl1 significantly increased cellular resistance to STM9005, whereas viability did not improve in cells overexpressing METTL1MUT/Mettl1MUT (Fig. 3g,h and Extended Data Fig. 4k,l), confirming that STM9005 exerts its effects through the inhibition of the catalytic activity of METTL1. Moreover, the reduction in the levels of known m7G-dependent protein substrates, such as CDK4 and KDM1A, is reversed when WT METTL1 is overexpressed, while the same is not seen with overexpression of METTL1MUT (Extended Data Fig. 4m). This further accentuates that STM9005’s activity is specifically driven by the catalytic inhibition of METTL1.

To assess the wider downstream effects of STM9005 treatment on global translation, we used ribosome sequencing (Ribo-seq). After treatment with STM9005, Ribo-seq and mRNA sequencing (mRNA-seq) changes were moderately correlated (r = 0.6368; Extended Data Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 6), suggesting that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 affects gene expression at both the transcription and translational levels. Ribosome-protected RNA fragment (RPF) density analysis showed that, after treatment with STM9005, there was a significant increase in A-site ribosome occupancy at codons associated with m7G-modified tRNAs compared with those associated with non-m7G modified tRNAs (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c and Supplementary Table 7), suggesting ribosome stalling at sites that are dependent on m7G-modified tRNAs for decoding. Importantly, treatment did not reduce the protein levels of METTL1 (Extended Data Fig. 1k), METTL3 and WDR4 (Extended Data Fig. 5d) at any of the concentrations tested, confirming that the effects seen can be attributed to the catalytic inhibition of METTL1, rather than a global translation defect. To further validate our Ribo-seq findings, we compared genes downregulated in our Ribo-seq dataset with a published SILAC-based proteomic dataset from METTL1 knockdown and METTL1(WT)–WDR4 overexpression studies11. Genes downregulated after STM9005 treatment showed significant overlap with those reduced after short-hairpin-RNA-mediated depletion of METTL1 (shMETTL1; P < 1 × 10−5; Extended Data Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 8) and were likewise enriched among genes upregulated by METTL1(WT)–WDR4 overexpression (P < 1 × 10−5; Extended Data Fig. 5f and Supplementary Table 8), further confirming on-target, catalysis-dependent effects on the METTL1-regulated translatome. This demonstrates that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 using STM9005 selectively alters the m7G-modified tRNA pool and therefore impacts translation, in concordance with our previous findings using genetic downregulation of METTL1 levels11.

To assess the molecular changes caused by treatment with STM9005 on the mRNA transcriptome, we performed mRNA-seq and differential expression analysis using three cancer models (OE21, LoVo and B16F10) treated with either vehicle or STM9005 (Supplementary Tables 9–11). Gene Ontology analysis of differentially expressed genes showed that treatment with STM9005 dysregulates several key oncogenic pathways, including pathways such as those regulated by MYC, PI3K–AKT–mTOR, p53 and, as shown earlier, the cell cycle (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Tables 12–14).

Previous studies have associated METTL1 with the transcriptional regulation of MYC and its pathways12,34. However, there is a lack of evidence directly linking the catalytic function of METTL1 to the regulation of MYC. To directly address this, we investigated whether the observed changes in expression of MYC, caused by isolated catalytic inhibition of METTL1, were evident at the MYC protein level. Indeed, western blot analysis confirmed that treatment with STM9005 leads to a dose-dependent decrease in MYC protein levels in two independent cancer models (Extended Data Fig. 6b), while the same reduction was not seen at the mRNA level (Extended Data Fig. 6c), showing that METTL1 regulates MYC protein levels through its catalytic function. To explore the potential of STM9005 treatment impacting cancer growth through the downstream regulation of MYC levels, we performed rescue-of-phenotype experiments by overexpressing MYC in a human and a mouse solid cancer model. Our experiments showed that MYC overexpression increased viability after treatment with STM9005 compared with the empty vector control (Extended Data Fig. 6d–g), indicating that the negative impact of STM9005 on cancer cells could be partially connected to negative regulation of MYC and its pathways.

Finally, we confirmed that, despite the transcript and protein level dysregulation of several cancer-associated pathways after treatment with STM9005, transcript and protein levels of METTL1 remained unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 6h and Extended Data Fig. 1j), highlighting again that the effects observed were due to the catalytic inhibition of METTL1.

Taken together, our mechanistic analysis further confirms the specificity and selectivity of our small-molecule approach and that treatment with STM9005 affects METTL1-mediated m7G modification levels, which in turn causes defects in the translation and gene regulation of cancer-essential biomarkers.

Given our strong evidence for potency, specificity and anti-cancer efficacy of STM9005 in vitro, we performed a series of in vivo experiments using both solid cancers and leukaemia models.

Initially, we tested the in vivo activity of STM9005 using three solid tumour models from different tissues (melanoma, pancreatic ductal carcinoma (PDAC) and lung adenocarcinoma). For the first in vivo solid-tumour experiment, we transplanted immunocompetent mice subcutaneously with B16F10 mouse melanoma cells and treated them twice daily with 30 mg per kg STM9005 for 5 days (Extended Data Fig. 7a). This treatment plan led to a significant decrease in tumour size of the STM9005-treated cohort in comparison to the vehicle-treated mice (Fig. 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 7b). To confirm on-target activity of STM9005 in vivo, we quantified m7G levels on tRNA extracted from melanoma tumours and kidney tissues of control and treated mice. Notably, we detected significantly lower levels of m7G tRNA modification in the tumours (Fig. 4c) and kidneys (Fig. 4d) of animals treated with STM9005 compared with the vehicle-treated cohort, demonstrating catalytic inhibition of METTL1 in vivo. We also confirmed a significant decrease in MYC and, simultaneously, a significant increase in p53 after in vivo treatment of melanoma tumours with STM9005 (Fig. 4e–g), providing strong proof of a mechanism consistent with reduction of cancer proliferation in vivo and complementing our previous in vitro findings (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b).

a–d, Representative image of tumours (a), the tumour volume (at day 11; b) and normalized tRNA-Val m7G levels in the tumours (c) and kidneys (d) from animals transplanted with B16F10 melanoma cells, treated twice daily with vehicle (n = 6 (b and d) and n = 5 (c)) or 30 mg per kg STM9005 (n = 9 (b), n = 5 (c) and n = 8 (d)). e–g, Western blot analysis of MYC, p53 and β-actin (e) and normalized protein levels of MYC (f) and p53 (g) in the tumours of animals transplanted with B16F10 melanoma cells, treated twice daily with vehicle (n = 6 independent animals) or 30 mg per kg STM9005 (n = 6 independent animals), normalized to β-actin. h–j, Representative image of the tumours (h), tumour volume over time (i) and the tumour volume at the end point (day 26; j) from animals transplanted with mPDAC1 cells and treated twice daily with vehicle (n = 5) or 30 mg per kg STM9005 (n = 9). k–n, Representative image of the tumours (k), the tumour volume over time (l), the tumour volume at the end point (day 23; m) and the normalized tRNA-Val m7G levels in the kidneys (n) from animals transplanted with A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells and treated twice daily with vehicle (n = 5 (tumour analysis) and n = 4 (kidney analysis)) or 30 mg per kg STM9005 (n = 5) at 23 days after transplantation. o,p, Kaplan–Meier survival analysis of animals transplanted with primary mouse MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+ AML (o) or AML-491 PDX (p) cells treated twice daily with vehicle (n = 5) or 30 mg per kg STM9005 (n = 7). P values were calculated using the log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test. q, The levels of hCD45+ cells in the bone marrow of mice transplanted with AML-491 PDX and treated twice daily with vehicle (n = 4) or 30 mg per kg STM9005 (n = 5), measured 43 days after transplantation. The green line indicates ongoing treatment. Data are mean ± s.d. P values were calculated using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests (b–d, f, g, i, j, l–n and q).

We followed up with two further in vivo experiments using solid cancer models, one using a mouse PDAC35 (mPDAC1) model driven by Kras and a second using the human lung adenocarcinoma model A549, both transplanted subcutaneously into immunocompromised mice and treated with 30 mg per kg STM9005 or vehicle twice daily for 9 days (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). As with the B16F10 model, treatment with STM9005 significantly impaired the growth of pancreatic and lung adenocarcinoma tumours compared to the control cohorts (Fig. 4h–m) and reduced tRNA m7G levels (Fig. 4n). Importantly, while STM9005 showed strong anti-cancer efficacy in vivo, it did not cause any acute or lasting signs of toxicity, and caused no measurable effects on the body weight of either immunocompromised or immunocompetent mice (Extended Data Fig. 7e–g).

Having established the anti-proliferative potential of STM9005 treatment in solid tumours, we next investigated the effect of pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 on haematological malignancies. First, we transplanted an aggressive primary mouse AML model driven by MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+ into NSG-SGM3 mice and treated them with 30 mg per kg STM9005 or vehicle, twice daily for 5 days (Extended Data Fig. 7h). Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 significantly prolonged the survival of STM9005-treated mice compared with the vehicle-treated controls (Fig. 4o), thereby demonstrating efficacy in both haematological and solid cancer models.

To accentuate these observations in a clinically relevant context, we next used a patient-derived AML xenograft (AML-491 PDX) and treated the mice twice daily with either vehicle or 30 mg per kg STM9005 for 10 days (Extended Data Fig. 7i). The STM9005-treated PDX cohort had a significantly longer lifespan compared with the vehicle-treated mice (Fig. 4p) and illustrated a significantly lower AML burden in the bone marrow, as measured by the presence of hCD45+ cells (Fig. 4q). Finally, analysis of weight and blood count measurements covering the duration of the AML PDX experiment (Extended Data Fig. 7i) showed no significant differences or signs of toxicity between the vehicle- and STM9005-treated cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 7j–o), consistent with our previous profiling illustrating no off-target toxicity (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3).

To investigate the impact of STM9005 on normal cells, we assessed the effects of STM9005 on primary cells ex vivo. STM9005 treatment did not impair the colony-forming potential of WT mouse bone marrow cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a) or primary human CD34+ cord blood cells (Extended Data Fig. 8b). Similarly, treatment of primary human hepatocytes from normal donors had no effect on cell viability, in contrast to doxorubicin-treated positive controls, which showed a significant reduction in viability (Extended Data Fig. 8c).

To assess the long-term effects of STM9005 on normal tissues in vivo, WT C57BL/6J mice were treated with vehicle or 30 mg per kg STM9005 twice daily for 12 days, and samples were collected 30 days after treatment. The organ weights of the spleen, liver and kidneys showed no differences between treatment groups (Extended Data Fig. 8e–g, respectively). Moreover, there was no differential impact observed on bone marrow cellularity (Extended Data Fig. 8h) and colony-forming potential of bone marrow cells (Extended Data Fig. 8i,j). Haematological parameters during the treatment period (day 7 after treatment initiation), including white blood cell counts, red blood cell counts, platelet counts and haemoglobin levels, were unaffected by STM9005 treatment (Extended Data Fig. 8k–n). Furthermore, haematopoietic cell composition in the bone marrow and spleen (Extended Data Fig. 8o,p), and analysis of major haematopoietic stem and progenitor compartments (Extended Data Fig. 8q–v), also revealed no significant differences between groups. Finally, histological assessment of heart, liver, kidney and spleen illustrated no morphological evidence of tissue pathology in either treatment group (Extended Data Fig. 9).

Taken together, our data show that isolated catalytic inhibition of METTL1 using STM9005 is highly efficacious in vivo, leading to detrimental effects on the proliferation of both solid and haematological malignancies, with no measurable signs of toxicity or long-term adverse effects.

The therapeutic potential of pharmacologically targeting different epitranscriptomic regulators is largely underexplored. Recently, we and others have demonstrated that small-molecule inhibition of RNA-modifying enzymes is a credible therapeutic avenue. However, most of the preclinical and clinical efforts to date have been focused on the m6A modification on poly(A)+ RNA24,25,26,27. There are numerous studies suggesting that tRNA-modifying enzymes could be therapeutic vulnerabilities in cancer6,29,36. Yet, the true therapeutic potential of targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme pharmacologically remains unclear. Here we illustrate the development and preclinical characterization of a bona fide first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor, STM9005—a potent, specific and bioavailable small molecule that selectively blocks the catalytic activity of the m7G-writer METTL1.

We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 affects a range of aggressive malignancies through distinct cellular and molecular activity. STM9005 treatment selectively decreases the deposition of m7G on a key subgroup of tRNAs previously associated with oncogenic transformation, cancer stemness, maintenance and aggressiveness11,20,37, which in turn impacts the translation of their mRNA/protein substrates. This molecular mechanism of action affects key oncogenic and therapeutically relevant pathways, such as those related to cell cycle regulators, p53 and MYC-associated proteins, consistent with our previous findings11.

Using a specific and potent catalytic inhibitor of METTL1 enabled us to generate multiple unique datasets to examine the direct effects of inhibiting the catalytic activity of the METTL1–WDR4 complex. It also enabled us to investigate the therapeutic potential of METTL1 inhibition, illustrating robust and on-target anti-proliferative efficacy of STM9005 in vivo using a range of aggressive mouse and human cancer models, including PDXs. Although we illustrated robust tumour growth inhibition in vivo, we did not observe tumour regression, potentially due to short periods of STM9005 dosing. These findings pave the way for further investigations, including possible combinatorial treatments of STM9005 with other cancer drugs, ultimately leading to the improvement of outcomes of current anti-cancer treatments.

Overall, this study provides a strong proof of concept of the in vivo activity and therapeutic efficacy of a specific and selective tRNA-methyltransferase inhibitor against cancer, identifying this class of inhibitors as a promising opportunity for the development of therapies against malignancies with a clear unmet medical need.

Sf21 cells in Sf-900 II serum-free medium (Gibco, 11497-013) were co-infected at a multiplicity of infection of 1 for both His-tagged METTL1 and Flag-tagged WDR4 baculovirus preparations. The infected cultures were incubated for 72 h at 110 rpm and 27 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 3,400g for 15 min at 4 °C and the pellets were stored at −80 °C.

The pellets were lysed in 25 mM Tris pH 8.0 (Invitrogen, 15568025), 300 mM NaCl (Merck, S6546), 1 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 20490), 5% glycerol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 327255000), 0.25% CHAPS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 28300), 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 36978) supplemented with protease inhibitor tablets (Roche, 4693124001) and 10 U ml−1 benzonase (Merck, E8263). Homogenization was achieved by two cycles at 20 kilopounds per square inch using an IKA high pressure homogenizer. Lysates were briefly centrifuged in between cycles (2,000 rpm for 15 min) to remove foam and finally cleared by ultracentrifugation (45 min at 150,000g, 4 °C).

The protein complex was purified sequentially by immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC), desalting, ion-exchange chromatography (IEX) and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC). IMAC purification was performed on the 5 ml HisTrap FF Crude column (Cytiva) at a flow rate of 4 ml min−1. The columns were washed in IMAC buffer A (25 mM Tris pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 5% glycerol and 20 mM imidazole (Merck, 56749-1KG)) and protein complexes were eluted in a gradient of 0–100% IMAC buffer B (buffer A + 500 mM imidazole) over 15 column volumes (CV). Desalting was performed using a HiPrep 53 ml desalting column (Cytiva) at a flow rate of 5 ml min−1 and buffer containing 25 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP and 5% glycerol. Further purification by IEX was by 5 ml HiTrap Q HP anion-exchange chromatography at a flow rate of 4 ml min−1. The columns were washed in IEX buffer A (25 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP and 5% glycerol) and protein complexes were eluted in a gradient of 0–100% IEX buffer B (25 mM Tris pH 8.0, 1 M NaCl, 1 mM TCEP and 5% glycerol) for 15 CV and 100% IEX buffer B for 5 CV. Finally, SEC purification was on the Superdex S200 26/60 (320 ml) column (Cytiva) at a flow rate of 2 ml min−1 in buffer containing 25 mM Tris pH 8.0, 300 mM NaCl, 1 mM TCEP, 5% glycerol and 3 μM SAM (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-286738C) before the samples were concentrated through an Amicon-15 10,000 MWCO centrifugal filter (Merck).

The METTL1–WDR4 substrate pre-tRNA-Phe2 was generated using the TranscriptAid T7 High Yield Transcription Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, K0441) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. DNA templates were purchased from IDT as complementary upper- and lower-strand DNA Ultramer oligonucleotides (Supplementary Table 15) containing the T7 promoter sequence (TAATACGACTCACTATAGGG).
