IVT products were purified using the RNA Clean & Concentrator-25 Kit (Zymo Research, R1018) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For denaturation and renaturation, the tRNA was diluted into 1× annealing buffer (10 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl and 1 mM EDTA (Invitrogen, AM9260G)), heated to 94 °C for 5 min and allowed to slowly cool down to room temperature (Thermomixer Comfort, Eppendorf). The samples were snap-frozen and stored at −80 °C.

The enzymatic assay was established to determine IC50 values for the inhibition of RNA methyltransferase activity. The enzyme used was full-length His-tagged human METTL1 co-expressed with full length Flag-tagged human WDR4 in a baculovirus expression system. The enzyme complex was purified as described above. Enzymatic reactions were performed as described previously23, with the following modifications: a 25 nM final concentration of the METTL1–WDR4 complex was pre-incubated with variable compound concentrations for 10 min, followed by addition of 1 µM final concentration of the in vitro transcribed substrate pre-tRNA-Phe and 1 µM final concentration SAM. The reaction was incubated for further 90 min at 37 °C and then quenched with 40 µl 7.5% TCA with two internal product standards (D4-SAH and 13C10-SAH). After termination, the plates were sealed, centrifuged and stored at 4 °C until analysis.

METTL1–WDR4 activity was measured label-free using the RapidFire MS platform, as described previously27.

Compound IC50 values were calculated by measuring enzyme activity over a dilution series of inhibitor concentrations. The relative inhibition was normalized to control wells with full inhibition (1 µM sinefungin, Merck, S8559) and without inhibition (DMSO only). Data were evaluated using a four-parameter logistic equation in GraphPad Prism (v.10).

Characterization of compound binding to METTL1 was carried out on a Biacore 8K instrument (GE HealthCare) using Series S NTA chips (GE HealthCare) at 20 °C.

For kinetic studies, approximately 2 to 3 kRU His–METTL1–WDR4 complex was immobilized to flow cell 2 of the sensor chip, preactivated with EDC/NHS according to the manufacturer’s protocol in a running buffer of 20 mmol l−1 HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mmol l−1 NaCl, 1 mmol l−1 TCEP and 0.05% Tween-20. After protein capture, surfaces were washed with 60 s pulses of ethanolamine and 10 mmol l−1 EDTA, respectively. Serial dilutions of the compound in 20 mmol l−1 HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mmol l−1 NaCl, 1 mmol l−1 TCEP, 0.05% Tween-20 and 2% DMSO were injected using single-cycle kinetics mode with 90 s association time at a flow rate of 80 μl min−1. Dissociation of the samples was monitored for 5,000 s. Data processing was performed using Biacore Insight Evaluation software v.3.0.12 (Biacore, GE HealthCare). Sensorgrams recorded on the reference flow cell 1 of the same channel without protein were subtracted from sensorgrams recorded on the METTL1–WDR4 surface. For double-referencing, injections of the running buffer without compound were run.

Solvent correction was applied to all sample sensorgrams to correct for buffer mismatches. To determine kinetic parameters, data were fitted to a simple 1:1 Langmuir interaction model.

The selectivity profile of STM9005 was assessed by testing the level of inhibition in a panel of methyltransferases (Reaction Biology). Inhibition of five additional RNA methyltransferases was tested using RapidFire MS assay, as described previously27. Data were plotted using GraphPad Prism (v.10).

Additional selectivity profiling was performed using commercial SAFETYscan47 and KINOMEscan scanEDGE panels (Eurofins DiscoverX), according to the provider’s standard protocols.

Protein boundaries were designed to mimic those used in PDB structure 3CKK, namely residues 32–265 of METTL1, with an N-terminal His-tag followed by a TEV cleavage site. This construct was synthetically cloned into the vector pTriIJ-HV (Evotec). The protein was expressed in BL21-CodonPlus (DE3)-RIL cells, grown in Terrific broth (Teknova, T7060) at 37 °C, before induction with 1 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG; Melford Laboratories I56000-5.0) at an optical density at 600 nm of 1.5, and subsequent expression for 18 h at 15 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 4,000g for 20 min at 4 °C, before storage at −80 °C.

Cells were lysed with a cell disruptor (Constant Systems) at 25,000 psi, 4 °C in a buffer of 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 2 mM β-mercaptoethanol (Merck, M3148-100ML), 5% glycerol, 1 mM PMSF, 40 µl l−1 benzonase. Cell debris was removed through centrifugation at 200,000g, 4 °C for 45 min, before the remaining supernatant was applied to a 5 ml HisTrap crude FF column (Cytiva). The loaded column was then washed with 10 CV of buffer A (20 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol and 50 mM imidazole), before elution with buffer B (20 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol and 250 mM imidazole). The protein was dialysed for 18 h at 4 °C in buffer C (20 mM HEPES pH 7.4 and 250 mM NaCl) in the presence of TEV protease (Evotec). Dialysed protein was loaded onto a 5 ml HiTrap SP HP ion-exchange column washed with buffer D (20 mM PIPES pH 6.5, Merck, P6757-500G) and eluted with a linear gradient with buffer E (20 mM PIPES pH 6.5 and 500 mM NaCl). Protein was concentrated with a 10 kDa molecular weight cut-off centrifugal concentrator to 28.7 mg ml−1 and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen until use for crystallography.

Protein samples were thawed to 4 °C before incubation on ice for 1 h with 10 mM compound STM00005451 (STM5451; final DMSO concentration of 2%; Supplementary Note 1c). Crystals were grown through hanging-drop vapour diffusion in a solution of 100 mM Bis-Tris pH 5.5 (Molecular Dimensions, MD2-004-PH), 200 mM LiSO4 (Molecular Dimensions, MD2-250-45) and 20% (w/v) polyethylene glycol 3350 (PEG 3350; Molecular Dimensions, MD2-250-9) (1 µl of protein + 1 µl reservoir). Seeding was used to enhance crystal reproducibility, and crystals grew overnight at 22 °C.

To replace STM5451 with STM9005, crystals were transferred into reservoir solution (2 µl) with 25 mM STM9005 (5% DMSO), before incubation for 24 h at 22 °C. Crystals were cryo-protected in soaking solution supplemented with 15% PEG before collecting into liquid nitrogen.

Data were collected at 100 K on ID17B at APS, with a 1.0 Å and processed with autoPROC and STARANISO38,39,40,41,42,43. An in-house generated PDB (originally derived from PDB 3CKK) was used for molecular replacement using dimple44,45. Iterative cycles of model building and refinement were performed using Coot46 and Buster47. STM9005 was fitted using restraints generated by Grade248. The final structure statistics are provided in Extended Data Table 1, with 100% Ramachandran-favoured protein residues. The structure was deposited to the PDB under accession code 9RYL. The structure was analysed using Molecular Operating Environment (Chemical Computing Group), and images were generated using PyMOL Molecular Graphics System (v.2.6.0a0, Schrödinger).

Cell target engagement of STM9005 was measured by thermal shift using InCELL Pulse technology (Eurofins DiscoverX). HeLa cells were transfected with 9 µg of pcDNA3.1-WDR4-P2A-METTL1-ePL and 21 µg pcDNA3.1(+) plasmid (empty vector as carrier) using FuGENE transfection reagent (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Then, 24 h after transfection, cells were frozen and stored in liquid nitrogen until the day of the assay.

For the thermal shift assay, 100 nl compound dilutions (eleven-point threefold dilutions, top concentration in assay: 50 μM) were spotted into assay plates (Greiner, 384-well, 784201) using a Mosquito instrument (SPT Labtech), resulting in a final DMSO concentration of 0.5%. Assay-ready, frozen WDR4-P2A-METTL1-ePL HeLa cells were thawed, washed in Opti-MEM (Gibco, 11058021) and seeded into the assay plates at 1,500 cells per well in 20 µl Opti-MEM. Plates were sealed with aluminium foil and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2. For the heat pulse, the plates were submerged for 5 min in a water bath at 60 °C, further incubated for 10 min at room temperature and finally centrifuged briefly to gather the liquid in the bottom of each well. Subsequently, 25 μl of detection solution (InCELL Detection Kit, DiscoverX; working solution: 16.7% EA reagent, 16.7% lysis buffer and 66.7% substrate reagent) was dispensed into each well and incubated for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. Subsequently, 42 µl of the reaction volume was transferred to the measurement plate (Corning, 384-well, 11058021), the assay plate was centrifuged for 1 min at 100g at room temperature and luminescence was measured using the EnVision multimode plate reader (Perkin Elmer). Relative luminescence values were normalized to the control wells with full stabilization (50 µM reference compound) and without stabilization (DMSO only). IC50 values were obtained by plotting data using GraphPad Prism (v.10).

HL-60, K562, Loucy, MOLM-13, MV-4-11, PEER, H1299, H1975, OE21 and OE33 were cultured in RPMI-1640 with l-glutamine (Gibco, 21875-034), supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco, A5256701) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich, P0781). B16F10, mouse PDAC (mPDAC1, 9091 PK –p48-Cre+/–, LSL-Kras+/–, ∆Tva+/−; mPDAC2, p48-cre+/−, LSL-Kras+/−)35, and HEK293FT cells were maintained in DMEM with l-glutamine (Gibco, 41965-039) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. A549, LoVo and SK-MES-1 cells were cultured in F-12K nutrient mix with l-glutamine (Gibco, 21127-022), supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. SW982 was maintained using DMEM with l-glutamine, supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% sodium pyruvate (Gibco, 11360-070) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. OCI-AML2 and OCI-AML3 cells were cultured in Alpha-MEM with l-glutamine (Gibco, 12509-069), supplemented with 20% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. HeLa cells were grown in MEM (Gibco, 11090-081), supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% l-glutamine (Gibco, 25030-149), 1% non-essential amino acids (Gibco, 11140-050).

Primary mouse MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+, MLL-AF4/Flt3ITD/+, Npm1cA+Flt3ITD/+ and MLL-ENL/Flt3ITD/+ cells were generated as described previously31. Npm1cA+NrasG12D/+ mice were described previously49. Primary mouse Dnmt3aR882H/+Npm1cA/+ cells were obtained by crossing Dnmt3aR992H/+ mice50 with Npm1cA/+ mice45. Finally, Npm1cA/+NrasG12D/+Idh1R132H/+ cells were obtained from mice generated by crossing Npm1cA/+NrasG12D/+ mice with Idh1R132H/+ mice51. All primary mouse cells were maintained in X-VIVO 20 (Lonza, LZBE04-448Q) supplemented with 5% FBS, 1% GlutaMax (Gibco, 35050-038), 1% penicillin–streptomycin, 50 ng ml−1 mouse stem cell factor (SCF) (Peprotech, AF-250-03), 10 ng ml−1 mouse IL-3 (Peprotech, AF-213-13) and 10 ng ml−1 mouse IL-6 (Peprotech, AF-216-16).

All cells were maintained at 37 °C, 5% CO2. MOLM-13, K562, HL-60, MV-411, PEER, Loucy, OCI-AML2 and OCI-AML3 cells were obtained from the Sanger Institute Cancer Cell Collection. OE21 and OE33 were purchased from Merck. All of the other cell lines were purchased from ATCC. All cell lines used were negative for mycoplasma.

Cas9 was introduced into cells using the pKLV2-EF1a-Cas92ABsd-W (Addgene, 68343) lentiviral vector, as described previously52. Guide RNAs (gRNAs) were cloned into pKLV2-U6gRNA5(BbsI)-PGKpuro2AmAzamiGreen (Addgene, 67976), as described previously30. A list of all gRNA sequences used in this study is provided in Supplementary Table 15.

Overexpression vectors pLKO.1-puro-ΔU6-Arg-TCT-4-1 and control pLKO.1-puro-ΔU6 were described previously11.

The pKLV-EF1a-puro-TY1 vector was constructed as follows. First, we removed the Cas9 fragment from the pKLV-EF1a-puro2AhCas952 vector, replaced it with a 2×TY1-tag, and introduced XmaI and XbaI restriction enzyme sites. Human CDK4 and MYC genes were amplified from cDNA obtained from MOLM-13 cells; the human METTL1 gene was amplified from cDNA obtained from A549 cells. The pKLV-EF1a-puro-TY1 vector and the PCR products were digested with XmaI and XbaI and ligated (T4 DNA ligase, M0202, NEB) into the vector, resulting in pKLV-EF1a-puro2A-2×TY1-hCDK4, pKLV-EF1a-puro2A-2×TY1-hMYC and pKLV-EF1a-puro2A-2×TY1-hMETTL1, respectively. Mouse Cdk4, Myc and Mettl1 were amplified from cDNA obtained from B16F10 cells. For Cdk4 and Myc, the PCR products and pKLV-EF1a-puro-TY1 plasmid were digested with XmaI and XbaI and ligated into the vector, resulting in pKLV-EF1a-puro2A-2×TY1-mCdk4 or pKLV-EF1a-puro2A-2×TY1-mMyc, respectively. For Mettl1, the pKLV-EF1a-puro-TY1 plasmid was digested with SmaI and XbaI and the PCR product was digested using PmeI and XbaI and ligated together, resulting in pKLV-EF1a-puro2A-2×TY1-mMettl1. The METTL1-mutant vectors were created using the Q5 site-directed mutagenesis kit (E0554, NEB), by introducing the following amino acid changes into the WT overexpression vectors: human METTL1, L160A and D163A; mouse Mettl1, L154A and D157A. A list of the primer sequences used is provided in Supplementary Table 15.

Viruses for competition assays and Arg-TCT overexpression were prepared by transfecting HEK293FT cells with the appropriate gRNA lentiviral vector together with packaging plasmids pPAX2 and pMD.2G at a ratio of 1:2.5:0.05 in 12-well plates. The supernatant was collected 48 h after transfection, filtered through a 45 μm PVDF filter and stored at −80 °C until further use.

Viruses for the introduction of Cas9, CDK4, MYC and METTL1 overexpression and the relevant controls were produced by transfecting HEK293FT cells with the appropriate lentiviral vector, pPAX2 and pMD.2G at a ratio 1:1:0.2 in 15 cm dishes. The supernatant was collected at 48 and 72 h after transfection and filtered through a 0.45 μm PVDF filter. The two yields were mixed and concentrated by centrifuging overnight at 6,000g at 4 °C; after centrifugation, the viral pellets were resuspended as 10× concentrates in PBS.

Suspension cells were seeded at 0.25 × 106 cells per well and transduced with appropriate viruses in a total medium volume of 2 ml and supplemented with polybrene (Merck, H9268)—8 μg ml−1 for human cells or 4 µg ml−1 for mouse cells—followed by spinfection (1 h, 900g, 32 °C). Adherent cells were seeded at 0.05–0.5 × 106 cells per well; the cells were transduced with appropriate viruses, in a total medium volume of 2 ml and passaged after reaching confluency. At day 4 after transduction, the transduction efficiency was confirmed to be 50% (±10%) using flow cytometry, and changes in the percentage of transduced cells were monitored by flow cytometry over time at days 7, 10 and 13. DAPI (Sigma-Aldrich, D9542) was used as a live/dead stain. Flow cytometry analysis of stained cells was performed using CytoFLEX (Beckman-Coulter). Further data processing and analysis were done using FlowJo (FlowJo, BD Biosciences). Gating strategies for all flow cytometry experiments are provided in Supplementary Fig. 2.

Cells were transduced with overexpression viruses as described above. On days 3 and 5 after transduction, cells were treated with 1 µg ml−1 puromycin (Merck, P8833) to select for transduced cells. Downstream experiments were initiated 6–10 days after transduction.

Suspension cells were seeded at 12,500 cells per 100 µl, and were treated for 3 days with vehicle or the indicated concentrations of STM9005 (100 μM to 781 nM). Then, 3 days after treatment, the cells were passaged and retreated with fresh compound, such that the resulting cell density matched the initial seeding density. Adherent cell lines were seeded at different densities, so they would reach 80–90% confluency on day 6 and treated with vehicle or the indicated concentrations of STM9005 (100 μM to 781 nM). All adherent cell lines were retreated on day 3. On day 6 after treatment, the CellTiter 96 AQueous Non-Radioactive Cell Proliferation Assay (Promega, G5430) was used, absorbance values at 490 nm were acquired using the CLARIOStar Plus microplate reader (BMG Labtech) and these values were used to calculate the relative cell proliferation.

Cells were seeded in 96-well culture plates at an initial seeding density of 400 (A549), 1,000 (OE21) or 2,500 (LoVo) cells. Cells were incubated for 18 h at 37 °C under 5% CO2. The next day, the medium was aspirated from all wells and replaced with assay medium (OE21: RPMI 1640 with GlutaMAX (Gibco, 61870-010) + 2% FBS; A549 and LoVo: F-12K nutrient mix with l-glutamine (Gibco, 21127-022) + 2.5% FBS). The cells were treated for 7 days. For quantification, the culture medium was aspirated and 50 µl PBS was added per well, before addition of 50 µl of CellTiter-Glo (Promega, G7572) working solution per well (prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions). The plates were incubated for 30 min at room temperature and luminescence signal was read on a multimode plate reader (SpectraMax i3x, Molecular Devices or EnVision, Perkin Elmer).

Human liver tissue was obtained from liver biopsies from deceased organ donors with informed consent. Liver biopsy samples were mechanically and enzymatically dissociated and plated following established protocols53. Primary human hepatocytes were cultured in modified HM medium, as described previously54. In culture, primary human hepatocytes were treated with vehicle or STM9005 for 72 h and viability was assessed using CellTiter-Glo (Promega, G7572) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Doxorubicin (Sigma-Aldrich, D5220) was used as a positive control. Each experiment was performed in three biopsy samples from two donor livers. All liver samples were obtained with informed consent for use in research and ethical approval (Research Ethics Committee (REC) 23/NS/0106).

Adherent cells were seeded in 12-well plates at densities that would lead to confluency in 3 days in control cells. At days 3, 6 and 9 after treatment, the cells were passaged and retreated with fresh compound, such that the resulting cell density in each well matched the initial seeding density.

At days 3, 6, 9 and 12, the plates were stained with 1% methylene blue (Merck, M9140), dissolved in 70% ethanol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 16685992), incubated at room temperature for 20 min and washed with distilled water to remove excess staining. The plates were then dried and scanned using an Epson Perfection V850 scanner.

The acquired images were further analysed using ImageJ (v.1.54), and relative confluency for each treatment was calculated by normalizing to untreated controls.

For replating assays of mouse cells, 100,000 WT bone marrow cells or 10,000 primary mouse MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+ cells were resuspended in 3 ml of methylcellulose (StemCell Technologies, M3434), supplemented with 1% penicillin–streptomycin, and split between two wells in six-well SmartDish plates (StemCell Technologies, 27371). The colonies were imaged and counted 7 days later (STEMvision, StemCell Technologies), replated to match the starting density and recounted a week later. In drug treatment experiments, the semisolid medium was supplemented with 1 µM, 2.5 µM STM9005 or vehicle, and replenished with each plating.

Human methylcellulose complete media (StemCell Technologies, H4434) was selected to determine the function of STM9005 on colony-forming capacity in CD34+ hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) from four healthy donors according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, mononuclear cells were isolated from cord blood from three healthy donors by density centrifugation. CD34+ HSPCs were next positively selected from mononuclear cells by using the CD34+ MicroBead Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-046-702). Finally, 1,000 CD34+ HSPCs, with vehicle or STM9005 treatment (2.5 μM and 5 μM), were suspended in 110 μl of IMDM (Gibco, 12440-053), supplemented with 2% FBS and seeded in 35-mm culture dishes (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10038820) with 1.1 ml of methylcellulose complete medium. The cells were cultured for 14–16 days and the colony numbers were counted by microscopy. All human cord blood samples were obtained with informed consent under local ethical approval (REC 24/EE/0116).

Adherent cells were seeded at different densities, so they would reach 70–80% confluency at assaying time points; cells were retreated at days 3 and 6. Cell cycle analysis was performed on days 5 and 7 after treatment, using 0.5 × 106 cells using the APC BrdU Flow Kit (BD Pharmingen, 557892), with a 2 h BrdU incubation for suspension cells and a 4 h BrdU incubation for adherent cells, according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Flow cytometry analysis of stained cells was performed using the CytoFLEX or CytoFLEX LX (Beckman-Coulter) system. Further data processing and analysis were done using FlowJo (FlowJo, BD Biosciences). Gating strategies for all flow cytometry experiments are provided in Supplementary Fig. 2.

Suspension cells were seeded at 0.1 × 106 cells per well in 12 well plates in a total of 2 ml medium, supplemented with vehicle or 1 µM and 2 µM of STM9005; cells were retreated at day 3 and day 6. Adherent cells were seeded at different densities, so they would reach 70–80% confluency at assaying time points; cells were retreated at days 3 and day 6. Apoptosis analysis was performed on days 3, 5 and 7 after treatment, staining 0.1 × 106 cells per reaction using the APC Annexin V Apoptosis Detection Kit (BioLegend, 640930) and propidium iodide (Sigma-Aldrich, P4170), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Flow cytometry analysis of stained cells was performed using CytoFLEX or CytoFLEX LX (Beckman-Coulter). Further data processing and analysis were done using FlowJo (FlowJo, BD Biosciences). Gating strategies for all flow cytometry experiments can be found in Supplementary Fig. 2.

For differentiation assays, cells were seeded at 0.25 × 106 cells per well and treated with vehicle or STM9005 (10 µM, 5 µM, 2.5 µM, 1 µM). On days 3 and 6, the cells were stained with 1:250 anti-mouse Ly-6G/Ly-6C (Gr-1)-APC (BioLegend, 108412, RB6-8C5) for mouse cells and 1:250 anti-human CD11b-APC (BioLegend, 982604, ICRF44, AB_2632619) for human cells. On day 3, cells were passaged and retreated with fresh compound, such that the resulting cell density matched the initial seeding density.

Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, 15596018) coupled with RNA Clean & Concentrator-100 column purifications (Zymo Research, R1019), according to the RNA Clean & Concentrator manufacturer’s instructions.

RNA quantity was measured by Qubit RNA Broad Range (BR) assay (Invitrogen, Q10211). Quality control of RNA was assessed and the RNA integrity number value was determined using either the Bioanalyzer RNA 6000 Nano kit (Agilent, 5067-1511) or the 4200 TapeStation system (Agilent).

For quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis, RNA was extracted using GenElute Mammalian Total RNA Miniprep Kit (Merck, RTN350), according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

Cells treated with STM9005 at the concentrations and time points indicated at figure legends were lysed using prewarmed HB42 buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 (Invitrogen, 15567-027), 750 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA pH 8.0, 1% SDS (Merck, 05030) and 15% formamide (Merck, F7503)) and the lysates were heated for 20 min at 95 °C with agitation. The lysates were then snap-frozen and stored at −80 °C.

For the MSD assay, Streptavidin-coated plates (Mesoscale Discovery, L21SA) were blocked with 50 µl blocking buffer (5% BSA, 100 µg ml−1 salmon sperm DNA solution (Invitrogen, 15632-011) in 1× Tris-buffered saline (TBS) (Alfa Aesar, J60877.K3) containing 0.05% Tween-20 (Merck, P1379)) for 1 h at room temperature with 400 rpm agitation. Plates were then washed twice with 50 µl MSD1 buffer (1× TBS containing 0.05% Tween-20) and once with 50 µl MSD2 buffer (2 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA pH 8.0). To each well, 20 µl of a 12.5 nM stock solution of the biotinylated capture oligo (/5Biosg/CGAACGTGATAACCACTACACTACGGAAAC) was added (final concentration of 0.25 pmol per well) and incubated for 1 h at room temperature with 450 rpm agitation. The plates were washed twice with MSD1 buffer and once with warm HB42 buffer. The previously frozen cell lysates in HB42 were first thawed to room temperature, heated to 95 °C for 10 min and then slowly cooled down to 42 °C (at a rate of 1 °C min−1). The lysates were kept at 42 °C until use. From the cell lysates, 25 µl was transferred to each well on the MSD plate and incubated at 42 °C overnight with 300 rpm agitation.

The next day, the plates were washed once with warm HB42 buffer (42 °C) supplemented with RNase inhibitors (final concentration, 0.002 U µl−1), followed by two washes with MSD1 buffer supplemented with RNase inhibitors (Invitrogen, AM2696), to a final concentration 0.002 U µl−1. The anti-m7G antibody (MBL, RN017M) was diluted to 0.2 µg ml−1 in 1% BSA, 100 µg ml−1 salmon sperm DNA, 0.05 U µl−1 RNase inhibitor in MSD1 buffer, and 30 µl per well was dispensed and incubated for 2 h at room temperature with 400 rpm agitation. The plates were washed three times with MSD1 buffer supplemented with 0.002 U µl−1 RNase inhibitors, followed by addition of 30 µl per well anti-mouse SULFO-TAG antibody (Mesoscale Discovery, R32AC-1) diluted to 1 µg ml−1 in 1% BSA, 0.05 U µl−1 RNase inhibitor in MSD1 buffer. The plates were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with 400 rpm agitation. The plates were then washed three times with MSD1 buffer supplemented with 0.002 U µl−1 RNase inhibitors, then 50 µl per well 1× MSD read buffer T (Mesoscale Discovery, R92TC-3) was added and plates were immediately read on a Sector 600 Mesoscale Discovery reader (Mesoscale Discovery). Dose–response curves were calculated by a four-parameter nonlinear regression model with variable slope using GraphPad Prism (v.10).

Alternatively, for total RNA preparations from cell lines or animal tissues and tumour samples, the tRNA-Val MSD assay was performed as described above with the following adjustments: total RNA was diluted to 20–40 ng µl−1 in HB42 buffer for 0.5–1 µg input in 25 µl per well. The diluted total RNA was heated to 95 °C for 10 min and then slowly cooled down to 42 °C (at a rate of 1 °C min−1) before being transferred to the 384-well MSD plate for the overnight incubation at 42 °C with 300 rpm agitation.

Total RNA extracted from cell lines or animal tissues and tumour were subjected to SEC. The fractions were separated in isocratic 0.1 M ammonium acetate in water (pH 5.5) at 65 °C with a flow rate of 1,000 µl min−1 for 7.5 min on an Agilent SEC-5 1000 Å 4.6 × 300 mm column using the Thermo UltiMate 3000 HPLC system with on-line ultraviolet detection at 260 nm.

Nucleosides were prepared and quantified as described previously27. All data were plotted using GraphPad Prism (v.10).

For experiments in Figs. 2j,k and 4e and Extended Data Fig. 1k, whole-cell protein lysates were prepared using RIPA lysis buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 89901) supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, 4693124001) followed by incubation on ice for 30 min. Protein lysates were cleared by centrifugation (20,000g, 15 min, 4 °C). Quantification of total protein was carried out using the Pierce BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23227) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

For experiments in Extended Data Figs. 4k–m and 6b, cells were lysed using RIPA lysis buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 89901) supplemented with 1× protease inhibitor cocktail (Merck, P8340), 1× phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 2 (Merck, P5044), 1× phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 3 (Merck, P5726), followed by incubation on ice for 10 min. The protein lysates were cleared by centrifugation (20,000g, 10 min, 4 °C). Total protein was quantified using the Pierce BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23227) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

For experiments in Fig. 3d and Extended Data Figs. 2b, 4b,i,j, 5d and 6f,g, cells were lysed using whole-cell lysis buffer (0.2% IGEPAL CA-630 (Merck, I8896), 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 450 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1× protease inhibitor cocktail (Merck, P8340), 1× phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 2 (Merck, P5044), 1× phosphatase inhibitor cocktail 3 (Merck, P5726) and 1 mM DTT (Epigentek, R-1104-1)) and incubated on ice for 10 min. The lysates were then centrifuged at 20,000g and 4 °C for 10 min. The supernatant was quantified using Bradford Assay (Bio-Rad, 5000006).

After quantification, the samples were supplemented with 1× NuPAGE LDS sample buffer (Life Technologies, NP0007) and 1× NuPAGE Sample Reducing Agent (Life Technologies, NP0009). They were then incubated at 70 °C for 10 min and were snap-frozen until further use.

Western blots were performed using 10–20 µg of protein on SDS–PAGE gels and blotted onto a PVDF membrane.

Western blots in Extended Data Fig. 1i were performed using the following antibodies: anti-METTL1 (Proteintech, 14994-1-AP), anti-GAPDH loading control monoclonal antibody DyLight 680 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA5-15738-D680), donkey anti-rabbit IgG HRP (Cytiva, NA934-1ML, AB_772206) and sheep anti-mouse IgG HRP (Cytiva, NA931-1ML).

Western blots in Fig. 2j,k were performed using anti-CDC2 (CDK1, Cell Signaling Technology, 9116), anti-CDC25A (Abcam, ab92892), anti-cyclin B1 (CCNB1, Cell Signaling Technology, 12231), anti-p21WAF1/CIP1 (CDKN1A, Cell Signaling Technology, 2947), anti-human CDK4 (Cell Signaling Technology, 12790), anti-human cyclin A2 (CCNA2, Cell Signaling Technology, 67955), anti-GAPDH loading control monoclonal antibody DyLight 680 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA5-15738-D680), anti-alpha tubulin-Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 53-4502-82), donkey anti-rabbit IgG HRP (Cytiva, NA934-1ML, AB_772206) and sheep anti-mouse IgG HRP (Cytiva, NA931-1ML).

Western blots in Extended Data Fig. 2b were performed using anti-H3 (Abcam, ab1791), anti-METTL1 (Proteintech, 14994-1-AP), anti-β-actin (Abcam, ab8442), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L Alexa Fluor 680 (Abcam, ab175775), goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L Alexa Fluor 790 (Abcam, ab186697), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Western blots in Fig. 3d were performed using anti-human CDK4 (Cell Signaling Technology, 12790), anti-KDM1A (Abcam, ab17721), anti-β-actin (Abcam, ab8442), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Western blots in Extended Data Fig. 4b were performed using anti-human CDK4 (Cell Signaling Technology, 12790), anti-mouse/human CDK4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AHZ0202) anti-β-actin (Abcam, ab8442), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Western blots in Extended Data Fig. 4i,j were performed using anti-mouse/human CDK4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AHZ0202), anti-β-actin (Abcam, ab8442), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Western blots in Extended Data Fig. 4k,l were performed using: anti-METTL1 (Proteintech, 14994-1-AP), anti-β-Actin (Abcam, ab8442), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Western blots in Extended Data Fig. 4m were performed using anti-KDM1A (Abcam, ab17721), anti-mouse/human CDK4 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AHZ0202), anti-β-actin (Abcam, ab8442), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L Alexa Fluor 680 (Abcam, ab175775) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Western blots in Extended Data Fig. 5d were performed using anti-METTL3 (Abcam, ab195352), anti-human WDR4 (Abcam, ab169526), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Western blots in Extended Data Fig. 6b,f,g were performed using anti-MYC (Y69) (Abcam, ab32072), anti-β-actin (Abcam, ab8442), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Western blots in Fig. 4e were performed using anti-MYC (Y69) (Abcam, ab32072), anti-p53 (1C12, Cell Signaling Technology, 2524), anti-β-Actin (Abcam, ab8442), goat anti-mouse IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab205719) and goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (HRP) (Abcam, ab6721).

Uncropped Western blots for all figures are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1.

For differentiated blood panel staining in bone marrow and spleen (Extended Data Fig. 8l,m, respectively) after treatment and erythrocyte lysis, cells were stained as described previously50 with the following antibodies: anti-mouse CD4-PE/Cyanine5 (PE/Cy5; BioLegend, 100514, 1:400), anti-mouse CD8a-PE/Cy5 (BioLegend, 100710, 1:400), anti-mouse/human CD45R/B220-PE/Cy5 (BioLegend, 103210, 1:400), anti-mouse Ly-6G/Ly-6C (Gr-1)-Alexa Fluor 700 (AF700; BioLegend, 108422, 1:400), anti-mouse/human CD11b-AF700 (BioLegend, 101222, 1:400) and anti-mouse/human CD45R/B220-AF700 (BioLegend, 103232, 1:400). B cells were defined as B220-PE-Cy5+B220-A700+, T cells as CD4-PE-Cy5+CD8-PE-Cy5+AF700− and myeloid cells as CD11b-AF700+Gr1-AF700+PE-Cy5−.

For analysis of the progenitor compartment (Extended Data Fig. 8n–s), freshly isolated BM cells after erythrocyte lysis were stained with the following antibodies, as described previously50: BD Pharmingen biotin mouse lineage panel (B220, TER119, CD11b, CD3e, Gr1; BD Biosciences, 559971, 1:300 each) detected with Streptavidin-Brilliant Violet (BV) 510 (BioLegend, 405233, 1:900), anti-mouse Ly-6A/E (Sca-1)-Pacific Blue (PB; BioLegend, 122520, 1:100), anti-mouse CD117 (KIT) (2B8)-APC-eFluor 780 (AF780) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 47-1171-82, 1:100), anti-mouse CD48-BV605 (BioLegend, 103441, 1:200), anti-mouse CD150 (SLAM)-BV650 (BioLegend, 115932, 1:100), anti-mouse CD135-PE (BD Pharmingen, BD Biosciences, 553842, 1:100), anti-mouse CD34-FITC (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11-0431-82, 1:50), anti-mouse CD16/32-PerCP-Cyanine5.5 (PerCP-Cy5.5; BioLegend, 101324, 1:100), 7AAD (BioLegend, 420404, 1:100). LK cells were defined as 7AAD−Lin−KIT-AF780+Sca1-PB−; LSK cells were defined as 7AAD−Lin−KIT-AF780+Sca1-PB+. Megakaryocyte–erythroid progenitors (MEPs), common myeloid progenitors (CMPs) and granulocyte–monocyte progenitors (GMPs) were gated on LK cells and defined as follows: MEP, CD34-FITC−CD16-32-PerCP-Cy5.5−; CMP, CD34-FITC+CD16-32-PerCP-Cy5.5−; GMP, CD34-FITC+CD16-32-PerCP-Cy5.5+. Short-term haematopoietic stem cells (ST-HSCs), long-term haematopoietic stem cells (LT-HSCs), multipotent progenitor 2 (MPP2) cells and multipotent progenitor 3 (MPP3) cells were gated on LSK cells and defined as follows: ST-HSC, CD150-BV650−CD48-BV605−; LT-HSC, CD150-BV650+CD48-BV605−; MPP2, CD150-BV650+CD48-BV605+; MPP3, CD150-BV650−CD48-BV605+. Haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), multipotent progenitor (MPP) cells and lymphoid-primed multipotent progenitor (LMPP) cells were gated on LSK cells and defined as follows: HSC, CD135-PE−; MPP, CD135-PEmedium; LMPP, CD135-PE+.

Gating strategies are provided in Supplementary Fig. 2. Flow cytometry acquisition was performed using LSRFortessa (BD Biosciences) and BD FACSDiva Software (BD Biosciences), and the data were analysed in FlowJo (FlowJo, BD Biosciences).

cDNA was synthesized using SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Invitrogen, 11756500) and 500 ng of RNA in 10 µl reactions, according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

The levels of specific RNAs were measured using the PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, A25742) and the QuantStudio 5 Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A list of all of the primer sequences used in this study is provided in Supplementary Table 15.

Total RNA samples isolated from in vitro treatment with either vehicle or 1 µM STM9005 of OE21 and LoVo cell lines as well as from in vivo B16F10 tumours from mice treated twice daily for 5 days with either vehicle or 30 mg per kg STM9005 were subjected to eukaryotic strand-specific mRNA sequencing provided as service by Novogene. In brief, the mRNA-seq service entailed RNA sample quality control, directional mRNA library preparation (with poly(A) enrichment) and sequencing of libraries in a paired-end 150 bp run mode (PE150) on the NovaSeq X Plus instrument (Illumina). The minimum output was 11 Gb per sample (>60 million reads per sample). For each condition, three individual replicate samples were processed.

Fastq files were processed using the Nextflow nf-core RNA-seq pipeline (v.3.9 and v.3.13.2). The pipeline aligned reads to the reference genomes for human (Ensemble GRCh38) and mouse (Ensemble GRCm39) using the STAR aligner55. Transcript expression was quantified with Salmon56. Differential gene expression analysis was performed on per gene read counts by DESeq257, after the removal of genes with fewer than 10 reads. DESeq2 log2[FC] statistics of treatment versus control was used to rank genes for gene set enrichment analysis (clusterProfiler package, pAdjustMethod=“BH”, pvalue.cutoff=0.05) with the hallmark gene set from MSigDB58. All data analysis was performed using R.

mim-tRNA-seq was adapted from a previous study59 to enable profiling of tRNA levels as well as methylation levels at the G46 position of tRNAs. Total RNA (5 µg in 19 µl) was incubated for 45 min at 37 °C with 1.5 µl 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 9.0) and 1 µl SUPERase.In RNase Inhibitor (Invitrogen, AM2694) to deacylate tRNAs. This was then incubated for 30 min at 37 °C with 67 µl nuclease-free water, 10 µl T4 PNK buffer and 1 µl T4 PNK (NEB, M0201L) to dephosphorylate the 3′ end of tRNAs. RNA was recovered by ethanol precipitation with 10 µl 3 M sodium acetate (pH 5.2) and 2 µl GlycoBlue coprecipitant (Invitrogen, AM9516) and resuspended in 5 µl nuclease-free water. Abasic sites at m7G modified positions were generated by incubation for 40 min on ice with 3 µl 37 mM m7GTP (Jena Bioscience, NU-1122S), 5 µl 3 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.2), 2 µl nuclease-free water and 15 µl 1 M sodium borohydride15 (NaBH4, Merck, 21346). The reaction was stopped by adding quenching buffer (180 µl 1 M sodium acetate (pH 4.5), 120 µl nuclease-free water, 2 µl GlycoBlue and 990 µl ethanol). RNA was recovered by ethanol precipitation. RNA was resolved by gel electrophoresis on a 10% TBE-urea gel. tRNAs were selected by excising RNAs between 65–90 nucleotides and generated into libraries for sequencing as described previously59. The libraries were sequenced in a single-end 100 bp run mode (SE100) on the NextSeq 2000 (Illumina) system.

Fastq files were demultiplexed and trimmed using cutadapt59,60. The mimseq command (--cluster-id 0.97 --threads 15 --min-cov 0.0005 --max-mismatches 0.075) within the conda mimseq package (v.1.3.8) was then used to obtain counts for each isodecoder as well as summarized counts for each anticodon and the proportion of misincorporation at the G46 position. log2[FC] values in tRNA levels after treatment and P values, adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, for the significance of these changes were then calculated using the DESeq2 R package57. log2[FC] values in the proportion of misincorporation at m7G46-modified sites were calculated for each replicate, as were P values using a two-tailed t-test to check the significance of any change in mean misincorporation.

Up to 2 µg total RNA isolated from control or METTL1 inhibitor-treated cells or 0.5 µl of the low molecular mass marker (Affymetrix/USB, J76410) were diluted to 5 µl and mixed with equal volume of 2× Novex TBE-urea sample buffer. The samples and marker were heated to 80 °C for 10 min before loading onto 10% Novex TBE-Urea polyacrylamide gels, stained as described above and imaged on a ChemiDoc MP imaging system (Bio-Rad). Nucleic acids were transferred onto positively charged Nylon membrane (Cytiva Amersham Hybond N+, RPN203B) by semi-dry electroblotting (3.3 mA cm−2 for 1 h) using the Trans-Blot Turbo transfer system (Bio-Rad). After completion of transfer, nucleic acids were cross-linked to membranes using a Stratalinker UV crosslinker with 120,000 µJ cm−2 of total energy. Membranes were additionally baked for 10 min at 80 °C and stored at −20 °C until further use.

For hybridization with specific biotinylated oligonucleotides, membranes were cut into strips and incubated with 7.5 ml preheated 1× North2South hybridization buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 37549) for 30 min at 55 °C. Biotinylated oligonucleotide probes (~30 nucleotide length) for specific tRNA molecules were diluted to 10 µM and heat denatured for 10 min at 98 °C. Per membrane in 7.5 ml buffer, 2.5 µl of the denatured oligonucleotide probe (equal to ~250 ng) was added and further incubated overnight at 55 °C. The next day, hybridization buffers were discarded, and membranes were washed three times with 7.5 ml preheated 1× North2South hybridization stringency wash buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 37555) for 15–20 min each at 55 °C. After stringency washes, the membranes were processed for Streptavidin-HRP incubation and subsequent detection of biotin-streptavidin complexes using the Chemiluminescent Nucleic Acid Detection Module Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 89880) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations and imaged on the ChemiDoc MP imaging system (Bio-Rad). Images were processed using ImageJ or Image Lab (Bio-Rad).

Cell culture medium was removed and cells were incubated (2 min, 37 °C) with new medium supplemented with 100 µg ml−1 cycloheximide (Merck, C4859), washed with PBS supplemented with 20 µg ml−1 cycloheximide, and lysed with 400 µl lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2 (Invitrogen, 89880), 1 mM dl-dithiothreitol (DTT, Merck, 43815), 1% Triton X-100 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10671652), 0.1% IGEPAL CA-630 (Merck, I8896), 100 µg ml−1 cycloheximide, 25 U ml−1 TURBO DNase (Invitrogen, AM2239) using a cell scraper. The lysates were triturated ten times through a 26-gauge needle and cell debris pelleted by centrifugation at 20,000g, 5 min, 4 °C. Total RNA was purified from 100 µl cleared lysate and mRNA-seq libraries were generated using the NEBNext Poly(A) mRNA Magnetic Isolation Module (NEB, E7490S) and NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB, E7760S). RPFs were generated by incubating (45 min, 23 °C, 1,400 rpm) cleared lysates (120 µl) with 3 µl RNase I (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AM2294). Digestion was stopped with 4 µl SUPERase.In. Ribosomes were enriched by passing 100 µl through a pre-equilibrated Illustra MicroSpin S-400 HR column (GE Healthcare, 27-5140-01) and equilibrated by gravity flow with 3 ml equilibration buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2). RNA was extracted from the flowthrough using TRIzol reagent according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

rRNA was depleted from 6 µg of RNA using the Ribo-seq rRNA depletion kit (siTOOLs, dp-K024-000042) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and RNA was purified using the RNA Clean & Concentrator kit (Zymogen). RPFs were selected by excising RNAs between 27 and 32 nucleotides after electrophoresis on a 15% TBE-Urea gel and extracted by incubating (15 min, 70 °C, 1,400 rpm) gel pieces in RNA extraction buffer (0.3 M NaOAc (pH 5.2), 0.25% SDS, 1 mM EDTA (pH 8.0)) and precipitating the RNA with isopropanol and GlycoBlue. RNA was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min with 1 µl T4 PNK buffer, 1 µl T4 PNK and 1 µl SUPERase.In. RNA was purified using the RNA Clean & Concentrator column, and libraries were generated using the NEBNext Small RNA-seq kit for Illumina (NEB, E7330S). mRNA and RPF libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq X Plus machine (Illumina) in a PE150 run mode to a depth of >40 million or >100 million reads, respectively.

Read 1 fastq files were adapter trimmed and filtered for reads with length between 20 and 40 nucleotides using cutadapt60. rRNA, tRNA, snoRNA and snRNA reads were removed using SortMeRNA54. Reads were then aligned to a transcriptome index generated from the MANE Select transcript set (GRCh38, Ensembl release 108) using STAR55 (--alignEndsType EndToEnd, --outFilterMultimapNmax 1, --outFilterMismatchNmax 2, --alignIntronMax 1). Bam files were then processed using riboWaltz61 to determine the codon that was at the ribosome A-site for each RPF, filtering for read lengths from 26 to 32 nucleotides and using the signal within a frame of −1 to +1 around the first nucleotide of each codon. log2[FC] values (treated/control) in Ribo-seq unit step transformation (RUST) ratios of observed/expected RPF density62 for each A-site codon transcriptome-wide, excluding the first 40 and last 20 codons of transcripts and transcripts with fewer than 80 codons, were then calculated for each replicate. This can be interpreted as the log2[FC] in ribosome occupancy when each codon is at the ribosome A-site. For the box plot, codons were assigned to m7G or non-m7G categories depending on the m7G status of the tRNA(s) that recognize them. In cases in which two tRNAs with opposing m7G statuses recognize the same codon, the m7G status of the cognate tRNA was selected unless the expression of this tRNA was undetectable in OE21 tRNA-seq data. Individual codons showing a significant (P < 0.05) increase in RUST ratio were calculated using a one-sample, one-tailed t-test. To calculate the significance of grouped m7G and non-m7G codons, a two-sample, two-tailed t-test was used.

mRNA fastq files were adapter-trimmed and gene counts were obtained using salmon56. An integrative differential expression analysis of RNA-seq and Ribo-seq gene counts was carried out to determine genes regulated at the level of transcription or translational efficiency63. This gives four categories of genes showing significant changes (adjusted P < 0.2): forwarded, significant change in the same direction and at the same rate for both translation and transcription; intensified, significant change in the same direction for both translation and transcription but with greater change in translation; exclusive, significant change only for translation; buffered, significant change in opposite directions for both translation and transcription.

Pairwise overlaps between differentially expressed gene sets (|log2[FC] | > 1, adjusted P < 0.05) were quantified using Jaccard similarity. Statistical significance of overlaps was assessed using a one-tailed hypergeometric test against a background of 20,000 protein-coding genes. The probability of observing at least k overlapping genes by chance was calculated as P(X ≥ k), where k is the observed overlap, A and B are the sizes of the two gene sets, and N represents the background gene universe. P values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. All reported overlaps remained significant after FDR correction (FDR < 0.001).

For histological analysis, samples were fixed in 10% formalin (CellStor Pot, CellPath, BAF-6000-08A), dehydrated and embedded in paraffin (Paraplast Plus, Sigma-Aldrich, P3683). Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks were sectioned at a thickness of 5–7 μm using a microtome Leica RM2255 microtome and mounted onto microscopy slides (Superfrost Plus Adhesion Microscopy slides, Epredia, J1800AMNZ) for further analysis. Haematoxylin (Pioneer Research Chemicals, PRC/R/51/2) and eosin staining (Pioneer Research Chemicals, PRC/66/1) was performed on FFPE sections. All images were acquired using a ZeissApoTome2.0 with Zen Blue software (Zeiss). Biopsy tissue samples from both groups were reviewed by two blinded clinicians with experience in mouse histology. No gross histological differences were observed between groups.

For all animal experiments, STM9005 was prepared using 20% (2-hydroxypropyl)-β-cyclodextrin (Merck, H105-5G) in water (Merck, W3500).

For the pharmacokinetic analysis of STM9005, male C57BL/6J mice were given i.p. injections of 10 mg per kg or 30 mg per kg STM9005 (3 mice per dose) and sampled serially up to 12 h after dosing. For oral dosing, 10 mg ml−1 STM9005 stock solution was administered at 30 mg per kg through oral gavage. Blood was collected from the tail vein at the indicated time points and collected in K2-EDTA tubes. Plasma was isolated by centrifugation, and 5 µl of sample was mixed with a precipitant solution of 200 µl acetonitrile and internal standard. The supernatant from this precipitation was transferred to a new plate and 3 μl injections were characterized by liquid chromatography coupled with MS (LC–MS) on a LC–MS/MS–AU Triple Quad 6500+ instrument attached to an LC instrument and autosampler (Waters ACQUITY UPLC I-Class PLUS System).

STM9005 was resolved on an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column (Waters, 1.8 μm particles, 2.1 × 50 mm) with an increasing gradient of 15–95% B over 78 s. Mobile phases consisted of (A) 0.1% formic acid and 2 mM ammonium formate in water and of (B) 0.1% formic acid and 2 mM ammonium formate in acetonitrile/water (v/v, 95:5). The flow rate was held at 0.6 ml min−1. Retention time for STM9005 was 0.86 min, mass/transition for STM9005 was 462.1/219.1 Da. A calibration curve for STM9005 was run at 2.00–3,000 ng ml−1 and the lower limit of quantification was set at 2 ng ml−1. Data were plotted using GraphPad Prism (v.10).

For all subsequent experiments, each animal was treated twice a day i.p. with 30 mg per kg STM9005 or vehicle.

For experiments in Fig. 4a–g and Extended Data Fig. 7a,b, B16F10 cells were transplanted subcutaneously into female C57BL/6J mice with 0.5 × 106 cells per mouse. mPDAC1 (Fig. 4h–j and Extended Data Fig. 7d,e) and A549 (Fig 4k–n and Extended Data Fig. 7j) cells were transplanted into male NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1WjTg(CMV-IL3,CSF2,KITLG)1Eav/MloySzJ (NSG-SGM3) mice with 1 × 106 and 2 × 106 cells per mouse, respectively. All cells were resuspended in a 1:1 mixture of Matrigel (Corning, 354234) and PBS (Merck, P4474-500ML). Treatment for all subcutaneous models was initiated after detection of palpable tumours using digital callipers and lasted 5 days for B16F10, and 9 days for A549 and mPDAC. Tumour sizes were monitored regularly for the duration of the experiment and all animals were collected after the tumours of vehicle-treated animals reached the humane end point described in the study plan. Tumour and kidney tissue was collected for further analysis.

For experiments in Fig. 4o and Extended Data Fig. 7h, male NSG-SGM3 mice were transplanted intravenously (i.v.) with MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+ cells at 0.5 × 106 cells per mouse. Daily treatment for 5 days was initiated 12 days after transplantation. Disease progression was monitored by weekly bleeds. In brief, 20 μl of blood was collected from the tail vein using a capillary pipette containing anticoagulants (EDTA) (Microvette 100 EDTA K3E, Sarstedt, 20.1278). The blood samples were used to obtain a complete blood count using Vet abc Plus (scil). The mice were collected after reaching the humane end points described in the study plan. In parallel, C57BL/6J were treated for 5 days, and monitored for signs of toxicity and changes in weight (Extended Data Fig. 7g).

For experiments in Fig. 4p,q and Extended Data Fig. 7i–o, female NSG-SGM3 mice were i.v. transplanted with a patient-derived AML xenograft (AML-491 PDX)64. Daily treatments with either vehicle or STM9005 for 10 days were initiated 22 days after transplantation. Disease progression was monitored by weekly bleeds, as described above, and mice were collected when humane end points were reached. For the experiment in Fig. 4q, a subset of mice was collected on day 43 after transplantation, the bone marrow was stained using 1:250 anti-human CD45 FITC (BioLegend, 304006) and engraftment was quantified using flow cytometry.

For the experiment in Extended Data Fig. 8a, bone marrow was isolated from 4 WT CB57BL/6J mice and used for colony serial plating assays.

For the experiments in Extended Data Figs. 8d–s and 9a,b, C57BL/6J mice were treated for 12 days twice daily with either vehicle or 30 mg ml−1 STM9005. Tissues were collected at 30 days after treatment. Bone marrow was isolated and used to assess colony-forming potential. Bone marrow and spleen were used for flow cytometry interrogation of haematopoiesis. Heart, liver, kidney and spleen were used for histology.

In vivo absorption–distribution–metabolism–excretion studies were conducted at WuXi AppTec in accordance with IACUC standard animal procedures and guidelines and in compliance with the US Animal Welfare Act and Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. All animal experiments related to Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 7 and Extended Data Fig. 8 were performed under project licences PP3797858 (PDX, MLL-AF9/Flt3ITD/+), PP9816216 (A549, mPDAC1), PP3042348 (long-term haematopoiesis experiment) or PP7037913 (B16F10) issued by the United Kingdom Home Office, in accordance with the Animal Scientific Procedures Act 1986.

No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size. The experiments were not randomized. The investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment. Statistical tests and sample sizes used are included in all relevant figure legends.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

All datasets related to STM9005 used in this study can be accessed from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under accession codes GSE302586 and GSE303386. STM9005’s structure has been deposited at the PDB (9RYL). Source data are provided with this paper.

The code used to process and analyse the tRNA and Ribo-seq datasets is available at GitHub (https://github.com/storm-therapeutics/mettl1_stm9005_manuscript).

Jamie Carragher has described Declan Rice as comfortably the best midfielder in the Premier League after another commanding performance helped Arsenal secure a huge 1-0 victory over Liverpool at Anfield.

Rice was named Player of the Match as Mikel Arteta’s side ended a 14-year wait for a league victory at Liverpool.

The England international also created the decisive goal, delivering the ball for Kai Havertz to score in the 16th minute as Arsenal moved top of the Premier League.

Speaking on Sky Sports, as also reported by Metro, Carragher left little doubt about where he ranks Rice among the league’s midfielders.

He said: “He’s the best midfield player in the Premier League by a long way. It’s not even a debate.”

Carragher also dismissed comparisons with Chelsea midfielder Moisés Caicedo, arguing that a debate existed last season but that Rice has now moved clearly ahead.

He added: “He’s a world-class midfield player. There’s absolutely no doubt about it. One of the best midfield players Arsenal have ever had.”

Carragher even placed Rice alongside some of Arsenal’s historic midfield greats, referencing Patrick Vieira and Liam Brady while insisting the 27-year-old deserves to be included in that conversation.

Rice’s display at Anfield backed up those words. He recorded more touches than any other Arsenal player, provided the match-winning assist and repeatedly helped protect the defence when Liverpool applied pressure.

Carragher’s claim will inevitably provoke debate, especially with players such as Caicedo competing at a similar level, but Rice’s influence on Arsenal is becoming difficult to question.

He can protect the defence, carry the ball through pressure, press aggressively, dominate duels and now regularly decide matches in the final third.

That last development has taken his game to another level.

Against Liverpool, Arsenal needed discipline more than flair. Rice delivered both. His assist decided the match, but his work without the ball was equally important as Liverpool failed to register a shot on target despite sustained pressure.

The comparison with Vieira will always be difficult because of what the Frenchman achieved at Arsenal, but Rice is building his own legacy.

If he continues producing decisive performances while Arsenal compete for major trophies, Carragher’s claim that he belongs among the club’s greatest midfielders may soon sound far less controversial.

Tottenham are still keeping close tabs on Nottingham Forest midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White and could revisit a deal in January if the England international becomes available.

The 26-year-old has been on Spurs’ radar for well over a year and came close to moving to North London in 2025 before the deal collapsed amid a dispute between the two clubs.

He later signed a new three-year contract with Forest, but speculation over his future has returned after another strong individual run of form.

According to Football Insider, Tottenham continue to monitor Gibbs-White and are considering another attempt to sign him in 2027.

The midfielder has been one of the Premier League’s most productive attacking midfielders in 2026, scoring 13 league goals since the start of the calendar year.

Forest’s difficult start to the current season could also increase the chances of him reassessing his future.

Tottenham’s interest is well established. CaughtOffside reported in September that Spurs were ready to revisit a move for Gibbs-White after failing to land him previously, with Roberto De Zerbi keen to add more creativity and control to midfield.

Gibbs-White has also earned major praise from his Forest teammates. Ola Aina said: “Morgan has the potential to be a very top player.”

He also described him as “the real deal” and “a fantastic player.”

This move still makes plenty of sense for Tottenham.

Gibbs-White would give De Zerbi a midfielder capable of carrying the ball, creating chances and scoring regularly from advanced positions. His Premier League experience would also make him a relatively low-risk signing compared with bringing in another player from abroad.

The biggest issue is Forest’s willingness to sell.

Gibbs-White is under contract and remains one of their most important players, so a January deal would likely require a significant offer. Forest are also unlikely to strengthen a Premier League rival without being well compensated.

But Spurs’ continued interest suggests they still see him as a long-term fit.

If Forest’s season continues to disappoint and Gibbs-White becomes open to leaving, Tottenham should be in a strong position to move quickly.

#1398. Chelsea 2-0 Manchester United PLAYER RATINGS: Who was 'sloppy' in possession? Which £70m star 'came up short'? And who is 'coming of age'?

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER

Published: 10:56 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 10:57 EDT, 31 October 2026

Things continue to go from bad to worse for Michael Carrick as his prospects of holding on to his position as Manchester United manager took another dent following this 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

United were the better team for 45 minutes but wasted their opportunities and were made to pay for it in the second half when Morgan Rogers fired Chelsea ahead.

From there, United capitulated, not helped by the ridiculous decision-making of Lisandro Martinez, who launched an elbow at Wesley Fofana on a corner, conceding a penalty and picking up a red card.

Cole Palmer scored that penalty and United never looked capable of getting back into the game as fans turned on the Argentine defender.

For Chelsea, this was the win they craved following a week in which they lost to Tottenham Hotspur in the Premier League and Liverpool on penalties in the Carabao Cup.

Daily Mail Sport's KIERAN GILL and CHRIS WHEELER were in position at Stamford Bridge to run the rule over both sides...

Morgan Rogers (left) and Cole Palmer (right) both scored to pile misery on Manchester United

Michael Carrick had his head in his hands as his side unravelled before going down to 10 men

Earned his first Premier League clean sheet as a starter. Denied Amad twice, including after one of Wesley Fofana's errors. Saved by the offside flag when Matheus Cunha scored at a corner, and tipped Bryan Mbeumo's rocket on to the crossbar.

Much-needed sliding challenge to stop Cunha from tapping in and a block to deny Bruno Fernandes amid other tidying up. The Cobham graduate was Chelsea's best defender here. He's coming of age.

Chelsea won, but we cannot pretend Fofana did not endure a shocker of a first half. Manchester United should have scored from at least one of his mistakes. But Fofana at least won his team a penalty when Martinez clattered into him at a corner.

Needed to attack crosses as United grew into the game in the build-up to half-time. A much easier – or enjoyable even – afternoon when the visitors dropped down to 10 men.

Had to fly forward down the left wing so that Morgan Rogers could drift inside. Got some mistakes out of his system in what was his first competitive start. A much more comfortable second half.

Marco Palestra struggled early on but managed to get mistakes out of his game as he settled

Replaced the unwell Jordan Henderson. Created Chelsea's opening goal as he brilliantly won the ball in midfield and gave it to Morgan Rogers. Regularly read passes before they happened. My star performer here overall. Back-to-back full 90s for him now.

Rarely is Caicedo upstaged by another midfielder, but even he knew his partner here was performing at an even higher level than him. A second-half showing full of control from Chelsea.

Chelsea fans demanded him. Xabi Alonso delivered him. Had two goals disallowed for offside on his first Premier League start of the season. Even hugged Alonso after he thought he had made it 3-0. Only for VAR to decide his shoulder had strayed offside. Such a positive performance.

Had hardly been in the game in an attacking sense when Chelsea were awarded a penalty, which he scored for 2-0. Would have tapped in another were it not for good defending from Harry Maguire.

Could not believe his luck as United's defence parted like the Red Sea to allow him through. He kept running and running and then chipped Lammens for 1-0. A lovely goal.

Rogers was a real livewire and couldn't believe United's defending as he went clear to score

Shot parried by Senne Lammens led to Estevao's offside tap-in. Had a good chance before half-time after winning the ball from Maguire but the angle was too tight for him to find the finish. Tried his best as a false nine.

The first half was poor, but he stood by his selection at the break, and Chelsea wound up winning comfortably. Good on him for finally using Estevao.

Eased back from injury by coming on with Chelsea leading 2-0.

Had no chance with Rogers' opener and Palmer's penalty. Got lucky when Caicedo hit the post in the first half, but did his best to keep United in the game and made a superb late save from Estevao.

Did well against Rogers in the first half but less so in the second as Chelsea's front line began to run United ragged. He wasn't alone in that respect.

Leny Yoro (right) started well and looked a bright spot but he faded as the game got away

Gave Rogers the freedom of Stamford Bridge to score the first goal. He had been solid up until then, apart from a slip that almost let in Neto, and got forward well at set-pieces.

Let his team down with a stupid challenge on Fofana at a corner shortly after being booked. Red card and penalty killed United's chances. A player of his experience should know better.

Continues to fill in at left-back and it's no easy task, especially when you are up against a winger like Estevao. Another player who did well up to half-time and suffered after that.

Crucially lost out in the 50-50 that led to Chelsea's opener. United paid £70m for Baleba to make a difference in those moments and he came up short. Substituted shortly afterwards.

United's other new defensive midfielder showed why he was never a first-choice at Chelsea. Powerless to stop the game turning in his old team's favour when they came on strong after the interval.

Andrey Santos (left) was powerless to stop Chelsea taking control of Saturday's early kick-off

How different might this game and result been if Amad had taken his chances? Could have had a hat-trick in the first half alone. By far United's liveliest player but finishing let him down.

The captain was back in the team after being dropped, and back in the No 10 role. Sadly, still not back to his best though. Too sloppy in possession and missed a great chance in the first half.

Another player recalled by Carrick. A handful on the left and when he alternated with Fernandes at No 10. Wanted to get on the ball and had a goal ruled out for a marginal offside, but faded after half-time.

Inches away from giving United a lifeline when he hit the underside of the bar in added time. Had more impact in the first half when he produced arguably the pass of the match to set up Fernandes.

These were the marginal games Carrick was winning last season. It was an improved performance from United but missed chances cost Carrick the game and may soon cost him his job.

#1397. Picture: Furious Inter ultras slam players after derby defeat

Inter ultras put up a banner after a 3-1 loss against Milan, criticising the players’ attitude during and after the game: ‘A derby lost without even playing. Not even the guts to say goodbye.’

Inter lost their first Serie A game of the season on Saturday, falling 3-1 to city rivals Milan.

Although it was only Inter’s first Serie A defeat in 2026-27, their ultras didn’t like the team’s attitude or that the players left the pitch without waving to the supporters in Curva Nord.

Lazio’s Sunday victory means Inter now sit second in the Serie A table, three points behind the Biancocelesti.

Poche parole, ma sufficienti a raccontare il malcontento di una parte della tifoseria nerazzurra. Nel mirino non c’è soltanto il risultato, ma soprattutto l’atteggiamento mostrato dalla squadra e quanto accaduto al termine della partita.

Manchester United are reportedly weighing up whether to sell Bruno Fernandes next summer rather than risk losing their captain for nothing when his current contract expires.

Fernandes is tied to Old Trafford until June 2027, although United retain an option to extend that deal by another 12 months.

That clause gives the club an important safety net and could become central to how they handle one of the biggest decisions of their 2027 transfer planning.

According to the Daily Mail, United are considering whether to negotiate fresh terms, trigger the one-year extension or cash in on Fernandes before his value drops further.

A report relaying the Mail’s latest information states that United are not prepared to overpay to keep the 32-year-old and could ultimately decide a sale makes more financial sense.

That would represent a significant shift from the summer, when United were publicly insisting Fernandes was not for sale. Talks over a new contract had also begun, but no agreement has been reached.

Recent report has suggested United are seriously considering activating the extra year in Fernandes’ contract specifically to protect his transfer value before potentially selling him in summer 2027.

Man United cannot afford to mishandle this situation.

Fernandes remains one of their most influential players, and Michael Carrick publicly reaffirmed only days ago that the captain is still fully committed despite their recent disagreement.

But sentiment cannot override basic squad planning. If United genuinely believe Fernandes could leave in 2027, allowing him to walk away for free would be poor business. Activating the extension would immediately strengthen their negotiating position and give them more control over the process.

There is already outside interest, with Atlético Madrid, AC Milan, Juventus and Galatasaray among the clubs previously linked.

The bigger question is whether United should sell at all.

Fernandes still creates more than almost anyone else in the squad, and replacing that influence would be expensive. But at 32, with the club considering another rebuild, this may be the last realistic opportunity to generate a meaningful fee.

Triggering the option first, then reassessing next summer, looks like the safest route.

#1395. Lethal Trent Alexander-Arnold sends Tuchel a statement in England victory

Thomas Tuchel has never been inclined to place much faith in the most famous right-back at his disposal, Trent Alexander-Arnold, once of Liverpool, now of Real Madrid, and – back in an England shirt – still capable of changing games in the blink of an eye.

England always looked likely to defeat a beleaguered Czech Republic team down to 10 men with just 25 minutes played, but it still required one man to conjure the moment of inspiration in this Nations League tie. This was the first cap in 15 months for the right-back now known simply as “Trent” in an England shirt – as well as his Real Madrid jersey – rather than the six syllables of his surname. With the game level at half-time, two minutes into the new half, he twice won the ball before landing a cross on the head of Anthony Gordon for the first goal.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3 goals in his last 3 games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/xmqPIULJ24

Will the Alexander-Arnold with England experiment survive? One feels that Tuchel will need a little more to convince him to abandon whatever reservations he has about the Liverpudlian. A week short of his 28th birthday, Alexander-Arnold was winning just his 35th cap. His Real Madrid team-mate Jude Bellingham, a second-half substitute, was earning his 58th cap less than two months after his 23rd birthday. Bellingham was on as captain in place of the man he replaced, Harry Kane, scorer of England’s second. Bellingham’s international career has taken a much less rocky path than that of his Real team-mate.

Having missed the World Cup finals this summer, and had little good fortune around previous tournaments, one wonders if Euro 2028 might be the watershed moment for Alexander-Arnold. Either way, against opponents who sit back, he is lethal when it is time for the big delivery. Alexander-Arnold may not have the breadth of England experience that some of his peers have accumulated, but he does have plenty of experience of big games.

“I make that run time and time again,” Gordon said of his anticipation of the Alexander-Arnold cross, “but only a set number of players have that ability, that technique and the bravery to risk a mistake to play that pass. And that’s why I have been dying to play with him [Alexander-Arnold]. He’s been on his own journey but has trained really well this week. He should have played more. Sorry – he would have loved to have played more.”

A Freudian slip from the Barcelona winger, another Liverpudlian in Spain, who himself has barely put a foot wrong for England of late. He has three goals in three games for England, including the World Cup semi-final against Argentina. This was an England team that Tuchel fine-tuned, first to give a rest to Bellingham and in other quarters, too. Lewis Hall started at left-back. Trevoh Chalobah won his third England cap at centre-back. Alex Scott, of Bournemouth, was given his debut off the bench in the second half and Rio Ngumoha won the second cap of his England career, just one month after his 18th birthday.

As for Kane, his 87th goal for England now puts him within two goals of Robert Lewandowski, among four greats in the seven ahead of Kane on the all-time international goalscorers’ list. By the end of this international break the England captain should have equalled Peter Shilton’s record 125 caps. It has been an astonishing career even if it ends tomorrow. Following the missed penalty against Spain, Kane was again the man in the right place at the right time when Morgan Rogers’s shot was blocked in the second half.

“Strange to get an early red card,” Tuchel said. “Not the best for the team and spectators. It’s an awkward one, but we kept going, got a win and that’s what counts.” Not quite a vintage Czech Republic team, either, and when their best player of the opening stages, the attacking midfielder Pavel Sulc, of Lyon in Ligue 1, was dismissed after 25 minutes, it certainly did not become any easier for the home team. Sulc, the Czech player of the year in 2025, had mistimed a tackle on Elliot Anderson, which on a VAR review, the Turkish referee Umut Meler decided was worthy of an upgrade from yellow to red. It was high on the right calf of the England midfielder.

Czech Republic DOWN TO 10 MEN! 🟥Pavel Šulc sees red for a dangerous challenge on Elliot Anderson#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/B2YOLuS0vL

England had looked once more a little open to the counter-attack in the early stages, with Sulc one notable runner. This was not an opponent of the quality of Spain and Tuchel’s players were able to recover the situation. When they lose the ball in the opposition’s half, England tend to look vulnerable.

Even before the red card Rogers had hit a post. Myles Lewis-Skelly, playing in midfield, was booked for a foul on Lukas Serv and was pursued thereafter by the Czech players hoping to get an upgrade on the yellow card. He was substituted at half-time, with Eberechi Eze on in his place.

“I spoke to Ant [Gordon] at half-time,” Alexander-Arnold said later to ITV, “and I said if I’m getting in those spaces make sure you get to the back post. You don’t expect to get it that fast, but it did and it worked.”

Two minutes after the break, Alexander-Arnold suddenly burst into life. He won the ball back in his own area and then drove forward in search of the return. When that did not come, he raced back to win the ball again and unleashed one of those right-footed outswingers to the back post, where Gordon guided in the header. “Really proud to score that,” Gordon said, “because I can’t tell you the number of hours I’ve spent practising headers.”

Kane scored the second just a minute before he was replaced and Bellingham took the captain’s armband and the role as a No 9. One day someone will have to step into those goalscorer’s boots on a permanent basis and try to replace Kane – although it may be a while yet.

Thomas Tuchel has backed Jude Bellingham as a future England captain after giving him the armband in the victory over the Czech Republic.

In the absence of Declan Rice, who was vice-captain at the World Cup, Bellingham assumed the role when he came on for Harry Kane, who is now in his 10th season as England captain and also scored in the 2-0 win in Prague.

Tuchel, who needs to check on Bellingham ahead of Saturday’s game against Croatia after a “niggle,” has praised the midfielder’s attitude during the extended international break one year after he was back from an injury but left out of the squad.

“If you are the captain at the end of these matches, you can be the permanent captain,” Tuchel said when asked whether Bellingham could eventually lead the team. “He was the captain against New Zealand before the World Cup. It is always a reward and always an honour.

“I think he loves to be with us at the moment. That’s what I feel, and we had this small talk today about his role. We felt in our hearts or our stomachs to say ‘let’s go again, let’s start again’ and also our heads told us maybe 30 minutes is enough for this match because he hasn’t played in this quick turnaround through this season. He has done it before, but not in the season, so we didn’t want to be the first ones to try that.

“But even in this little encounter, you can see that he’s confident and happy to help from the bench. So it’s a reward. It’s good. He had a little niggle at the end of the match, so hopefully it’s nothing serious, and he’s available for Croatia.”

Nico O’Reilly is a doubt for the Croatia match in Rijeka and there are also concerns over Ezri Konsa, who was on the bench but not fit enough to play.

Trent Alexander-Arnold provided an assist for Anthony Gordon in the Real Madrid full-back’s first cap in 15 months. Gordon, meanwhile, has now scored in the first two Nations League games of the campaign and is staking his case to be an indispensable player for Tuchel.

“He’s getting there. He’s defending his shirt, he’s defending his position, an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain,” Tuchel said.

“He was very decisive today and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult, but the technique and finishing was excellent. He scored against Spain, so he has decisive actions and he’s defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he’s a very important player.”

England returned to winning ways with a 2-0 win over Czech Republic in Prague.

Pavel Sulc’s first-half red card after a VAR review of his clumsy challenge on Elliot Anderson took the sting out of the initially lively hosts and Anthony Gordon gave Thomas Tuchel’s men a deserved lead early in the second half.

The forward headed home a fantastic cross by Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start under the German coach, before skipper Harry Kane scored to settle any nerves.

So who played well for England and who failed to impress? Rate each player with our voting tool, and have your say in the comments.

I thought we were very professional second half. We stepped up and needed to be more dynamic, bring more urgency into our play, which we did. We kept that intensity going and and the effort was till there. Deserved victory.

Strange to get an early red card. Not the best for the spectators, not the best for the team. It’s an awkward one. But we got the win.

To guide it into the goal, there was an awful lot [for Anthony Gordon] to do. Good pass, good goal. Both full-backs were good. The position in the second half suited Trent more than the position in the first half. Lewis was excellent on the other side.

We have used all the outfield players after two matches so credit to all of them. Now it’s important to relax and enjoy the evening, do a good recovery and prepare for Saturday.

I think it was good. They go down to 10 men and it should be easier for us to win the game, But in fact it makes it more difficult. They get very compact and defend with a lot of players around the box and it’s hard to break them down.

We got that [goal] at the start of the second half which is what we needed. The longer it’s 0-0, it gets harder and harder and harder.

[Where do you place your assist?]  It’s up there for sure. I spoke to Ant at half-time and said if I get into those half-spaces I’m looking to put it in so make sure you get to the back post. I didn’t expect it to work so quickly.

He’s a willing runner, great to play with him. I saw the run and was able to execute the pass,

The Professional Footballers’ Association has leapt to Cole Palmer’s defence following his withdrawal from the England squad.

The union’s CEO,  Maheta Molango, said the Chelsea forward is a victim of a “sick” system that is demanding too much from players physically.

“When England see five players who need to withdraw when the single most proud moment a player has is to be called up for the national team, you just ask yourself, what’s wrong about the industry?” Molango said at the Fifpro performance summit in London.

“You see people like Cole Palmer, someone who would have played four consecutive summers in a row had he gone to the World Cup, and you wonder why is he missing?”He’s missing because he’s a victim of the calendar and that’s something that needs to absolutely trigger the alarm bells.”
