#1374. Ryan Gravenberch Fighting for Liverpool Future After Iraola Decision vs Arsenal

Liverpool turned in a strong performance at Anfield but fell to a second defeat of the season against Premier League champions Arsenal on Sunday afternoon.

The Reds fell behind early to a Kai Havertz goal, but then created a number of chances and failed to trouble goalkeeper David Raya, as the Gunners held on for their first win on Merseyside in 14 years without conceding a single shot on target in the 90 minutes.

But the feeling after the game wasn't one of such big disappointment for many fans, as they were proud of the performance and they acknowledged that Arsenal are just at a higher level at this stage of their team building.

However, there was one decision by Andoni Iraola that took plenty of people by surprise ahead of the game, as the manager opted to name youngster Trey Nyoni in the starting lineup for the huge game.

It was his full Premier League debut, and the central midfielder turned in a very strong performance against top-level opposition to prove his manager correct, and show everyone that he is more than ready to play a big part in the first team.

He started alongside Alexis Mac Allister, offering protection and quality on the ball behind Florian Wirtz, and last season's player of the year Dominik Szoboszlai eventually replaced him after around an hour, with the team chasing an equaliser and the manager looking to inject a bit more experience into the side.

But it was evident during the game that when that substitution was made, Liverpool lost more control of the midfield area and it allowed Arsenal to get a footing on the game a little bit more, and eventually ride out their winning position until full-time.

Even more intriguing was the fact that during the game, Iraola didn't once look towards Ryan Gravenberch to enter the pitch and provide his attributes, and it's very possible that the boss feels the team is better without the Netherlands man being involved.

Gravenberch has been a regular at Anfield since joining from Bayern Munich, and was recently rewarded for his form in the last 12 months with a new contract worth £280,000-a-week, tying him to the club until 2032.

There's no doubting his qualities as a footballer, but this season he has struggled under Iraola and in the new system. He has consistently underperformed when given the chance to play, the structure of the team suffers when he's in the midfield, and he has been making a lot of individual errors, including giving away a penalty in the EFL Cup clash with Chelsea last week.

It now seems as though he is a fourth-choice midfielder in the squad, and there is talk that the club are keen to add another midfielder to their ranks in January. GIVEMESPORT sources understand that AS Monaco star Lamine Camara is a target, while Bournemouth's Alex Scott is also someone being looked at, although Chelsea lead the race for him.

But should someone else join, and Iraola continue to choose Nyoni ahead of him, then it's very possible that Gravenberch's time at Anfield is closer to the end than ever before.

Liverpool failed to register a shot on target against Arsenal on Sunday evening, and Florian Wirtz isn't the only Reds player who deserves criticism.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#1373. Buoyant Bairns are a different beast this year after summer rebuild... and that spells bad news for Celtic

Published: 15:07 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 15:14 EDT, 31 October 2026

Was there ever any doubt that Falkirk would eventually get over their sticky start to the season and begin making their way up the Premiership table?

Well yes, actually. Quite a lot of it, in fact.

A mass exodus over the summer saw 17 depart, including a host of key players who helped the side upset the odds last season by making the top six.

Barney Stewart and Calvin Miller left for West Bromwich Albion and Hearts respectively – both bringing in a tidy profit for the club in the process – with Dylan Tait making the move to Premiership rivals Dundee United and Ben Broggio going back to Aston Villa after an impressive loan spell north of the border.

The excellent defensive pair of Filip Lissah and Kyrell Wilson also returned to parent club Swansea, with the former now an automatic starter for the promotion-chasers while the latter is plying his trade in the Belgian top flight with Gent.

Replacing that lot was rightly viewed by most as a near-impossible task. Top six? Forget it.

And results over the first couple of months suggested that survival might have to be the main priority for this year.

Falkirk striker Jacob Murrell has scored four goals in his last five Premiership games

But as we enter November, it appears as though those fears were unfounded. We should have known better than to doubt Falkirk at all.

It’s taken a while – certainly longer than manager John McGlynn would have liked – but his new-look squad are finally starting to find their feet.

Winning three on the bounce in the Premiership is no small feat. Indeed, for all the plaudits Falkirk rightly earned on their march to the top half last season, that was something they failed to achieve.

And the most encouraging aspect of this mini-run is that they’ve managed to do it in a very un-Falkirk way.

Motherwell aside, Falkirk were the most entertaining side to watch in the top flight last term, just as they were as they swept away the opposition in League One and the Championship on their incredible journey up the divisions.

It’s not necessarily for a lack of trying, but the free-flowing style which has been the blueprint for so much of their success in recent times has been all but abandoned over the past fortnight.

Aside from two moments of real quality from striker Jacob Murrell at Easter Road, the three points were largely earned thanks to a gritty, dig-your-heels-in kind of performance.

Murrell and fellow American CJ Fodrey have been taken into the hearts of Bairns fans

The 3-0 victory against Kilmarnock the following week was fairly comfortable in terms of the scoreline. But the hoolie provided by Storm Boelo rendered that affair a war of attrition rather than a game of football.

And then up at Pittodrie midweek, McGlynn himself admitted that the display was one to be endured rather than enjoyed.

That his side have collected nine points from nine in their last three outings despite being miles off their top level bodes well going forward. Not chucking in late goals has certainly helped spark this upturn in fortunes too.

Dundee United, St Johnstone and Dundee have all taken points off the Bairns this season with virtually the last kick of the ball. They could be five points better off at this stage had they managed to hold out. All ifs and buts, of course.

Yet, at the moment, they don’t even look like conceding. From back to front, the team is gelling together nicely.

Winning with a swagger is all good and well, and that will always be the aim for as long as McGlynn is at the helm. But we’re now seeing a side demonstrating they are every bit as capable of doing it the ugly way if required.

In some ways, the manager might take greater satisfaction in that, at least in the short term.

McGlynn, of course, deserves the bulk of the credit for turning things around. He has completely rebuilt this squad without complaint. The nature of the job and all that.

John McGlynn has once again proven himself a master in the art of squad rebuilding

And, in that regard, he has put several others with significantly bigger budgets to shame. Not that he has ever needed a particularly big budget to succeed anyway.

His eye for a player remains razor sharp. Nineteen-year-old Owen Eames isn’t realistically going to produce anything like the numbers supplied by his predecessor Miller – few could. But the Derby County loanee has taken no time at all to settle into this team. He’s getting better with each passing week.

The same can be said of the chap playing in front of him. Murrell has come a long way from missing two absolute sitters against Rangers on his home debut back in September, scoring five in his seven appearances since.

The American was never remotely prolific throughout his time with DC United in the MLS. In truth, there was little on his CV that would suggest he would be able to cut it. But fair play to him – and the Falkirk scouting team for that matter – for proving the rest of us wrong.

Murrell will no doubt be rubbing his hands at the prospect of going up against a Celtic defence which has been a doddle to get at all season long.

He is playing with the confidence of a guy who only needs one chance to find the back of the net. Against this opposition – top of the table or not – he may well get a few opportunities.

Falkirk have lost their last ten against Sunday’s visitors. However, considering the way they’re playing, this should be viewed as a genuine opportunity to halt that horrid sequence.

#1372. Carrick Ready to Unleash Unseen Man Utd Partnership vs Roma to Save His Job

Manchester United are in crisis, and they will be welcoming AS Roma to Old Trafford on Tuesday night in the Champions League while trying to turn things around.

The Reds fell 2-0 to Chelsea on Saturday afternoon at Stamford Bridge, bringing their winless run to nine games in all competitions and leaving them with just two wins in 13 this season. But INEOS have made the decision to stick by Carrick despite the poor performances and results, with the belief that he can turn things around.

It's understood that the situation will be reviewed during the next international break, which will take place after the weekend clash against Aston Villa on Sunday, which gives Carrick two games to find more results and potentially save his job.

What's clear is that the manager must try new things to get new results, because what he has been doing over the last two months simply hasn't been good enough.

Against Chelsea, Carrick made the decision to leave Youri Tielemans out of the side for the first time since taking over, and the performance was good in the first half especially, with the performance crumbling following Lisandro Martinez's red card at 1-0 down.

But the manager was able to welcome Kobbie Mainoo back into the fold as a substitute after missing several games with a muscle injury, and that will be a major boost to the manager and the team going forward.

After a big splurge in the transfer market during the summer, Carrick is yet to have had all of his midfield options available to him at the same time. That changes against Roma, and it means there is a chance for him to finally name his top two options alongside each other.

Tielemans has struggled with a lack of athleticism, and covering ground is a major part of the problem United have had. Andrey Santos has been good in recent games too, but defeats have been a regular occurrence, and he doesn't quite have the ability on the ball to be a help going forward.

Baleba and Mainoo offer the perfect balance of athleticism, duel winning, quality on the ball, and ability to carry the ball forward into space, and Carrick will surely now unleash the pair for their first minutes together in what is arguably the biggest and most important game of his reign.

Carrick made it abundantly clear during his interim spell in charge that the midfield was hugely important to how he wanted to play. He wants to control possession, pin the opposition in their own half, and work openings. That hasn't happened this year.

But with a pairing of Baleba and Mainoo, we could finally start to see the image of the manager come to fruition. Roma like to play a similar way, and winning the midfield battle against Manu Kone and Bryan Cristante will be the key to coming out on top.

The attack against Chelsea was dangerous but wasteful, and he has the options in Shea Lacey and Joshua Zirkzee to potentially change things if he wishes. Considering we're now in November, though, it's mad to think that United haven't been able to name their best midfield in a team together at any stage.

That will surely change against Roma, and it could be the kickstart this team needs to be able to finally pick up a victory and turn their season around, and save Carrick's job in the process.

Manchester United should be somewhat optimistic about how they performed for long periods against Chelsea.

#1371. Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first

The 125th cap was no different to the first for Harry Kane, who has now been in the business of goal accumulation for so long that it is only at the landmark moments, that all of us are obliged to step back and take in the full scale of the work he has created.

Peter Shilton took 20 years to rack up his 125 caps, while for Kane it has been just 11 – and then there are the goals. Two more on Tuesday took him to 91 which means that only 12 other England players in history have more England caps than Kane has England goals. This unassuming man from Chingford, who looks like a mildly rebellious academic from the late 1950s, was at it again: the first-time strike, the back-post header. He has some misses across these 11 years, most infamously from the penalty spot against France at the Qatar World Cup almost four years ago, so, yes, there are some regrets too. But what sticks is the way he has taken his chances – again and again.

ONE-TOUCH BRILLIANCE! ✨ Anderson, Rogers and Kane combine beautifully to double England's lead 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Cap No. 125, goal No. 90 for the skipper 👏 https://t.co/otMcxlXyps

Following his debut goal in 2015 against Lithuania, Kane has missed just 27 of the 152 England games since. He has added to the total like a great Test batsman patiently moving the scoreboard along. There was a bad run without goals in 2020 and before that in 2018. He scored only five in his first 17 caps and then scored 14 in his next 10. Against a very mediocre Czech Republic team this was classic late-era Kane, picking his moments and taking those chances with the usual absence of nerves. He was even substituted before the end.

Hall ➡️ Kane! The Newcastle fullback swings in the corner and it's the England captain who rises highest to head home 💥 https://t.co/5EhAcNZUqm

Afterwards at a Wembley press conference to mark the occasion, he invoked the cricket analogy himself on the question of scoring 100 England goals. “Being in the 90s, I try not to think about it too much, and it’s like I guess being a cricketer in the 90s. The more you think about the hundred… you don’t always get there.” There has still not been the elusive major trophy in the Kane England years but there has been success relative to the three decades that came before it. Semi-finals, finals – a good team if not a winning team.

At the centre of it has been a man around whom there has never been any scandal or, by the usual measure, much that might be described as spectacular. Rather it has been the scope of Kane’s career that is the most striking. The volume of the goals, of appearances, the capacity to be available – to play, to score – and the absolute quality of the player himself. He is determined to wring the very last drop out of his talent and usually refuses to acknowledge the prospect of the end, although there was a nod to it this time. “At some stage you know this opportunity isn’t going to be here,” he said. “I’m not going to be around forever, and I still hope that’s a long way away. But ultimately, of course, there’s times you’re tired or you’re injured, but I know I’ll miss it when it’s done. I try to always remind myself that and always try to make myself available.”

One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

England lead! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿⚽️ A great ball from Kane and a great finish from Coufal - unfortunately for the defender, it's in the wrong net...🫣 https://t.co/h54xQnunZM

The second goal, on 40 minutes, was one for the ages. Anderson’s ball out to the right was met first time by Rogers for the cross and Kane ran into the space, as he has done so many times, to deliver a finish struck with customary assuredness. Bellingham almost flicked in Rogers’s cross on 56 minutes and from the corner that came after, Kane nodded in a header at the back post from Lewis Hall’s cross. All said, the defending was woeful but there was nothing wrong with the finish.

Thomas Tuchel believes England have taken a step forward from their World Cup heartbreak over this international break and said he was “honoured” to hear fans sing his name.

England finished their four Nations League games with a 3-0 win over Czech Republic, in which Harry Kane scored twice on his record-equalling 125th appearance.

It meant that Tuchel’s team have won three and lost one, against Spain, of their four games since the World Cup, after which the England head coach was heavily criticised for the semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Tuchel seems to have won the forgiveness of some England supporters, who sang his name at the start and the end of Tuesday’s game.

“It means a lot,” Tuchel said. “It’s amazing to have a song. It’s the biggest honour. And I’m very happy and very honoured. They can be sure that I will give my absolute best to make our team win and play well.”

Asked if he sensed a change in mood around his England team since the fall-out from the World Cup, Tuchel said: “I do and I think it’s necessary to move on. I think I can only repeat that we didn’t go out in the group stage. Sometimes it feels like that and we didn’t. As I said, our aim was always to progress, move forward and improve.”

Tuchel snapped back at a reporter who questioned why he felt it necessary to repeat that England had not gone out in the group stage of the World Cup, claiming the criticism had felt a “little bit” too harsh.

But on whether England have shown they are a step ahead of where the team were at the World Cup during this international camp, Tuchel was far more positive and replied: “Of course and that’s what we have to do. That is our goal to constantly improve and develop.

“We had these experiences together and we had a big tournament together, and it was very positive. It’s necessary to move forward and improve, especially in sports. This is what we’re trying to do.

“We adjusted some details in our structure and we didn’t compromise on the effort and the intensity, and on the togetherness of the team. The players who were with us in the World Cup took care of these standards and of the culture within the team, off the pitch and on the pitch, and I think that’s what you could see.”

We played a very good match, very fluid and to put it into context it was the fourth match in 11 or 12 days. We dominated the whole match, had some good opportunities, scored some beautiful goals. Subs were strong. Very good performance again.

[Leading the way, Mr Kane] Of course. That’s what he does. I don’t take it for granted. It’s just exceptional, every single match. It’s just difficult to find new words to express it.

Training, attitude, cohesion, belief, of course [is why they’re stronger than ever].

[Has the World Cup made England stronger?]  Of course, we got the first medal in 60 years. We didn’t go out in the group stage. We had a strong qualification, strong World Cup and strong camp. All four matches were on a high level. The camp throughout from the first day was on the highest level. You learn every day together. We grew stronger.

I was happy that everyone who was in the camp was contributing. Everyone was on the pitch. Everyone showed he was willing to give everything for the team and for the shirt. The guys who were with us for the World Cup set the standards high, made everyone feel welcome and everyone had a good camp.

He’s the best England player evert to wear the shirt and it’s an honour to play with him. And he’s only getting better.

A perfect night for me personally and also for the team. It’s been a tough camp, a long camp with some difficult games so it’s nice to finish it off all together. An extremely proud evening for me.

You saw some fantastic football out there tonight. The way we’re moving, the one-touch stuff, a fantastic ball from Elliot to Morgan and then a first time cross which was as good as it gets. As a striker you’re just waiting for those opportunities.

It started in the first game [reaching a higher level] although the result didn’t go for us. First game after a tournament, obviously this was a four-game camp, we had to find it [a higher level] and find it quickly. That’s the most pleasing thing.

This is the England team. There’s always going to be competition for places. It’s about taking the opportunity whether it’s 90 minutes, five minutes, whatever it was, make the most of it. You’re seeing that, everyone wants to be part of this. That’s only going to make us better for sure.

[Now for cap 126 next month?] That would be nice for sure.

Because places between teams who finish on the same points in the first instance are decided on head-to-heads, Croatia will have to beat England 8-0 at Wembley next month to have any hope of stopping them from qualifying for the quarter-finals.

Secret to Harry Kane’s England longevity? ‘He strikes the ball better than Ronaldo’

Right foot, goal. Left foot, goal. Edge of the area, goal. Inside the area, goal. Under pressure, goal, Right foot, save. Left foot, goal. That was Harry Kane’s warm-up prior to England’s 7-0 demolition of Croatia and it underlined just why the striker will equal Peter Shilton’s appearance record on Tuesday night.

As demonstrated in Rijeka, Kane’s career has been a non-stop pursuit of excellence that has led him to the very top of the national game. England’s record goalscorer will also become the joint most-capped player with Shilton, when he makes his 125th appearance against the Czech Republic at Wembley on Tuesday night.

Eberechi Eze is set to start for England in the clash against Czech Republic tonight. The Arsenal forward is poised to come in for Anthony Gordon, who has started in the three matches during the Nations League international break. Trent Alexander-Arnold is also due to play at right-back, with Jarell Quansah moving to centre-back to cover for Ezri Konsa.

Alex Scott has been ruled out through injury, which has upset Bournemouth after he played in the win over Croatia at the weekend. Myles Lewis-Skelly is expected to get a recall to the team after playing against Czech Republic in Prague last week when England won 2-0. Morgan Rogers, who scored against Croatia, is in line to start in place of Bukayo Saka.

Probable England team: Pickford; Trent, Quansah, Guehi, Hall; Lewis-Skelly, Anderson; Rogers, Bellingham, Eze; Kane

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of England vs Czech Republic from Wembley in the fourth and mercifully final round of fixtures in this sprawling Nations League international break. Tonight Harry Kane will win his 125th cap and equal Peter Shilton for England appearances.

Shilton’s took him 20 years as Gordon Banks was simply too good in the couple of years following his debut and then a couple of managers, Don Revie and Ron Greenwood, preferred Ray Clemence until the latter finally plumped for Shilton as No 1 in 1979. Kane’s, by contrast, have taken him 11. In that time he has been rested for a handful of friendlies but has not been unused in a competitive match when fit since Gareth Southgate left him out of the 5-0 victory over Sam Marino in 2021’s World Cup qualifier when Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored two and Ollie Watkins one goal on his debut.

England played the Czech Republic a week ago, winning 2-0 in Prague by virtue of Anthony Gordon’s cute header and Kane’s clever shot through a defender’s legs but they huffed and puffed for ages against a team harshly reduced to 10 men until they blew the house down. They went on to marmalise Croatia 7-0 in their next game in front of a crowd that sounded like a cross between the choirs on Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2 and There’s No One Quite Like Grandma.

In the past England have had problems backing up their best performances – the 4-1 evisceration of the Dutch at Euro 96 was followed by the cagey display in the quarter-final against Spain before prevailing on penalties, the 5-1 victory in Munich in 2001 led to a drab 2-0 win against Albania at St James’ Park the following Tuesday, in 2016 they went to Berlin and beat world champions Germany but were thumped by Netherlands, who had not even qualified for Euro 2016, a couple of days later. Even their thrilling, second-half showing against Croatia in their World Cup opener in June preceded the dreary 0-0 draw with Ghana.

Given the attacking fluency in Rijeka, Thomas Tuchel must be tempted not to to ring the changes and replace seven or eight players. He will have to find replacements for the injured Alex Scott and Ezri Konsa, however, and Calvert Lewin, who has had seven minutes of action, Rio Ngumoha 19, Morgan Gibbs-White 27 and Jarrad Branthwaite one, may feel they deserve a fairer opportunity to show what they can do in a match.

#1370. Spalletti: ‘Juventus players deserve credit for victory, but we need fans by our side’

Luciano Spalletti said Juventus players ‘deserve all the credit’ for the 2-0 win over Napoli, but hits back at the boo boys. ‘We need our fans by our side, the real face of this stadium.’

The Bianconeri mood was dire going into this game, especially after the 2-0 defeat to relegation battlers Genoa on Wednesday evening.

Juan Cabal hit the woodwork, and Guglielmo Vicario needed a stunning early save on Lorenzo Lucca, but there were two moments of magic late on to seal the 2-0 victory.

Kerim Alajbegovic and Jeremie Boga hit screamers from outside the box, around a Luca Marianucci second bookable offence.

At the final whistle, the coach pulled his staff members into a massive embrace.

“They suffer along with me, they too work from morning till night, I am the first to arrive and the last to leave, but they are usually there with me for most of it,” Spalletti told DAZN Italia.

“However, the credit this evening must go to the team. They managed to dig into themselves and find that desire to take the first step, to go forward, think positive, and then they managed it in the second half with a few adjustments.

“I think tonight they fully deserved the victory, restoring some of the self-esteem in the football they can play.”

It was for long spells far from a convincing performance, but this result can be a massive confidence-booster going forward, so how did it come about?

“The most important speech was made by Carnevali, because they are not accustomed to hearing his voice, so that alone forced the players to prick up their ears, listen and absorb those words, as it was the first time he’d done that,” revealed Spalletti.

“All we can do is be by their side, but there are players who genuinely plunge into this spiral and lose confidence in everything they do, even the most normal things. When there’s a misplaced simple pass or hesitation in making a decision, which is worse than making the wrong decision, that lack of confidence gets transferred to the rest of the team.

“Napoli had started the match well, we hit back two or three times, but as the game wore on, the lads did really well in making the right choices, pushing forward, thinking positive and leaving space behind them that is hard to defend against. The players deserve all the credit this evening.”

There were some fresh concerns, as Weston McKennie went off at half-time with an adductor issue, while Alajbegovic was spotted on the bench with an ice pack strapped to his calf after the goal.

When Spalletti was asked if this Juventus side can be structured to win with the current group or if they need big investments in future, he was not impressed.

“I know the game you are playing, with the pressure to put on the other, to have an advantage. At this moment, we are not structured in anything, because tonight I had to take McKennie off, Sarr had a fever and couldn’t play, all the substitutions I made were forced ones, and we’ve got to play again on Thursday.”

Fans in the Allianz Stadium were shouting insults and calling for the team to show guts from the very first minute of tonight’s match with Napoli, with a protest outside the stadium before kick-off.

“We’ve just got to keep going. This is a moment we have to handle, then you can talk about what you want. Right now, we must be solid, along with a stadium whose real face is that of the second half, fighting alongside the team,” he added.

“You can say Spalletti’s no good, that player’s no good, get rid of everyone, but right now we need to be united, and this stadium must return to being our fortress. Even if we don’t make them that happy, we still need our fans by our side, so we thank all those today who applauded us and stayed with us.

“This is a moment where we need to hold hands and stand together, try to push forward and be positive, which isn’t easy when there are so few of us available. It was a victory deserved by the players, who deserve a big round of applause. Well done, lads.”

#1369. MLS 2027 Sprint Season: Key Details & Transition Explained

Major League Soccer is about to go through the biggest shake-up in its 31-year history. Historically, the league has always run on a calendar-year schedule, but from summer 2027, it will switch to the summer-to-spring calendar used by the Premier League, La Liga and most of the world's top leagues. To bridge the gap, the league is introducing something entirely new: the 2027 sprint season.

Had MLS kept its old system, teams would have gone up to seven months without a fixture, with nothing scheduled between December 2026 and July 2027. The new 'Sprint Season' fills that hole with a short, high-stakes mini-campaign that still carries a full MLS Cup and places in continental competitions.

The sprint season is a shortened, one-off season that serves as the bridge between the old calendar and the new one. It runs from February through May 2027, including the MLS Cup Playoffs and MLS Cup, before the new summer-to-spring calendar begins in July 2027.

Each club will play 14 regular-season matches, seven at home and seven away, playing just once against each of the other 14 teams in their conference. Once the regular season ends, the top eight teams in each conference will qualify for the 2027 MLS Cup Playoffs, from which, each conference plays a single-elimination bracket to find its champion. The champions from the Eastern and Western conferences will then meet in the MLS Cup final.

Importantly, all playoff games, including the MLS Cup itself, will be hosted by the team that finished higher in the final 2027 Supporters' Shield standings, meaning that with only 14 games, every point, goal and clean sheet could decide who plays at home in the May final.

Firstly, the current season, which started in February 2026, culminates with the MLS Cup final on 18th December 2026. The league will then take a break over the winter, before the sprint season starts in February 2027. The 14-match regular season will then run until April 2027, followed by the MLS Cup playoffs and final in May.

Following a short break, the 2027/28 season will kick off roughly eight weeks later, in mid-July 2027. This season will then see the league return to the 34-match campaign it currently uses whilst adhering to the new summer-to-spring calendar.

However, unlike most major European leagues, the MLS will take a slightly longer winter break, with games stopping mid-December, before resuming in February, meaning that no games will be played in January.

One of the most obvious upsides to the adjusted schedule is that the MLS off-season will now line up with most other major leagues, and more importantly, it will lineup with the summer transfer window. This means that teams no longer have to worry about disrupting a squad, in the heart of the season, with summer transfers, and instead allows teams to plan ahead of the new season. It also means that the MLS' schedule will line up with FIFA international windows and big summer tournaments such as the Copa América and the World Cup, whilst also giving the playoffs more prominence in global football.

MLS itself has said that the calendar shift does not change its commitment to national and international cup competitions. As usual, five MLS clubs will qualify for the 2028 Concacaf Champions Cup through the sprint season, with the 2027 MLS Cup winner, 2027 Supporters' Shield winner, the regular-season winner of whichever conference didn't produce the Shield winner, and the next two best clubs in the Supporters' Shield standings all earning a spot at the tournament.

The top nine clubs from each conference will earn qualification to the 2028 Leagues Cup, whilst the three Canadian MLS clubs will all still be able to compete in the 2028 Canadian Championship.

As for the US Open Cup, details are yet to be released regarding the 2028 tournament. However, for the 2027 edition, all 27 US-based MLS clubs will enter the competition in the Round of 64 in July, and will receive hosting priority for their opening match.

#1368. Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections.

Homeostatic synaptic plasticity can involve pre- or postsynaptic mechanisms. In response to a global change in activity, mammalian central neurons alter the expression of glutamate receptors1,5,6,7. By contrast, a presynaptic form of homeostasis occurs at the neuromuscular junction. First established in Drosophila melanogaster, this involves increased release of glutamate in response to reduced postsynaptic receptor function8,9. An effect of activity on neurotransmitter release has also been reported at central synapses10,11,12,13,14,15,16,17,18. Although previous work has identified several elements that are required for the different forms of homeostatic plasticity, the mechanisms involved remain poorly understood.

To determine the time course over which presynaptic homeostatic plasticity develops, we suppressed network activity by treating primary mouse hippocampal cultures, which contain almost entirely glutamatergic neurons (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b), with the glutamate receptor antagonists 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) and 3-(2-carboxypiperazin-4-yl)propyl-1-phosphonic acid (commonly known as APV). We monitored the consequent changes in transmitter release using a fusion of the strongly pH-sensitive GFP variant ecliptic pHluorin to a luminal loop of the vesicular glutamate transporter VGLUT1 (VGLUT1–pH). Quenched at the low pH of synaptic vesicles (SVs), the pHluorin-based reporter brightens on exposure to the higher external pH at exocytosis; the reacidification that accompanies endocytosis results in requenching. Figure 1a,b shows that silencing with CNQX and APV increases both the rate and the extent of VGLUT1+ SV exocytosis. The reacidification that accompanies endocytosis also slows (Fig. 1a,b), but stimulation in the presence of the v-type H+-ATPase inhibitor bafilomycin to block SV reacidification results in an increase in the proportion of VGLUT1+ SVs available for release, independent of any change in endocytosis16 (Fig. 1c). We detect no change in the punctate distribution of SVs or the active zone (Extended Data Fig. 1c). To assess the initial release probability, we monitored glutamate release at individual presynaptic boutons using the glutamate sensor iGluSnFR (ref. 19). Stimulating at a low frequency (0.2 Hz), we find that silencing the cultures increases the proportion of synapses that release glutamate (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1d). Because a change in release probability can reflect a change in the presynaptic Ca2+ entry that triggers release, we monitored presynaptic Ca2+ with the low-affinity Ca2+ dye Fluo5F. Figure 1e,f shows that silencing the cultures greatly increases the presynaptic Ca2+ response to both 5-Hz and 25-Hz stimulus trains. This large increase in Ca2+ entry might be expected to increase the release probability more than the doubling that was observed, but we used iGluSnFR only to indicate whether release occurred, and this binary measure underestimates the actual increase in release probability. In addition, stimulation at 1 Hz and 5 Hz triggers Ca2+ entry with near 100% reliability in all presynaptic boutons (Extended Data Fig. 2). Thus, silencing cannot increase the proportion of responsive boutons, excluding effects on action potential invasion of the nerve terminal. Ongoing neural activity thus seems to reduce glutamate release by suppressing presynaptic Ca2+ entry.

a, Wild-type (WT) hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH were treated with CNQX (10 μM) and APV (50 μM) for the times indicated and stimulated at 25 Hz for 20 s. The fluorescence response normalized to total fluorescence was revealed in 50 mM NH4Cl. b, Left, peak response and initial rate (first 4 s) of fluorescence increase. Right, time constant (τ) of endocytosis (0 h and 24 h, n = 20/3 (see end of legend for explanation of n numbers); 3 h, n = 14/3; 6 h and 48 h, n = 16/3). c, WT hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH were silenced for 24 h, stimulated at 25 Hz for 120 s in the presence of 100 nM bafilomycin A1 (Baf) and the response was normalized as above. Scatter plots show exocytosis rate and recycling pool size (control, n = 14/3; CNQX + APV, n = 16/3). d, WT hippocampal neurons expressing iGluSnFR–stargazin were silenced for 24 h and stimulated 30 times at 0.2 Hz to measure the release probability (Pr). Pr is shown as a cumulative frequency distribution and as a box-and-whisker plot, with centre line indicating the median, box bounds 25th−75th percentiles and whiskers minimum and maximum values (n = 12/3). e,f,h, WT hippocampal neurons silenced with CNQX + APV (e,f) or 1 μM TTX (h) for 24 h and loaded with Fluo5F were stimulated at 5 Hz for 5 s (e) (control, n = 16/3; CNQX + APV, n = 18/3) or stimulated repeatedly at 25 Hz for 5 s each, with 15 s between bursts and fluorescence normalized to baseline (f,h) (f, control, n = 14/3; CNQX + APV, n = 20/3; h, n = 10/2, both conditions). Scatter plots show the slope of fluorescence increase and the fluorescence at the end of the stimulus (g, control, n = 11/3; CNQX + APV, n = 10/3; i, n = 14/3, both conditions). Data are mean ± s.e.m.; n = x/y, where x indicates the fields examined and y the number of independent experiments. Significance by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (c–e), one-way (b) or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (f–i).

To determine whether activity can reverse the effects of silencing, we stimulated the neurons with repeated 25-Hz bursts. We find that two to three bursts reduces the Ca2+ entry in silenced neurons back to baseline, with no effect on presynaptic Ca2+ entry in unsilenced cultures (Fig. 1f). To assess the effects on release, we imaged VGLUT1–pH. Stimulation at 25 Hz also reverses the increased rate and extent of release due to silencing, with no effect on the unsilenced neurons (Fig. 1g). Thus, activity can acutely reverse the homeostatic increase in transmitter release. Stimulation reverses the effects of silencing despite the continued presence of glutamate receptor antagonists, indicating that the mechanism does not require the activation of postsynaptic receptors and is thus induced presynaptically. Silencing with tetrodotoxin (TTX) for 24 h similarly enhances presynaptic Ca2+ entry and transmitter release that reverses rapidly with repeated 25-Hz stimulation (in the absence of TTX) (Fig. 1h,i), supporting the role of neural activity, rather than being a phenomenon restricted to the inactivation of glutamate receptors.

To determine whether activity suppresses release in a more physiological preparation, we extended the analysis to Schaffer-collateral synapses in the stratum radiatum of CA1 hippocampus. We compared the effect of 100 action potentials (APs) delivered at either 5 Hz or 50 Hz (followed by a 20-s gap to allow some recovery) on the response to test stimulation at 5 Hz. With intervening stimulation at 5 Hz, the final stimulus train shows incomplete recovery of the first response but synaptic depression similar to that observed with the first train (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a), indicating that the properties of release have not changed. Despite delivering the same number of APs, intervening stimulation at 50 Hz increases facilitation and reduces subsequent synaptic depression (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). This suggests a reduction in the initial release probability that enables the accumulation of Ca2+ without depleting SVs20—a fundamental change in the properties of release.

We wanted to understand how high-frequency stimulation suppresses subsequent transmitter release. Previous work has shown that the heterotetrameric adaptor protein AP-3 produces a subset of SVs from endosomes21,22, distinct from the production of canonical SVs at the plasma membrane (or immediately after endocytosis) by clathrin and the related adaptor AP-2 (refs. 23,24,25). We previously found that loss of AP-3 impairs release specifically to stimulation at a high frequency3,4. Thus, we investigated whether loss of AP-3 impairs the suppression of release that follows high-frequency stimulation. Slices from mocha mice, which lack AP-3, show increased rather than reduced synaptic depression after 50-Hz stimulation (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3b). Consistent with the role of AP-3 in producing SVs that are responsive specifically to strong stimulation (that is, of low release probability), AP-3 is thus required for the suppression of release after high-frequency stimulation, and previous work has shown that loss of AP-3 has little effect on response to the 5-Hz test stimulation itself3.

The dependence on AP-3 predicted that a specific component of SVs made by this adaptor is responsible for the suppression of release after strong stimulation. Indeed, a small subset of SV proteins depend on AP-3 for targeting to SVs. These include the zinc transporter ZnT3 (ref. 26), the phospholipid flippase ATP8A1 (ref. 3) and the endolysosomal v-SNARE (vesicular soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) VAMP7 (refs. 27,28). Because a zinc transporter seemed to be more likely to influence postsynaptic glutamate receptors29 than to affect release, we focused on the two other proteins. Although enriched in mossy-fibre terminals, ATP8A1 and VAMP7 are highly expressed throughout the hippocampus, including in CA1 and CA3, and localize to SVs30 (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis indicates that both genes are expressed in CA3 pyramidal neurons31 (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Western blot analysis confirms the enrichment of both proteins in SVs from the stratum radiatum and stratum lacunosum-moleculare (Extended Data Fig. 4d). In hippocampal slices from Atp8a1-knockout (KO) mice, 50-Hz stimulation still reduces subsequent synaptic depression in the CA1 stratum radiatum (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3c). However, loss of VAMP7 (Vamp7 KO) increases synaptic depression, and 50-Hz stimulation does not alter the increased depression (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3d). Loss of VAMP7 thus seems to account for the role of AP-3 in the effect of high-frequency activity on subsequent release.

Differences in synaptic depression might result from differential recruitment of Schaffer-collateral input, but varying the stimulus intensity threefold does not affect the kinetics or the extent of short-term depression with 5-Hz stimulation (Extended Data Fig. 3e). The effect also persists under more physiological recording conditions (1.5 mM Ca2+, 1 mM Mg2+), which reduce the initial release probability but still allow 50-Hz stimulation to reduce the subsequent release probability in wild-type (WT) but not in Vamp7-KO slices (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f).

To assess the release probability directly, we took advantage of the use-dependent N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonist MK-801. Slices pre-incubated in MK-801 were subjected to a conditioning train at either 5 Hz or 50 Hz while the postsynaptic cell was held at −70 mV. Stimulating at 0.2 Hz to assess the ‘initial’ response, NMDAR-EPSCs were then recorded at +40 mV in the continued presence of MK-801. As shown in Fig. 2f, previous 50-Hz stimulation of WT slices slows MK-801 blockade to a greater extent than does previous stimulation at 5 Hz, whereas blockade by MK-801 in Vamp7-KO slices does not change with previous stimulation. Thus, high-frequency stimulation reduces the release probability, and loss of VAMP7 blocks this effect.

VAMP7 is widely expressed throughout the nervous system (Extended Data Fig. 5a). We thus examined three other facilitating synapses: perforant-path synapses formed by layer 2 and 3 neurons of the entorhinal cortex onto dentate granule cells; corticothalamic synapses made by cortical layer 6 pyramidal cells onto ventrobasal thalamic relay neurons; and cerebellar parallel-fibre synapses onto Purkinje cells. Similar to CA1 stratum radiatum, 50-Hz stimulation at each of these synapses reduces synaptic depression (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In addition, loss of VAMP7 increases synaptic depression and eliminates the effect of 50-Hz stimulation, supporting a general role for VAMP7 in neurotransmission. Loss of VAMP7 does not affect the presynaptic expression of canonical SNARE proteins in SVs, the punctate distribution of SVs or the active-zone protein Piccolo (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b), suggesting that VAMP7 has a specific effect on release.

If VAMP7 is required for suppression of release after high-frequency stimulation, it should also have a key role in the increase in release due to silencing. We thus used VGLUT1–pH to monitor SV exocytosis. In unsilenced cultures, loss of VAMP7 increases SV exocytosis relative to WT across a range of stimulation frequencies (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Although silencing with glutamate receptor antagonists increases release from WT neurons, silencing does not further increase release in Vamp7-KO neurons (Fig. 2g). Thus, the increased release observed in the absence of VAMP7 occludes the effect of silencing, suggesting that silencing inactivates VAMP7. Consistent with the hypothesis that VAMP7 has a role in the inhibition of release, overexpression of VAMP7 inhibits the exocytosis of VGLUT1–pH and VGLUT2–pH, particularly at a high frequency (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d).

We next investigated how VAMP7 suppresses release. In hippocampal slices, loss of VAMP7 impairs synaptic facilitation and increases depression with low-frequency stimulation (Fig. 3a,b and Extended Data Fig. 7a), consistent with the results in culture and suggesting an increased initial release probability. Mossy fibres in the hippocampus express high levels of VAMP7 (refs. 28,32), and a recent study33 has investigated the properties of mossy-fibre synapses in the absence of VAMP7. In contrast to our findings in CA1 stratum radiatum, this study found no change in the properties of transmitter release at mossy-fibre synapses33. This might reflect a difference between the two synapses, but the experiments were also performed at room temperature rather than at the 35 °C used here. We thus repeated the analysis of Schaffer-collateral synapses in CA1 stratum radiatum at room temperature, and found that the effect of Vamp7 KO on 5-Hz and 25-Hz stimulus trains disappears (Extended Data Fig. 7b). Vamp7 KO has no effect on the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) at room temperature, but at 34–35 °C it results in a clear reduction in the PPR, consistent with an increased release probability at this more physiological temperature34 (Extended Data Fig. 7c). At 34–35 °C, mossy-fibre synapses show modestly reduced facilitation in the absence of VAMP7 (Extended Data Fig. 7d), consistent with an increase in the release probability at this synapse as well as at Schaffer collaterals. Temperature thus accounts for the discrepant results, and VAMP7 has qualitatively similar effects at both Schaffer-collateral and mossy-fibre synapses.

The analysis of initial release probability after stimulation suggested that loss of VAMP7 increases the release probability (Fig. 2f). A direct comparison of WT and Vamp7-KO slices confirms this observation (Fig. 3c). Because the initial release probability mostly reflects Ca2+ entry, we varied the external Ca2+ concentration and found that 4 mM Ca2+ occludes the effect of Vamp7 KO on release by Schaffer collaterals (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with an increase in Ca2+ entry owing to the loss of VAMP7. To determine whether loss of VAMP7 affects Ca2+ at individual presynaptic boutons, we used the low-affinity Ca2+ indicator Fluo5F to monitor Ca2+ entry at the boutons of cultured hippocampal neurons labelled with the red-shifted styryl dye FM4-64 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Figure 3e shows that at all frequencies tested (1–50 Hz), cultured Vamp7-KO neurons exhibit higher evoked Ca2+ transients than do WT cells, and that the low-affinity Fluo5F does not saturate under these conditions (Extended Data Fig. 8b). At a high frequency, Vamp7-KO but not WT neurons progressively accumulate Ca2+, perhaps because an increased Ca2+ load overwhelms the mechanisms for Ca2+ clearance.

To determine whether the effect of VAMP7 on Ca2+ entry extends to other v-SNAREs, we used lentiviral transduction of the light chain of tetanus toxin (TeNT) to cleave the canonical SV SNARE VAMP2 (ref. 35). Despite complete cleavage of VAMP2 (Fig. 3f) and the resulting inhibition of release (Extended Data Fig. 8c), TeNT has no effect on the punctate localization of SV and active-zone proteins (Fig. 3g), and does not alter the presynaptic entry of Ca2+ at a wide range of stimulation frequencies in WT or Vamp7-KO neurons (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). Because TeNT also cleaves the related v-SNAREs VAMP1 and VAMP3 but not VAMP7 (ref. 36), the regulation of presynaptic Ca2+ entry by v-SNAREs seems to be unique to the non-canonical v-SNARE VAMP7.

VAMP7 localizes mainly to intracellular membranes, so we wondered how it could suppress presynaptic Ca2+ entry evoked by stimulation. Depolarization of the nerve terminal activates voltage-gated channels to allow Ca2+ entry, but release from intracellular stores might contribute37,38,39. To determine whether VAMP7 inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane, we took advantage of a mutation that blocks the endocytosis of VAMP2, trapping it at the cell surface40 (Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). Introducing the equivalent mutation (M140A) into VAMP7–pH disrupts its punctate localization at presynaptic boutons in hippocampal cultures (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 9c), greatly increases the surface fraction, as determined by quenching with cell-impermeant, low-pH buffer (Fig. 3j and Extended Data Fig. 9d), and eliminates the response of VAMP7–pH to stimulation at multiple frequencies (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 9e). VAMP7(M140A) thus localizes almost exclusively to the plasma membrane. In Vamp7-KO neurons, VAMP7(M140A) reduces presynaptic Ca2+ entry back to the level observed in WT neurons (Fig. 3l) and inhibits SV exocytosis to the same extent that WT VAMP7 does (Extended Data Fig. 9f). Thus, VAMP7 inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ entry at the plasma membrane.

The presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels that trigger transmitter release generally belong to the N and P/Q types41. To determine which type is inhibited by VAMP7, we took advantage of neurotoxins that block specific channel types. Figure 3m shows that ω-agatoxin IVA, which targets Cav2.1 (the P/Q/-type voltage-gated calcium channel), greatly reduces the increased presynaptic Ca2+ entry that is triggered at a wide range of stimulation frequencies in cultured Vamp7-KO neurons, including the progressive increase in Ca2+ that is observed with high-frequency stimulation. ω-Agatoxin also inhibits Ca2+ entry in WT neurons, but the extent of inhibition is greater in Vamp7-KO neurons. Consistent with this, previous work has shown that Ca2+ entry specifically through P/Q-type channels changes as a function of neural activity17. By contrast, the N-type Ca2+ channel inhibitor ω-conotoxin GVIA has a more modest effect that is similar in Vamp7-KO and in WT neurons (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 10a). The L-type Ca2+ channel inhibitor nimodipine and R-type inhibitor SNX-482 have little effect on presynaptic Ca2+ entry in WT neurons, and little effect in Vamp7-KO neurons stimulated at a low frequency (Extended Data Fig. 10b). However, nimodipine substantially reduces Ca2+ entry in Vamp7-KO neurons stimulated at 25 Hz (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Thus, VAMP7 inhibits P/Q-type Ca2+ channels at all frequencies and L-type channels at a high frequency. Because previous work has implicated intracellular Ca2+ stores in transmitter release42,43, we also depleted intracellular Ca2+ using the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) inhibitor thapsigargin. Thapsigargin reduces Ca2+ entry at low and high frequencies, but loss of VAMP7 has no effect on the extent of inhibition (Extended Data Fig. 10c).

To determine whether the observed effect of VAMP7 on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels accounts for the changes in transmitter release in the Vamp7 KO, we used slice recording. ω-Agatoxin IVA inhibits release (1 AP) to a greater extent in Vamp7-KO slices than it does in WT slices (Extended Data Fig. 10d,e), consistent with the disinhibition of P/Q-type channels. By contrast, ω-conotoxin has the same, small effect in both WT and Vamp7-KO slices, and nimodipine has essentially no effect on the response to single stimuli in either genotype (Extended Data Fig. 10d,e). A change in Ca2+ entry should also influence short-term plasticity. Extended Data Fig. 10e,f shows that ω-agatoxin reduces synaptic depression to a much greater extent in the Vamp7 KO than in the WT, reflecting a greater reduction in release probability. By contrast, ω-conotoxin has little effect in either WT or Vamp7 KO. Thus, loss of VAMP7 increases the reliance on P/Q-type channels specifically for release.

Next, we examined how VAMP7 contributes to the inhibition of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels. Previous work has shown that the t-SNAREs syntaxin and SNAP25 interact with N- and P/Q-type Ca2+ channels at a specific (‘synprint’) site between the second and third homology repeats44,45,46. In heterologous expression systems, the t-SNAREs inhibit voltage-gated Ca2+ channels47, but when assembled with synaptotagmin, their disinhibition has been suggested to promote the coupling of release to Ca2+ entry48,49,50. The role of v-SNAREs in this form of regulation has remained unclear. We find that loss of VAMP7 does not alter the punctate distribution of Cav2.1 or Cav2.2, or their colocalization with the SV protein synaptophysin or with the active-zone protein Piccolo (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 11a,b). However, loss of VAMP7 reduces the colocalization of syntaxin 1 with Cav2.1 (Fig. 4b), whereas colocalization with Cav2.2 does not change (Extended Data Fig. 11c). In terms of biochemical interaction, VAMP7 and syntaxin 1 co-immunoprecipitate with P/Q-type channels in synaptosomes from WT mice (Fig. 4c). In membranes from Vamp7-KO mice, however, less syntaxin co-immunoprecipitates with the channel, suggesting that VAMP7 stabilizes the interaction of syntaxin with Cav2.1. By contrast, the association of SNAP25 with the channel does not depend on VAMP7 (Fig. 4c).
