#1349. Kevin Nisbet's lack of cool proved so costly for Aberdeen at Hampden... and underlines why he's not a man for the big occasion

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 18:27 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 18:32 EDT, 31 October 2026

In the build-up to this Premier Sports Cup semi-final, Aberdeen captain Kevin Nisbet spoke about the players needing to step up and deliver.

On a woeful run of form as they arrived at Hampden, and with huge pressure mounting on Stephen Robinson, Nisbet insisted the players owed the manager a performance and a result.

Just to take the heat off as much as anything else. With 76 minutes on the clock in this tense and cagey affair with Rangers, Nisbet had a golden opportunity.

With the score locked at 0-0, Stuart Armstrong fed a pass into Nisbet’s path and the ball was crying out to be struck first time.

Nisbet could probably see the whites of Ivor Pandur’s eyes. In the context of the game, it was as good a chance as Aberdeen could have hoped for.

But his finish was absolutely awful. Nisbet hesitated when he should have pulled the trigger straight away, allowing Olwethu Makhanya to make a block.

Aberdeen striker Kevin Nisbet reflects on a golden chance to fire Aberdeen ahead at Hampden

On such moments are cup semi-finals won and lost. Just seven minutes later, at the other end of the pitch, Ryan Naderi prodded home from close range to send Rangers through to the final.

Nisbet will surely be haunted by his miss. He has scored 13 goals this season. For all Aberdeen’s struggles, some have even touted him for a Scotland recall.

But he is not up to scratch at the top level. In some respects, he finds himself in the same boat as Lawrence Shankland.

Any time Shankland has been given an opportunity with Scotland, he hasn’t really taken it. Particularly in the World Cup in the summer.

Nisbet is a decent enough striker at Scottish Professional Football League level. But in the big moments in big games, he’s not good enough.

It was a chance he had to take. In the end, Aberdeen were left to rue what might have been as Rangers, who were poor for much of the game, edged through to the final.

All in all, this is a defeat which just piles more pressure on Stephen Robinson. His team did not play poorly but they did not win.

Nisbet took too long with the ball and allowed Olwethu Makhanya the chance to block his shot

There is no sense in trotting out excuses about being competitive and unlucky. Aberdeen were not unlucky.

They had a glorious chance to go in front late in the game and their captain wasted it. That is not misfortune. It is profligacy.

Robinson and his players now face a huge game against Hibs at Pittodrie next Saturday.

With the international break just around the corner, a time when clubs invariably change manager once the rot has set in, it could well be last-chance saloon for Robinson.

#1348. Thiago Motta among candidates for Lyon job if Fonseca leaves

Reports in France claim that former Juventus and Bologna head coach Thiago Motta is among the candidates to take over at Ligue 1 side Olympique Lyonnais in the event that Paulo Fonseca departs in the near future.

Despite sitting in third place in Ligue 1 after nine matches of the 2026-27 season, recent reports suggest that former Milan head coach Fonseca could leave Lyon in order to his native Portugal to take over from Rui Borges as head coach of Sporting CP instead.

Fonseca has reportedly requested to leave Lyon according to recent reports from l’Equipe.

If Fonseca does leave, Lyon will be left needing a replacement, and according to l’Equipe, Thiago Motta is among the list of potential replacements.

Motta has been available since leaving Juventus in March of 2025, less than a year after he was appointed as Bianconeri head coach. He had been handed the job after an impressive season with Bologna, which ended with Champions League qualification at the end of the 2023-24 season.

Though he left Juventus in March of 2025, Thiago Motta remained on the club’s payroll for more than a year afterwards, before seeing his contract formally terminated at the start of June this year. This means that he is fully available and does not need to terminate any other outstanding agreements if he is to take on a new job in the near future.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1347. Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Image sensors are critical components in artificial intelligence1,2,3, yet conventional approaches bond detector arrays to readout integrated circuits (ROICs), a process that increases complexity and cost4. The ideal alternative—growing the detector directly on the ROIC from solution using raw materials—has remained elusive owing to the difficulty in achieving electronic-grade films through a ROIC-compatible process5,6. Here, inspired by biomineralization principles7, we demonstrate monolithic in situ integration (MISI) of high-performance lead sulfide (PbS) photodetectors on ROICs by means of a room-temperature aqueous process. By regulating Pb–OH complexation and suppressing environmental perturbations, we achieve quasi-single-crystalline PbS films with excellent electronic properties (carrier density approximately 2 × 1015 cm−3, mobility 124 cm2 V−1 s−1) and wafer-scale, pixel-level uniformity. Through antimony doping, the resulting photodiodes exhibit a record specific detectivity of 4.4 × 1011 Jones at 2.5 µm, surpassing commercial InGaAs detectors8. We further fabricate a 640 × 512-pixel focal-plane array that captures clear infrared images and also integrate devices directly onto flexible ROICs. This solution-based MISI approach offers a scalable and transformative route for advanced optoelectronics and sensors.

a, Calculated concentration of the growth-active species HPbO2− (black, left axis) and its differential response to hydroxide concentration, dCHPbO2−/dCOH− (red, right axis), as a function of pH at a total Pb concentration of 17.8 mM. b, Concentration of HPbO2− and its differential response to total Pb concentration, dCHPbO2−/dCPb, over a total Pb concentration range of 0.1–100 mM. c,d, Differential responses of the Pb–Cl complex (c) and Pb–acetate complex (d) to total Pb concentration at the indicated logarithmic ligand concentrations. The equilibrium calculations were performed using Visual MINTEQ. Together, these results identify an alkaline chemical window in which HPbO2− is abundant and comparatively buffered against variations in pH and precursor concentration, supporting stable control of supersaturation during aqueous PbS growth.

a, Texture factor of the PbS (200) reflection for films grown at pH values ranging from 11.0 to 11.4. Each point represents an independently prepared film and the distributions were obtained from seven independent measurements at each pH. The highest (200) texture factor was obtained at pH 11.2. b, Dynamic-light-scattering-derived particle counts as a function of reaction time at the indicated pH values. Solid lines represent the mean values and shaded regions indicate the variation across three repeated scans. The negligible particle signal at pH 11.2, together with the enhanced (200) texture factor, is consistent with the suppression of homogeneous nucleation and preferential PbS growth at the substrate interface.

a, Measured velocity spectra for applied vertical vibrations spanning 0.1–100 Hz. b, Enlarged velocity spectra near 40 Hz at the different driving amplitudes used in d; the peak velocity was taken as the vibration velocity amplitude. c, PbS (200) diffraction peak intensity (black, left axis) and FWHM (red, right axis) as functions of vibration frequency. The dashed lines indicate the corresponding values measured without externally applied vibration (0 Hz). d, PbS (200) peak intensity and FWHM as functions of vibration velocity amplitude at a fixed frequency of 40 Hz. Data in c and d are presented as mean ± standard deviation from n = 3 independently prepared films for each condition. The reduction in diffraction intensity and accompanying peak broadening at higher vibration frequencies and amplitudes are consistent with decreased crystallographic ordering under stronger mechanical perturbation.

a, Schematic illustration of the customized in situ synchrotron XRD configuration used to monitor aqueous PbS crystallization directly on a CMOS ROIC. b, Photograph of the experimental set-up, including the beamline configuration, sample holder and vibration-isolation platform; the growth cell is indicated by the red arrow. c, Representative one-dimensional radial intensity profiles obtained by integrating the two-dimensional diffraction patterns at selected reaction times. The PbS (002) peak near q ≈ 2.3 Å−1 increases progressively, whereas the reflections originating from the CMOS substrate remain detectable throughout the measurement. The PbS diffraction intensity increases continuously over the 200-min growth period, whereas the substrate signal gradually decreases. These time-resolved measurements directly reveal sustained PbS crystallization and film accumulation on the CMOS ROIC during aqueous growth.

a, Representative photographs of the substrate before and after aqueous PbS deposition, showing uniform film coverage over the full substrate area. b, Spatial distribution of the PbS film thickness measured by spectroscopic ellipsometry at the indicated sampling positions. The thickness variation across the wafer is limited to approximately 50 nm. c, Spatial distribution of the integrated intensity of the PbS (200) diffraction peak. d, Spatial distribution of the FWHM of the PbS (200) diffraction peak. Black points in b–d indicate the measurement positions and the continuous maps were generated by interpolation between these points. The colour scales represent film thickness in nm, diffraction intensity in arbitrary units and FWHM in degrees, respectively. Both the PbS (200) peak intensity and FWHM remain broadly uniform across the mapped region. Although minor localized variations are present, no systematic spatial degradation or large-scale gradients are observed, supporting well-controlled film growth and crystallographic uniformity over the inch-scale substrate.

a–c, Pole-figure maps of the PbS (220) (a), PbS (200) (b) and PbS (111) (c) reflections. The colour scales indicate diffraction intensity, whereas grey points denote positions with no detectable diffraction above the background. The (200) pole figure exhibits a strongly localized maximum at the centre, consistent with preferential alignment of the PbS (200) planes parallel to the substrate surface. The discrete symmetry-related maxima observed in the (220) and (111) pole figures, together with the absence of continuous diffraction rings, indicate a highly textured film with a limited population of randomly oriented grains. These measurements support the dominant out-of-plane orientation and low orientational dispersion of the MISI-grown PbS films.

a,e,i, Chemical-potential stability regions for In-doped, Sb-doped and Bi-doped PbS, respectively. Red points 1–3 denote S-rich, intermediate and Pb-rich conditions, respectively. b–d,f–h,j–l, Calculated defect-formation energies as functions of Fermi level under the corresponding chemical-potential conditions. Vertical dashed lines mark the equilibrium Fermi levels. Among the three dopants, substitutional SbPb exhibits the lowest formation energy and weakest competition from compensating acceptor defects, allowing the equilibrium Fermi level to approach or enter the conduction band. In-doped and Bi-doped PbS show comparatively higher donor-formation energies and stronger compensation, indicating narrower processing windows for stable n-type doping.

a–c, SEM image (a), high-resolution TEM image (b) and XRD pattern (c) of an undoped PbS film grown under optimized MISI conditions. d–f, Corresponding SEM image (d), high-resolution TEM image (e) and XRD (f) of an Sb-doped PbS film. The Sb-doped film retains a dense and continuous morphology without obvious pinholes or phase segregation. The measured lattice spacing decreases locally from 0.292 nm in the undoped film to 0.285 nm after Sb doping, consistent with local lattice contraction associated with Sb incorporation. The nearly unchanged position and intensity of the PbS (200) diffraction peak indicate that the average crystal structure and preferred orientation are preserved after doping.

a, Photograph of a PbSe film deposited directly on a CMOS ROIC substrate by the MISI process at room temperature. b, Surface SEM image of the on-chip PbSe film, showing dense and continuous crystalline coverage. c, XRD pattern of the PbSe film. The dominant PbSe reflections are indexed to the rock-salt phase, whereas the extra peaks originate from the Au and SiO2 layers of the CMOS ROIC; the reference PbSe diffraction pattern is shown at the bottom. d, Pole figure of the PbSe (200) reflection, indicating a pronounced preferred crystallographic orientation. e, Time-dependent current response of a PbSe photoconductive device under repeated on–off illumination from a 573-K blackbody source at a bias of 10 V and an incident power density of 0.1 mW cm−2. f, Normalized spectral photoresponse of the PbSe device, extending into the mid-wave infrared range. Together, the preserved film morphology, preferred crystallographic orientation and functional infrared photoresponse provide a proof-of-concept demonstration that the MISI strategy can be extended from PbS to PbSe.

#1346. Pioli analyses Juventus 2-0 Napoli: ‘Kolo Muani is working hard from what I can see’

Stefano Pioli shared his thoughts following Juventus’s 2-0 victory over Napoli in Serie A on Sunday evening, suggesting that the hosts’ ‘desire’ is what got them over the line, and that Luciano Spalletti is doing everything he can to get the best out of Randal Kolo Muani.

Juventus picked up a much-needed 2-0 victory at home against Napoli in Serie A thanks to goals from Kerim Alajbegovic and Jeremie Boga on Sunday evening, bouncing back after a midweek 2-0 defeat away against Genoa.

The Bianconeri are now up to seventh place with 17 points from their first 10 league matches of the season, whilst Massimiliano Allegri and Napoli are on 14, one place behind them in the table.

Pioli was a guest in the Sky Sport Italia studio for Sunday’s coverage of Juventus’s 2-0 victory over Napoli and shared his thoughts on the game after full-time.

“It was an exciting game in the first half, but Juventus went on to show the desire to win and it’s a game that will give the Bianconeri a bit more trust,” said the former Milan, Inter, Fiorentina and Lazio head coach (via TMW).

Juventus have recently been playing in a 3-5-2 with Randal Kolo Muani and Nick Woltemade up front with injuries to several key attacking players, but then decided to bring on more natural wide players in Jeremie Boga and Edon Zhegrova in the second half.

Asked whether it makes a big difference if Juventus play with wingers or with a two-man striker partnership, Pioli said: “I think so, but Juventus have a lot of wingers. The pairing of Woltemade and Kolo Muani makes sense, but Spalletti made good changes and interpreted the game well. The Bianconeri had a lot of shots from outside the box and they were rewarded for that tonight.”

And on Kolo Muani specifically, Pioli said: “As long as he shows a willing attitude, Kolo Muani is working hard from what I can see, he’s just missing that decisive moment. You have to help him on a psychological level, being there for him and giving him confidence or putting him in different areas on the pitch: In short, basically what Spalletti is trying to do.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

Muani played too many games and played multiple roles in every game. Its very harsh to criticize him. Most of the time very few players are involved in the counter-attack transition, which is the main reason that the team scored only a few goals.

not that hard to criticize him. persistent mistakes.misplaced passes like Sunday with the 2 on 1.

#1345. RANGERS 1 ABERDEEN 0: Ryan Naderi the Hampden hero as Light Blues squeeze past dogged Dons to reach final

Published: 16:41 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 18:41 EDT, 31 October 2026

Ryan Naderi is developing the happy knack of turning up in the right place at the right time for Rangers. And, by Jove, how they needed him to deliver something to break the deadlock in this one and book a spot in the Premier Sports Cup final back at Hampden next month.

Derek McInnes’ side weren’t as bad at the national stadium as they were midweek in scraping a 2-2 draw away to Hearts, but they certainly weren’t all that good. Aberdeen turned up to frustrate them last night and succeeded for the large part, making a number of notable chances themselves.

There’s an obligation to drop in some kind of pun about Hallowe’en in this account of what went down between these two sides, so let's discuss how Dons’ captain Kevin Nisbet must have spent last night suffering nightmares following his own personal horror show just 14 minutes from time.

With the game back hanging in the balance in the wake of a strong period of Rangers pressure, Stephen Robinson’s side broke forward in numbers and, even after Nisbet had failed to find substitute Mitchy Ntelo with a pass, the ball was picked up by Stuart Armstrong and fed back into the skipper’s path on the right-hand side of the box.

He had to smash it first-time. Hard and low across the keeper. Inexplicably, for a guy who does know how to find the net and has done it plenty of times throughout his career, he took a touch and allowed Olwethu Makhanya the opportunity to get across and put in a crucial block.

In that instant, you wondered if the Dons’ big chance had come and gone. Naderi provided the answer just seven minutes later.

Rangers striker Ryan Naderi celebrates his late semi-final winner at Hampden Park

Rangers boss Derek McInnes enjoys the moment at full-time as his side are through to the final

The Czech internationalist endured a grim start to the season as a lone frontman, but has come into his own since being deployed beside Kevin Kelsy and shown that precious ability to score goals that really change things, really matter.

He scored the winner at Celtic Park in September, of course, as well as a home winner against Motherwell. Last time out against St Johnstone, his second-half effort to notch the second goal of what ended up a 4-0 romp was expertly timed as his team-mates had failed to wake up at the start of the second 45 and looked like they might fall flat on their faces.

Once again, he rode to the rescue here, reading the play, making a run, getting into space and finishing from close-in for his eighth of the campaign. The kind of bread-and-butter goal you want your strikers to score.

A cross in from the left from Rangers’ best player Badredine Bouanani, turning up on the wrong wing for some reason, was cleared by Connor Ronan to substitute Dan Neil 25 yards out.

His short pass to James Penrice resulted in a low shot into the area and Naderi timed his run perfectly to ghost in and convert from close range.

It was a sickening blow to under-pressure Robinson and his players. They had dug in really well, pulled off the game plan nicely and kept themselves in it throughout. Their display belied the league form that has put the manager’s job on the line ahead of next Saturday’s teatime visit of Hibernian.

It all counts for nothing in the end, though. As they reflect on events in Mount Florida, they will know that they came up against a Rangers side that most definitely dominated possession — and probably deserved the win in the end — but was vulnerable at times and failed to function as McInnes would have wanted.

The Ibrox boss pulled something of a surprise in his starting line-up by dropping vice-captain Neil and putting left-back Penrice in beside skipper-for-the-night Nico Raskin. It didn’t really work, though.

Listen, those guys weren’t exactly the core of the problem. A lot of the time, the ball wasn’t even being played through midfield, but the switch-up just didn’t feel like it worked. The balance wasn’t right.

For most of the first half, in particular, not very much was right about Rangers. They had plenty of the ball but Aberdeen set up in a 5-3-2 formation and kept them quiet while managing to create good chances of their own on the counter-attack.

Rangers were too slow. Not creative enough. Everything truly positive and dangerous they did went through Badredine Bouanani on the right, but there has to be infinitely more variation in their play rather than just getting it to the on-loan Algerian and hoping those quick feet of his can work some magic.

It was heartbreak for Aberdeen's Nicky Devlin as they fell just short in the semi-final

When he was brought in from German side VfB Stuttgart, the chat was that the management team saw him as an ideal weapon to break down teams playing a low block. He has the ability to beat a man, play in tight spots, have a shot.

However, there’s got to be more about Rangers than that. In this game, as with the 2-2 midweek draw with Hearts at Tynecastle, there just wasn’t enough in the way of fluent, purposeful play. They’ve looked nothing like the side that blew St Johnstone away last weekend with some exhilarating football and that must be a worry for McInnes.

By this stage of the season, they should be starting to find their stride, develop more in the way of consistency.

It took Rangers 44 minutes, for example, to fashion a shot on target. Naturally, it came from Bouanani, a low effort from a central position being saved low to his right by Aberdeen goalkeeper Marius Muller.

Up until that point, the better of the opportunities had fallen to the Dons. Midway through the opening period, Raskin played a pass wide to Dujon Sterling that carried just too much jeopardy.

Nesta Guinness-Walker nipped in to steal possession and then took the ball for a run all the way into the final third before releasing a decent low effort which Ibrox No1 Ivor Pandur had to save to his left.

With ten minutes of the half to play, Nisbet then sent a header wide from a great position after moving onto a cross from Brad Lyons.

At that stage, all Rangers had to shout about was an appeal for a penalty turned down on the 16-minute mark when Dons striker Ayoub Mouloua clearly handled the ball in his own area under pressure from Manny Fernandez.

Referee Ryan Lee didn’t give the award with VAR John Beaton backing up that call. It was controversial and no mistake.

Towards the end of the first half, however, it looked like things might be starting to click for McInnes’ men. Naderi put a header just over from a Raskin cross after getting in behind Jack Milne and Min-su Kim, massively disappointing again and eventually replaced by Djeidi Gassama, sliced an effort wide directly in front of goal.

Yet, it remained stodgy for Rangers after the restart. In the wake of Naderi just failing to get on the end of a low shot from Bouanani at the back post, a deflected Nisbet shot at the other end had to be saved low and smartly by Pandur.

Kelsy missed a sitter just after the hour when putting a header miles wide from a brilliant Bouanani cross and Muller had to block a shot from the Algerian wide man with his right boot as Rangers enjoyed their most dangerous and insistent period of the match.

It didn’t last, but Nisbet dallied when it mattered while Naderi just let his instinct take control for a sharp little conversion from that Penrice effort.

McInnes now has his first shot at silverware as Rangers manager pending and that’s what he wanted going into this game.

However, he needs to find a way to get this team slicker, tighter, more joined-up. More relentless. More focused. More composed in key areas.

As if a reminder of that was needed, it came in time added-on when Armstrong picked up the ball at the edge of their box and bent a fine effort just wide of Pandur’s left-hand post.

So near and yet so far. The story of Aberdeen’s night, really. A night where a big chance definitely existed, but just couldn’t be taken.

#1344. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b

Was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

"Enjoy the ride and smile" Erling Haaland with a message for Man City fans ahead of their trip to Anfield this weekend 🎙️🩵 https://t.co/H7so0fk6XE

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1343. Experts call for Curtis Jones after disappointing Barella display in Milan derby

Nicolo Barella is among the Inter players to come under criticism after Saturday’s 3-1 defeat against Milan in the Derby della Madonnina, and experts including Paolo Di Canio feel that it is only a matter of time before summer signing Curtis Jones becomes the starter in the Italian’s preferred position.

Inter were beaten 3-1 by Milan in the derby on Saturday: They have now gone eight matches without a victory in the Derby della Madonnina, drawing twice and losing six times since their most recent victory over the Rossoneri in April of 2024.

Saturday’s defeat against Milan also ended Inter’s unbeaten start to the 2026-27 Serie A season and has seen them knocked off top spot by Lazio, who have collected 28 points from a possible 30 after 10 league matches.

Among the Inter players facing criticism after the derby defeat is Italy international Barella, who committed the foul just outside the penalty area that led to Diego Moreira’s excellently-taken free-kick, which sent Milan into a 3-1 lead.

Paolo Di Canio, on punditry duty with Sky Sport Italia on Sunday, feels that this isn’t an uncommon thing for Barella.

“Inter suffered against Milan. It was a team that looked terrified, especially after going 3-1 down. Barella commits the foul and it’s a bad one, the one that led to the goal for 3-1. It’s things we’ve spoken about before, impromptu little heel kicks and things like that,” said Di Caino (via TMW).

“They confirmed it themselves by saying that they might’ve lost a bit of hunger or that they’ve taken their foot off the gas. We’re not making that up. They are still the strongest team, but they didn’t bounce back against Milan. It’s a team that has a few problems. Most importantly, they need to get their best players back.”

Di Canio feels that Inter would be better off with Jones starting in Barella’s position in midfield.

“Remember: Curtis Jones will be a starter. He brings aggression and also helps out in front of the defence. He will play, he’s their most evolved midfielder.”

Jones has made four Serie A appearances for Inter following his €35m summer transfer from Liverpool, but has missed the last five with an adductor injury, which has kept him out of action since the September-October international break.

Stefano Pioli, also in the Sky studio on Sunday, agreed with Di Canio’s verdict on Jones: “I like him a lot, he’s an all-rounder,” said the former Nerazzzurri head coach.

Pioli feels that the absence of Lautaro Martinez is hurting Inter more than anything right now, though.

“There’s an Inter with Lautaro and an Inter without him. Every coach wants a captain like that. He fights for every ball and plays every game with passion and a desire to help the team. I’ve always really admired him.

“Sometimes in the dressing room, what a teammate says to you can be the most important thing.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

Trust me, Barella is way better than Jones. The former just needs some rotation. The problem is nobody could replace or be closer to the turkey player. The other midfielders are very similar.

#1342. Stats not good enough! Derek McInnes issues warning to his Rangers players over their profligacy in front of goal

Published: 18:38 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 18:47 EDT, 31 October 2026

Rangers manager Derek McInnes last night warned his side they have to ramp up the killer instinct in front of goal after branding their attacking stats in the one-goal Premier Sports Cup semi-final win over Aberdeen ‘embarrassing’.

The Ibrox outfit had 25 shots on goal with only five on target at the end of a Hampden tussle settled by a close-range finish from striker Ryan Naderi with just seven minutes left to play.

McInnes feels his players are making too many bad decisions in the final third of the field and has told wide men such as Badredine Bouanani and Kim Min-su, who has yet to record an assist or goal this term, that they need to start pitching in with better figures.

He accepts there is a lack of top-level experience among a group of attackers notable for their youth, but knows there must be improvements in the quest for silverware.

‘We came with the intention of making sure we got the club into a cup final by hook or by crook, and we’ve done the job, so I am really pleased and delighted with the players, in the main, for their perseverance, for keeping going,’ said McInnes.

‘Semi-finals aren’t easy to get through, particularly when you play the way we did in the first half.

Derek McInnes labelled his team's attacking statistics 'embarrassing' after their Hampden win

‘We were ponderous when we needed to be quicker. When we needed to be calm in the final bit, we snatched and made poor decisions.

‘In terms of the stats, it is actually embarrassing we have had 25 shots and only five on target. It says a lot about the inexperience at the top end of the pitch.

‘That’s for another day. Today was just all about getting through. It’s so important for the club and the supporters to look forward to a cup final.

‘We need to keep arriving in cup finals and get the job done to win trophies.

‘I always feel there’s goals in us,’ said the Ibrox boss. ‘Equally, I was still a bit concerned on counter-attacks. Aberdeen had a couple of moments that gave them oxygen and belief that maybe they could get in the final, but the better team won.

‘Naderi, like all good strikers, is going that way when the defenders are on their heels and he gets these scruffy goals that you want your striker to score.

‘He’s always in the middle of the goal when the ball gets into good areas, but a lot of the time we don’t feed him enough. We make too many bad decisions.

Kevin Kelsy watches a header fly wide on a rare off night for the Venezuelan front man

‘Some of the stats that we’re seeing more or less every week at the minute, it’s like making poor decisions, snatching at things, rushing crosses, not making the right pass, not putting the extra pass in. I’m going to keep saying that we’re a young team up there and it’s hard sometimes.

‘You need an old man up there, an old head, nous, who knows just how to bring a bit of savvy and calmness to it.

‘Thankfully, we had that with the goal today, but there were so many other times where we could, if we just take more care, be less rushed and stay calm in those moments, create better opportunities rather than just 25 shots and 20 of them flying over the bar.

‘Those shots on target become double, triple more of what we get, and it’s those wee bits that we need to sharpen up if we’re going to be successful this season.’

Asked if he felt there would be more goals in man-of-the-match Bouanani, McInnes replied: ‘There had better! The wide players need to start scoring goals.

‘Min-su needs to get that demand on himself, Gassama. Bouanani’s got so much quality.

‘The thing with Bouanani is, as soon as he steps on the pitch on that left side, 25 yards out, you think it’s in the net because he does it time and time again in training. If he keeps chapping at the door, I’m sure the goals will come.

‘I’d like to have enjoyed this a wee bit more. Enjoyment comes now, a wee bit of satisfaction when I see the lads in the dressing room celebrating together, but the job now is to go and win the thing.

Badredine Bouanani goes close with a curling effort but McInnes wants to see more from him

‘We’ll get six weeks now between now and then where we need to get better at things I just spoke about.

‘We’re on a really strong run just now in terms of wins and being unbeaten over a period of time, but we know we’re not perfect. It’s important that we keep searching for those improvements.’

Naderi lapped up his eighth goal of the season and insisted the right team won.

‘It was wonderful. I am so happy. It was a wonderful second half and we deserved it. It was just a question of time until we scored,’ said Naderi.

‘We had so many corners back-to-back, so much pressure, so many shots on target.’

Captain-for-the-night Nico Raskin, meanwhile, agreed with McInnes’ view that the team has to become more ruthless in front of goal.

‘Their goalkeeper made loads of saves and we could maybe have been a bit more calm in front of goal, but I am just so happy for Ryan and the team we got the goal,’ he said.

‘It is about trying to be more clinical now and enjoying the game more as it is always tense at 0-0 or 1-0. We want to come back to Hampden and win the cup now.’

#1341. Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea)1,2,3. The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights4,5 but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia);6,7,8 these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales4,5. All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes9. Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome c oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea–eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis10, with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification.

Understanding how complex eukaryotic cells emerged from their prokaryotic ancestors is a fundamental challenge in biology. The widely discussed endosymbiotic theory posits that the last eukaryotic common ancestor was derived from a host cell that had taken up an alphaproteobacteria-related symbiont that later became the mitochondrion11,12,13,14. Although the identity of the putative host cell in this theory has long been enigmatic, recent metagenomic and phylogenetic analyses indicate that eukaryotes probably evolved from a lineage closely related to members of the archaeal group Asgard archaea2,6,7,15,16,17, which has now been formally classified as the phylum Promethearchaeota within the kingdom Promethearchaeati3. This relationship is further reflected in the presence of abundant eukaryotic signature proteins (ESPs) in their genomes15,16,18. Moreover, several of these ESPs exhibit structural and functional similarities to those found in eukaryotes19,20,21,22.

What has remained unclear was the cell structure and physiology of the archaeal group; both have important implications for how archaea may have transitioned towards eukaryotes. On the basis of the presence of abundant and diverse ESPs in these archaea, studies hypothesized that the archaeal ancestor to eukaryotes may have already evolved a complex internal cell structure (that is, an endomembrane system) before endosymbiosis of the alphaproteobacterial ancestor of mitochondria (that is, mito-intermediate or mito-late)1,23,24,25. Cultivation efforts yielded one isolate, Promethearchaeum syntrophicum strain MK-D13,4, as well as enrichment cultures predominated by ‘Candidatus Lokiarchaeum ossiferum’5 and ‘Candidatus Nerearchaeum marumarumayae’26, all revealing a typical prokaryotic internal structure without a persistent eukaryote-like endomembrane system4,5,26 and potential evidence for an actin-based cytoskeleton5,27. All of the Promethearchaeaceae strains gain energy from anaerobic degradation of peptides/amino acids (and/or sugars) through symbiotic metabolic (that is, syntrophic) interactions with H2-consuming methanogenic archaea or sulfate-reducing bacteria3,4,5,26. A metagenomic study also observed organotrophic H2 generation as a shared metabolic feature across four classes of Promethearchaeota23. Collectively, these data suggest that anaerobiosis, H2 generation and prokaryotic cell structure may have been relevant to the evolutionary transition between archaea and eukaryotes.

However, whether features found in these Promethearchaeia (formerly Lokiarchaeia) cultures are relevant to the origin of eukaryotes remains a matter of debate1,7,27. First, metagenomic predictions suggest a wide diversity of physiologies across Promethearchaeota (such as autotrophy, organotrophy and rhodopsin-based phototrophy)23,28,29,30,31. Second, according to recent phylogenetic analyses, the class ‘Candidatus Heimdallarchaeia’ or its order ‘Candidatus Hodarchaeales’ may branch as a sister group to eukaryotes6,7,8. On the basis of these observations, a variety of features, including complex internal cell structure4,7,8,23,24,25, have been proposed for the last archaea (specifically ‘Ca. Heimdallarchaeia’) eukaryote common ancestor (LAECA). Another potential feature of this ancestor that has recently attracted attention is aerobic respiration7,23,30,32. If LAECA were capable of oxygen respiration, this would substantially alter some models of eukaryogenesis that posit an anaerobic archaeal host interacting syntrophically with an alphaproteobacterial endosymbiont capable of aerobic respiration. Studies find that some ‘Ca. Heimdallarchaeia’ possess terminal oxidases (Cox)7,23 and further propose LAECA may have been aerobic30,32. These observations suggest that LAECA already had the beginnings of structural and respiratory features associated with eukaryotes. However, the cell structure of ‘Ca. Heimdallarchaeia’ has yet to be elucidated and the simple presence of such enzymes cannot distinguish between aerotolerant anaerobes and (facultative) aerobes given that many obligately anaerobic organisms possess terminal oxidases for oxygen tolerance33,34. In light of this, cultivation of class ‘Ca. Heimdallarchaeia’ from habitats exposed to oxygen is essential to identify how these archaea may interact with oxygen and determine the cell structures and physiologies that are potentially relevant to LAECA1.

Here we successfully cultured two strains of Heimdallarchaeia belonging to the order Hodarchaeales from a biofilm submerged in anoxic subsurface-derived brine water but exposed to air hourly. One was isolated in a pure syntrophic co-culture and another in a pure tri-culture with methanogenic partners. The strain in co-culture had terminal oxidases and yet exhibited strict dependence on anaerobic metabolism. We further report the cultivation procedures, cellular structures, physiological characteristics and genomic features of these strains, and their implications for the origin of eukaryotes.

To culture members of ‘Heimdallarchaeia’ and examine their potential relationship with oxygen, we capitalized on previous experience in cultivation of P. syntrophicum MK-D14,35. We attributed successful isolation of this strain to a long-term bioreactor-based increase in metabolic activity, acclimatization to artificial conditions and selection against other populations (that is, enrichment)3,4,35. Previous studies also hinted that the presence and activity of anaerobic methane-oxidizing microbial consortia were probably important in supporting the growth of Promethearchaeota members, presumably through the excretion of organic compounds35,36. Here we looked to a gas production well in the Boso Peninsula, Chiba Prefecture, Japan, which is operationally similar to our previous cultivation methane-fed bioreactor (Extended Data Fig. 1). Methane-bearing saline groundwater (that is, brine) upwells into the well and supports a biofilm on the walls containing populations identical or similar to those found in marine sediments, according to 16S rRNA gene tag-sequencing (iTag) analysis37. In contrast to our previous anoxic reactor, the biofilm is intermittently exposed to air (and therefore oxygen) due to periodic eruptions of brine, akin to geysers, that cause the water level to drop temporarily37. Enriched in these biofilms were small populations of Heimdallarchaeia, which we targeted for isolation (Supplementary Table 1).

We aimed to culture the biofilm microbial community in the laboratory while mimicking natural conditions. Filtered brine from the well was used as the basal medium and supplemented this with methane and magnetite to attempt co-enrichment of Promethearchaeota members with anaerobic methane-oxidizing archaea (Supplementary Note 1). While typical anaerobe cultivation procedures call for addition of reducing agents (such as sodium sulfide and/or cysteine) to the culture medium to scavenge oxygen, we omitted these to retain exposure to low concentrations of oxygen. After approximately 3 months, we detected several 16S rRNA gene sequences of Hodarchaeales, Heimdallarchaeales and Promethearchaeales (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). We implemented proteinaceous substrates, casamino acids and powdered milk (each 0.005%, w/v), as energy sources for subcultures to enhance the growth of these archaea, based on our previous observation that syntrophic degradation of amino acids/peptides is a widespread feature across the phylum4 (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Table 1). To also select against other organisms, we supplemented the medium with five antibiotics: ampicillin, vancomycin, kanamycin, streptomycin and erythromycin.

a, Maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny of 16S rRNA gene sequences, showing the phylogenetic position of cultured strains. The 16S rRNA genes obtained from isolated strains, enrichment culture and metagenome assemblies are shown in red, orange and bold black font, respectively. The branches have bootstrap support ≥0.9 unless otherwise noted. b, Phase-contrast photomicrograph of pure co-culture of HC1 and Methanocalculus sp. MC2. The relative abundance of each member (in late-exponential phase) was estimated using 16S rRNA gene-tag-sequencing (iTag) analysis and is shown as a pie chart. c, Growth curves of HC1 in anaerobic medium supplemented with casamino acids (CA), peptone and yeast extract (YE) (0.005% (w/v) each). d, Phase-contrast photomicrograph of strain SC1 in a tri-culture; the relative abundance of each member in late-exponential phase is shown based on an iTag analysis. e, Growth curves of SC1 in anaerobic medium supplemented with CA, peptone, powdered milk (PM) and yeast extract (0.005%, 0.005%, 0.005% and 0.005% or 0.05% (w/v), respectively). For b and d, the phase-contrast microscopy images of HC1 and SC1 are representatives of n = 126 and 65 recorded images, respectively. The relative abundances shown in the pie charts in b and d were determined after 15 and 11 transfers of HC1 and SC1 cultures, respectively (Supplementary Table 1), and similar community compositions were consistently observed in subsequent transfers. The grey arrows indicate Methanocalculus cells. Scale bars, 10 µm (b,d).

For cultures that sustained Promethearchaeota members according to iTag analysis, we subcultured twice in fresh medium of the same composition at roughly 100-day intervals; cultures that enriched one population of Hodarchaeales over other Promethearchaeota were further subcultured using a synthetic medium mimicking natural brine supplemented with casamino acids, powdered milk and five antibiotics (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). By omitting reducing agents, we were able to retain microoxic conditions (281 ± 123 nM dissolved oxygen, n = 5) that would possibly select for Hodarchaeales over Promethearchaeales members, each presumably associated with more oxidized and reduced lifestyles3,23. After four successive transfers under the same cultivation conditions, the culture retained aerobic bacteria (that is, Mariniphaga and Alcanivorax), contained a higher abundance of the Hodarchaeales population (1.8% in relative abundance) and lost the Promethearchaeales members (Supplementary Table 1). This suggested that the Hodarchaeales population can at least tolerate low-oxygen concentrations and is probably more adapted to oxic conditions compared with the Promethearchaeales members.

In subsequent subcultures, reducing agents were introduced and peptone was added as an additional energy source. The Hodarchaeales population reached up to 30% in relative abundance and maximum cell densities up to 106 16S rRNA gene copy numbers per ml. As for the other populations, only Mariniphaga, Alcanivorax and Methanocalculus remained (Supplementary Table 1). We isolated the Mariniphaga and Alcanivorax species, identified antibiotics that they are sensitive to (Supplementary Table 2) and applied these antibiotics (gentamycin, ciprofloxacin, cephalothin or ofloxacin) to the Hodarchaeales-dominated cultures (Supplementary Table 1). In parallel we also optimized the cultivation temperature and energy source types and concentrations (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Three years after the original sampling, we isolated Hodarchaeales in a purified co-culture with a single partnering methanogen population (Methanocalculus), each designated as strains HC1 and MC2, in an anaerobic medium supplemented with casamino acids, peptone and yeast extract (each 0.005%, w/v) at 30 °C (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Under these cultivation conditions, HC1 required 25–35 days to reach full growth with a doubling time of approximately 7–12 days, reaching a maximum cell density of 106 16S rRNA gene copies per ml (Fig. 1c). HC1 cells were morphologically similar to Promethearchaeales members3,4,5, with coccoid cells, albeit with larger diameters of 0.8–2.3 µm (1.3 µm on average; Supplementary Table 3) and multiple protrusions extending from the cell surface (Fig. 1b).

Using a cultivation strategy similar to that for HC1, we successfully isolated another Hodarchaeales strain and also enriched other Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeaceae members (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Note 2). One Hodarchaeales strain, designated SC1, was isolated in a purified tri-culture with Methanocalculus sp. strain MC3 and Methanolobus sp. strain MLB, with relative abundances of approximately 40%, 60% and <0.3%, respectively, based on iTag analysis (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 1). The tri-culture is stably maintained in anaerobic medium supplemented with casamino acids, powdered milk, polypeptone peptone (0.01%, w/v) and yeast extract (0.05%, w/v). SC1 required approximately 60 days to reach maximum growth with a doubling time of approximately 14–20 days, reaching a maximum cell density of 106 16S rRNA gene copies per ml (Fig. 1e). The 16S rRNA gene sequence identity between SC1 and HC1 was 77.55% based on BLAST analysis. SC1 cells were morphologically similar to HC1 but with a smaller diameter, 0.6–1.2 µm (0.9 µm on average) (Fig. 1d).

We sequenced the genomes of both strains. HC1 and SC1 possess circular genomes 7.91 Mb and 6.75 Mb, respectively (Supplementary Tables 4–6). HC1 has a larger genome than all reported Heimdallarchaeia metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs)32. Phylogenetic analyses showed that both strains belonged to the family-level clade LC-3 in Hodarchaeales (Fig. 1a). We tentatively propose the names ‘Candidatus Margulisarchaeum peptidiphilum’ and ‘Candidatus Flexarchaeum multiprotrusionum’ for strains HC1 and SC1, respectively, under the family ‘Candidatus Margulisarchaeaceae’ (Supplementary Note 3).

According to our analyses, HC1 and SC1 each possess 27 and 29 types of ESPs (Supplementary Table 7), putting them in the top quartile of Heimdallarchaeia. Both strains have numbers of ESP types for each ESP category greater than or equal to the average among Heimdallarchaeia. As such, we propose that HC1 is a suitable representative of extant Heimdallarchaeia or Hodarchaeales for examining whether these lineages harbour any intracellular cell structures related to or resembling eukaryotic complexity.

Observation of HC1 and SC1 cells in late exponential and early stationary phases using electron microscopy (EM) revealed that both strains have signatures of typical prokaryotic cells (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3). Cells are coccoid and generally found as individuals, occasionally in aggregates (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Figs. 2c and 3c,d,s). Cells divide through binary fission and, during this, exhibit a ring-like structure (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3e). Both strains produced membrane vesicles (Extended Data Figs. 2o–s and 3w). On the basis of cryo-EM, the cytoplasm and protrusions contained actin-filament-like structures and ferritin-like membrane-less granules (Fig. 2j–n, Extended Data Figs. 2h–j,m, 3t–w, 4 and 5, Supplementary Tables 5 and 6, Supplementary Figs. 2–4, Supplementary Notes 4–6 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). On the cell surface, we observed regular S-layer-like structures under cryo-EM and quick-freeze deep-etch replica EM (QFDE-EM) (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Figs. 2g,l and 3r,s,v,w). A combination of protein multimer structure prediction using AlphaFold338 and glycoproteomics revealed S-layer proteins conserved across many Promethearchaeota lineages that form symmetric homotetramers with a central vertical pore and are N-glycosylated like S-layer proteins of other archaea39 (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Table 8). In addition to the S-layer, we observed that the cell body and protrusion surfaces of HC1 are covered with very thin filaments (around 55 nm in length and approximately 1 nm in diameter), although their function remains unclear (Extended Data Fig. 2i–k,m,n).

a–e, SEM images showing single (a), dividing (b), protrusion-producing (c) and methanogen-attached (d) cells, and a magnified view of the image in d (e). f, QFDE image. g,h, Ultrathin section. i, Fluorescence image of cells stained with DAPI (blue) and hybridized with nucleotide probes targeting the rRNA of HC1 (green) and Methanocalculus (red) (Extended Data Fig. 7). j, Immunofluorescence image of cells stained with SYBR Green I (yellow/green) and labelled with an HC1 actin-specific antibody (red) (Extended Data Fig. 4). k–n, Cryo-electron tomogram (cryo-ET) slices (k,m) and corresponding 3D volume segmentations (l,n). Intracellular vesicle-like structures were infrequently observed in the images in m and n. Red, ferritin-like granules; yellow, actin filaments; blue, cell membrane; light blue, intracellular vesicle-like structure. The images c, f, h and i–n were obtained from cultures in the late-exponential phase, and the others were obtained from cultures in the mid-exponential phase. SEM, QFDE, ultrathin section, FISH and immunofluorescence images are representatives of n = 98, 48, 60, 21 and 36 recorded images, respectively. Cryo-ET images were obtained from 11 recorded tilted cryo-EM images. The white arrows indicate Methanocalculus sp. strain MC2 cells. Scale bars, 1 µm (a–j) and 500 nm (k,m).

After mid-exponential phase, most cells possess multiple protrusions of uniform diameter (approximately 370 nm), varying lengths, branching and bulbous expansions (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3), morphologically similar to P. syntrophicum MK-D13,4 and ‘Ca. L. ossiferum’5. Based on observations using scanning EM (SEM), protrusions were absent in all cells that appear to be undergoing cell division (cells that are in the middle of separating into two cocci with characteristic rings in both cocci marking where cell division probably began; Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3e), suggesting that protrusion generation and cell division are mutually exclusive processes. The protrusions often comprised more than half the volume of each cell (roughly 1.7 µm3 or 142% of the main cell body, on average; Supplementary Table 3), suggesting they have an important role in the physiology of these archaea. Notably, both protrusions and cells were flexible and were observed to sway by Brownian motion (Supplementary Videos 3 and 4). We found that fixation with formaldehyde tended to disconnect their protrusions (Supplementary Fig. 5), indicating that caution must be taken in defining morphology using fixed cells. The protrusions of all isolated and highly enriched Promethearchaeota3,4,5 were observed to physically attach to syntrophic partners. For HC1 and SC1, helical filaments on the protrusion surface tended to be found at the protrusion–partner interface (Fig. 2d,e, Extended Data Figs. 2e,f and 3g–j and Supplementary Note 7). Given the consistent presence of protrusions in Promethearchaeota cultures, we suspect that LAECA also probably possessed such structures.

We further microscopically investigated whether these Hodarchaeales strains have a complex eukaryote-like internal system. The eukaryote endomembrane system is characterized with universally conserved, physically persistent organelles (the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum) and structurally transient compartments (such as Golgi apparatus and lysosomes), all integrated by regulated membrane trafficking. Based on transmission EM (TEM) and cryo-EM, we did not observe any persistent internal membrane structures shared among all HC1 or SC1 cells (Fig. 2g,h,k,l, Extended Data Figs. 2h–j and 3k,l,t,u,w and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). Meanwhile, although infrequent, low-electron-density intracellular vesicle-like structures were observed in some cells (Fig. 2m,n, Extended Data Fig. 3m,n,v and Supplementary Video 1). This indicates the absence of persistent eukaryote-like organelles and presence of transient internal structures. Consistent with this, a Heimdallarchaeales archaeon (‘Candidatus Yibarchaeum umbracryptum’) enriched by a recent study lacked persistent organelles and possessed transient intracellular vesicles of unknown function that appeared during early growth stages40. With current data, it is unclear whether the transient structures are related to ESPs, a primitive endomembrane system, or neither.

Despite the absence of conserved internal membrane structures, nearly all HC1 and SC1 cells showed spatial separation between DNA and rRNA based on fluorescence microscopy using DAPI and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) (Fig. 2i, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Video 5), as also previously observed in other Promethearchaeia and Heimdallarchaeia41,42. The reason for this spatial localization is not yet clear, but histones may mediate DNA compaction43. All microscopically studied Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeales—albeit three strains only—consistently lack conserved, persistent eukaryote-like organelles. Despite this cell architecture, HC1 and SC1 have a comparable number of ESPs associated with endosomal sorting and trafficking (11 and 10 out of 34 types) to other Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeia (10 ± 2 and 10 ± 2 types on average, respectively) (Supplementary Table 7). These suggest that other extant Heimdallarchaeia may also lack persistent internal structures. Given that only 9 out of 34 of the endosomal sorting and trafficking-related ESP types are moderately conserved across Heimdallarchaeia (found in at least 50% of the genomes associated with each order), LAECA may have also possessed few such ESPs. Although this suggests the possibility that LAECA also lacked persistent internal cell structure, the genomic composition of LAECA remains to be resolved.

The HC1 co-culture and SC1 tri-culture both contain H2-using methanogenic archaea, and addition of the methanogenesis inhibitor 2-bromoethanesulfonate (10 mM) to the cultures completely suppressed growth. This shows that both HC1 and SC1 depend on H2-mediated symbiosis with methanogens. Such a metabolic symbiosis is known as syntrophy, in which an organotroph performs a hydrogen and/or formate-yielding metabolism that is thermodynamically inhibited by these products and a partner organism scavenges these products to low non-inhibitory concentrations44. Accordingly, amending high concentrations of hydrogen gas or formate also suppressed the growth of both strains (Supplementary Table 9). In the SC1 tri-culture, we detected a methanogen that uses only methylated compounds, Methanolobus sp. MLB, and suspect that SC1 may generate methanol through formate reduction through the expressed aldehyde reductase and alcohol dehydrogenase (Supplementary Table 6), a recently discovered pathway and phenomenon45. Given that syntrophy and symbiosis have been hypothesized to be relevant to the origin of eukaryotes4,12,23, the identification of these features in Heimadallarchaeia has major evolutionary implications.

Both strains are clearly dependent on peptides, as supplementation with non-proteinaceous substrates did not stimulate growth of HC1 and SC1, and neither strain could grow when peptide substrates were replaced with a mixture of 20 proteinogenic amino acids (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 9). Ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC)-based analysis of macromolecule distributions in the cultures indicated clear consumption of higher-molecular-mass molecules (Fig. 3b,c, Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Note 8). Genome analyses revealed that both strains encode extracellular peptidases, peptide transporters, amino acid degradation pathways of glutamate, aspartate, threonine, methionine, glycine, serine, alanine and cysteine in both strains, and NiFe hydrogenases for syntrophic peptide degradation (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). Energy is conserved through ATP synthesis through substrate-level phosphorylation and proton motive force generation coupled with ferredoxin-driven H2 generation (Fig. 4). Transcriptomic and proteomic data further confirmed their expression (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). Glycoproteomics revealed that peptide/nickel transport system substrate-binding proteins of both strains were highly N-glycosylated like P. syntrophicum MK-D146 (Extended Data Fig. 8, Supplementary Table 8 and Supplementary Note 10), further evidencing the importance of peptides for the growth of these strains. Collectively, we demonstrate that both strains are obligately syntrophy-dependent peptidotrophic archaea.
