Gene-expression signature scores for WNT expression, comprising all 19 WNT ligand genes, hot tumour signatures, CAF signatures and stem-like T cell signatures were calculated from normalized expression matrices using predefined gene sets. Expression values for INHBA and LRP6 were extracted directly from the same normalized expression matrices.

To define target tumours for downstream analysis, tumours were first filtered using predefined cutoff values for WNT expression, hot tumour signatures and CAF signature scores. Tumours exceeding the defined thresholds for all three features were included in the target-positive cohort. In this cohort, k-means clustering was performed with k = 2 using three variables: stem-like T cell signature score, INHBA expression and LRP6 expression. For each cancer type, WNT expression, stem-like T cell signature scores, INHBA expression and LRP6 expression were compared between the two identified groups.

Public bulk tumour transcriptomic datasets from patients treated with ICIs were collected across three solid cancer types: gastric cancer, lung cancer and ovarian cancer. The following datasets from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and GEO were analysed: ENA: PRJEB25780 (ref. 81) for gastric cancer; GEO: GSE126044 (ref. 82), GSE274975 (ref. 83) and GSE248378 (refs. 84,85) for lung cancer; and GSE188249 (ref. 86) and GSE206422 (ref. 87) for ovarian cancer. Where applicable, curated immunotherapy transcriptomic resources, including TIGER88, were used to obtain or cross-check expression matrices and response annotations.

For each cohort, pretreatment or baseline tumour bulk expression profiles and clinical response annotations were obtained from the corresponding public repositories or processed data resources. Gene identifiers were harmonized to official gene symbols before downstream analyses. Clinical responses were converted into binary response groups according to the annotations provided in each source dataset. Complete response, partial response and pathological complete response were classified as responders, whereas stable disease, progressive disease and non-pathological complete response were classified as non-responders. Samples without evaluable binary response annotations were excluded.

Gene-expression signature scores were calculated using within-cohort gene-wise z score normalization. For each signature, genes available in the expression matrix were z-score-normalized across samples and averaged to generate a sample-level score. WNT expression was calculated using all 19 WNT ligand genes, and stem-like T cell signature scores were calculated using established markers of stem-like and progenitor-exhausted T cells22,29,46,47,48. INHBA and LRP6 were analysed as individual gene-level features and were z-score-normalized in each cohort.

Samples in each cancer type were retained if their WNT expression score was above the 10th percentile of the corresponding cancer-specific pooled cohort. An integrated joint score was calculated to quantify coordinated enrichment of stem-like T cell, INHBA and LRP6 features. For each cohort, percentile ranks were calculated for the stem-like T cell score, INHBA z score and LRP6 z score, and summed to generate the integrated joint score.

scRNA-seq datasets from four cancer cohorts obtained from the GEO were analysed: gastric cancer (GSE206785)89, lung cancer (GSE131907)90, ovarian cancer (GSE192898)91 and prostate cancer (GSE176031)92. For each cohort, cell-level expression matrices were merged with metadata containing patient identifiers and publication-derived cell-type annotations. Cell-type labels were harmonized across datasets into major compartments, including tumour and epithelial cells, fibroblasts and CAFs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells, T cells, B cells, NK cells, plasma cells, mast cells and other cells.

For each patient, tumour WNT expression was quantified as the mean expression of all 19 WNT ligand genes in tumour cells. Patients with evaluable tumour WNT expression were retained for downstream analyses. In these target patients, CAF-associated INHBA and LRP6 features were quantified as the proportions of CAF and fibroblast cells expressing INHBA, expressing LRP6 or co-expressing both INHBA and LRP6. The proportion of stem-like CD8+ T cells was quantified as the proportion of CD8+ T cells expressing stem-like signatures.

In each cancer cohort, patients were stratified into high and low groups using a composite score calculated on the basis of the proportion of stem-like CD8+ T cells and the proportion of INHBA+LRP6+ CAFs. For each cohort, patient-level heatmaps were generated using tumour WNT expression, stem-like CD8+ T cell proportion, INHBA+ CAF proportion, LRP6+ CAF proportion and INHBA+LRP6+ CAF proportion. Values were z-score-normalized in each cohort for visualization. Patients were ordered by group and tumour WNT expression. Cell-type-level heatmaps for INHBA and LRP6 were generated across the four cancer cohorts using the union of cell types observed across cohorts, with missing cell types indicated separately.

Total RNA was extracted using a RNeasy Plus Mini kit (Qiagen). First-strand cDNA was synthesized using a High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription kit (Applied Biosystems) using oligo(dT) primers. RT–qPCR was performed using SYBR Green Supermix (Applied Biosystems) in a One-Step Cycler (Applied Biosystems). Gene expression was normalized to GAPDH.

Samples were rinsed in PBS, fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 24 h at 4 °C on a rotator and paraffin-embedded. For RCC organoids, specimens were first embedded in 3% agarose to form agarose blocks, fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 24 h at 4 °C on a rotator and then processed for paraffin embedding. Paraffin blocks were sectioned at 4 µm on a rotary microtome and stained with H&E for histopathological evaluation.

For frozen sections, samples were washed twice with PBS and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min at 4 °C. Samples were embedded in OCT compound (Leica), and 10–25 µm sections were cut on a Leica CM1860 cryostat. Sections were post-fixed in 4% PFA for 15 min at 4 °C, washed 3 times in PBS and blocked for 1 h at room temperature in PBS containing 0.25% Triton X-100 (PBS-T) and 2% goat serum. The following primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer were applied overnight at 4 °C in a humidified chamber: rabbit anti-CA9 (1:400, Novus), rabbit anti-TCF1 (1:300, Cell Signaling), mouse anti-COL1A1 (1:200, Cell Signaling), rabbit anti-CD8 (1:200, Abcam), rat anti-CD8 (1:200, Invitrogen), mouse anti-pan-keratin (1:400, Cell Signaling), chicken anti-vimentin (1:500, Millipore), mouse anti-αSMA (1:200, Abcam), rat anti-KRT8/18 (1:500, DSHB), rabbit anti-CD45 (1:200, Abcam), rabbit anti-LRP6 (1:200, Invitrogen) and rabbit anti-cleaved caspase-3 (1:200, Cell Signaling). After 3 washes in PBS-T, sections were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with Alexa Fluor–conjugated secondary antibodies (488, 594, 633 or 647; 1:1,000 in PBS-T) together with DAPI, washed twice in PBS-T and mounted using ProLong Gold (Invitrogen).

For paraffin sections, deparaffinized sections underwent heat-mediated antigen retrieval in 10 mM Tris-EDTA buffer (pH 9.0) at 60 °C overnight and were cooled to room temperature. After 3 washes in PBS-T, sections were blocked for 1 h at room temperature in blocking buffer, incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies diluted in the same buffer, washed 3 times and incubated for 1 h at room temperature with the appropriate secondary antibodies (1:1,000 in PBS-T) and DAPI. Slides were washed and mounted using ProLong Gold.

For whole-mount staining, samples were fixed in 4% PFA for 15 min at room temperature, washed 3 times in PBS and blocked in PBS-T containing 2% goat serum for 4 h at room temperature with gentle agitation. Samples were incubated with primary antibodies for 24 h at room temperature with agitation, washed 3 times (1 h each) in PBS-T and incubated with secondary antibodies and/or 2 µM CellEvent Caspase-3/7 Detection reagent (Invitrogen) plus DAPI. After two final PBS-T washes, samples were imaged by fluorescence microscopy.

Fluorescence images were analysed using NIS-Elements BR software (v.6.02). Flow cytometry data were analysed using FlowJo (v.10.10.0). Statistical analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism (v.10). P < 0.05 was considered significant.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The Degust web application (Degust Classic v.3.1.0; https://degust.erc.monash.edu/) was used for differential gene expression analysis. Gene ontology enrichment analysis was performed using the Gene Ontology web resource (http://geneontology.org/)77 with versions archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14083199, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17382285 and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19377705)78,79,80. The Visium spatial transcriptomic data from previously published RCC tissue samples were obtained from the GEO database under the following accession codes: GSM6415705 (ref. 40) for responder samples and GSM5924038 (ref. 41) for non-responder samples. Public TCGA bulk RNA-seq data and clinical annotations for gastric cancer, lung cancer, ovarian cancer and prostate cancer were obtained from the UCSC Xena platform using the TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas dataset (https://xena.ucsc.edu/). The following public bulk RNA-seq datasets from patients treated with ICIs were obtained from the ENA and GEO: ENA: PRJEB25780 (ref. 81); GEO: GSE126044 (ref. 82), GSE274975 (ref. 83), GSE248378 (refs. 84,85), GSE188249 (ref. 86) and GSE206422 (ref. 87). The following public scRNA-seq datasets used for cross-cancer analyses were obtained from the GEO: GSE206785 (ref. 89), GSE131907 (ref. 90), GSE192898 (ref. 91) and GSE176031 (ref. 92). scRNA-seq, RNA-seq and GeoMx data have been deposited into the publicly accessible Korea BioData System (K-BDS) database under the following accession codes: KAP242588 (scRNA-seq data), KAP242587 (bulk RNA-seq data) and KAP242586 (GeoMx data). Processed whole-exome sequencing data, including mutation calls and summary tables, are provided in the Supplementary Data. All other data supporting the findings of this study are available in this paper. Source data are provided with this paper.

a, Schematic of patient-specific RCC assembloid generation. CA9+ and CA9− cells, CAFs and TII cells were isolated from pretreatment RCC tissues, reconstituted at patient-matched ratios and cultured on a shaker for 7 days. Histopathology, mutational profiles, cellular composition and transcriptomic profiles of assembloids were compared with those of the corresponding parental tumours. Assembloids were then treated with anti-PD-1, and in vitro responses were compared with each patient’s clinical outcome to ICI therapy. b, Schematic workflow for the establishment and maintenance of RCC-derived cultures. For tumour cells, dissociated single-cell suspensions were separated into CA9+ and CA9− populations, each embedded in Matrigel to generate and maintain CA9+ and CA9− organoids, respectively. CAFs were isolated as adherent spindle-shaped cells and expanded in adherent culture. TII cells were maintained and expanded in suspension/adherent culture. c, Representative immunofluorescence images of RCC organoids established without separating CA9+ and CA9− cells at an early stage of culture (top) and maintained in prolonged culture (bottom). Scale bars, 100 μm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. d, Representative immunofluorescence images of CA9+ (top) and CA9− (bottom) RCC organoids, with corresponding H&E staining. Scale bars, 100 µm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. e, Oncoplot showing somatic mutations identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. f, Relative fractions of six base substitution types identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. g, Variant-class composition of somatic mutations identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations. h, TMB in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. CR, complete response; NED, no evidence of disease; PD, progressive disease; PR, partial response; SD, stable disease.

a, Representative immunofluorescence images of patient-derived CAFs. Scale bars, 100 μm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. b, Gating strategy for the analysis of CAFs. c, Flow cytometry plots of primary CAFs from RCC tissues (top) and cultured CAFs (bottom). Three technical replicates were analysed per group (n = 3). d, Heatmaps showing the relative expression of representative myCAF, iCAF and apCAF marker genes in primary and cultured CAFs derived from six RCC patients, as assessed by RT–qPCR. For box plots (d,g,m,n), centre lines indicate medians, box limits indicate the interquartile range and whiskers extend to the most extreme data points within 1.5 × the interquartile range.

In this study, we identified dynamic interactions among tumour cells, CAFs and CD8+ T cells that determine tumour responses to ICIs in human RCC. CAF-derived activin A promotes the maintenance and expansion of the TCF1+ stem-like CD8+ T cell pool in inflamed tumours, thereby establishing a responding hot tumour state. In this setting, tumour-derived WNT2B induces activin A production in LRP6-positive CAFs, which in turn sustains CD8+ T cell stemness and drives expansion of the stem-like T cell pool. By contrast, when activin A expression is minimal or absent in inflamed settings due to the presence of tumour-adjacent LRP6-deficient CAFs, it fails to sustain CD8+ T cell stemness, resulting in non-responding hot tumours and resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy.

#1321. A chip off the old block? Wayne Rooney's son Kai, 16, is dazzling in Man United's academy after scoring FOUR goals in a game - insiders reveal the secrets behind his rise

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 07:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 07:06 EDT, 1 November 2026

Just over 24 years ago, a 16-year-old footballing phenomenon called Wayne Rooney made his mark with that goal for Everton against Arsenal.

Fast-forward to now and his eldest son, Kai, enhanced his burgeoning reputation while in action for Manchester United's Under 18s on Tuesday.

The 16-year-old, who turns 17 on Monday, scored four goals for the young Red Devils in a 6-0 thrashing of Burnley's U18s in the Under-18 Premier League North.

His four goals showed his repertoire of skills as the forward scored two with his preferred left foot, one with his head and the other a fine run that was finished with his right foot.

His four goals came in 44 minutes across half-time - with the latter three coming in a devastating 15-minute second-half spell (49, 63 and 66 minutes).

As Manchester United's own match report on their website details the teenager 'was the star of a clinical showing after the break from Darren Fletcher's side'.

Kai Rooney opens the scoring at Burnley for our #MUAcademy U18s 💪Watch live coverage on MUTV ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/KFr8B2hWNY

Kai Rooney scored four goals for Manchester United U18s as they thrashed Burnley U18s 6-0

One of his goals came was a penalty during Tuesday's Under-18 Premier League North fixture

Rooney's father Wayne scored that goal against Arsenal as a 16-year-old for Everton in 2002

Rooney then followed that performance with another goal in Saturday's comeback 4-1 win at Blackburn Rovers U18s, although he was later sent off for two bookable offences.

Just like his dad Wayne, Kai is fixated on football and is following in his father's footsteps in a number of ways.

As detailed by Daily Mail Sport in January, one of those is with regards to diet.

Akin to his famous father - who is United's all-time record goalscorer - in his Old Trafford heyday, Rooney Jr eats plenty of carbohydrates two days before a game. This then changes to salmon and rice followed by rice pudding the night before matches.

His dietary discipline has been recognised by those within the United academy - who are impressed by Rooney's focus.

The teenager does allow himself some respite at times though with the family's go-to is Chinese takeaway 'WowYauChow' in Altrincham. As revealed in Manchester United Confidential, crispy chilli beef is a particular favourite of the rising footballer.

Cooking has also become a passion for Rooney off-the-pitch and he is also fluent in Spanish - a trait that will only stand him in good stead in the multicultural world of football.

Rooney has had to deal with accusations of nepotism, due to the legendary figure of who his dad is, but he has always wanted to form his own path - even from a younger age than he is now.

'Kai told Wayne to stop coming to football games when he played grassroots tournaments and stuff, because he used to get swarmed, and he couldn't even watch the game,' his mum Coleen explained during her time in the I'm A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here! jungle almost two years ago.

Kai is pictured with parents Coleen and Wayne signing his Man United contract when younger

Rooney is fixated with football like his father but wants to forge his own career within the sport

'How do you say to all of these kids, "Go away, I'm watching my son?" Adults, it's different, you could speak to them, so he [Kai] just said, "Oh, dad, there's no point you coming because you don't even watch me play anyway". Which is sad, but it can't be helped.'

Speaking in August 2024, Rooney underlined that he is intent on doing things his own way.

'I'm trying to make a name for myself, not try and be my dad because I'm my own person,' Kai said back in August 2024.

'I want to see how my career goes, obviously try to do the best I can and try to reach the biggest stages.

'I'm just focusing on me and to try to not let any pressure get to me and just keep working on me day by day, month by month.'

Rooney Jr has copied his father's diet when he was a professional - which includes salmon

His parents, meanwhile, have been keen to stress that they are keeping the pressure off their young son.

'He has great coaches at Manchester United, so I take a stand-off approach,' Wayne told the BBC last year.

'I speak to him, but for me it’s all about his mentality and his mindset, to make sure he keeps enjoying it – that’s the main thing for me.'

Meanwhile Coleen told The Times earlier this year: 'He’s lived it (being Wayne's son) from a young age. When we used to go to matches when he was younger, he’d get a lot of people coming up saying, "Oh, are you Wayne Rooney’s son?"

'But he’s strong-minded, always has been. I’ve got no worries in the way he deals with it.'

A Puma ambassador since he was 12, Kai used to play football in laceless boots after previously breaking both of his feet.

The youngster was signed up by Puma at the age of 12 - and has pursued a football career

Against Burnley his boots had laces as he tied his opponents in knots, something he will look to continue to do as he makes his own way in the game.

And while replicating his father seems fanciful, the iconic 'remember the name' piece of commentary could be updated for Kai in the future.

#1320. Athletic Club academy trio score first senior goals in 6-1 Copa del Rey win at Prat

Three academy players scored their first goals for Athletic Club's senior side inside four minutes as Edin Terzić's team beat Prat 6-1 in the Copa del Rey. The late burst came from substitutes in a side rotated with the Basque derby in mind.

On Thursday 29 October, Athletic met Prat in the Copa del Rey round of 128. The tie was played at the Estadi La Feixa Llarga in L’Hospitalet de Llobregat. Its closing stages belonged to Athletic’s academy.

Each of the late scorers had come off the bench. Selton Sánchez finished the night with the sixth goal, teed up by Vizcay, whose own strike had started the flurry.

Aritz Conde earned an 8.2 rating from the data provider for his half-hour on the pitch. Imga, aged just 17, had made his first-team debut alongside Vizcay against Getafe the previous Sunday.

#1318. FIFA awards inaugural Women's Club World Cup in 2028 to United States

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The United States will play host to another major women's soccer tournament. FIFA announced that the inaugural FIFA Women's Club World Cup will be held in the U.S. in January 2028, giving the country another marquee event for the women's game.

The flagship quadrennial tournament will begin Jan. 5 and run through Jan. 30, and it will feature 19 of the world's best clubs across six confederations. It will be the third flagship competition hosted in the United States for the foreseeable future.

The choice of the United States was no accident. The country is coming off co-hosting a record-setting 2026 FIFA Men's World Cup and will host the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

FIFA Chief Women's Football Officer Dame Sarai Bareman said the governing body ran a detailed assessment before settling on a host, and the American bid came out on top.

"We undertook a detailed assessment to identify the most suitable host for the inaugural edition of the FIFA Women's Club World Cup," said Bareman.

"Ultimately, the United States' recent excellence in staging top FIFA tournaments, combined with the significant interest in women's football there plus its elite sporting infrastructure, made the country the standout option. Alongside the vibrant and passionate women's football ecosystem in the United States, the qualified clubs, government, host cities, our commercial and media partners, and more, our mission will be to set an impressive standard for global women's club football and a benchmark for the future."

The timing seems to fit a larger picture. With Los Angeles as host of the 2028 Summer Games, and the Women's Club World Cup set to kick off the year in January, American soccer fans will have another stacked calendar of football to partake in as the best clubs and national teams compete in winter and summer tournaments.

Looking further ahead, the United States is on track to host the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup and hosted the men's Club World Cup in 2025. No official announcement has been made on that tournament, but the U.S. Soccer Federation launched a bid alongside co-hosts Mexico, Costa Rica, and Jamaica for the next World Cup, and they are currently leading an uncontested bid.

The 2031 tournament will be an expanded format, welcoming 48 teams for the first time. An official vote by the FIFA Congress is expected by Nov. 23 in Zurich. The initial bid of host cities has already expanded, with recent additions of Chicago and Portland.

Already home to two first-division women's pro soccer leagues, the NWSL and Gainbridge Super League, the United States remains a model for club, national team, and tournament standards. Excitement around a future World Cup, the Olympics, and now a Women's Club World Cup cements the country as a go-to destination for women's tournament soccer from club competitions to the national-team stage.

For the sport and the women's game, there are logistical stakes at play. A successful first edition of the Women's Club World Cup could set standards for how club soccer is marketed, packaged, and watched worldwide.

Seven teams have already qualified for the upcoming tournament, setting the tone for some of the world's most iconic football brands, including Arsenal (England), FC Barcelona (Spain), and Club América (Mexico). Gotham FC (USA), SC Corinthians (Brazil), Wuhan Jiangda WFC (China PR), and Naegohyang Women's FC (DPR Korea) round out the primary seven qualified teams.

That group blends traditional European powers with champions from across the globe, including a U.S.-based side Gotham FC and rising global powerhouse Club America from Mexico.

"These seven clubs, and a dozen more, will come together to show the strength and depth of women's club football to a global audience," said Bareman. "They will have the opportunity to tell their story, expand their fan base and represent their club on the world stage. They have thoroughly earned this opportunity to be part of history in the United States."

The complete confederation slots for the Club World Cup:

FIFA will prioritize continental champions from seasons ending in 2024 to 2027, in line with the FIFA council's previous decision on how clubs qualify for the inaugural Club World Cup. FIFA plans to work with confederations to establish club ranking methodologies based on sporting merit, and existing Concacaf and UEFA mechanisms will apply to those respective confederations for the inaugural edition.

With six qualifying slots for UEFA, the premier club competition champion qualifies, and the remaining spots are determined by club rankings. A cap of two clubs per member association typically applies, unless more than two clubs from the same country have won the UEFA Women's Champions League in the window.

Confederations with fewer than four slots will send their highest-ranked clubs from their respective premier competitions, with no country cap.

FIFA will review the access framework after the 2028 edition.

Closer than the 2028 Club World Cup is the 2027 FIFA Women's Champions Cup. The second edition of FIFA's tournament for the six continental champions following the years between the Women's Club World Cup. The FIFA council moved to increase visibility by changing the semifinal dates.

The semifinals in Miami, Florida, will now be played on consecutive days at Nu Stadium, home of Inter Miami CF. On January 26, Club America will meet the winners of the AFC, CAF, or OFC round two tie. FC Barcelona will then face the winners for CONMEBOL's Libertadores Femenina on Janu. 27. The third-place match and championship final will feature as a double-header on Jan. 31.

Finally, the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil earned a significant financial boost following the meeting. The first-ever Women's World Cup tournament hosted in South America will receive increased financial distribution. Players, clubs, and member associations will receive the increases, including preparation money of $2.5 million -- matching the 2026 men's World Cup. The total amount was $1 million increase from the 2023 Women's World Cup.

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he launched a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a big game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

That Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

#1312. Athletic end Real Sociedad’s four-game league run as visitors protest Berenguer penalty

Athletic Club beat Real Sociedad 2-1 at San Mamés on Sunday 1 November to end their rivals' run of four straight league wins. The visitors have formally disputed the first-half penalty that decided the derby, while Athletic lost another striker to injury.

Every goal in the Bilbao derby arrived before half-time.

Nico Williams provided the assist for the opening goal. Luka Sučić equalised on the half-hour. A crowd of 50,092 watched the game.

Before kick-off, Unai Simón presented his Yashin Trophy to the home crowd. A minute’s silence was also held for the victims of the Urda rail accident.

The visitors left Bilbao angry about the decisive spot-kick. In its official match report, Real Sociedad called it a penalty that never was and criticised VAR for not stepping in. The club statement added that the chip inside the match ball shows Jon Aramburu made contact with the ball in his challenge on Nico Williams.

Pellegrino Matarazzo said that for him it was clearly not a penalty. The Real Sociedad coach could not understand why VAR had not intervened to cancel it. He was booked for dissent in the 65th minute, a minute after Mamadou Sarr received a yellow card for the same offence. Referee Alejandro Hernandez showed Real Sociedad four yellow cards in total, against two for Athletic.

The statistics point in two directions. Real Sociedad dominated the ball, completing 514 accurate passes to Athletic’s 307. Terzić’s side created the clearer chances, however. Unai Simón made four saves, while Álex Remiro made one. Sučić was the highest-rated player on the pitch at 7.52.

The victory came at a cost. Maroan Sannadi felt his hamstring early in the game. Athletic will need one or two more days to know how long he will be out. His injury follows Gorka Guruzeta’s serious knee injury at Valencia on 17 October, which left the squad short of strikers.

With 83 minutes on the pitch, Navarro created four key passes and was rated 7.2.

The win was Athletic’s third in a row across all competitions, after a 6-1 victory over Prat and a 4-0 win against Getafe. They sit seventh, two points behind Sevilla. Real Betis are four points clear of Real Sociedad.

#1311. Coventry heap more misery on Sunderland: Insipid Black Cats hit new low to leave Regis Le Bris looking haunted by grim prospect of relegation after 3-1 defeat

Published: 13:38 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 08:38 EDT, 1 November 2026

Call it a horror show that left Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris looking increasingly haunted and clinging a little less securely to his job.

Brand it the stuff of nightmares for the furious supporters who made the long journey back to the north-east fearing relegation.

Roll out the clichés because they all apply after this ghoulish display had Le Bris and his players well and truly spooked.

It was x-rated stuff from insipid Sunderland in what had been billed as an early-season relegation shoot-out.

They lacked intensity, were a shambles defensively and remain rock-bottom after being well beaten by a Coventry side who deserved everything they got.

As the ska classic Ghost Town by legendary Coventry band The Specials boomed out over the public address system, it was Sunderland who were left looking like dead men.

Jack Rudoni (right) was the key man again for Coventry as they dismantled Sunderland

Regis Le Bris's side remain bottom of the Premier League with their season looking bleak

Le Bris said: 'Are we in a relegation scrap? It’s obvious when you look at the table.

'Are we worried? Always. It’s football and you can’t relax.

'We won’t give up just because it’s a bit tough. I feel the unity of the club and the players.'

Coventry’s acclimatisation to the Premier League after 25 years away has not been plain sailing.

Frank Lampard’s men are clearly a united force, however, and that togetherness harvested back-to-back victories at Nottingham Forest and home to Newcastle a few weeks ago.

A reality check came with defeats at Tottenham and a 1-0 reverse to Fulham here last weekend when the Sky Blues were booed off.

But they were comfortably the better side against Sunderland as they chiselled out a third win from five Premier League games.

They led in the 17th minute when Tatsuhiro Sakamoto produced a stunning left-foot finish which flew into the net after Sunderland failed miserably to clear their lines.

The manner in which Taiwo Awoniyi strode through the Sunderland rearguard to fire home and double Coventry’s lead 20 minutes later was far more shocking.

Sunderland fans booed their team off at the break but things got worse in the 52nd minute when Jack Rudoni’s deflected left-foot strike beat Robin Roefs.

Frank Lampard's side now have three wins this season after 25 years away from the league

Could Coventry beat the drop? You would have your doubts.

But only a fool would turn his back on the Sky Blues now.

There is too much energy, and too much drive, coursing through the veins of a football club with momentum behind it.

Lampard, whose side climbed out of the drop zone, said: 'I’m very happy with the energy we showed and the quality in the goals we scored.

'The positivity in the performance rubbed off on the stadium. It’s a nice feeling to be out of the bottom three but things can change very quickly and there’s such a long way to go.'

Sunderland, let it be remembered, finished seventh last season and qualified for Europe for the first time in 53 years.

But second-season syndrome is threatening to hit the Wearsiders like a tonne of bricks.

During the first half, they created precious little as Brian Brobbey scuffed a low shot wide when Coventry led 1-0.

That felt like a big moment and they finally got off the mark in the 67th minute through Enzo Le Fee’s penalty after Ethan Pinnock’s handball.

But it never looked anything else but consolation for Sunderland, whose supporters made their feelings clear, although many had cleared off long before the end.

Le Bris said: 'It’s normal to react like this but I know they believe in the club and we’ll stick together.'

It is now one win in nine for the Black Cats, who look a pale shadow of the side who had 17 points at this stage last season.

Sunderland look a shadow of the side that finished seventh in their first year back last year

If Coventry are to defy the odds and beat the drop this season, the influence of Rudoni will be crucial.

The midfielder's educated left boot again proved an important weapon for his team and he is likely to be attracting admiring glances from some higher-placed clubs.

He scored a goal and was in the thick of things when Alderete was sent off in the closing stages.

Rudoni's technical qualities are certainly of the Premier League and he should not be short of offers if Lampard's men fail to beat the drop.

#1310. Vincent Kompany hospitalized after collapsing at Bayern Munich training ground

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany was hospitalized after collapsing on Friday. The Belgian coach collapsed following a training session and reportedly required emergency transport. According to BILD, a rescue helicopter landed at the training ground earlier in the day. Kompany's need to go to the hospital was announced by the club on Friday afternoon.

"Vincent Kompany had to seek medical treatment on Friday after collapsing during training for FC Bayern's second team," the statement said. "The first-team coach had been watching the second team's session. Kompany will undergo thorough examination in the hospital and remain in medical care. For the time being, his coaching staff will manage training and match operations."

Kompany also missed sessions on Monday and Tuesday ahead of the club's Champions League fixture against Arsenal, which were overseen by assistant coach Aaron Danks. The 40-year-old contracted a viral infection last week and skipped post-match interviews after Bayern's 6-1 victory over RB Leipzig, though he still managed the match from the sidelines. Danks confirmed in a pre-game news conference that the virus had affected Kompany's legs, with the manager feeling pain in them. It's not known if that same virus has any relation to Friday's collapse.

It's not the first medical emergency that Bayern have dealt with this season as midfielder Jamal Musiala had also collapsed due to microseizures related to a neurological dysfunction. During preseason, he went down off the ball after playing five minutes before needing to receive medical treatment.

Next up, Bayern Munich will face Freiburg in the Bundesliga on Sunday. Currently undefeated to start the season, they are level atop the league table with Borussia Dortmund while sitting 14th in the Champions League standings.

#1309. Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits2, prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions3,4,5. Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

Emotion regulation is a core determinant of mental and physical health1. It encompasses the strategies that people use, intentionally or automatically, to influence their emotional experience. Among these, cognitive reappraisal—changing the interpretation of a situation to alter its emotional impact—has received particular attention in psychology, psychiatry and the broader public. It is central to cognitive-behavioural therapy and linked to resilience, lower symptom burden and improved daily affect1.

Neuroimaging studies have extensively mapped the neural basis of reappraisal. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) consistently implicates a network of lateral and medial prefrontal regions, often along with reduced amygdala activation during reappraisal of negative stimuli2. These findings have informed neuromodulatory interventions for emotion regulation deficits6,7,8. Still, they are based primarily on within-person designs that contrast experimental conditions such as ‘reappraise’ versus ‘view without regulation’ in the same individuals, and many studies and broader theories extend these neural within-person mechanisms to explain between-person individual differences in well-being or psychopathology4,5. This extension is not necessarily warranted.

Extending within-person neural mechanisms to explain between-person differences risks the ecological fallacy9: associations at one level need not hold at the other. For instance, people who habitually use reappraisal report better well-being than others. However, in daily life, reappraisal often occurs in response to stressors and may therefore coincide with worse-than-average momentary mood.

Compounding this, prefrontal regions that are engaged during reappraisal also participate in working memory, response selection and pain processing10—limiting their specificity as emotion-related markers of regulatory function. Task designs, moreover, may not mirror naturalistic regulation, raising questions about ecological validity and relevance for individual-difference research11,12. A recent systematic review found partial effect convergence in prefrontal and amygdala circuits, but studies were underpowered13 (median n = 25) and too heterogeneous for formal meta-analysis3. In turn, meta-analyses on reappraisal in mental disorders have yielded mixed results, with inconsistent findings in the prefrontal cortex4,14,15.

To resolve this, we conducted a preregistered consortium analysis of 40 fMRI datasets on the neurobiology of emotion regulation capacity (NIDER consortium; n = 2,175;  Methods, ‘Consortium procedures’ and Supplementary Table 1)—approximately 20 times larger than previous efforts3—with sufficient power to detect even small between-person associations (r = 0.10; Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’). In this context, reappraisal capacity refers to individual differences in whether, and how effectively, people use reappraisal to reduce negative affect. We focused on three widely used indices that are often assumed to reflect related facets of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation during reappraisal. Prior work has linked these three indices with each other and with prefrontal activity during reappraisal3,16,17,18,19. To our knowledge, this assumption has not been tested at scale. Notably, the most widely used trait questionnaires are generally understood to index self-reported habitual tendencies to reappraise rather than the ability to implement reappraisal. We nonetheless included them given their proposed functional link to such ability16,17,18 and their widespread use.

We explored whether the three indices converge on a shared core, and whether any of them relate to activity in canonical emotion regulation circuits during common reappraisal tasks2. Our findings have direct implications for neuromodulatory interventions, biomarker development and the validity of individual-difference research in affective neuroscience.

In a first step, we aimed to assess the overlap between the three main indices of cognitive reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation. If these three indices represent a similar core construct, or are otherwise functionally related, they should show a meaningful association. Individual consortium study teams calculated the correlations between the three indices of reappraisal capacity based on a standardized coding protocol using functionally predefined regions of interest, ensuring that higher values on each index indicate higher reappraisal capacity. Study-level results were aggregated with random-effects meta-analyses, which is statistically equivalent to person-level random-effects mega-analysis for the preregistered analyses and was intended to circumvent data sharing thresholds (Supplementary Methods, ‘Meta- vs mega-analytic approaches’). The evidence for null results was further quantified using Bayes factors (Methods, ‘Bayesian evidence’).

There was a statistically significant association between amygdala down-regulation and task-based affective ratings (P = 0.010; Table 1 and Forest plots in Extended Data Figs. 1–3). As hypothesized, participants with stronger down-regulation of the amygdala via cognitive reappraisal showed a better down-regulation of task-based affective ratings. Yet, the effect size was comparatively small (r = 0.08): To detect this effect size with a statistical power of 80%, a single study would need to test 1,105 participants (Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’).

There was no significant association between trait questionnaires and either outcome—that is, amygdala down-regulation or task-based affective ratings (P > 0.06, BF10 ≤ 0.16; Table 1). Confidence intervals ruled out even small effect sizes (r = 0.10), for which statistical power was above 88% given the maximal observed between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.07; Supplementary Fig. 1). The overlap (shared variance) between the three indices of cognitive reappraisal capacity is shown in Fig. 1, which indicates no shared overlap between all three. Bayes factors substantially favoured the null hypothesis for associations with trait questionnaires (BF10 ≤ 0.16). Between-study heterogeneity was not statistically significant in any of the three tests (P > 0.17) and was particularly small for the non-significant correlations (τ = 0.00 and 0.06), indicating that these null findings are unlikely to be explained by differences in study design.

Pairwise overlap between three widely used indices of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation. Overlap is shown as shared variance derived from the corresponding pairwise random-effects meta-analytic Pearson correlations, which are displayed next to each intersection. The correlations were: task-based affective ratings with amygdala down-regulation, r = 0.08, P = 0.010, k = 26, n = 1,377; trait questionnaires with task-based affective ratings, r = 0.05, P = 0.067, k = 28, n = 1,397; and trait questionnaires with amygdala down-regulation, r = 0.01, P = 0.807, k = 33, n = 1,833. All tests were two-sided and uncorrected.

All studies made use of trait questionnaires that primarily assess beliefs about habitual reappraisal use. Although relations to implementation ability, as measured by experiments, are theoretically and empirically expected16,17,18, trait questionnaires that directly measure beliefs about such abilities might show stronger associations. To test this, we performed a subsequent analysis based on three large studies that additionally administered modified versions of the emotion regulation questionnaire to capture such beliefs about abilities20. Fixed-effects meta-analysis confirmed that beliefs about habitual use and implementation ability are strongly related (r = 0.67; Table 1). Supporting the null results for habit questionnaires, there was substantial evidence against an association between these ability trait questionnaires and task-based affective ratings (BF10 = 0.13). By contrast, the association between trait ability questionnaires and amygdala down-regulation was statistically significant (P = 0.010), but in the opposite direction, meaning that beliefs in higher reappraisal capacity were related to less effective down-regulation of the amygdala. This represents strong evidence against an effect in the expected direction (one-sided BF10 = 0.05).

To address the second research question, we examined whether individual differences in the three reappraisal indices were systematically related to neural activity during cognitive reappraisal beyond the amygdala. We first tested these associations in canonical emotion regulation networks derived from prior meta-analytic work2 (Fig. 2a) and then complemented these confirmatory analyses with exploratory whole-brain analyses, both outlined in the preregistration (Methods, ‘Statistical analyses’). This strategy was intended to assess whether the three indices showed associations with established regulatory circuitries and whether any observed effects converged on overlapping or distinct neural regions.

Significant associations are shown at the whole-brain level after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q < 0.05, two-sided). All significant effects were negative. The shared colour bar indicates Pearson’s r, with more intense colours reflecting stronger negative correlations. The colour bar was truncated at −0.30 for visibility reasons, although larger negative correlations were frequent for amygdala down-regulation (d). For the full distribution of correlations with amygdala down-regulation, see Extended Data Fig. 5. In d, negative correlations reflect positive associations with amygdala responses during reappraisal as amygdala down-regulation was coded using the inverse contrast [view negative − reappraise negative]. Slices are displayed in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space: x = 4, y = 0, z = 0 (a); x = 4, y = 0, z = 0 (b); x = −44, y = 7, z = 4 (c); x = 0, y = 0, z = 0 (d). Anatomical backgrounds are based on the MNI152 template (© 1993–2009 Louis Collins, McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, Montreal Neurological Institute, McGill University).

There was no statistically significant association between trait questionnaires and neural activity during reappraisal (Fig. 2b). The correlations with average activity in the two predefined networks were negligibly small and the null hypothesis strongly favoured by Bayes factors (both |r| ≤ 0.03, P > 0.25, uncorrected, BF10 < 0.02; k = 37, n = 2,091). No voxels survived the correction for multiple comparisons in the voxel-wise networks of interest or the whole-brain approach. All brain-wide effect sizes were smaller than |r| = 0.11 (mean = −0.01, range −0.10 to 0.09).

These null results were stable when using a jackknife procedure—that is, no statistically significant voxels when repeating the meta-analysis while leaving out one study at a time. They were further supported by Bayesian posterior odds for voxels across the canonical emotion regulation networks2 (that is, Bayes factors corrected for multiple comparisons; Methods, ‘Bayesian evidence’). The null hypothesis was decisively favoured for 98% of voxels with odds over 100:1, there were no voxels with favourable odds for the existence of an effect, and only two voxels favoured the null in an ambiguous range below 3:1. The power to detect a small effect (r = 0.10) was 96% for average network responses (τ = 0.07). Power in voxel-wise analyses was mostly above 80% in simulated scenarios for this effect size, especially for the network of interest approach (Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’).

As in the previous section, a fixed-effects meta-analysis of three studies that provided trait questionnaires specifically targeting beliefs about ability yielded no statistically significant results (both a priori networks |r| < 0.04, P > 0.511, BF10 < 0.07, uncorrected; k = 3, n = 444). No voxels survived thresholding; all Bayesian posterior odds favoured the null hypothesis (mean = 0.00, range 0.00 to 0.25).

As for trait questionnaires, there was no statistically significant association between average down-regulation of task-based affective ratings and average neural activity during reappraisal in the preregistered regulatory networks, with strong support for the null hypothesis by Bayes factors (both |r| < 0.03, P > 0.22, BF10 < 0.03, uncorrected; k = 31, n = 1,958). No voxels within these networks survived correction for multiple comparisons in voxel-wise analyses.

Within canonical emotion regulation networks2, about 98% of voxels showed null effects that were decisively supported by Bayesian posterior odds (mean = 0.00, range 0.00 to 0.29), with only 12 voxels falling into an indecisive range (mean = 0.84, range 0.34 to 2.52). By contrast, five voxels in the brainstem (caudal pons) provided substantial evidence for an effect (mean = 7.31, range 4.84 to 13.89). Using uncorrected Bayesian posterior odds, evidence for effects was observed in 55 voxels exceeding 3:1 odds, including the amygdala (mean = 69.63, range 3.02 to 1,055.27). This pattern aligns with the uncorrected preregistered findings from the amygdala region-of-interest analyses (see ‘Divergence of capacity indices’).

For whole-brain analyses, the jackknife procedure indicated that results were highly sensitive to the inclusion of data from Brehl et al.21 (Extended Data Fig. 4), potentially owing to its large sample size in combination with study-specific effects (for example, data were collected in the context of the first COVID-19 outbreak). In the full analysis, a negative association with task-based affective ratings was observed in a cluster of 86 voxels outside the canonical regulatory networks. Excluding data from Brehl et al.21 increased the extent of significant voxels substantially to 587, mainly in sensorimotor and dorsal attention regions, with smaller clusters in visual cortex, caudate nucleus and brainstem (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Table 1). Across these regions, better down-regulation of negative emotions was associated with lower activation (mean = −0.11, range −0.16 to −0.09). Together, these results suggest that classically emotion-generating regions, but not emotion-regulating regions, are indicative of emotion regulation capacity, albeit with small effect sizes.

To facilitate the psychological interpretation of the significant neural activation pattern, we conducted automated meta-analytic decoding using Neurosynth, which quantifies the association between whole-brain activation maps and large-scale term-based meta-analytic patterns derived from the neuroimaging literature (for example, ‘pain’, ‘fear’ and ‘motoric’). Neurosynth decoding against 50 topic maps from 11,406 fMRI studies indicated that the meta-analytic activation map is most similar to language processing (‘comprehension’: r = 0.17, ‘sentence’: r = 0.16 and ‘semantic’: r = 0.14) and most dissimilar to sensorimotor processing, consistent with the deactivation observed in whole-brain analyses (‘hand’: r = −0.25, ‘movements’: r = −0.22, ‘motor’: r = −0.17).

Top-down theoretical models predict that effective reappraisal should be associated with lower amygdala and higher prefrontal responses—an opposing pattern. Between-person differences in overall brain responsivity12,22, however, could blur such regional specificity.

Contrary to theoretical predictions, participants with stronger amygdala responses during reappraisal also showed substantially stronger responses throughout the rest of the brain in the same contrast (mean r = 0.27, range −0.08 to 0.68; Extended Data Fig. 5; correlation signs are reversed in the figures because amygdala down-regulation was coded as [view negative − reappraise negative]). This included both regulatory networks (first: r = 0.29, P < 0.001; second: r = 0.24, P < 0.001; k = 35, n = 2,088) and more than 170,000 voxels brain-wide, with only a single voxel showing a negative correlation (Fig. 2d). A person with a larger amygdala response than others, therefore, also tends to show larger responses in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and elsewhere—making the expected opposing pattern almost undetectable with standard fMRI individual-difference analyses.

This pattern was not unique to the amygdala. For all pairs among 489 anatomical regions23 (Methods, ‘Inter-region correlations’) in an independent reappraisal dataset24 (n = 33), any two brain regions were on average highly correlated across participants (r = 0.58, s.d. = 0.18).This means that individuals who respond more strongly in one region tend to respond more strongly everywhere across the brain, compared with other people. Crucially, this was not specific to reappraisal: the same pattern held across 18 studies spanning negative emotion, pain and cognitive control10 (mean r = 0.37; Fig. 3a), with between-person correlations among canonical resting-state network responses25 reaching 0.50–0.80 (Fig. 3b). Person-level whole-brain responsivity thus potentially reflects pervasive confounding processes for regional fMRI inference—an issue that affects not only reappraisal research, but also the broader task-based individual-difference literature.

a, Between-person correlations (that is, across participants) of regional activation across pairs of brain regions in an independent multimodal task–fMRI dataset spanning three domains—cognitive control, negative emotion and pain processing—with three subdomains per domain and two studies per subdomain (n = 15 per study; total n = 270). Each dot shows the mean Pearson correlation across all possible pairs of 489 regions; whiskers indicate the s.d. across region pairs. b, Between-person Pearson correlations of activation profiles between pairs of resting-state networks in the same dataset, additionally including a reappraisal dataset24 (n = 33). Colours encode the magnitude of Pearson’s r, and the top row shows the mean across studies. Networks were defined using the Yeo parcellation25. Rows show individual studies; columns show network pairs. dAttention and vAttention denote dorsal and ventral attention networks, respectively; Default denotes the default mode network.

These profound individual differences in global signal responses are in conflict with the argument that most fMRI tasks have been designed to elicit strong within-person effects, at the cost of meaningful between-person variance, despite their common use in individual-difference research26. We tested this potential misalignment by analysing trial-wise responses to negative pictures in two large samples with population-representative variance in negative emotional dispositions, using the most common reappraisal task12 (Methods, ‘Variance decomposition’). For trial-wise task-based affective ratings, the majority of variance was at the within-person level (92–93%; Fig. 4). By contrast, for neural responses in the amygdala and regulatory networks, about 60% of variance was on the between-person level. Thus, associations are likely to be reduced because common fMRI task designs prioritize robust within-person condition effects over between-person effects26, a mismatch that is further amplified by large individual differences in global signal responses.

Variance decomposition for three focal outcomes—task-based affective ratings, amygdala responses and regulatory network responses—in two large task–fMRI studies50 (the Pittsburgh Imaging Project (PIP) (study 1) n = 176, and Adult Health and Behavior Project, phase 2 (AHAB-2) (study 2) n = 180; Supplementary Table 1). Bars show the proportion of total variance attributable to between-person and within-person variability. Single-trial responses were extracted for each outcome and decomposed using intercept-only linear mixed-effects models, with the random intercept indexing between-person variance and the residual term indexing within-person variance. To obtain stable estimates, trial-level responses outside three times the interquartile range were removed within each participant, followed by removal of participants whose average responses fell outside three times the interquartile range. Between-person variance estimates were low for task-based affective ratings but substantially higher for amygdala and regulatory network responses. Exact proportions of total variance attributable to between-person differences were as follows. Study 1: ratings 0.07, 95% confidence interval [0.05, 0.09]; amygdala 0.64, 95% confidence interval [0.59, 0.69]; regulatory network 0.62, 95% confidence interval [0.57, 0.66]. Study 2: ratings 0.08, 95% confidence interval [0.06, 0.10]; amygdala 0.60, 95% confidence interval [0.55, 0.65]; regulatory network 0.56, 95% confidence interval [0.51, 0.61].

Finally, we tested whether multivariate neural signatures provide more sensitive indices of reappraisal capacity than anatomically defined regions or networks. Neural signatures are predictive decoding models that combine activity across many brain regions to estimate the presence or intensity of a psychological state in new individuals. We focused on three established candidate signatures: a negative affect decoder, a decoder of reappraisal as a dynamic state, and a decoder trained to predict individual differences in reappraisal success from task-based affective ratings (Methods, ‘Multivariate neuro-affective signatures’).

Using the four largest studies (n = 730), we first examined whether these signatures differentiated emotion generation from reappraisal (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Table 2). The negative affect decoder was strongly expressed during emotion generation (d = 0.69) but increased further during reappraisal (d = 0.15), indicating that its expression did not follow the expected reappraisal-related reduction in negative affect. The reappraisal state decoder showed stronger negative expression during emotion generation (d = −0.41) than positive expression during reappraisal (d = 0.30), suggesting limited specificity for reappraisal as opposed to variation in emotional state. The reappraisal ability decoder showed substantial negative expression across both contrasts (d = −0.22 for emotion generation and d = −0.37 for emotion regulation). Consistent with these ambiguous task-response profiles and univariate null findings, none of the three signatures was significantly associated with reappraisal capacity, whether indexed by trait questionnaires or task-based affective ratings (P > 0.08; Fig. 5b and Extended Data Table 3). Descriptive correlations were near-zero (|r| ≤ 0.06), with confidence intervals excluding effects larger than |r| = 0.15 and Bayes factors favouring the null hypothesis (BF10 < 0.25), especially for the negative affect decoder (BF10 < 0.09).

a, Responses of neural signatures, the amygdala and the regulatory network to the two main contrasts: emotion generation [view negative – view neutral] and emotion regulation (reappraise negative – view negative). Metrics are expressed as Cohen’s d. Smaller points indicate study-specific estimates; larger points and error bars indicate estimates aggregated across studies and their 95% confidence intervals (uncorrected, two-sided). Total n = 730; study 1 n = 180 (AHAB-250), study 2 n = 176 (PIP50), study 3 n = 139 (Doren et al., unpublished) and study 4 n = 235 (ref. 21). The negative affect decoder was not used in study 1, and the reappraisal ability decoder was not used in study 2 to avoid inflated effect sizes, as these were the training samples for the previously published decoders. For exact statistics, see Extended Data Table 2. b, Between-person Pearson correlations of the three neural signatures with trait questionnaires and task-based affective ratings. Smaller points indicate study-specific correlations; larger points and error bars indicate pooled correlations and their 95% confidence intervals (uncorrected, two-sided).
