A similarly unexpected pattern emerged for the broader systems commonly used to distinguish emotion generation from regulation. The regulatory network was involved in both processes, as recently observed27 (d = 0.22 for emotion generation and d = 0.37 for emotion regulation). Notably, removing the outlying study 4 altered the pattern substantially, resulting in a stronger preference for emotion generation (d = 0.18) than for regulation (d = 0.08), the latter having an inconclusive Bayes factor (BF10 = 0.90). By contrast, the amygdala was selectively engaged during emotion generation (d = 0.16) and was not modulated during reappraisal (d = 0.01, BF10 = 0.03; detailed statistics are in Extended Data Table 2).

Despite extensive research on the neural basis of cognitive reappraisal, the assumption that brain activity during reappraisal reflects individual differences in regulatory capacity has rarely been tested at the scale needed for robust effects. Here we found a notable lack of convergence among three widely used indices of reappraisal capacity. Only the association between task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation was statistically significant, yet with an effect size (r = 0.08) so small that more than 1,000 participants would be needed for 80% power—far exceeding typical sample sizes in the field. Trait questionnaires showed no association with either index, with Bayes factors favouring the absence of effects. None of the three indices showed the expected relation with activity in canonical prefrontal emotion regulation circuits. These findings call for a fundamental reassessment of how reappraisal capacity is measured and interpreted across behavioural and neural levels of analysis.

The lack of convergence challenges a central assumption in affective neuroscience and clinical neuroimaging: that questionnaires, task-based affective change and neural responses provide complementary windows onto a shared underlying regulatory capacity, albeit with unique aspects. This matters because the extent to which common reappraisal task findings inform claims about emotion, psychopathology and intervention targets may be overstated if individual indices capture only distinct aspects of regulatory functioning. Indeed, research on emotional coherence shows that experiential, behavioural and physiological channels often diverge because they operate on different time scales and are shaped by different causal influences and biases28. Trait questionnaires reflect recollected beliefs about reappraisal habits and ability across diverse real-life contexts; task-based affective ratings capture momentary regulatory effects under constrained experimental conditions; and neural responses may additionally reflect processes outside conscious awareness29, while being shaped by neurovascular and scanner-related factors that are unrelated to regulation. The present findings therefore do not merely show weak measurement convergence; they suggest that common indices of reappraisal capacity, in fact, may carve the construct at different joints, without the widely assumed contribution of the prefrontal cortex.

For task-based affective ratings, we found associations in emotion-generative rather than prefrontal emotion-regulatory regions: the amygdala, the caudal pons, and—when excluding an outlier dataset from the early COVID-19 era—sensorimotor and dorso-parietal attention networks, outside of canonical emotion regulation regions. The role of the amygdala remains debated: although it tracks concurrent negative affect in well-powered studies30,31, it also responds to positive and otherwise salient stimuli4,32. We further confirmed with four large samples that it is not consistently modulated by reappraisal27. The amygdala is better understood as a neuromodulatory hub facilitating attention, memory encoding and consolidation33, and allostatic responding—processes that are relevant to emotion generation but not specific to it. One possibility is that reappraisal changes the quality or valence of an emotional response without proportionally reducing its salience.

Our finding of sensorimotor associations is consistent with extended process models that assign a role to sensorimotor cortices and the brainstem in the action phase of regulation27. Recent large-scale evidence indicates that even in the absence of overt motor responses, sensorimotor cortices carry rich information about emotion generation27, are modifiable by reappraisal strategies27, are related to individual differences in stress vulnerability12,34, and are a promising target for neuromodulation in depression35. Neurosynth decoding further indicated language-related activation, consistent with the verbal nature of reappraisal. Together, these patterns suggest that individual differences in affective down-regulation are more closely tied to salience-allostasis and perception–action-related processes than to canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits36. Notably, canonical regulatory circuits were similarly engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging the commonly assumed dichotomy between bottom-up excitation and top-down control in emotion regulation27.

The absence of associations between trait questionnaires and task-based or neural indices points to an explanatory gap that can be understood through process models of emotion regulation1,27. Most trait questionnaires capture habitual tendencies across multiple temporal stages, including encountering and recognizing reappraisable situations, deciding whether to regulate, and selecting reappraisal over competing strategies. From one angle, previous work showed associations between reappraisal habits, ability and neuro-behavioural implementation16,17,18, including causal evidence that neuromodulation affects reappraisal habits19. Similarly, we found a very strong correlation between habit and ability questionnaires, pointing towards a functional relation on a conceptual level. From another angle, standard fMRI tasks bypass much of the naturalistic reappraisal sequence: participants are instructed when and how to regulate, receive practice trials and respond to standardized stimuli optimized for reliable group-level effects. Therefore, individuals with higher reappraisal capacity might derive their real-world advantage less from universally superior neural implementation than from selecting, initiating and sustaining reappraisal in personally meaningful contexts, and from encountering environments that more readily afford successful reappraisal37. Relatedly, higher self-reported reappraisal tendency may partly reflect greater regulatory need rather than greater regulatory success: individuals experiencing stronger negative emotions may have more occasions to engage in reappraisal38. At the same time, highly intense negative emotions may render reappraisal less suitable than alternative regulation strategies39, relating reappraisal success to situational demands and individual differences in emotional reactivity4,12. This aligns with broader arguments that successful self-regulation reflects complex person-situation interactions rather than being governed by a context-general regulatory resource40. Future paradigms should therefore additionally engage other regulatory stages including strategy selection, personally relevant stimuli and spontaneous deployment.

The gap between task-based affective ratings and concurrent neural responses raises a different set of issues. Within persons, trial-by-trial affective ratings can be decoded from neural responses with large effect sizes, particularly with distributed multivariate neuro-affective signatures30. Even anatomically localized responses, such as the amygdala, track within-person fluctuations in affect with smaller but theoretically meaningful effect sizes30,31. This robust within-person correspondence demonstrates that brain–behaviour alignment is achievable and supports the value of process-oriented research for identifying neuromodulation targets.

Between persons, however, brain–behaviour associations are systematically much smaller12—a dissociation also observed for non-fMRI physiological markers of emotion28. Neural degeneracy provides one principled account: multiple neural configurations can support similar regulatory outcomes, and the specific configurations recruited may differ markedly across individuals41, particularly in higher-order association cortices where anatomical variability is substantial42. Yet degeneracy alone cannot explain the magnitude of the within–between discrepancy. Process-oriented fMRI studies routinely identify replicable regional response patterns, as reflected in meta-analyses of reappraisal2, and population-level models trained to decode within-person affective states generalize well to unseen healthy and clinical cohorts43. This indicates substantial representational overlap between individuals on a process level.

Three additional factors are likely to contribute. First, we demonstrated that established multivariate neuro-affective signatures can produce large effect sizes (dmax = 0.69) while conflating emotion generation and regulation, limiting their psychological interpretability and showing no association with reappraisal capacity. Second, standard reappraisal tasks were designed for process-based research and may not elicit the stable individual differences needed for strong brain–behaviour associations26. In support of this, we found little variance on the between-person level in task-based affective ratings (7–8%), even in two large samples with population-representative variance on affective traits12. Third, we found that between-person fMRI responses are strongly shaped by person-level whole-brain responsivity—potentially owing to factors such as neurovascular variation22—producing highly correlated regional responses that limit anatomical specificity. This extends to canonical resting-state networks, where correlations reached 0.50 to 0.80 across multiple task domains. This complicates efforts to interpret individual differences in task–fMRI responses through influential clinical models, including the triple-network model, suggesting antagonistic relations between canonical networks44. These global effects are not removed by calculating contrasts between conditions. As a result, most between-person variance in neural responses likely reflects confounded individual differences, in stark contrast to task-based affective responses. This highlights a fundamental misalignment, potentially alleviated by tasks designed to specifically induce individual differences while accounting for whole-brain responsivity12,45.

These findings might have direct implications for how neural correlates are used to guide clinical inference and neuromodulatory interventions. The absence of prefrontal individual-difference associations does not invalidate process-oriented findings: the neural systems identified in within-person reappraisal research could remain viable targets for neuromodulation, as they reflect the implementation of reappraisal regardless of between-person variation. However, our results support caution against inferring individual regulatory capacity from regional brain activation—whether in the prefrontal cortex, amygdala or elsewhere—as is common in clinical neuroimaging models of emotion dysregulation4,5. The success of neuromodulatory interventions targeting these regions8,19 may reflect distributed network reorganization rather than correction of a specific regional deficit35,46, consistent with evidence that different stimulation sites can achieve similar clinical outcomes. This fits a systems neuroscience perspective where single regions cannot be interpreted in isolation. Supporting this, recent well-powered studies linked individual differences in affective functioning with reappraisal-contingent connectivity between the amygdala and prefrontal areas (ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC), dlPFC and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC))47, as well as shifts along primary gradients of macroscale neurofunctional organization48. Further testing these approaches represents a natural next step for the NIDER consortium and individual-difference neuroimaging of emotion regulation more broadly.

Our sample comprised non-clinical populations, limiting generalizability to groups with greater symptom severity and variability. A population-representative sample would show 1.3–1.5 times greater variance in reappraisal habits49, potentially enabling slightly larger effect sizes. More importantly, transdiagnostic samples covering the full range of clinical dimensions could reveal meaningful individual-difference associations that are absent in non-clinical adult individuals, while also introducing potential confounders. Most included studies used habit-oriented questionnaires,although the small number of studies with additional ability-focused measures still had sufficient power for most small effect sizes in fixed-effects analyses. Finally, whereas our meta-analytic approach is statistically equivalent to mega-analysis for voxel-outcome correlations, subject-level data would enable person-specific decoding models—a promising direction for future work on neural heterogeneity.

Together, our findings challenge the assumption that prefrontal activation during reappraisal reflects individual differences in regulatory capacity. The three most commonly used indices of reappraisal capacity do not converge, and none relates to canonical emotion regulation circuits in the expected direction. More broadly, person-level whole-brain responsivity represents a pervasive methodological challenge for task-based fMRI research on individual differences—one that extends across emotional, cognitive and pain domains. Large-scale resting-state studies with sample sizes in the thousands have similarly failed to identify replicable neural correlates of emotion-related traits13, underscoring the need for better alignment between theoretical constructs, behavioural tasks, and neural measures12. Progress will require methodological refinements—including connectivity and gradient-based approaches—as well as a conceptual re-framing of what reappraisal capacity means, how its multiple components are best measured, and the level of analysis at which each measure is expected to predict real-world emotional well-being. Until then, strong claims about a person’s emotion regulation capacity based on any specific brain region should be made with considerable caution.

Studies were eligible for inclusion if they measured (1) task-based fMRI (2) during a cognitive reappraisal task, (3) using negative stimuli, (4) to compare a down-regulation condition with a view-without-regulation condition, and (5) included a trait-like questionnaire measure for cognitive reappraisal (6) in a healthy sample. The latter criterion was used to avoid excessive heterogeneity in disorder presentation and medications (see ‘Towards transdiagnostic neural systems’).

Contributing research groups were invited using two strategies. First, we conducted a systematic literature search, contacting 64 authors via e-mail or Researchgate. Second, we used mailing lists of academic societies to advertise the consortium. In total, this led to 32 contributing research teams with 40 datasets comprising up to 2,175 participants. For an overview of study characteristics see Supplementary Table 1. Nine studies were unpublished. For 31 studies (77.5%), teams indicated they had not performed any of the targeted main analyses of the present paper. There were no further assessments of selection bias. Most papers used the emotion regulation questionnaire (ERQ)51 to measure reappraisal, while six used the cognitive emotion regulation questionnaire (CERQ)52, and only one study used a different questionnaire (FEEL-E)53. The majority of studies used pictorial stimuli. Two studies used videos, one study used autobiographical memory cues, one study used Cyberball, and one study used a different game task.

We conducted a systematic literature search of articles using the PubMed, Web of Science and PsychINFO databases. See Supplementary Fig. 2 for a flow chart depiction of the screening and selection of studies via literature search. We searched for the following keywords: ‘emotion regulation’ cross referenced with ‘fMRI’ or ‘neuroimaging’ or ‘functional magnetic resonance imaging’ or ‘functional MRI’. This search process yielded a total of 2,633 potentially relevant articles on 7 July 2021 (after duplicates were removed). Two independent reviewers (J.Z. and M. Schweizer) systematically examined titles and relevant abstracts using the Rayyan website54 to determine whether an article fulfills the criteria to be screened. The following criteria were applied: The study included original empirical results, was written in English or German, included adult healthy participants, and assessed an explicit emotion regulation paradigm during fMRI measurement. In a next step, for all remaining studies full texts were screened by three independent reviewers (J.Z., M. Boll and D. Lang) and they were included if (1) participants were told to use reappraisal strategies to modulate a negative emotion, (2) an emotion regulation questionnaire was assessed (for example, ERQ), (3) a control condition was included in which participants were confronted with emotional stimuli but did not regulate their emotions, and (4) negative stimuli were used in the emotion regulation task. Finally, a total of k = 61 studies fulfilled all inclusion criteria. Relevant articles in the authors’ library were also reviewed for titles that might have been missed by our literature search. Studies identified in this manner (k = 3) were collected for inclusion. Of the k = 64 studies, k = 17 reported the correlation between fMRI BOLD activation (‘reappraise negative’) and emotion regulation questionnaire data. The authors of all 64 studies were contacted.

Research groups prepared up to three unthresholded group-level statistical images, containing voxel-wise t-statistics for the between-person correlation of the whole-brain neural response in the [reappraise negative – view negative] contrast and the three outcomes of interest. These outcomes were (1) trait questionnaires of cognitive reappraisal, (2) the person-wise averaged decrease of task-based affective ratings during ‘reappraise negative’ versus ‘view negative’ conditions, and (3) and person-wise averaged decrease of amygdala responses during ‘reappraise negative’ versus ‘view negative’ conditions.

A homepage with detailed instructions and a Matlab example analysis script was provided to support analyses. Contributors were instructed to compute the three measures of reappraisal capacity so that higher values correspond to better reappraisal capacity. For task-based affective ratings, this entailed (re-)coding for higher values to correspond to a more negative emotional response and calculating person-wise averaged down-regulation of affect from the contrast [view negative – reappraise negative]; thus, a greater reduction in negative affect via reappraisal leads to higher values. Similarly, for amygdala down-regulation, average activity was extracted from the [view negative – reappraise negative] contrast, as higher values correspond to a better down-regulation of the amygdala for sign congruence with the other two outcomes. A standardized amygdala mask was provided for all research groups based on the intersection of an anatomical amygdala mask (SPM anatomy toolbox v2.2b) and a functional emotion-generating network from an emotion regulation meta-analysis2, which ensures the anatomical and functional specificity of the amygdala region of interest.

Furthermore, contributors provided direct bivariate correlations between the three reappraisal outcomes (for example, trait questionnaires and task-based affective ratings) as well as demographic and other study information (Supplementary Table 1).

Images were quality controlled individually by plotting t-values on a brain template, histograms, and performing brain-wide thresholding at false discovery rate (FDR) = 0.05 to check for plausibility. Collectively, quality was controlled by checking for outlier studies within the same emotion regulation outcome category (for example, mean whole-brain activation, Mahalanobis distance, and covariance matrices). Two images were removed from whole-brain analyses due to insufficient coverage55,56. Effective sample sizes for tests are reported in the results section.

Study-level estimates were aggregated within a random-effects meta-analytic framework. Under standard assumptions, this approach closely approximates subject-level mega-analysis for the associations examined here, while reducing barriers to data sharing57 and potentially increasing the number of includable studies and overall precision58,59 (see Supplementary Methods, ‘Meta- vs mega-analytic approaches’ for details).

First, we assessed the concordance between the three outcome measures (trait questionnaires, task-based ratings, amygdala down-regulation) using random-effects meta-analysis implemented in the R package meta using the DerSimonian and Laird approach to estimate between-study heterogeneity60.

Second, we tested associations between the three outcomes and two neural emotion regulation networks based on a recent process-based meta-analysis on emotion regulation2; networks 1 and 2 (Fig. 2). These networks are thought to be predominantly implicated in the cognitive control (versus emotion-generating) aspects of emotion regulation and mostly include regions in the prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortex. Images were resampled to the same spatial resolution of 2 × 2 × 2 mm³. The statistical core procedure was done in three preregistered stages. In the first stage, we tested the correlation between average activity in the two networks of interest, respectively, and reappraisal capacity, with Bonferroni corrections for two tests. In the second stage, we performed voxel-wise tests in the combined two networks with FDR correction based on the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (FDR = 0.05, approximately 10,000 voxels). In a third stage, we repeated the second-stage analysis on the whole brain (approximately 180,000 voxels). Between-study heterogeneity was tested for statistical significance based on whole-brain data and corrected with the same FDR procedure.

To perform the image-based fMRI meta-analysis, we developed custom Matlab code which interfaces with the fMRI-specific functionality of the CanlabCore toolbox23. Our procedure converts study-wise unthresholded t-maps to correlation maps and therefore, together with sample size information, offers voxel-wise estimates of effect size, statistical significance, and between-study heterogeneity via the DerSimonian and Laird approach61,62. The code was validated by testing congruence with meta-analytic packages in R as well as performing a small meta-analysis on six openly available group-level images of physical pain, which detected typically involved brain regions and was successfully decoded as ‘pain’ using Neurosynth63 (Supplementary Methods, ‘Testing the custom meta-analytic functions’). Neurosynth decoding was performed analogously as described in the main text.

We calculated Bayesian posterior odds for focal effects to quantify the relative evidence for the null hypothesis (that is, no effect exists) against the alternative hypothesis (that is, an effect exists) based on established interpretational thresholds64. These analyses were performed using Bayesian model-averaged meta-analysis65. We used objective literature-based prior distributions for effect sizes and between-study heterogeneity. For effect sizes, we used a normal moment prior66 approximating the empirical distribution of meta-analytic correlations across individual-difference research67, with a mode at r = 0.20 (Supplementary Fig 3). For between-study heterogeneity (τ), we used a one-sided t-distribution (scale factor = 0.15, df = 1), approximating the empirical distribution found for over 700 meta-analyses68 (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Bayesian posterior odds were not corrected for multiple comparisons in the three preregistered overlap tests (see ‘Divergence of capacity indices’) and the preregistered tests on average network activation. Therein, the null and alternative hypothesis are assumed to be equally likely (prior odds = 1:1), making the Bayesian posterior odds identical to the Bayes factor. For voxel-wise tests, we calculated Bayes factors across all four canonical networks involved in emotion regulation, including both aspects of emotion regulation and generation2, consisting of about 20,000 voxels. Due to this large number of comparisons belonging to the same global hypothesis, we performed Bayesian corrections for multiple comparisons by adjusting the prior odds to be equal for the global null (no effect across all voxels) versus the alternative hypothesis (an effect in at least one voxel) using Jeffrey’s method69. Like Bonferroni correction, this method is conservative when tests are not independent. Therefore, we calculated the number of effective independent tests based on the spatial correlation structure70, indicating 53 independent tests as a basis for multiplicity correction.

Anatomical regions were defined using the CANlab 2018 combined atlas in MNI152 space, which integrates cortical and subcortical regions from several established parcellations23. The full set of 489 regions, including atlas labels, anatomical or network descriptions and references to source parcellations, is provided in the Supplementary Atlas File. For each pair of regions, between-person Pearson correlations were calculated across participants using region-wise activation estimates. Correlations were then summarized across all region pairs to characterize the overall degree of shared between-person variation in regional activation.

To obtain trial-level neural responses, additional first-level general linear models (GLMs) were estimated using a beta-series approach in which each trial’s (n = 45) viewing epoch was modelled with a separate regressor, yielding 45 trial-specific parameter estimates for subsequent ROI analyses. Additional regressors in the beta-series GLM included a regressor reflecting all rating periods (to account for motor responses) as well as the six realignment parameters (to account for head motion-related activation). Subsequently, each trial-specific beta map was used to extract mean amygdala and regulatory network response scores for each trial and used for the variance decomposition, parallel to the task-based affective ratings.

To stabilize variance estimates for all three outcomes, we first removed outlier observations outside 3-times the interquartile range within each participant (9–113 out of 16,155 observations). Then, we removed whole outlier participants outside 3-times the interquartile range based on their average ratings (1–4 out of 359 participants). Next, we fit intercept-only linear mixed models to decompose variance between (random intercept) and within (residual) individuals.

Analyses included three candidate signatures: a negative affect decoder trained to predict task-based affective ratings (affective state)30, a decoder discriminating reappraisal from other competing processes (reappraisal state)71, and a decoder trained to predict individual differences in reappraisal success from task-based affective ratings (affective trait)72. All three were developed in relatively large samples, while the first two were additionally validated in multiple independent samples. Generally, these neural signatures consist of brain images containing regression weights. For each decoder, person, and condition, we calculated the signature expression by taking the dot product between the respective contrast (beta) image and the signature image. Pattern-expression scores, as well as the amygdala and regulatory network responses, were z-standardized within studies to transform them from the arbitrary site-specific fMRI metric to a comparable Cohen’s d metric. Specifically, for differences between conditions, values were standardized on the pooled within-condition variance separately for each study. Then, a linear mixed model was calculated with condition, study, and their interaction as fixed effects and a random intercept for each participant. Aggregate estimates and confidence intervals were obtained from estimated marginal means averaged equally across studies73. For correlations with reappraisal capacity, pattern-expression scores were calculated for the contrast [reappraise negative – view negative]. Pattern-expression scores and reappraisal capacity measures were z-standardized within studies and then analysed using pooled individual-level linear regressions across studies. These approaches equate to fixed-effects mega-analysis (that is, without study-specific random intercepts and slopes), as modelling between-study heterogeneity is severely limited with only four studies.

For model-derived contrasts, approximate Bayes factors were calculated from the corresponding t-statistics and denominator degrees of freedom using the default Cauchy prior for standardized mean differences implemented in the BayesFactor package74.

Aims, literature search strategy, and statistical analyses were preregistered on PROSPERO: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42021243155. A notable error in the preregistration was the statement that only studies using pictures as stimuli are included. Rather, the meta-analysis included all types of stimuli, which we stated correctly on the accompanying homepage and the mailing list advertisements. Regardless of this error, the overwhelming majority of studies used pictures as stimuli (88%) and the low, statistically non-significant between-study heterogeneities as well as the jackknife procedures indicate that stimulus type does not influence the results.

The participating studies followed their respective institutional approval processes at the time of data collection, including applicable ethical approval and informed consent procedures. For the present meta-analysis, participant-level analyses were performed locally by the contributing research groups, and only study-level summary statistics and group-level statistical images were shared. No new data were collected and no participant-level or identifiable information was accessed by the meta-analysis team. Therefore, no separate institutional review board approval or formal exemption was sought for the present secondary analysis.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The 40 primary task–fMRI datasets contributing to the consortium are listed individually, together with their study references and sample characteristics, in Supplementary Table 1. Participant-level data were not centrally collected as part of the present study and remain under the governance of the respective contributing research groups. Study-level summary statistics and group-level statistical images used for the meta-analyses are available at https://github.com/MaurizioSicorello/NIDER_project. The repository has been archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22084628 (ref. 75)). The systematic literature search was conducted using PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), Web of Science (https://www.webofscience.com/) and PsycINFO (https://www.apa.org/pubs/databases/psycinfo). Neurosynth was used for automated meta-analytic decoding (https://neurosynth.org/). Publicly available group-level statistical images used for validation of the image-based meta-analytic procedure were obtained from NeuroVault (https://neurovault.org/); permanent image identifiers are provided in the accompanying studyInfo_neurovault.xlsx file in the GitHub repository (https://github.com/MaurizioSicorello/NIDER_project). Source data are provided with this paper.

Custom MATLAB and R code used for the analyses is available on GitHub (https://github.com/MaurizioSicorello/NIDER_project) and has been archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22084628 (ref. 75)). The custom code is released under the MIT License (https://opensource.org/license/mit).

#1307. Barcelona vs. Real Madrid: Who has the edge in El Clasico in goal, defense, midfield and attack?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

On Sunday, Barcelona will host Real Madrid at the Spotify Camp Nou for what's expected to be one of the most exciting moments of the season. On top of that, Sunday's game will feature the return of Jose Mourinho to the stadium where he fought some of his incredible battles against Barcelona from 2010 to 2013, when he coached Real Madrid for the first time. The reception is expected to be heated, especially considering what happened in the recent weeks.

Real Madrid striker Vinicius Jr. will miss El Clasico against FC Barcelona after being suspended for four games for the red card he received in Real Madrid's home game against Villarreal at the Bernabeu last week. Despite the appeal, Vinicius Jr. won't be part of the game and will be back playing for the Blancos after the international break in the domestic league.

Let's take a closer look at both squads and compare their strengths to determine which team has the edge:

Let's start with the goalkeepers, and here Thibaut Courtois is probably still one of the best in his role and can directly make an impact on the result of a match. Joan Garcia, on the other hand, still has some room for improvement, and he's at a different stage of his career, with plenty of potential to evolve more. Although Courtois is nine years older than Garcia, making a direct comparison is somewhat unfair given their different stages of development; the Real Madrid goalkeeper still has the edge right now in terms of experience, consistency, and overall quality. At least when he's fit.

Barcelona: Joan Garcia, Wojciech Szczęsny, Dominik Livakovic.

Real Madrid: Thibaut Courtois, Andriy Lunin, Fran Gonzalez.

Things get more complicated when it comes to the defensive lines. Both Barcelona and Real Madrid have strong lineups in these roles, but they also concede a lot of goals. The new Real Madrid signings such as Denzel Dumfries, Marc Cucurella or Ibrahima Konate are yet to show their full potential, while the Barcelona young defenders like Pau Cubarsi, Eric Garcia or Xavi Espart are showing to be in a better form.

Barcelona: Joao Cancelo, Alejandro Balde, Pau Cubarsi, Xavi Espart, Andreas Christensen, Gerard Martin, Jules Kounde, Eric Garcia.

Real Madrid: Raul Asencio, Eder Militao, Dean Huijsen, Trent Alexander-Arnold, Ibrahima Konate, Marc Cucurella, Alvaro Carreras, Antonio Rüdiger, Ferland Mendy, Denzel Dumfries.

Both sides have some incredibly talented players, as usual. Barcelona signed Rodri in the summer, after the Spanish captain refused to join Real Madrid before signing for the Blaugrana. Apart from that, the players in the roster led by Jose Mourinho are just as incredible: Jude Bellingham, Federico Valverde, Arda Guler, Aurelien Tchouameni and Bernardo Silva, who signed as a free agent in the summer. Despite the qualities of the Barcelona midfielders, Real Madrid look much stronger in this sector.

Barcelona: Brian Farinas, Gavi, Fermin Lopez, Pedri, Rodri, Dani Olmo, Frenkie de Jong, Marc Bernal.

Real Madrid: Jude Bellingham, Eduardo Camavinga, Federico Valverde, Aurelien Tchouameni, Arda Guler, Bernardo Silva, Thiago Pitarch, Jorge Cestero.

The most challenging one. It's almost impossible to decided between Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe, Yan Diomande, Raphinha, Anthony Gordon and more. But there is a big difference ahead of Sunday's game: the absence of Vinicius Jr., who will miss El Clasico after receiving a four-game ban. Even if he didn't have his best start to the season so far, there is a difference without him. This is why I'm going for Barcelona this time.

Barcelona: Gabriel Jesus, Lamine Yamal, Raphinha, Karim Adeyemi, Anthony Gordon, Roony Bardghji, Jesse Bisiwu, Hamza Abdelkarim.

Real Madrid: Vinicius Junior, Endrick, Kylian Mbappe, Rodrygo, Cristian Espi, Brahim Díaz, Yan Diomande.

This is arguably one of the most difficult calls to make as both managers are considered among the best around the world. While Jose Mourinho shaped the last two decades of the game, Hansi Flick is now doing it as well. With two LaLiga titles won in his first two years at Barcelona, Flick now needs to win outside the country as he did at Bayern Munich before. Mourinho was called back by Real Madrid owner Florentino Perez to re-establish Real Madrid supremacy in Spain, but it won't be easy at all against Flick and Barcelona.

#1306. Inter Miami's MLS Cup credentials take hit with midfield problems that are too big for Lionel Messi to solve

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

HARRISON, N.J. – The sun was beginning to set as thousands clad in pink jerseys settled into their seats, hoping to see a show. The wait was not particularly long – with Lionel Messi temporarily a member of a captive audience, 17-year-old midfielder Adri Mehmeti made World Cup winner Rodrigo de Paul march to the beat of his drum. Red Bull New York were up on reigning MLS Cup champions Inter Miami seconds later thanks to a Casemiro own goal, the lead fully deserved.

Adri Mehmeti starts it with some filthy tekkers 😱Julian Hall opens the scoring against @InterMiamiCF! pic.twitter.com/sufccNHZub

A moment of brilliance from a rising local star is now a weekly occurrence in MLS, especially from those who took part in the U.S. men's national team's generational shift-themed friendlies this fall. It was perhaps one of few guarantees on Saturday, the main one being Messi's presence. He was the reason, after all, that Sports Illustrated Stadium was actually full, this time with spectators who jumped out of concession lines in the 56th minute to see Messi enter the pitch. He's the person whose name is chanted more often than any of the home team's players by a very healthy margin, no matter the MLS stadium. It's the kind of request Inter Miami always feel obliged to grant because of his inexplicable excellence, even if he was in Oviedo, Spain, two days earlier to accept the Princess of Asturias award for sport. The appetite for Messi is insatiable in that way, to the point that the vast majority of people in the building believed he would flip the game on its head in a single moment.

Miami fell flat in a 2-0 defeat to the Red Bulls, who precariously sit in the final playoff position with three games to go. The 16 points and six places that separate them in the Eastern Conference indicated that Miami would at least assert themselves at times on Saturday, but they failed to make a dent in more ways than one. Mehmeti's ability to outperform De Paul for the game's opening goal set the tone for the evening in a lot of ways, losing the game as soon as they lost the midfield battle. It was not that they lacked the opportunity to impose themselves – they had 65.9% possession, took 906 touches and completed 86.3% of their 714 passes. That possession never translated to an actual ability to dominate the game, their performance disjointed and ineffective in the end.

"Our build-up play from the back was slow, and we lost possession in areas where we simply cannot afford to lose the ball," Miami head coach Cristian "Kily" Gonzalez said post-match. "Because of these turnovers — whether due to poor passing, bad touches, or other errors — we ended up being caught too spread out as a team. I don't want to take any credit away from our opponent, but I believe the main issue was our own failure to maintain the style of play that defines us — specifically, avoiding so many turnovers in the midfield. We were also caught out by passes played behind our lines and we weren't compact enough. We improved a little bit after halftime, but I'm certainly not satisfied. We're in a phase where we cannot afford to relax — not even for a moment — or else we'll face serious consequences. We weren't the best team before, and we certainly aren't the worst now; we just need to get back to our usual way of playing and regain our rhythm."

The Red Bulls are hardly the team one would expect to exploit Miami's weaknesses, notably ineffective in their own way. The 2-0 scoreline was generous to Miami, the hosts wasteful with 19 shots and 3.24 expected goals, the likes of Julian Hall and Jorge Ruvalcaba missing sitter after sitter. It is not much of a surprise for a team that ranks inside MLS' top five for expected goals with 57.02 but has just 41 goals to show for it but even then, they succeeded fully in exploiting Miami's weaknesses. Mehmeti's outing, one of the best of his young career, was the foundation for a Red Bulls performance, particularly in a dominant first half.

"Honestly, the maturity he has is unbelievable," the Red Bulls' Mohammed Sofo said. "The vision he has – he knows when to play for it, when to come down. Sometimes he does things, I'm like, 'Wow.' For me as a No. 8 or also as a No. 10, I try to find myself in the pockets and sometimes he finds me with just two touches. Other players need to take a first touch, look for it and then play but for him, from the second touch, he finds you."

Mehmeti's excellence allowed the Red Bulls to survive even once Messi entered the game.

"We all know how good he is," Red Bulls coach Michael Bradley said. "We all know how special he is. I said last week, for me, he's the best player of all time but I also know that you don't want to let really good players just do whatever they want and to just back off and admire the qualities, that doesn't get you what you want so you know that he's going to be able to twist and turn and dribble through tight spaces and find his way out of a certain spot. You know that he's going to be able to play certain passes but we still talked and worked all week on the idea of making the game really hard, not just on Miami but on Messi in particular and again in the middle of all that, there's still going to be certain plays but we wanted the first guy ready to close down and take away the direct path to goal. We wanted the second guy coming ready every single time on the inside. We wanted in certain moments a third guy ready, close and so that part was generally good when he came on and so I was more pleased with that part."

Messi, of course, did what he could to help Miami but at 39 years old and after two transatlantic flights in a handful of days, the spark was not there. He was hardly at his freshest, generating 0.13 expected goals plus expected assists and creating two chances along the way. Miami looked a bit better as a whole after his arrival, generating 0.51 expected goals from five shots. It was technically an improvement from the 0.3 expected goals they mustered in the 55 minutes before Messi's substitution but for a title-contending team, the results were not impressive in the slightest.

This, of course, is not Messi's fault. He is the perfect, and perhaps only, player a team can build an entire strategy around. Even on the days where he is mostly absent, he can still turn up – only three months have passed since Messi was kept at bay in a World Cup semifinal for 85 minutes, only to notch two assists and send Argentina to the final. It is genuinely worth asking if that approach is actually a sustainable one, though. There was only going to be so much gas in the tank of a team fueled by Messi – and for that matter, Luis Suarez – in the final years of their careers. Miami won MLS Cup last year with their help but also with an actual plan by ex-head coach Javier Mascherano, who was out of a job four months later.

Gonzalez, who had a 32.5% win percentage in a coaching career that had only consisted of jobs in Argentina before Miami hired him in late summer, has not found the solutions to Miami's problems. If three wins in seven games was not enough for Mascherano to keep his job, Gonzalez's identical record is not much better. Miami, though, look more aimless now than they have since Messi joined the club three years ago and are running out of time for Gonzalez to fix it before the playoffs begin next month.

In a team sport, Miami's problems might just be too big for Messi to solve all by himself.

While fans fill stadiums to see the likes of Messi, LAFC's Son Heung-min and the Chicago Fire's Robert Lewandowski, they are often treated to something else entirely these days – a teenager doing what he can to leave a strong impression. Mehmeti did just that on Saturday, an appropriate feat for a freshly-capped USMNT player who has been the talk of MLS sporting executives for some time. Bradley was quick to remind, though, that his quick rise is impressive even if his potential was easy to spot.

"He has personality," Bradley said. "He has technical ability, the technical ability that you need to play in that spot in the center of the field when spaces are tight and things happen fast. He has a feel and an understanding for the game and obviously, the way things have gone this year, we've thrown an incredible amount at him. I've also said this a bunch of times. I didn't know coming into the season what exactly it was going to mean for Adri, or Julian, or Matty dos Santos, or any of our young guys. We knew that they were going to be a real part of the first team and in the end, it was going to be we were going to see how things played out, how they responded every day, how they took to ideas, how they pushed themselves along in the group, how they earned respect and the way it has gone means that we have put a lot on Adri's plate. We expect a lot of him. He has a lot of responsibility in our team for a 17-year-old, and he doesn't bat an eye."

Mehmeti's strong outing against Miami came after two games where he was substituted off before the hour mark, all on the back of a first camp with the U.S. team where his international teammates popped off more than he did. Growth is hardly linear, though, especially for a 17-year-old in the midst of his first season as a professional.

"Are there things that need to continue to improve? Yeah, absolutely," Bradley said. "Have there been certain games where, for this reason or that reason, we end up feeling like no, tonight's a night where we got to make a change and get him off a little bit earlier? Yeah, there have been but generally speaking, when you talk about a 17-year-old kid who has played in that spot on our team and when you think about the way that we play and what gets asked of him in that role, he's doing really well."

Mehmeti's settings are ideal as he continues to chart an upward trajectory. USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino has described MLS as a strong place for young players to begin their professional careers, while Bradley himself will have plenty of insight to offer Mehmeti. The Red Bulls head coach was once the celebrated midfield engine of the USMNT, the former national team captain winning 151 caps and playing in two World Cups during his career.

"I just think the full package has improved in every way," he said about Mehmeti's progress this season. "He has taken the qualities that he has and has made them hold up as games get better and harder and faster and as opponents get that much better and within that, there are little things that need to continue to get better. We've talked a little bit lately about his understanding in certain situations when we can't be aggressive or when it's not a real counter-pressing moment and he has to then slide out a little bit on an angle and deal with an attack or just his understanding of how to take a good angle and make sure that he can control that situation so it doesn't turn into anything more dangerous and so as I said, these are all normal things that when you're a young player playing in that position and there is that much responsibility, you have to live it. You have to play through it. You have to make certain mistakes so that you understand, 'I can't do that exactly the same way again,' and so he's moving himself forward in a really good way."

#1305. Andoni Iraola has Liverpool's fearsome frontline firing, Alexis Mac Allister back to his best and is unlocking the best of Florian Wirtz... it is far too soon to count them out of the title race, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 22:00 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 08:57 EDT, 1 November 2026

Are Liverpool in the title race? The question has been bandied around this week — and conversations will only grow louder if they beat Arsenal at Anfield tomorrow.

The clash feels like an early six-pointer but regardless of the result, we can make this point — Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool are on the up and, whether this year or next, will soon be competing for the top prizes again.

This follows a season of strife in which the football was boring, the title defence fell apart and fans turned mutinous — booing, leaving early and moaning at manager Arne Slot.

The Dutchman paid with his job and in came Iraola, who — with respect to Bournemouth and Rayo Vallecano — had no experience of managing the day-to-day stresses and demands of a club of this size.

Three months into his reign, the Basque is yet to receive the plaudits he deserves. Maybe because Arsenal are champions and the two Manchester clubs are never out of the headlines, Liverpool have gone under the radar.

But they have lost just once, when down to 10 men against Manchester City, and have won their last five games, including some potential banana skins. So is it time to stop sleeping on this team’s chances?

Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool are on the up and will soon be competing for the top prizes again

Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola are starting to fire for Iraola

We can go position by position and analyse how the Reds have improved under Iraola. In attack, there was a potential narrative of a post-Mohamed Salah slump, but the absence of the Egyptian has rarely been mentioned.

In the summer, Iraola said he wants his forwards to be ‘game changers’ and he has plenty of those — Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz, Cody Gakpo and Rio Ngumoha have all fulfilled that role, plus Hugo Ekitike when he returns from injury.

In midfield, Alexis Mac Allister is back to his best and Iraola sees the Argentine as his coach on the pitch, a man who reads the game better than anyone. Wirtz is getting better while young Trey Nyoni, 19, has been outstanding when he has featured.

At the back, Jeremy Jacquet has been a revelation. Fellow new signing Ronald Araujo is only on loan from Barcelona — there is an option to make that permanent — but is becoming a cult hero.

Iraola has also got the fans back on side. It is fair to say the Kop was unsure of him when he arrived but he has won them over with a front-footed, exciting style in a system that demands hard work and relentless pressing.

There is the perfect blend of youth and experience and it is clear the team are fighting for one another again.

‘It’s not just winning,’ Iraola said. ‘At Anfield, everyone feels when the team goes for it and when everyone is giving everything, trying his best… then the supporters will be there. Even when we have been losing, they have helped us massively.’

Florian Wirtz endured a difficult first season at Anfield but is starting to show why the club paid big money to sign him from Bayer Leverkusen in 2025

Jeremy Jacquet has been a revelation in the Liverpool defence

Captain Virgil van Dijk added: ‘The fans definitely like what they’re seeing and, of course, you feel that energy and it’s great. I’ve been feeling that energy for quite a while and when you miss it then to get it back is obviously very good.’

So, title race? Absolutely. Beat Arsenal and they are only three points behind the Gunners, so why not? Lose and it is nine points, which would not be insurmountable with 29 games and six months to go, but would certainly reduce the margin for error.

Usurping the Gunners might be a step too far this season, but Liverpool are certainly stronger than last term — and Iraola says there is still plenty of room for improvement.

Just look at his Bournemouth side. Winless in their first nine games, they barely looked back as they qualified for Europe. Liverpool had a rocky first month with obvious deficiencies, but are now building a head of steam.

Arsenal visit on Sunday having not won at Anfield since 2012 - last season this fixture was won by Dominik Szoboszlai's stunning 35-yard free-kick

The small details are also improving, such as solidity from set-pieces — an issue that bugged them last term with a league-high 20 goals conceded. The fitness of Isak is a huge factor, while Alisson looks in top condition again.

Asked where his team can improve, Iraola said: ‘Almost everywhere. We are defending really well lately but still we have some situations where we need to improve. In the league, we have been less dangerous offensively.

‘So it is still too early to make big conclusions but there are improvements needed everywhere.’

Arsenal might not be wary of Manchester City given potential points deductions but, should Liverpool beat them on Halloween weekend, the champions will certainly be running scared.

#1304. Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

The giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

If you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had said he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

“He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

As Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

#1302. Real Madrid finally show their potential under Jose Mourinho in convincing El Clasico win over Barcelona

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There is an air of inevitability when a player is in peak form, to the point that their teams develop a very entertaining type of dependence on them. At the team's best, the player is merely the focal point in a harmonious system; otherwise, that player is almost resigned to the reality that they exist in large part to bail their team out of trouble. Barcelona felt like the best-case scenario before El Clasico after both Lamine Yamal and Raphinha got off to strong starts to their seasons, Tuesday's 4-2 loss at Paris Saint-Germain doing little to dampen their spirits. If anything, it was Real Madrid who have become overly reliant on Kylian Mbappe over the years, Sunday's game slated to be no exception.

Over the course of Real Madrid's 2-1 win at the Camp Nou, though, the roles had reversed.

Mbappe and Raphina were each on the scoresheet, neither feat much of a surprise considering each of their exploits this season. Early in his third season with the club, Mbappe notched his 99th and 100th Real Madrid goals on Sunday while Raphina registered his 13th goal in nine LaLiga games this campaign. Both showcased the inherent ability of a dependable superstar, each of them providing a unique snapshot of the teams they represent.

The France World Cup winner was the finishing piece of a team whose defensive efforts won them the game, neutralizing a Barcelona team that had won nine games out of nine to start the domestic campaign. The visitors opted to cede play to the possession-oriented hosts, holding the ball just 37.6% of the time in the process. Los Blancos also let the attack-minded Barcelona roll out Plan A, outshooting the visitors 18 to 10 along the way. Jose Mourinho's side were fully prepared for the challenge, their positional discipline designed to ensure their opponents would be unable to do much with all of their efforts. Hansi Flick's side registered just 1.19 expected goals from all their attempts, well below their average tally of 3.5 expected goals per game in LaLiga this campaign.

Yamal and Raphinha, as well as winger Anthony Gordon, had the ball at their feet on multiple occasions and looked certain to go for goal. They were often restricted to taking shots from sundial positions, Real Madrid's defensive shape holding nicely for much of the game. In the moments the Barcelona players' individual brilliance came through, a Real Madrid defender would find a way to shut things down before it was too late. Aurelien Tchouameni led the charge at the base of Los Blancos' midfield, excellent as the visitors resisted Barcelona's press and prevented them from racking up opportunities in moments of transition. He was hardly alone – Federico Valverde excelled at right back, while Marc Cucurella came in clutch on the flip side. Even Arda Guler and Yan Diomande maintained their standing in their wide attacking positions, limiting Barcelona's ability to create much despite racking up touches and passes.

It allowed Mbappe to pounce when the ball finally landed, even if he was less visible over the course of the 90 minutes than usual. He took just 36 touches and three shots, down from his average in LaLiga this season of 52.7 touches and 5.2 shots per game, but he is the exact type of player to survive a game state like this one. His first was a gift from Barcelona's back line while his second was a team effort, one that showcased his own brilliance as much as it did Eduardo Camavinga's abilities off the bench in maintaining Los Blancos' structure before notching the game-winning assist.

AN UNREAL TEAM MOVE FROM REAL MADRID ENDS WITH MBAPPE PUTTING THEM AHEAD LATE IN ELCLÁSICO!A BRACE FOR MBAPPÉ 😱 pic.twitter.com/qkFvVPWulg

Mbappe exploited a Barcelona back line that had tried to turn over a new defensive leaf this season, perhaps haunted by the mistakes their aggressive high line has made since Flick took the job two years ago. Rodri, whose Golden Ball award goes hand-in-hand with Spain's World Cup win this year, is as well-positioned as any to be a one-man solution but he was unable to fix Sunday's problems by himself. The injuries to Barcelona's defense have not helped, another coming midway through the first half when left back Xavi Espart came off for Alejandro Balde, but Mbappe was not alone in getting the better of the hosts' back line. Jude Bellingham had his moments, while Guler played a key role in the build-up to Mbappe's first goal.

GERARD MARTIN'S CLEARANCE GOES OFF MBAPPE AND REAL MADRID OPEN THE SCORING IN ELCLÁSICO 😮 pic.twitter.com/g5gBxFH7i8

In the process, Real Madrid closed the gap atop LaLiga to three points and rebooted a title race that many were ready to call two months into the season. Unlike the 2023-24 team that picked up the team's last major title, they found a way to win on Sunday not on the back of excellent individuals who are living, breathing cheat codes. For the first time since Xabi Alonso's surprise dismissal in January, they notched a convincing win on the back of a strong game plan and an even more impressive ability to execute it.

#1301. Why you can't blame Aston Villa chiefs for fighting back at Jamie Carragher as Fulham refuse to follow pundit in backing down as they earn deserved point, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE

Published: 18:11 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 09:34 EDT, 1 November 2026

Aston Villa might have had an apology from Jamie Carragher but Unai Emery’s men found Fulham far more awkward opponents on a difficult night at Villa Park.

After Villa had threatened legal action, the Sky Sports pundit said sorry for telling ‘Aston Villa fans’ to ‘shut the f*** up’ on Saturday. The Holte End let Carragher know what they thought of him within a minute here.

Unfortunately for Villa, Fulham were in no mood to back down as Carragher had. John McGinn missed a penalty for the home side early on and though Nicolas Jackson gave them a half-time lead, Fulham deservedly equalised when Zion Suzuki – outstanding until then – carried Alex Iwobi’s corner over his own line.

Though Villa were very poor in the second half, this remains a team in transition and there will be bumps in the road. And thanks to the dispute with Carragher, the main talking point on Saturday was away from the pitch.

Villa have been mocked for this response but look at it from their point of view. The club feel that at every turn, the established order are trying to slow their progress.

Consider the financial regulations that favour historically wealthy clubs who make money off the pitch, over those who have started to succeed on it.

Nicolas Jackson has been on fire this season and netted again to give Villa the lead

Villa would certainly have settled for Champions League fixture pile-ups 10 years ago

Imagine the frustration of finishing fourth in the Premier League, winning the Europa League and then having to sell six starters from the Final.

Now he has to listen to ex-players with significant influence telling the world that Villa can never satisfy Emery’s ambition.

Carragher is probably guilty of nothing more than expressing an opinion, however crudely he may have done so. But if Sawiris is fed up of various voices and organisations trying to put Villa back in their box, who can blame him?

Whenever Antonee Robinson charged down the Fulham left, Villa were in trouble. The US international had a superb match but until his error, the visitors found Suzuki in excellent form.

He made one outstanding stop from Oscar Bobb and produced decisive interventions to deny Gonzalo Garcia, Josh King and Alex Iwobi.

There is plenty of technical ability in this side and when they move forward they are great to watch. But Garcia does not look a ruthless finisher in the style of Jackson and he missed chances here. At the back, too, they look flimsy. As well as Jackson took his goal, the challenges from Timothy Castagne and David Affengruber were weak.

Yet in Josh King and Oscar Bobb they have twinkle-toed attackers capable of threatening any defence. After a poor start to his tenure, it looks as though Alvaro Arbeloa is starting to find his range at Craven Cottage and had they won here, it would have been fully merited.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki got into a terrible mess to gift Fulham an equaliser

Villa would certainly have settled for Champions League fixture pile-ups ten years ago, when they were eking out a 1-1 draw at rivals Birmingham in the Championship, but their recent schedule has been unforgiving.

With Villa facing Barca at the Nou Camp on Tuesday, the Fulham game was brought forward from 2pm on Sunday to the late fixture on Saturday. That is exactly 72 hours after the Carabao Cup defeat to Bournemouth, and 72 before they face the Spanish champions.

Given Villa made several changes at Bournemouth, surely there was a case making this a 12.30pm kick-off, or even a 3pm kick-off on Saturday? Given the short turnaround before facing one of Europe’s strongest sides, Villa will be glad to have won their opening three games.

That gives them a clear shot at the last 16, either by qualifying directly or through the play-offs. Barcelona also opted not to rest players and fielded a strong side against Alaves in La Liga on Saturday, which was also an 8pm kick-off.

The bad news is that Hansi Flick’s side were 4-0 up at half-time and went on to win 6-1. If Fulham were able to cause Villa this much trouble with sharp passing and movement, what about the club most associated with those qualities?

Emery and his squad will certainly travel to Barcelona a little nervously on Monday afternoon.
