#1275. Nobel Prize in literature: How the winner is secretly chosen

Can Xue is considered one of this year's favorites; Margaret Atwood and Salman Rushdie are other strong contenders. But what goes on behind the scenes in the selection of the Nobel Prize in literature?

On Thursday, October 8, at around 1:00 p.m. CEST, all eyes in the literary world will be set on Stockholm.

That's when the new permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, will hold a press conference to announce the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature, marking the end of a lengthy selection process that officially began a year earlier.

The Swedish Academy is the body responsible for awarding the prize. Its 18 members consist of writers, professors and intellectuals.

In September of the previous year, the Academy's Nobel Committee sends forms to hundreds of individuals and organizations eligible to submit nominations for the Nobel Prize in literature.

According to the Nobel Prize website, these include professors of literature and linguistics at universities and colleges, previous Nobel laureates in literature and the heads of writers' associations that represent the literary community in their respective countries. Anyone from one of these groups who has not received a form may also submit a nomination.

"The list can reach 200 names per year of nominated authors," explains Gisele Sapiro, research director at France's National Centre for Scientific Research. She studies how the Nobel Prize, as a global institution, influences the international circulation of literature, power dynamics in the literary world and translation markets.

"The committee can also add names itself, such as authors who were nominated in previous years," she says.

In the spring, the Nobel Committee then selects five names through a multistage process and presents them to the Academy. Over the summer, Academy members read the nominees' works and discuss them. The Academy always announces the decision in early October.

As for the criteria the Academy uses to make its decision, it prefers to keep them to itself.

The public doesn't learn which nominees missed out until 50 years later — that's how long the Academy waits before releasing the list.

Sometimes decades pass between an author's first nomination and actually receiving the prize. Danish writer Johannes V. Jensen, who won the Nobel Prize in literature in 1944, waited 40 years. Doris Lessing received the award in 2007 after 35 years, while Thomas Mann, who won in 1929, had to wait 27 years.

In his will, Alfred Nobel, the prize's founder, stipulated that it should be awarded to the person who had produced "the most outstanding work in an idealistic direction." That leaves plenty of room for interpretation.

According to Gisele Sapiro, the Academy aims to honor ambitious, influential literature that has, for example, given rise to a new literary movement. "At the same time, the work has to be universal, being able to transcend its own culture," she says.

Translations can be one indication of this. "I noted in my research, however, that all the laureates since 1990 had been translated into English, French and German — except for Abdulrazak Gurnah [the Tanzanian-British 2021 Nobel laureate], who had not been translated into German before winning — meaning that I think these three languages are the most important," Sapiro explains.

Sapiro says it is also a major advantage if nominees have already won other major literary awards, such as the International Man Booker Prize, the Cervantes Prize or the Büchner Prize.

Politics can also influence the Swedish Academy's decisions.

On several occasions, the prize has gone to writers who openly opposed the regimes in their home countries, such as Belarusian writer Svetlana Alexievich in 2015. She is an outspoken critic of authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko.

Genre, on the other hand, does not matter. In the past, laureates have been honored not only for novels but also for poetry and plays. In 2016, singer-songwriter Bob Dylan received the prize for his song lyrics.

So far, only 33 of the 122 laureates have come from outside Europe. There is also a clear gender imbalance: only in the past eight years have men and women alternated as winners, significantly increasing women's share of the total number of laureates to 14.9%.

#1274. Harry Kane is 'still processing' his Ballon d'Or win, so he went back to the only thing he knows

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MUNICH – Less than an hour into a casual second-round cup match, a pocket of Bayern Munich fans in one corner of the Allianz Arena had moved on from reveling over Michael Olise's brace against second-division side Magdeburg. Their attention was instead on the group of substitutes who were warming up behind the opponent's goal and one person in particular.

It was a likely place for Harry Kane to spend a Wednesday evening, no matter the circumstances. Considering Bayern's relative strengths, the coaching staff had already hoped to give Kane the night off, especially with Borussia Dortmund awaiting this weekend and a trip to Atletico Madrid in the UEFA Champions League coming up on Tuesday. This was no ordinary midweek cup game, though, the pre-match guard of honor from his teammates as clear a sign as any of the occasion. It was Kane's first time back since winning the Ballon d'Or on Monday, doing so in his hometown of London.

The warm-ups were the only glimpse the crowd got of him on Wednesday, Bayern getting business done swiftly with a 6-1 win. Yet, Kane's appearance on the sidelines alone was celebratory, both after becoming the first Englishman to win the individual accolade in 25 years and the first player from the Bundesliga to do it since Matthias Sammer accomplished the feat in 1996. It was the type of thing that required an afterparty that allegedly stretched long after a delayed, bloated ceremony came to an end at around 11 p.m. local time, though Kane insisted he "didn't party too hard." It also allowed him to follow up a crowning achievement the only way he knows how – "straight back to work."

Kane trained on Tuesday and would have been ready to play if called upon on Wednesday, and is expected to prepare as usual for Saturday's clash with Dortmund. It comes as little surprise for a player who has rarely chased individual accolades. He has repeatedly insisted that his goal every four years is to win the World Cup with England, not the golden boot and left boyhood club Tottenham Hotspur for greater collective opportunities with Bayern in 2023 despite being just 47 goals behind Alan Shearer's Premier League goalscoring record at the age of 30. The spotlight has followed Kane for much of his career but he has always chosen to share it. There is no flexibility with the attention the Ballon d'Or carries, though; only one person can win it, no matter how team-oriented that person happens to be.

"It's strange," Kane said. "It's not my normal thing to enjoy. Even the guys, when I was walking out to warm up and they're all there clapping. I don't know. I get quite, maybe, embarrassed by it, but I know this is a big deal and I felt that obviously in the event, I felt that since with the reception and how much messages I've got from not just friends and family but people sending my number to other coaches and people just that have known me or know of me and they all wanted to just say well done. I think I'm still processing everything, to be honest, but look, I know it's a really big deal so I appreciate everyone, and you know, even on Saturday, I know we're going to do something before the game and all this, and it's important to do because it's a big celebration as well."

Even in his hometown on Monday, surrounded both by loved ones and his Bayern teammates who chanted his name in the London Palladium as Ronaldo revealed he had won the sport's ultimate individual prize, Kane felt out of place.

"A lot of nerves and just different emotions compared to a football match or anything like that and a lot of waiting around and just trying to picture what it'd be like if I did win but honestly, just really special," he said. "The support I've had from friends, family, fans, text messages, social media has just been overwhelming almost."

There is a lot Kane has not considered about life post-Ballon d'Or, either, like where the trophy might rest or what will come of the gold-flaked schnitzel that was made by a Bavarian restaurant and delivered to his home.

"I didn't actually eat it yesterday," he said. "With the match being today, I have a routine of what I eat and stuff but now, obviously, I appreciate it. It's a nice tradition that we have so to have a gold one, let's just keep them coming."

True to form, Kane has found the most comfort in a busy week in a return to his familiar routine.

"I think just being back to football," he said. "It feels like the Freiburg game [on Sunday] was six weeks ago. So much has happened in 48 hours. It was nice just to be back. A bit of normality, seeing the fans, getting a reception before the game, obviously, and then honestly just being back with the boys and just watching football and watching the boys play again so it's been a whirlwind of a 48 hours, and it's nice to just kind of be here and feel at home again."

He admitted he needs to add a new item to the routine at home, though – protecting the Ballon d'Or from his four children, aged nine to three.

"My wife and kids are still in London right now," he noted. "They get back on Friday so I haven't actually seen my kids since I won. I spoke to them, obviously, on FaceTime and stuff so I'm excited to see them and show them the trophy. I know they'll be trying to play with it and pick it up and it's quite heavy and so I might have to keep an eye on it this time but normally, the two boys, especially, just smash the ball around and then whoever wins picks up the trophy that I bring home but I'll have to explain it's a little bit more precious, so we'll have to keep an eye on it."

#1273. Paramount and Warner Bros merge into one Hollywood giant

Paramount has completed an $81 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, as its owner Skydance creates a new entertainment behemoth. Billionaire David Ellison's hostile takeover bid defeated rival efforts from Netflix.

Paramount on Tuesday finalized its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing a hostile acquisition that was months in the making and almost faltered at several hurdles.

The takeover cost a total of around $81 billion (roughly €72 billion), or almost $111 billion including the Warner Bros. debts passed on as part of the deal.

The merger brings together two of the oldest US filmmaking studios and will form a new giant called Skydance Corporation.

The new name Skydance hails from billionaire investor David Ellison, who first bought out Paramount and its subsidiaries and then moved on to target the much larger fish that is Warner Bros.

The bid faced stiff competition in a bidding war with Netflix, and later scrutiny from US regulators and politicians, but ultimately went through.

"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose family has ties to US President Donald Trump.

Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker SKYD, while Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share.

The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.

As well as the two giant film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, the deal also brings together the CBS News and CNN news networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Ellison says he plans to merge the subscription streaming platforms Paramount+ and HBO Max.

Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO of the new company. Former Mattel boss Ynon Kreiz is operating as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations.

Skydance Corp. looks set to have a total revenue in the region of $70 billion, based on the performance to date of its component parts. It says it's targeting cost savings of around $6 billion within three years as it takes advantage of overlaps created by the merger.

#1272. Mikel Arteta's mission to conquer his Anfield demons: Why Arsenal boss must overcome psychological damage from his playing days and take the handbrake off as he plots first win at Liverpool, writes ISAAN KHAN

Published: 08:47 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 11:13 EDT, 1 November 2026

The word 'Anfield' still haunts Mikel Arteta.

It was there, 12 years ago, that the Spaniard suffered a chastening experience after losing 5-1 there as an Arsenal player in February 2014.

In a subsequent interview with Spanish newspaper Marca, Arteta used the term 'pajara' - a Spanish phrase com monly associated with cyclists who suddenly run out of energy - to describe a sensation mirroring mental paralysis. He had been caught up in an Anfield tornado.

'Suddenly I could only see red shirts flying around, the game is passing all over me and I cannot react,' Arteta reflected.

'Everyone is thinking, 'What is he doing?' I cannot react, emotionally, physical. I cannot cope, everything goes fast and I only had that feeling in my career once - and it was at Anfield.'

Such was the impact of that trauma that Arteta felt compelled to bring a slice of Anfield to Arsenal's London Colney base ahead of a league meeting in November 2021.

Mikel Arteta (right) has consistently found life tough when managing away at Anfield

Going to Anfield has become something akin to a hoodoo - and it shows no signs of abating

Arteta surrounded the training pitch with enormous speakers which blared out 'You'll Never Walk Alone' during a training session, in hope the noise would ready his players to tackle the very atmosphere he himself wilted in. It was to no avail.

The Gunners found themselves on the end of a 4-0 drubbing and Arteta on the end of mocking from critics for his alternative methods.

Five years later, Arsenal's away day hoodoo against the Reds has shown no signs of abating.

The north London club's league record against Liverpool away under Arteta reads: six games, three draws, three defeats. Arsenal's most recent league victory there was in September 2012, in which Arteta played in the 2-0 victory.

Their results against Manchester City at the Etihad - their other closest title rivals in recent years - under Arteta are no better either. Seven games have resulted in five defeats and two draws.

In fact, across the 27 Premier League teams Arteta's Arsenal have faced away from home during his seven-year reign, his lowest points-per-game ratios are against Man City (0.29) and Liverpool (0.50).

These matches are more than difficult away trips. They are a test of both Arteta's tactical flexibility and the psycho logical resilience of his team in the face of hostility.

Andoni Iraola's side have appeared to turn a corner in the league after beating the impressive Brighton last weekend. With a cloud of uncertainty hanging over Man City and whether their sanctions for breaching financial rules will be enacted before the season ends, Liverpool may well end up as Arsenal's closest challengers for the title.

Beating Arsenal on Sunday, certainly, would go some way to announcing themselves as true contenders.

Arsenal are champions but they have consistently struggled away against the very best teams

So where have Arteta's Arsenal gone wrong at Anfield and the Etihad Stadium? Well, Arteta's tactical approach has arguably been too cautious in these fixtures for a start.

The 1-0 defeat in August 2025 against Arne Slot's Liverpool smacked of restraint and a concession that a point would be good enough before Dominik Szoboszlai's stunning late free-kick winner.

Arsenal's defensive organisation has long been a major strength under Arteta. He has built his Arsenal from the backline, reinforcing it with excellent back-up options before assessing the forward positions.

Yet, in these high-profile away matches, the pursuit of defensive security can come at the expense of attacking ambition.

There's a big drop in attacking output between when Arsenal face Liverpool at Anfield under Arteta compared with when the Gunners face other league opponents on away turf across the last two seasons.

Possession drops from 56.3 to 43.2 per cent, expected goals from 1.6 to 1.1 and big chances created from 3.1 to 1.8.

The impact of the fervent Anfield atmosphere can't be ignored, either. Ray Parlour understands this better than most, making his Arsenal debut at Anfield in January 1992 aged 18.

The Gunners legend, part of Arsene Wenger's Invincibles side, has a word of advice for the current crop.

'I made my debut there, I know exactly how tough it is to play there. But mentally, you've got to get ready,' Parlour tells Daily Mail Sport.

'For me, the crowd in the first 15 to 20 minutes is always very important at Anfield, because you have to silence them if you can.

Arteta's attack routinely suffers as he seeks defensive solidity in the toughest away games

Arsenal are very strong when they score first but slow starts have proven their Achilles heel

'You've got to start on the front foot, put them under pressure, and I think they can leak goals, Liverpool. To try score that first goal is always important.

'We know defensively Arsenal are a very strong side, so if they go and get that first goal, then they might have a good afternoon there.'

Parlour raises a pertinent point. Arsenal's slow starts at Anfield have left themselves with a mountain to climb. Of the 26 league games Arsenal won last season, they scored first in 24 of those matches. Whereas in the six away matches against Liverpool under Arteta, the Gunners have taken time to getting going.

More shots (from 27 to 30) and an increased xG (from 3.2 to 3.5) were registered in the second period compared to the first half in those games.

Arsenal need to start quicker - and be more clinical, too. At the Emirates, Arteta's men have struck 10 goals against Liverpool, but just six at Anfield despite creating more big chances at Anfield (1.8 per away game vs 1.1 per home game).

Parlour references Arsenal's 3-0 pummelling at Brighton last month as a key example. Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler admitted telling his players to 'win the small battles first' and that's exactly what they did.

'Win the first header, win the first tackle, win the first throw in, win the first corner,' revealed Hurzeler when asked about his pre-match message to his players. The Gunners can use this as a lesson to overcome their bogey team.

'Look, they're champions. They've got to play in all different sort of atmospheres,' explains Parlour.

'There's a lot of experienced players out there, so you know what to expect.

Arteta played in Arsenal's last league win at Anfield - a 2-0 victory 14 years ago against Brendan Rodgers' Liverpool. He will look to end that streak as a manager on Sunday

Former Arsenal midfielder Ray Parlour wants to see a bravery that can help navigate the storm

'It's going to be a tough place to play, but you've just got to go there and play your game. Individuals win their battles, which is very important in football.

'You see Brighton when they turned over Arsenal, they won their battles that day, so you've got to make sure you get one over on the players you're playing against.

Ultimately, if Arteta is to banish the Anfield demons that have lingered for 12 years, Arsenal must arrive with the courage to impose themselves from the first whistle - and the resilience to withstand the inevitable storm. Only then can the Spaniard finally rewrite a story that has haunted him for so long.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1270. From last place to the playoffs: How the Philadelphia Union pulled off MLS's most stunning turnaround

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

CHESTER, Pa. -- At the end of the World Cup, the Philadelphia Union were at the bottom of the Eastern Conference and all of Major League Soccer with only seven points, moving on from Supporters' Shield-winning head coach Bradley Carnell and turning to 36-year-old Ryan Richter to save the season. Given Richter's path as someone who oversaw the Union's MLS Next Pro side before becoming an assistant under Jim Curtin with the first team, it seemed like a moment where the Union would be in the process of preparing for next season and seeing what they did next.

But with the return of a familiar face in Kai Wagner, a meeting at Two Persons Coffee in South Philadelphia between captain Alejandro Bedoya and Richter, and one of the most impressive runs that we've seen of youth talent in league history, the Union were able to clinch a place in the MLS Cup playoffs, and they did it in impressive fashion, too, by playing Nashville SC to a scoreless draw away from home without 17-year-old phenom Cavan Sullivan being available for the match. It caps off a turnaround that has seen the Union pick up 40 points since the World Cup, winning 12 matches, drawing four, and only losing one. Those 40 points outpace the second-best team in the time range, which is Nashville SC, by five.

Sullivan has been one of the spark plugs of this improvement with seven goals and 11 assists, with most of that coming after the World Cup break, but with 38 of the Union's 59 league goals absent for that game as Bruno Damiani and Milan Iloski missed out on the match, it truly showed the mentality that the squad has.

Plenty preach about "next-man-up" mentality, but matches like this one show why no one should want to face the Union in the playoffs. If the season ended today, they'd face Inter Miami in a three-game series, which would be sure to bring fireworks after the scuffle that their last meeting created, but there's still more work to do with two games remaining, as the Union could slide down to the eight-versus-nine play-in game if they lose their final two games of the regular season.

Under Carnell, the Union were a traditional high-press team that tried to force their opponents into mistakes. While it worked with only MLS games to play, adding in the Concacaf Champions Cup saw the team unable to keep up that intensity, especially without Wagner at left back and with Neil Pierre on loan in Denmark instead of being with the squad. While Richter did benefit from both of these players being in the mix, he has also dialed things back to more of a zonal press, allowing the midfield to have time to rest in between plays so that they can keep the same intensity at minute 90 as they have entering the game.

Pierre and Nathan Harriel on the back line have assisted greatly with that, being mobile centerbacks in their own right. Richter knows the impact of having a 6-foot-7 defender like Pierre, who is also comfortable when being on an island, and it's clear how he helps the attack function.

"We can be super aggressive because Neil is comfortable in one-on-one situations. If it's a direct ball, he wins; he eats all of these. If it's open space that he has to defend, physically, he can deal with that, and he's also a good defender," Richter said. "The way he puts out so many fires allows us to be aggressive higher up the field, because we know when they play the ball long that we have someone who cleans this up almost every time."

Putting that in front of three-time MLS Goalkeeper of the Year Andre Blake, it's easy to see why the Union's defense has improved from the first half of the season, but the attack is where major strides have been made.

You'd have to be living under a rock to have not heard the name Cavan Sullivan by now, and for good reason, as the 17-year-old has been taking MLS by storm and helping push the Union attack forward with his creativity. Since the World Cup break, Sullivan is second only to Evander in assists with nine and has pitched in goals alongside that. He may not be the biggest or fastest player on the pitch, but the quick bursts that he has into space have been tormenting defenses.

Alongside Pierre and Frankie Westfield, he was able to earn his first national team cap under Mauricio Pochettino and also didn't look out of place there either, but when speaking to him and people around the team, the shift in mentality is clear. Sullivan asked to do extra training during the World Cup break instead of taking the time off, and has come back a more complete player. Already set to join Manchester City when he turns 18 next year, the path for future development is clear (assuming City are in the Premier League), but this is one of the best American soccer prospects ever developed. Being able to play alongside his older brother Quinn also helps with this transition, but Cavan has grown into a player of his own, and while this season has been a coming-out party for him in many ways, the playoffs are going to be a moment that can thrust him into the stratosphere as he looks to lead his hometown club to the first MLS Cup title in their history.

Which American has the most goals in Major League Soccer? Usually, the answer to that question is Brian White, but this season, it also resides in Philadelphia in Milan Iloski, a longtime journeyman, he has found a home in Philadelphia and has scored 19 goals with seven assists, which is third in the league. After moving Tai Baribo to D.C. United, there were valid questions of where the Union's goals would come from, and Iloski has delivered and shown that there isn't a finish that he doesn't have in his locker, and he's not overperforming, either, with an xG of 18.77.

Alongside him, Bruno Damiani has stepped up with 12 goals, and the Uruguayan could be key to any serious playoff run that the team has. If teams crowd Sullivan and Iloski, other people on the team need to be able to make them pay, and Damiani is chief among them. The hope was that new signing Ezekiel Alladoh would be able to take on that mantle, but with one goal and one assist in 26 appearances, he may find minutes hard to come by in the playoffs unless there's an injury. While it's unlikely that they'd upset the likes of Nashville and Miami to win the MLS Cup, the mantra of "Why not us" has always carried Philadelphia and looking at these numbers, you can't say that they don't have a chance. Given that, it is also only a matter of time until the interim tag is removed from Richter's coaching title, but that's an offseason issue to deal with; right now, there are more soccer games to win.

#1269. Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19, subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta8,20. Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.

According to the adiabatic theorem, a time-dependent, two-level quantum system remains in its ground state during a slow evolution21. By contrast, driving the system faster than its intrinsic timescale through an avoided energy crossing can create a finite occupation of the excited state by means of non-adiabatic transitions called Landau–Zener–Majorana (LZM) tunnelling22,23,24. This mechanism is central for strong-field light–matter interaction7,10,25,26. Yet, a direct observation of this foundational quantum effect in momentum space is still missing. The unique properties of graphene27 form the ideal test bed for observing LZM transitions. Its quasirelativistic electron dispersion and the robustness under irradiation with intense light have made this material a prime test ground for lightwave electronics26,28, including the demonstration of the first lightwave electronic logic gates7 and Floquet–Bloch states18,19. This has opened revolutionary prospects for quantum control, quantum sensing and quantum computation applications10,11,29.

Understanding and shaping the opportunities offered by lightwave control of electrons requires a direct observation of how LZM transitions dictate strong-field light–matter interaction. Attosecond spectroscopy has reached sufficient temporal resolution to access these dynamics30,31, and time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (trARPES) in combination with momentum microscopy32 has visualized electron dynamics directly in the band structure of quantum materials or in the orbitals of molecular layers12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,33. trARPES with subcycle temporal resolution8,20 has combined these approaches but offered only limited 1D momentum space access. To track coherent strong-field phenomena and scattering-induced momentum redistribution, observing carrier dynamics across the entire momentum space is imperative.

Here we expand subcycle band-structure videography to the entire first Brillouin zone (BZ). The new platform overcomes previous restrictions of momentum microscopy and subcycle ARPES, increasing the momentum area accessible with subcycle resolution by more than two orders of magnitude and the available field strengths by one order of magnitude. Exploiting few-cycle mid-infrared (MIR) field transients with large peak amplitudes, we drive coherent electron dynamics at the BZ edge of graphene. This approach reveals the simultaneous displacement and distortion of the light-driven electron distribution, uncovering the interplay between coherent intraband and interband dynamics underlying LZM transitions in graphene. Moreover, tracking the non-thermal subcycle distributions in 2D momentum space reveals how different scattering processes affect lightwave-driven dynamics.

When low-intensity, short-wavelength light interacts with electrons in a solid, it can induce perturbative interband quantum jumps in momentum regions in which the occupied and unoccupied bands are separated by an integer multiple of the photon energy (Fig. 1a). In graphene, the non-trivial pseudospin texture influences the dipole moments between the lower and upper halves of the Dirac cone, leading to a distribution of excited carriers only along the direction orthogonal to the light field34,35. Conversely, a strong low-frequency field transient can adiabatically accelerate carriers within their bands on subcycle timescales, deflecting the Fermi surface in momentum space according to Bloch’s acceleration theorem (Fig. 1b). During their excursion, electrons experience an energy gap, which, in graphene, varies linearly near the K point to form an avoided crossing. Thus, field-driven acceleration may drive prototypical LZM transitions, which leave a markedly different occupation in momentum space compared with Fig. 1a. If the driving field is periodic, the phase accumulated between consecutive non-adiabatic events—the Stückelberg phase—results in so-called Landau–Zener–Stückelberg–Majorana (LZSM) interference36,37.

a, Illustration of the fundamental electronic processes governing light–matter interaction in undoped graphene at the K point in the weak-field regime. Here electrons can be promoted from the valence band to the conduction band by absorption. In graphene, the optical selection rules favour transitions in the momentum direction perpendicular to the polarization of the electric field. b, In the strong-field regime, electrons can undergo ballistic acceleration by an electric field (dashed blue arrow). Simultaneously, the field can drive interband LZM transitions on subcycle timescales, allowing electrons to tunnel from the valence band to the conduction band (solid red arrows). This results in an elongated electron distribution in the previously unoccupied conduction band, with the weight of the electron population in the direction parallel to the field. c, In the experimental scheme shown in the bottom half, an s-polarized, phase-stable MIR pulse (red) drives a monolayer of graphene, and a p-polarized XUV probe pulse (purple) at variable time delay, t, provides snapshots of the induced dynamics with subcycle temporal resolution. The photoemitted electrons (blue) enter a photoemission momentum microscope. This enables the simultaneous detection of both parallel momenta, kx and ky, and kinetic energy for every individual electron. The upper half shows a femtosecond snapshot of the 2D band structure of a monolayer of graphene, recorded with the momentum microscope. The field of view extends over the entire first BZ, allowing tracking of the electronic occupation to slightly beyond the six K points.

To access this regime, we drive electrons in epitaxially grown monolayer graphene on SiC (ref. 38) with intense phase-stable MIR pulses (central frequency, 30 THz). After a delay time, t, extreme ultraviolet (XUV) pulses (central photon energy, 21.7 eV) photoemit the electrons with subcycle resolution. Their energies and momenta are detected with a time-of-flight photoemission momentum microscope (Fig. 1c and Methods). In equilibrium, the photoemission signal maps the occupied band structure. The high XUV photon energy and the large acceptance angle of the momentum microscope capture the electronic structural dynamics throughout the entire first BZ, including its six corners, in a single measurement with sub-10-fs resolution.

Figure 2a shows several momentum distribution maps in the vicinity of a K point at selected energies. The in-plane component of the p-polarized XUV radiation driving the photoemission process is set parallel to the kx-axis. Owing to the matrix elements in the photoemission process, the intensity exhibits the characteristic horseshoe-like distribution for energies far below the Dirac point39. The influence of the dark corridor at ky = 0 and positive kx − K values is suppressed for energies close to the Dirac point, ED, and the photoemission intensity forms a disc. To ensure that the relevant dynamics occur along a direction in which the two branches of the Dirac cone have equal photoemission intensities, we apply an s-polarized MIR field along the ky-axis. For large negative delays (t = −70 fs), a slice of the photoelectron intensity for kx − K = 0 (Fig. 2b) shows two linear bands with a slope of ħvF (with the Fermi velocity vF = 10.7 Å fs−1) and a Fermi level located 200 meV above the Dirac point. With increasing t, we observe an apparent shift of the overall band structure owing to momentum streaking20 of photoemitted electrons in vacuo by the MIR field. This effect can be used to retrieve the MIR waveform at the sample surface (Extended Data Fig. 2a and Methods). Compensating for this shift isolates the subcycle electron dynamics within the band structure.

The solid black lines represent the integration range in momentum space used in the three panels in b. b, Streaking-compensated and curvature-filtered view into the band structure of graphene at the Dirac point before the arrival of the MIR pulse (t = −70 fs) and for selected delay times during the interaction with the MIR pulse, t = −13.6 fs and t = 6.3 fs (raw data, Extended Data Fig. 2b). The last two snapshots show how the electron distribution is accelerated along the Dirac cone away from the equilibrium Fermi level. c, Current extracted from the occupation imbalance in the photoemission maps (blue points) and MIR waveform reconstructed from the momentum streaking (red points). Dashed black lines mark the temporal positions shown in b. The lightwave-driven current is extracted by tracking the imbalance in the occupation for positive and negative momenta (red and green shaded areas) in the raw photoemission spectra (inset) and normalized on the total amount of carriers in both regions before the pulse arrives. The grey shaded area indicates the normalized population increase in the conduction band extracted from a similar measurement.

A corresponding femtosecond snapshot of the band structure for t = −13.6 fs shows a highly non-thermal lightwave-driven electron distribution (Fig. 2b). In the upper half of the Dirac cone (E − ED ≥ 0), the ky > 0 branch is occupied up to about 1 eV, whereas the ky < 0 branch is completely unoccupied. Half a cycle of the MIR carrier wave later (t = 6.3 fs), the field direction is inverted and the electron distribution is mirrored. The extreme carrier redistribution on subcycle timescales clearly proves the non-perturbative nature of the light–matter interaction. This scenario is expected for the small Keldysh parameter near the Dirac point (γ = 0.075; Methods). Still, it is notable that the few-fs timescales accessible with our experiment allow us to see lightwave-driven intraband acceleration despite the extremely fast scattering processes in graphene33,35,40,41,42,43,44,45. Asymmetric electron distributions in momentum space correspond to the excitation of an intraband current. By tracking the imbalance in the band occupation for positive and negative ky momenta (Fig. 2c, inset and Methods), we extract the lightwave-driven intraband current density and directly compare it with the MIR driving waveform (Fig. 2c). Although the current density shows a similar envelope and oscillation frequency as the MIR transient, there is a non-trivial phase shift between the two waveforms.

From Bloch’s acceleration theorem20,46, we would expect that, in the absence of decoherence, the momentum accumulated by electrons follows the integral over the MIR field, resulting in a phase shift of π/2 between the current and the field. A Fourier analysis (Methods) allows us to retrieve this phase delay with attosecond precision. Notably, the average delay of 4.9 ± 0.2 fs is much smaller than the value associated with a fully coherent evolution (8.3 fs). Simulations based on the semiconductor Bloch equations (SBEs)6 in the relaxation time approximation (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Methods) reproduce this phase shift for a mean scattering time of 9.0 ± 0.7 fs. As non-adiabatic LZM transitions rely on the coherent and unperturbed field-driven evolution of charge carriers, this sets the time and length scales relevant for lightwave electronics. Despite the short scattering time, electrons in graphene can travel almost 100 Å owing to their large velocity of vF = 10.7 Å fs−1.

Most notably, the current is accompanied by an ultrafast increase of the total conduction-band population within the strongest MIR half-cycles (Fig. 2c, grey shaded area). Perturbative interband transitions are too weak to become effective on subcycle timescales and, in equilibrium, straightforward vertical interband transitions are prohibited in the doped sample by Pauli blocking. Hence, the observed electronic structural dynamics attest to an interplay between strong-field-driven intraband and interband currents. Next, we unveil the microscopic mechanisms by imaging the full 2D momentum space. With this capability, unavailable in previous subcycle photoemission experiments8,20, we can directly target the coherent light–matter interaction regime and the subsequent relaxation dynamics.

Before the interaction with the MIR transient, the equilibrium carrier distribution in the conduction band (E − ED ≥ 0) of n-doped graphene can be approximated by a disc centred about each K point (Fig. 2a). If the electrons were solely subject to an accelerating electric field, they would, in accordance with Bloch’s acceleration theorem46, collectively move along the ky direction and we would merely expect a time-dependent centre-of-mass (COM) displacement of this disc. Although the streaking-compensated 2D momentum maps (Fig. 3a) indeed show pronounced oscillations of the COM displacement with the frequency of the strong driving field and a maximum amplitude of 0.078 Å−1 (Fig. 3b), they also reveal a further notable change of their shape (Fig. 3a,c). The observed deviations from the initial shape of the distribution are on the same order as the COM displacement.

The inset indicates the position of the evaluated window in momentum space and the arrow shows the MIR polarization. The grey lines mark the BZ borders. The Gaussian fits illustrate the width of the projection of the carrier distribution on the kx-axis (brown) and the ky-axis (green). The fits of the first panel are shown in black in the later snapshots as a reference. Under the influence of the field, the carrier distribution is displaced along ky (t = −43.6 fs). Owing to LZM transitions, the carrier distribution is elongated along ky, forming an ellipse (t = 3 fs). For later delays (t = 26.3 fs), scattering leads to a broadening also along kx. For vanishing fields, the electron distribution relaxes back to its original shape (t = 233 fs). b, Displacement of the COM of the electron distribution. The inset shows the Fourier transform of the oscillating electron distribution (green line) and the driving field (red shaded area). Dashed black lines mark the temporal positions of the momentum maps in a. c, Evolution of the change in the size of the electron distribution, Δσ, characterized by the width of the Gaussians used to fit the carrier distribution along the kx-axis (brown) and the ky-axis (green). The Fourier transform in the inset reveals oscillations in the width of the distribution along the ky-axis, with pronounced components at the second harmonic of the driving frequency during the initial half-cycles of the driving field (grey shaded area). The vertical orange lines in b and c are guides to the eye to relate the oscillation in the width of the electron distribution to the motion of its COM.

Already after the first MIR field cycles (Fig. 3a, t = 3 fs), the Fermi surface is strongly elongated from 0.054 Å−1 to 0.096 Å−1 in the direction parallel to the field, whereas the change in the orthogonal direction is only 0.014 Å−1 (Fig. 3a, Gaussian fits). The Fermi surface is no longer circular but takes on an elliptical shape. The time-dependent change in the ky width (Fig. 3c, green line) directly correlates with the field strength. Furthermore, this width oscillates at twice the MIR carrier frequency while the COM displacement tracks the electric field similarly to the current plotted in Fig. 2c. Because the maximum broadening coincides with the peak COM displacement, we can rule out motion blur as the origin of the elongation in the ky direction. Notably, the electron distribution encompasses the Dirac point at all delay times, even for the largest displacements.

All of these intriguing dynamics can be microscopically explained by a full quantum-mechanical solution of the SBEs6 (Methods), which account for intraband and interband transitions as well as LZM-type interband coupling, on equal footing. A systematic switch-off analysis pinpoints how specific aspects of coherent strong-field light–matter interaction manifest in the observed dynamics (Extended Data Fig. 4a). The periodic COM shift of the electron distribution is clearly associated with field-driven intraband motion of charge carriers. Yet, the distribution retains its circular shape and separates from the K point for large displacement if interband dynamics are switched off. Once interband coupling is included, the theory shows the same elongation of the carrier distribution as the experiment (Extended Data Fig. 4b). The theory also qualitatively reproduces the increase in carrier density in the conduction band (Extended Data Fig. 5), confirming that interband transitions at the K point act like a well that feeds electrons into the upper part of the Dirac cone on subcycle timescales.

These transitions originate from strong-field interband coupling, whereas conventional perturbative interband photoexcitation is suppressed by orders of magnitude under our experimental conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6). Owing to pseudospin selection rules34,35, photoexcitation would occur in momentum regions with |kx − K| > 0, located perpendicular to the polarization of the incident light (Extended Data Fig. 6a). By contrast, the coupled intraband and interband dynamics of the LZM scenario leads to the observed unidirectional elongation of the electron distribution parallel to the electric field (Extended Data Fig. 6b). Simulations with varying field strengths confirm that this feature is characteristic of the strong-field regime (Extended Data Fig. 7).

The region in which LZM-type tunnelling can occur is determined by the field strength, E0, and the energy gap, which increases linearly with |kx − K|. For E0 = 1.57 MV cm−1, the transition region is confined to momenta |kx − K| ≤ 0.08 Å−1 (Fig. 3a, t = 3 fs), corresponding to a Keldysh parameter of γ ≤ 0.63. Accounting for scattering and limited momentum resolution, this value is in good agreement with the original LZM formula \({P}_{{\rm{L}}{\rm{Z}}{\rm{M}}}=\exp \left(-2{\rm{\pi }}\frac{\hbar {v}_{{\rm{F}}}}{2|e|{E}_{0}}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\right)\), which predicts diabatic transitions in a momentum range |kx − K| ≤ 0.04 Å−1 (probability 1/e2 width; Methods). This confirms that the linearly dispersing Dirac cone of graphene is a perfect realization of the original model Hamiltonian23. And even Landau, Zener and Majorana’s assumption that the energy levels intersect at a constant speed holds true, as the strong driving fields propel the electrons past the intersection point in less than 1 fs—much faster than the MIR oscillation period (Methods).

The interplay between intraband motion and LZM tunnelling also explains the modulations of the width observed at twice the driving frequency (Fig. 3c). Because the region close to the K point features the lowest tunnelling barrier, electron injection into the upper part of the Dirac cone becomes most efficient in the few-fs time window between a field extremum and the nearest peak displacement of the pre-existing population, which occurs twice per optical cycle. Scattering shortens this time window, shifting the optimal injection time. This situation should result in a step-like increase of the population in the conduction band, with a phase determined by the interplay of Pauli blocking, the evolution of the field amplitude and scattering (Methods). However, a step-like increase can only be reproduced by simulations using extremely strong dephasing that destroys the quantum memory between successive LZM transitions (Extended Data Fig. 9). For realistic dephasing rates, the step-like character transforms into pronounced 2ω oscillations. Their presence in the experimental width of the electron distribution suggests interference of electrons owing to their accumulated phase between individual tunnelling events, emphasizing the role of quantum coherence in light-field-driven devices.

Although LZM dynamics dominate at early delay times, scattering limits the time frame for fully coherent light–matter interaction. At t = 26.3 fs (Fig. 3a), the initially anisotropic electron distribution broadens also along the kx direction and approaches a circular shape with a radius of about 0.065 Å−1, before it contracts to a more equilibrated and isotropic distribution (t = 233 fs). This ultrafast change of the elliptical distribution (Fig. 3c) reflects the interplay between field-driven acceleration, LZM transitions, scattering and carrier relaxation. Our SBE simulations (Extended Data Fig. 10 and Methods) predict distinctive momentum fingerprints for electron–electron and electron–optical phonon scattering. 2D mapping thus allows us to identify their signatures (Fig. 4a). Neglecting all forms of scattering results in a broadening (up to 0.053 Å−1) and displacement (about 0.107 Å−1) of the carrier density along the ky direction and the distribution remains elliptical after the MIR pulse (t = 233 fs), retaining the momentum hallmark of LZM transitions. Moreover, the phase delay of the microscopic current (Fig. 4b) is approximately π/2, as expected for undamped intraband motion. Introducing electron–electron scattering, the initially strongly broadened and displaced momentum distribution (t = 27 fs) partially thermalizes (t = 233 fs) and shrinks to a circular shape with a radius of about 0.038 Å−1. Still, the peculiar angular dependence of electron–electron scattering41,47 retains a large ellipticity on shorter timescales, and the phase delay is only marginally affected. This is caused by the reduced phase space for scattering imposed by the pseudospin texture of graphene.

a, Simulated 2D carrier density, n, in the conduction band for selected delay times with different scattering contributions. The leftmost panels show how the carrier distribution behaves for intermediate and late delay times t, based on the SBEs without scattering. The light grey line marks the half-maximum contour, highlighting the shape of the carrier distribution. For comparison, the dark grey line shows the corresponding contour when also excluding interband coupling, emphasizing its role in reproducing the experimental observations. It is included in the other panels for reference. The middle and right panels show the carrier distribution including different scattering channels: electron–electron (ee) scattering and electron–electron combined with electron–optical phonon (ee + op) scattering, respectively. The cartoons in the insets illustrate the regions in momentum space accessible for an electron (small, blue sphere) through scattering (dark regions: accessible; bright regions: inaccessible). b, Time-dependent evolution of the extracted current for different scattering mechanisms (dotted purple line: no scattering; dotted light blue line: ee scattering; solid blue line: ee + op scattering). The driving field is shown as a red line. Without scattering (dotted curves), the distribution is broadened strongly only in the direction of the field. Simulations including scattering with Γ point longitudinal (LO) and transverse (TO) optical phonons reproduce the experimentally observed dynamics very well. For t = 27 fs, the electron distribution shows a substantial broadening in both the ky (about 0.051 Å−1) and the kx (about 0.041 Å−1) directions, associated with an isotropic redistribution of the charge carriers. This leads to a nearly circular distribution whose COM is shifted by only 0.008 Å−1 at t = 27 fs, much less than in the previous cases. This results from a large change in the phase delay (Fig. 4b), approaching a value of π/4. After the pulse (t = 233 fs), the distribution relaxes to a fully circular shape with a radius of approximately 0.031 Å−1. Both the phase delay and the time-dependent broadening of the electron distribution (Fig. 4c) are in good qualitative agreement with the experiment. We can, thus, identify the key limiting factor for coherent control dictated by the fastest momentum redistribution channel, which, in graphene, is electron–optical phonon scattering (Fig. 4b, solid blue line).

Our experiment opens the momentum horizon of subcycle photoemission over the entire first BZ of basically any quantum material. This universal tool enabled us to directly observe LZM transitions in the band structure of a solid. Attosecond-precision videography of graphene unravels how interband LZM tunnelling couples to field-driven intraband acceleration along the Dirac cone and how scattering influences and limits a fully coherent evolution. This platform may soon address other key questions of condensed matter physics and ultrafast information technologies, from optical band-structure engineering and phase transitions to light-field-driven sculpting of molecular orbitals.

The subcycle momentum microscopy setup (Extended Data Fig. 1a) is based on two ytterbium-doped potassium gadolinium tungstate (Yb:KGW) amplifiers (CARBIDE, Light Conversion Inc.). Each amplifier generates near-infrared light pulses with a duration of 250 fs, a centre wavelength of 1,030 nm and a pulse energy of 1.5 mJ, at a repetition rate of 50 kHz. In the probe arm, the second harmonic of the output of a four-stage noncollinear optical-parametric amplifier (NOPA; ORPHEUS-OPCPA, Light Conversion Inc.)48 yields carrier-envelope phase (CEP)-stabilized pulses centred at 400 nm with a pulse duration of 20 fs. These pulses are focused into a high-pressure argon gas jet to generate high-order harmonics (Extended Data Fig. 1b) in a vacuum beamline49. The seventh harmonic at a photon energy of 21.7 eV is spectrally selected by two multilayer mirrors (Extended Data Fig. 1b, grey shaded area). They feature a bandwidth of 0.9 nm around 57 nm and thus support a Fourier-limited pulse duration of less than 10 fs. The XUV pulses enter the experimental ultrahigh-vacuum (UHV) chamber, the momentum microscope32, through a 200-nm-thin aluminium foil, which also filters out the ultraviolet driving pulses.

Because the count rate in a time-of-flight photoemission momentum microscope is limited to only about one electron per laser shot, a high repetition rate is key for keeping measurement times at a reasonable amount while ensuring good statistics. In our experiment, this requirement entails the challenge of pushing the generation of the atomically strong, few-cycle phase-stable MIR pump pulses to new limits for a tabletop setup. Here the generated phase-stable MIR pulses feature, to the best of our knowledge, record-high average powers of up to 1 W and electrical peak field strengths of more than 200 MV cm−1. These field transients are obtained by difference frequency generation in a gallium selenide crystal between the outputs of two parallel (N)OPAs (ORPHEUS-MIR, Light Conversion Inc.)50. They feature pulse durations down to sub-50 fs and can be tuned between 4 µm and 15 µm. A small portion of the laser fundamental is picked off to pump a home-built single-stage NOPA. It is optimized to generate 10-fs pulses centred around 825 nm, which are used for electro-optic sampling (EOS) of the MIR waveforms. Extended Data Fig. 1c shows a typical MIR transient detected by EOS. A pair of wire-grid polarizers allows us to precisely control the polarization direction and power of the MIR pulses, which are then coupled into the UHV chamber through a diamond window.

The intense MIR pump (s-polarized) and the XUV probe (p-polarized) are spatially overlapped in the vacuum chamber with a custom-built off-axis parabolic mirror featuring a small aperture for XUV transmission and are focused onto monolayer graphene with an angle of incidence of 70°. A piezo-controlled delay stage in the excitation beam path allows us to set the delay between the MIR and XUV pulses with a temporal precision of 230 as. The emitted photoelectrons are detected by a time-of-flight momentum microscope (lens system: GST mbH; detector: HEX40, RoentDek)51. Multihit detection ensures linearity of the signal up to a repetition rate of 20 kHz. The combination of the 21.7-eV probe pulses with the large acceptance angle of the momentum microscope allows access to momentum regions up to ±2.14 Å−1, as compared with ±0.16 Å−1 in previous subcycle ARPES experiments8,20. The energy resolution is limited by the broad spectrum of the probe pulse. The bandwidth of the XUV pulse is tunable, setting a limit for the energy resolution of 180 meV. The momentum resolution is better than 0.01 Å−1. The custom-designed UHV chamber is shielded by a μ-metal liner and maintains a base pressure of 2 × 10−10 mbar. The samples were measured at room temperature.

Inducing field-driven dynamics in the monolayer requires a field that is parallel to the plane of the monolayer. To maximize the corresponding field component, the MIR pulse is s-polarized. The polarization of the XUV pulse is set to be perpendicular to the MIR pulse to prevent crosstalk between their fields that could introduce coherent artefacts effects in the observed dynamics. Finally, the rotation of the sample is chosen such that the MIR-induced momentum streaking in vacuum is minimized at one of the K points. This requires one K point to be at k∥ = 0, with k∥ being the momentum direction parallel to the electric field of the MIR pulse. This alignment also minimizes matrix-element-induced asymmetries along k∥ = 0 in the observed energy and momentum range. Although an asymmetry along the kx direction might persist, it is rather small at the observed energies. This is because the dark corridor only begins to set in at relatively high excitation energies, which do not occur along the kx direction in the experiment. This may also explain the slightly larger broadening observed in the simulations in which the matrix element was neglected.

For sample preparation, an n-doped 6H-SiC(0001) wafer was used as a substrate for growing an epitaxial monolayer graphene with 0° rotational alignment relative to the substrate lattice (0°-EMLG). The wafer was initially degassed in UHV at 880 °C for 30 min. The temperature was subsequently increased to 1,050 °C and maintained for 30 min under an external flux of Si atoms, resulting in a Si-rich (√3 × √3)R30° surface reconstruction. The sample was then further annealed at 880 °C for an extra 30 min, again under Si flux, resulting in the Si-rich (3 × 3) surface reconstruction. With this procedure, the oxide layer is removed from the SiC surface and atomic cleanness is achieved. In the next step, 0°-EMLG was obtained by annealing the sample at 1,400 °C for 30 min in borazine (B3N3H6) atmosphere with a partial pressure of 1.5 × 10−6 mbar. The borazine molecules act as surfactants on the heated SiC surface. They inhibit the formation of the conventional 30°-rotated graphene layer but instead force the homogeneous graphene layer in an unconventional 0° orientation with respect to the substrate lattice. For more details on the preparation of the 0°-EMLG, see refs. 38,52,53. Following growth, the surface morphology and crystalline structure were characterized using low-energy electron microscopy and low-energy electron diffraction. The average width of terraces on the SiC surface is approximately 160 nm and the surface is fully covered by 0°-EMLG. Subsequently, the sample was shortly exposed to air, transported in static vacuum (0.1 mbar) to the experimental chambers and degassed at 350 °C for 3 h before the measurements. The photoemission experiments reveal that the 0°-EMLG sample is n-doped, with the Fermi level approximately 200 meV above the Dirac point.

The acceleration of photoemitted electrons in vacuum allows for an in situ reconstruction of electric field waveforms20. In addition to acceleration within the sample, the s-polarized field also accelerates electrons after they have left the material. This causes a momentum change of the entire band structure parallel to the surface of the sample, Δk∥, that follows the vector potential of the field. The electric field waveform can thus be calculated by:

To extract Δk∥, the extracted photoemission data are shifted stepwise along k∥ and compared with a reference spectrum without a field. Within a fixed momentum window centred on the Dirac point, spanning +160 meV to −1.5 eV relative to the Fermi level (a range that, at equilibrium, encompasses predominantly the valence band), the sum of absolute pixel-wise differences between the measured data and the reference is computed at each iteration. The iteration with the smallest overall error gives the value for Δk∥. Repeating this procedure for every delay point, t, allows a reconstruction of the applied field E∥(t). To refine the retrieved waveform, a second method for extracting Δk∥(t) is used. Tracking the change in the number of electrons, integrated over all detected energies (+1 eV to −7 eV), with positive or negative momentum along k∥, yields a unitless quantity directly proportional to Δk∥(t), which is not subject to discretization caused by the binning of the data along k∥. The waveform that can be extracted in this way is then scaled by the peak electric field from the first method. The resulting waveform is shown in Fig. 2c.

The extracted Δk∥ is also used to compensate for the streaking in the photoemission spectra. As well as the trivial shift along k∥, a shift in energy, Δε, is connected to momentum streaking. The energy of every electron in vacuum is given by:

The change in energy caused by Δk∥ can therefore be calculated with:

Extended Data Fig. 2a shows band-structure snapshots taken without an applied field (left panel) and with a strong field applied before streaking compensation (middle panel) and after streaking compensation (right panel). The streaking-induced changes of energy and momentum were compensated for in all photoemission spectra before further analysis of the occupation of the band structure.

A parameter that is frequently used to distinguish between the weak-field and strong-field regimes of light–matter interaction is the Keldysh parameter

It was introduced by Leonid Keldysh in 1965 as the ratio between the carrier frequency of light ω and the tunnelling rate of an electron with mass \({m}_{{\rm{e}}+{\rm{h}}}^{\ast }\) through a barrier Δ, to show that tunnelling and multiphoton ionization in strong electromagnetic fields follow essentially the same physical laws54. This ratio scales linearly with frequency ω and the inverse of the electric field strength E0. Tunnelling dominates for γ ≪ 1, which holds for sufficiently strong fields and/or low frequencies. Equivalently, it can be expressed as \(\gamma =\sqrt{\Delta /{2U}_{{\rm{P}}}}\) by comparing the barrier Δ with the mean kinetic energy of a free electron in an oscillating electric field of amplitude E0, the ponderomotive potential \({2U}_{{\rm{P}}}={e}^{2}{E}_{0}^{2}/4{m}_{e+h}^{\ast }{\omega }^{2}\). Although similar considerations can be made for quasirelativistic motion of electrons in gapless graphene, it is more realistic for the present experiment to take the full Dirac cone with its distribution of barriers and effective masses into account (Extended Data Fig. 7a). In that case, we obtain a kx-dependent Keldysh parameter26

because both the gap, Δ = 2ħvF|kx|, and the effective mass at the gap, \({m}_{e+h}^{\ast }=\hbar |{k}_{x}|/2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}\), depend on the distance from the Dirac point. By identifying Δ with the MIR photon energy of 124 meV, we get γ = 0.075 for the peak electric fields of 1.57 MV cm−1. If we could switch off intraband acceleration, the relevant transition energy from the valence band to the unperturbed conduction band would increase to two times the doping energy of 200 meV, that is, to Δ = 400 meV. Even then, γ = 0.24 would comfortably place our measurements in the strong-field regime.

The microscopic intraband current density for each time instant, j(t), is directly extracted from the individual photoemission measurements, as in Fig. 2c. After compensation of momentum streaking, the photoemission intensity is integrated in two momentum regions with ky < 0 and ky > 0, respectively, and normalized by the total number of carriers in the two momentum regions at equilibrium. Subtracting the time-dependent number of counts with positive and negative ky components, we obtain a dimensionless value proportional to the microscopic current. To reveal the maximum amplitude of the current density, this procedure is performed for all carriers above the Dirac point (E − ED ≥ 0) within the momentum region |kx − K| < 0.15 Å−1. The result is then calibrated to physical values by multiplying with the Fermi velocity and carrier density in the conduction band of graphene with a Fermi level located 200 meV above the Dirac point, which can be computed from the density of states27. This yields a maximum current density of j(t) = 38.2 A cm−1. This value is very high, as it is even larger than in previous studies on topological insulators8,20, in which the scattering times were two orders of magnitude longer. Given the higher Fermi velocity and field amplitude, a higher current could be expected in the presented experiment. Yet, in a Drude-like regime, this would not be sufficient to compensate for the much higher scattering rate. This confirms that, in ballistic regimes, the current does not follow the Drude model. The same procedure is applied to the results of the simulations based on the SBEs.

To extract the relative timing between the microscopic current in the Dirac cone, j(t), and the electric field waveform, E(t), we apply a phase delay analysis. We compute the product between the Fourier transform of the field waveform, \(\mathop{E}\limits^{ \sim }(\omega )=F\{E(t)\}\), and the complex conjugate of the Fourier transform of the current, \(\mathop{j}\limits^{ \sim }(\omega )=F\{j(t)\}\):

The squared modulus of P(ω) peaks at the frequency of the pump field, whereas its phase corresponds to the timing difference (or phase delay) between the two oscillating quantities. We thus define the average phase difference as:

in which φ[P(ω)] is the complex phase of P(ω) and summations only consider frequencies at which |P(ω)| is larger than 50% of its peak value. To compute the phase delay, τi, we need to divide this quantity by the central frequency of the pump field. We then obtain the mean phase delay, τϕ, and the associated standard deviation of the mean over repeated measurements as:

in which i = 1,…, N runs over three different measurements performed on this sample geometry.

By performing a gated phase delay analysis, it is also possible to calculate a time-dependent phase difference, ϕ(t), which indicates the evolution of the scattering processes throughout the duration of the pulse. Here, however, the delay remains relatively stable over the first 100 fs of the driving pulse. We therefore use a single average phase shift, which we associate with a characteristic scattering time. In principle, however, this method could open new avenues for investigating relaxation dynamics across different samples with unprecedented temporal resolution.
