From the Hamiltonian, it is then possible to compute the equilibrium eigenenergies and eigenfunctions:

The out-of-equilibrium dynamics shown in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 9 were simulated on a 250 × 250 2D square (kx, ky) grid in momentum space. The grid is centred on one of the K points with coordinates kx,K = 1.703 Å−1 and ky,K = 0 and it has a side length of 0.73 Å−1. The simulated time axis ranges from −100 fs to 300 fs, with a step size of 2 fs. The electric field, E(t), is parallel to ky and its temporal profile is analytically fitted to the experimentally measured field. At the initial time instant (t0 = −100 fs), we assume peh(k, t0) = 0, whereas the electron distribution corresponds to a Fermi–Dirac distribution. The position of the Fermi level compared with the Dirac crossing is set to εF = 0.2 eV to match the experiment. Simulations comparing the dynamics at other driving frequencies, varying field strengths or different Fermi levels sometimes used analytically modelled waveforms and smaller grid sizes to keep up with increased demands for spatial or temporal resolution.

In simulations including scattering, the grid was adjusted to 50 × 50 while maintaining the size in momentum space, to save resources. To reproduce the time-dependent electron distribution observed in momentum space, it is imperative to realistically model the scattering rates:

On these timescales, two physical phenomena mainly contribute to the scattering rates:

in which \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}},{\rm{e}}{\rm{p}}}^{\alpha }\) and \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}},{\rm{e}}{\rm{e}}}^{\alpha }\) are, respectively, the electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering rates.

Starting from the electron–phonon interaction, the scattering rate can be written as57:

in which v is the phonon mode considered and α, α′ ∈ {e, h} are the band indexes. The first term thus describes transitions from an occupied (k′, α′) state to an empty (k, α) state owing to the interaction with a v phonon, whereas the second term describes the opposite process. Whereas in the former the state (k, α) is empty and becomes occupied (thus, the rate is positive), in the latter, the rate must be negative. The probability of these transitions is associated with the electron–phonon transition rate:

in which \({G}_{{\alpha }^{{\prime} }\alpha }^{v}({{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{\bf{k}})\) is the electron–phonon coupling constant, δ is the Kronecker delta imposing energy and momentum conservation, q and \({\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) are the momentum and angular frequency of a v phonon, respectively, and \({n}_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) is the number of v phonons with a given frequency and momentum, which is described by the Bose–Einstein distribution.

To simplify our description, we assume that: (1) Umklapp processes are negligible and (2) the number of phonons \({n}_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) is constant and equal to its value at equilibrium (phonon bath). Moreover, previous works explained the dominating contribution of LO and TO phonons34,47. We will thus limit our model to LO and TO phonons and, because they have similar phonon energies (\({\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{{\rm{LO}}}\simeq {\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{{\rm{TO}}}\simeq 164.6\,{\hbar }^{-1}\,{\rm{meV}}\)) and matrix elements but their angular dependencies compensate each other, we will treat them together with an effective electron–optical phonon coupling constant57:

The effective matrix element is constant in momentum space and its value is adjusted to reproduce the experimental data. Owing to the isotropic angular dependence of this term, electron–optical phonon scattering will lead to a rapid spreading of the electron distribution around the Dirac cone.

In the same spirit, the scattering rate for electron–electron interaction can be written as57:

in which \(\alpha ,{\alpha }^{{\prime} },\beta ,{\beta }^{{\prime} }\in \{{\rm{e}},{\rm{h}}\}\) are the band indices. The first term, therefore, describes the scattering between a pair of particles in the initial states (α′, k′) and \(({\beta }^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} })\) to the final states (α, k) and \((\beta ,{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast })\), and the second term refers to the opposite process. The associated transition rate can thus be written as57:

and q = |k − k′| and \({q}^{{\prime} }=|{\bf{k}}-{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} }|\). The Coulomb potential between electron pairs is:

with A = 4π2/Δk2. The screening of the Coulomb interaction is given by the dielectric function \({\epsilon }(q)=1+{v}_{{\rm{c}}}(q)D({\varepsilon }_{{\rm{F}}})\mathop{\Pi }\limits^{ \sim }(q)\)57,58, in which:

and rS is the Wigner–Seitz radius of graphene, kF = εF/(ħvF) the Fermi wavevector and D(ε) the density of states close to the Dirac point. This approximation holds for n ≥ nth = 1012 cm−2, thus if εF ≥ 37.14 meV, as in our case.

In this form, the scattering rate for electron–electron interaction is computationally extremely expensive. Therefore, we assume that the electron distribution for the second particle can be approximated by the equilibrium Fermi–Dirac distribution of the carriers:

This allows us to write a simplified expression for the electron–electron scattering rate:

in which we use that \({S}_{{\rm{ee}}}({\bf{k}},{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast },{{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} })={S}_{{\rm{ee}}}({{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} },{\bf{k}},{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast })\) and define:

In our simulations, we only focus on a small momentum space region around one of the six equivalent K points. In doing so, we neglect intervalley electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering processes, which are not expected to contribute notably in these conditions34. However, for electron–electron scattering, it is possible that an electron scatters from one state to another within the same valley by interacting with a charge carrier in a different one. For this reason, we effectively account for these processes by multiplying \({S}_{{\rm{ee}},\beta \beta {\rm{{\prime} }}}^{{\rm{eff}},1}\) and \({S}_{{\rm{ee}},\beta \beta {\rm{{\prime} }}}^{{\rm{eff}},2}\) by the number of equivalent K valleys, that is, six. To reproduce the experimental data, we assumed Veff = 4.386. It is important to notice that the dependence on the relative angle between k, k′, \({{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }\) and \({{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} }\) determines the characteristic angular dependence of electron–electron scattering in graphene47, also termed collinear scattering41. Notably, at variance with the relaxation time approximation, our approach does not enforce any specific electron distribution at any time instant, while matching our experimental results.

To reduce the computational costs when relating the phase delay to an effective scattering time, a customary approach when solving the SBEs is to invoke the relaxation time approximation6,20,55,56. In this context, the scattering rate \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}}}^{\alpha }\) is assumed to be inversely proportional to a time constant, T1, associated with the mean free time between scattering events. Defining \({f}_{\alpha }^{(0)}({\bf{k}})\) as the equilibrium electron distribution in the α band, we obtain:

It is important to notice that, even though this approach allows us to extract an effective time constant, it is not enough to reproduce the experimental data. In fact, in this approximation, the scattering rate at a given point k in momentum space will only depend on the instantaneous electron distribution at that point and not on any other point in momentum space. This makes it impossible to reproduce any carrier redistribution dynamics in momentum space owing to, for example, the interaction with optical phonons.

The original works of Landau22, Zener23, Majorana24 and Stückelberg36 considered a two-state quantum system with an energy separation Δε = ε1(t) − ε2(t) = αt that changes linearly with time and undergoes an avoided crossing with a half gap energy δ. The diabatic transition probability is then given by26

with the diabaticity parameter \(\varGamma =\frac{{\delta }^{2}}{\hbar \alpha }\). This simple formula can be used to estimate the region in momentum space in which transitions occur in our experiment. The model is applicable under the condition that the characteristic sweep time through the transition, τ = 2δ/ε, is short compared with the oscillation period T = 2π/ω of the driving electric field. In this case, the field can be considered quasistatic during the transition and we simply have \(\alpha =2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}\hbar |{k}_{x}-K|=2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}|e|{E}_{0}\). With δ = vFħ|kx − K|, we obtain \(\tau =\frac{\hbar | {k}_{x}-K|}{|e|{E}_{0}}=\frac{\gamma }{\omega }\). Because γ ≈ 0.1, the crossing indeed occurs very fast (τ < 1 fs). For the peak electric field E0 = 1.57 MV cm−1, the diabaticity parameter \(\varGamma =\frac{\hslash {v}_{{\rm{F}}}}{2|e|{E}_{0}}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\,\cong \) \(210\,{{\rm{\mathring{\rm A} }}}^{2}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\) becomes smaller than 1/π for |kx − K| < 0.04 Å−2. In this region around the Dirac point, 1 − e−2 = 86% of the transitions from the valence band to the conductions band are expected to take place as long as Pauli blocking can be neglected. This region roughly coincides with the momentum area in which the conduction band of our doped graphene samples is occupied. This shows that transitions can only take place after the electrons have been accelerated away from the Dirac point. After several driving cycles, the observed dynamics of the doped and a hypothetical undoped sample are expected to be similar (Extended Data Fig. 8).

For an empty upper Dirac cone, we expect the carrier injection rate owing to LZM tunnelling to closely follow the magnitude of the electric field and the electron population to increase stepwise, with the highest injection rates occurring at the largest absolute field values. In an n-doped system and for high injection rates, as in the present experiment, Pauli blocking modifies this simple picture (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Electrons can only be injected when there is sufficient empty space in the conduction band near the K point. Consequently, intraband transport plays a decisive role in determining the injection timing. Carrier injection happens most efficiently during the intervals between the extrema of the electric field and the carrier displacement. Our simulations clearly show that this results in a phase delay between the population jumps and the field, which grows as more population has been transferred. Beyond the effects of Pauli blocking and scattering, the injection dynamics can be strongly influenced by quantum interference59. Here we find that they can cause a deviation of a step-like increase in the conduction band population (or electron distribution width) by transforming the plateau regions, following a strong injection phase, into local minima through destructive interference of electron wavepackets (Extended Data Fig. 9). Although the signal-to-noise ratio of the measured conduction band population does not allow us to resolve the jumps in the population during carrier injection experimentally, the dynamics of the increase of the carrier density can be well reproduced with the theory.

The simulations also show that the elongation of the conduction band electron distribution in momentum space is closely tied to the carrier population (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Notably, the weak oscillations in the width of the electron distribution, which are superimposed on the stepwise increase, become more pronounced with scattering (Fig. 4c). This effect is probably caused by a shortening of the effective injection time window. In the absence of scattering, the electron displacement follows the vector potential and is therefore phase-shifted by π/2 relative to the electric field. With scattering, the phase shift between the electric field and the displacement of the electrons shrinks, such that periods of rapid population increase occur only a few femtoseconds before an extremum in the displacement (Extended Data Fig. 5). Experimentally, the oscillation of the width of the electron distribution at twice the frequency of the driving field is clearly visible during the first three cycles of the electric field, that is, at times when there is still substantial carrier injection (Fig. 3c). The observed relative phase with respect to the electric field transient and the COM displacement agrees well with the simulations that include scattering. The data thus support the picture of a well that is periodically driven by the electric field and opened and closed by the oscillating carriers in the conduction band.

The new experimental platform presented here was developed to give direct access to strongly driven electron dynamics without relying heavily on theory or models. This philosophy also translates to data processing: our conclusions only rely on features present in the raw data. The previously described streaking compensation is the first and only step in the data analysis pipeline that is required to ensure that the observed dynamics can be attributed to processes that are happening in the solid and not the vacuum. Following that, the general strategy is that filtering is only used to remove technical noise and signals related to the matrix elements before the data are analysed or to enhance visibility in the figures. To ensure full transparency, the following contains a summary of all notable data processing steps for the presented figures.

The raw data from the delay line detector are binned with a spacing of 0.084 eV × 0.022 Å−1 × 0.022 Å−1 for the data in Fig. 1 and with a spacing of 0.084 eV × 0.011 Å−1 × 0.011 Å−1 for all other photoemission data.

The 3D data in Fig. 1c are symmetrized to remove the decrease in photoemission intensity caused by the angle of incidence of the XUV pulse.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 2a are obtained by integrating the 3D data within an energy window of 0.33 eV around distinct energy levels (0.25 eV, −0.25 eV, −0.75 eV, −1.25 eV, −1.75 eV). Before plotting, the data are further processed to enhance the visibility in the figure. First, a 1D simple moving average along both momentum axes (window size: 0.08 Å−1) is applied to the data four times. The filtered data are further processed by a 2D curvature filter described by equation (11) of ref. 60 with C0 = 0.2. Finally, a 2D median filter with window size 0.045 eV × 0.045 Å−1 is applied three times to clean up numerical noise.

The band structure cuts in Fig. 2b are obtained by integrating the 3D data within a momentum window of 0.08 Å−1 around kx − K = 0. Before plotting, the data are further processed to enhance the visibility in the figure. First, a 1D simple moving average along the energy and momentum axes with window sizes of 0.59 eV and 0.08 Å−1, respectively, is applied four times. The filtered data are subject to a 2D curvature filter with C0 = 0.2. Finally, a 2D median filter with window size 0.34 eV × 0.045 Å−1 is applied three times. The raw data are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2b.

The applied field transient and current in Fig. 2c are extracted from the raw data as laid out in Methods sections ‘Electric field waveform reconstruction and streaking compensation’ and ‘Current extraction and Fourier analysis of the phase delay’. Before plotting, a 4-THz high-pass filter is applied to the data to remove slowly varying offsets. The data showing the increase of the carrier population in the conduction band were acquired under almost identical experimental conditions in which special care has been taken to align the MIR polarization such that the electric field exhibits no perpendicular component leading to coherent oscillations of the integrated photoemission intensity.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 3a are obtained by integrating the 3D data for energies higher than 170 meV. This energy level is chosen to minimize contributions of the valence band caused by the limited energy resolution of the setup. Before extracting the COM displacement and width, a Gaussian filter with a small window size 0.02 Å−1 × 0.02 Å−1 has been applied to the 2D data. We applied the same filter to the experimental 2D data for a better comparison between experiment and theory. For the theory data, this is necessary to reduce numerical or binning artefacts. Owing to its small window size, the filter does not change or remove any of the features retrieved for data analysis.

To extract the COM motion and change of the width of the carrier distribution shown in Fig. 3b,c, the plotted 2D maps are integrated along kx and ky. For the data along ky, a Gaussian distribution with a constant offset (accounting for the background) is fitted to the integrated distribution. For the data along kx, the previously constant offset is modified with a linear decrease for growing kx values to account for the decrease in background caused by the photoemission matrix element. The mean of the extracted fit for the ky distribution is used to characterize the COM motion. Before plotting, a 15-THz high-pass filter is applied to these data to remove a slowly varying offset. The change of the standard deviation, Δσ, of the extracted fits is used to characterize the change of the width of the carrier distribution along kx and ky.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 4a are obtained by integrating the simulated population of the conduction band and applying a Gaussian filter with a small window size of 0.02 Å−1 × 0.02 Å−1 to the 2D data, as described above for the data shown in Fig. 3a.

The extraction of the simulated current density and change of the width of the carrier distribution shown in Fig. 4b,c follows the procedures outlined for the experimental data.

a, A Yb:KGW oscillator seeds two Yb:KGW amplifiers, each providing a pulse energy of 1.5 mJ at a repetition rate of 50 kHz. Half of the output of one amplifier is upconverted to 400-nm pulses with a pulse duration of 20 fs, which are then used to generate sub-10-fs XUV pulses by high-harmonic generation in argon (left side). In parallel, widely tunable, intense, few-cycle and CEP-stable MIR pulses are generated by difference frequency generation (DFG) of the outputs of a dual-branch OPA, which is supplied with the remaining half of the output of the first amplifiers (middle). The output of the second amplifier is used to almost exclusively pump the last amplification stage in the dual-branch OPA. Furthermore, a NOPA generates 10-fs-long NIR pulses (right side), which can be used to detect the MIR waveforms (EOS). Finally, all beams are guided into the UHV chamber of the momentum microscope, in which they are spatially overlapped. b, Generated XUV spectrum. The intense seventh harmonic order centred around 57 nm is selected by multilayer mirrors (grey shaded area) and is used as a probe pulse in the subcycle momentum microscopy experiments. c, Typical MIR waveform measured by EOS.

a, Photoemission spectra in different streaking conditions. The first two panels show a band-structure snapshot taken in equilibrium (left panel) and a snapshot with strong streaking along ky by the s-polarized MIR field (middle panel). The electric field is reconstructed by matching the streaked band structures to the equilibrium case. Once the electric field is known, the streaking effects can be compensated (right panel). The dashed black lines are a guide to the eye representing the equilibrium band structure. Applying the calculated shifts along energy and momentum, according to the extracted field from the middle panel, to the dashed black line yields the solid black line. b, Unfiltered version of the data shown in Fig. 2, showing the raw photoemission data after streaking compensation.

Simulations based on the SBEs in relaxation time approximation reveal how the phase delay between an applied waveform (central frequency, 30 THz) and the lightwave-driven current scales with the scattering time. For very small scattering times, the phase difference converges to zero, whereas for longer scattering times, it converges to π/2. The strongest change in the phase delay can be observed for scattering times on the order of a half-cycle of the driving waveform.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering. a, Interband coupling switched off. b, Interband coupling switched on. It causes a large elongation of the carrier distribution along the polarization of the driving light field, filling the gap between the displaced electrons distribution and the K point.

a, Normalized carrier density in the conduction band extracted from our theory model with electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering (black curve) and from experimental data (grey curve). The observed difference in the number of extra carriers between theory and experiment is to be expected, as the theory does not account for inherent constraints of the measurement itself, such as matrix element effects. The population rises fastest during the time window between a maximum of the field (red curve) and the COM displacement (green curve). b, During the first few cycles, the evolution of the width of the electron distribution (green curve) closely follows the population dynamics (black curve).

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering in the weak-field and strong-field regimes. The interaction regime is defined by means of the Keldysh parameter for an energy gap corresponding to single-photon absorption. a, The weak-field regime is reached by using fields that are 200 times weaker than in the experiment. Here the interaction is dominated by perturbative absorption, which is strongly affected by the selection rules owing to the pseudospin texture of graphene. By removing the doping, the first row highlights how this leads to a population increase in regions perpendicular to the polarization of the light pulse. The second row depicts the situation with the same doping level as in the experiment. Here no change in the population can be resolved, even when exaggerating the colour map by a factor of 2,500. b, In the strong-field regime, the interaction with light is characterized by a unidirectional elongation of the electron distribution parallel to the electric field as well as a displacement of the Fermi surface.

a, Illustration of the distribution of bandgaps Δ and the varying Keldysh parameter γ in graphene. b, Simulated 2D change of the population in the conduction band (blue curve) and aspect ratio of the carrier distribution (red curve) after interacting with the electric field for different field strengths in an undoped sample without scattering. For Keldysh parameters γ ≫ 1, the number of excited carriers scales quadratically with the field (grey curve), indicative of single carrier absorption. At the same time, the aspect ratio of the carrier distribution shows that the distribution is broader along the momentum direction perpendicular to the light field (left inset). In the strong-field regime (γ ≪ 1), the number of excited carriers is trending towards saturation, indicative of light-field-induced tunnelling as the transition mechanism. Simultaneously, the aspect ratio of the carrier distribution inverts, resulting in the elliptical distribution observed in the experiment with broadening in the direction parallel to the applied field (right inset). The extracted sub-quadratic scaling of the excited carrier density for the field strength used in the experiment (grey shaded area) indicates that perturbative single-photon or multiphoton absorption does not play a substantial role in the interaction.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering and different doping levels. a, No doping. b, Moderate doping. c, High doping. Intrinsic (a) and the moderately doped graphene (b, Fermi level 200 meV) closely resemble each other. Higher doping levels (c) reveal the difference between the intraband and interband signatures.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for different dephasing times. a, T2 = 0.1 fs. b, T2 = 1 fs c, T2 = 5 fs. d, T2 = 500 fs. The 2D carrier distribution is shown after the first (left panel) and second (middle panel) cycles. For very fast dephasing, the efficiency for LZM transitions decreases substantially, manifesting in a lack of additional carriers in the second panel of a. For very slow dephasing, signatures of LZSM interference emerge after the second cycle (fishbone pattern in the second panel of d). They manifest in a modulation at the second harmonic of the driving field in the elongation of the electron distribution along the direction parallel to the electric field (right panel), as highlighted in the inset by its Fourier transform during the first half-cycles of the driving field (grey area). The scale of the vertical axis is fixed across the insets.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times with different scattering contributions. a, No scattering. b, Only electron–electron scattering. c, Only scattering with optical phonons. d, Combination of electron–electron scattering and scattering with optical phonons.

Lightwave-driven dynamics in graphene. The video shows the subcycle dynamics of lightwave-driven graphene in the vicinity of the K point. On the left side, the electron population in the conduction band is shown, whereas the right panel shows a cut through the band structure at the K point. The field-induced asymmetry in the number of carriers with positive or negative momenta testifies to a macroscopic lightwave-driven current. Meanwhile, the emerging elliptical shape of the electron distribution in momentum space highlights the presence of LZM tunnelling into the conduction band. For late delay times, the electron distribution becomes circular again and relaxes back to its original shape by scattering.

#1268. O'Neill admits new signings are struggling with demands of being a Celtic player after dispiriting loss at Falkirk

Published: 11:08 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 11:21 EDT, 1 November 2026

Celtic boss Martin O’Neill admitted his summer recruits need to prove that they have the character and quality to handle the pressure of playing for the club.

The league leaders went down 2-0 at Falkirk on Sunday afternoon – their sixth defeat in their last 10 in all competitions – as they missed the chance to extend their advantage at the top of the Premiership table to seven points.

First-half strikes from Ethan Ross and Scott Tanser had the Bairns ahead at the break, and despite peppering Scott Bain’s goal in the second period, the visitors were unable to find a response.

When it was put to O’Neill that some new members of his squad are still struggling to meet the club’s high expectations, he said: ‘Absolutely. You have to cope with the pressure to be a player.

‘Tommy Burns said it might be easier to play against Celtic than for Celtic but hopefully we have enough in the dressing room and players who have been big winners.

‘When you ask managers sometimes you think the best team is the one that has won convincingly, but there are a number of players who have arrived.

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill was unhappy with his team's defending at Falkirk

‘You can think someone is doing well in training but the only place to find where players fit is out there.

‘We’re not used to losing a lot of games. We were in a much worse position this time last year so we have to buckle down and win a game and win a game in Europe. Thursday [against Besiktas in the Europa League] is a big game and then the following Sunday is massive before we go into the international break.

‘We need to sort out a few things. I was asked about confidence. If you take Kasper [Hogh], he wanted to get a goal after some time.

‘Something might fall for him but it’s not just that something might fall for you. You have to work at it which is something us as a team and the players in particular need to do.’

O’Neill bemoaned the defensive lapses that allowed Falkirk to open up a two-goal cushion, but saw enough in his team’s performance in the attacking third to give him confidence that things will soon start clicking.

‘I’m naturally disappointed to have lost the game,’ he said. ‘We had a lot of chances. Their goalie was magnificent but naturally we’ve lost so I’m very disappointed.

Callum McGregor looks frustrated as Celtic are made to suffer in Falkirk

‘The goals were very poor from our viewpoint. We didn’t clear it for the first one then we let someone run through and pick his spot for the second. We had some really great chances we just weren’t able to convert.

‘At half-time I thought we were still in the game. I thought we’d played decent stuff. If you concede a magnificent goal you take it in your stride.

‘When you concede a bad goal, which from any viewpoint was a poor goal, then it’s tough to come back then the goalie makes some saves and it’s frustrating.

‘Despite mistakes at the back we had enough chances to get back.

‘We have conceded some poor goals and haven’t kept a clean sheet for some time which is the essence of a championship team, but we’re still top and we need to address it and that’s the way out of it.

‘We scored seven against Hearts which isn’t that long ago. I just thought the goalie had a magnificent game and we should have scored a number in each half.

‘When you don’t it becomes frustrating. We have to address that we were conceding. Hopefully we can still do that. It’s still a long season.’

#1267. Munich up against at least six competitors for 2036 Olympics

The International Olympic Committee has revealed the six other countries intending to bid for the 2036 Olympic Games. This comes after Germany selected Munich as its Olympic candidate.

Munich's bid for the 2036 Summer Olympics will be up against at least six candidates from Europe, Asia and Africa. On Tuesday, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced that, in addition to Germany, Hungary, Turkey, India, Qatar, South Korea and South Africa all intend to bid for the Games. All are currently engaged in the Continuous Dialogue stage of the bidding process with the IOC.

However, there could be further applicants, as the deadline for interested parties to submit a bid is October 31. The candidates are to present their plans virtually to the Future Host Commission in November. In March 2027, the IOC is to deliberate, analyze, and narrow down the field of applicants to a group selected to enter into the Strategic Dialogue stage.

A subsequent Targeted Dialogue stage with one or more bidders is planned for 2028, with the final decision on the 2036 Olympic host expected at the IOC Session in the summer of 2029.

However, the IOC did not disclose exactly which cities, alongside Munich, are in the running – although Ahmedabad, Doha, Budapest and Istanbul are seen as possible hopefuls.

Munich secured its bid late last month after beating the Cologne/Rhine-Ruhr region in a vote by delegates of the German Olympic Sports Confederation. The city last hosted the Games in 1972. Berlin had withdrawn its bid in the days leading up to the vote.

"Wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: Athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do," IOC President Kirsty Coventry said.

"As an athlete, you spend years working to make your Olympic dream come true. The experience you have when you finally reach the Olympic Games stays with you for the rest of your life," added the former swimmer who won gold in the 200-meter backstroke for Zimbabwe at the 2004 Athens and 2008 Beijing Summer Games.

"That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point."

The IOC is to evaluate the bidders' proposals based on "technical factors." These include a master plan for competition venues and the athlete experience, the financing strategy, political and public support, the capacity to deliver the event, and a sustainability strategy. The German Olympic Sports Confederation believes Munich is well-positioned in all these areas.

The Munich bid is not focused solely on 2036 but was also designed with 2040 and 2044 in mind. If it misses out on 2036, Munich can expect to face a similarly large pool of competitors for the following two Summer Games. According to an IOC statement, there are National Olympic Committees "taking part in noncommittal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036."

#1265. Inter and AC Milan unveil plans for new 71,500-seat Generali Stadium to replace iconic San Siro

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It was an historic day in Milan as Inter and AC Milan have finally unveiled the project for the new stadium that will replace San Siro, the current arena that hosts the home games of both teams. The new San Siro will be named "Generali Stadium" after the Italian insurance company Generali acquired the naming rights of the stadium in a deal worth €650 million ($725 million) over 20 years, according to multiple reports. The Generali Stadium will be ready by the 2031-2032 season, according to the two clubs, just in time for the UEFA 2032 Euro that will be co-hosted by Italy and Turkiye, with construction starting in 2028. The current San Siro will be demolished only after the new stadium is ready to be used by the teams, giving more time for fans to attend a match in the iconic Italian stadium that was built in 1926.

Let's now go into the details of the new arena: According to the joint news release from both clubs, it will be a "71,500-seat stadium designed around one of football's most iconic atmospheres, setting a new standard for the live fan experience". A bold architectural vision by Foster + Partners and MANICA, bringing together Lord Norman Foster and David Manica, the two architects who previously worked on the design of London's Wembley Stadium. The new arena will feature a striking X-frame structure and a sweeping double-curved roof, conceived to become Milan's next landmark. A "defining investment" by RedBird and Oaktree, AC Milan and Inter ownerships, to "strengthen sporting competitiveness, unlock future growth and help shape the next era of Italian football".

Two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, creating exceptional sightlines and an immersive connection between fans and pitch. At either end, the iconic Curvas rise as single, steep walls of support, drawn forward toward the field of play with seating inclinations of up to 37 degrees to amplify both atmosphere and visual impact. At the heart of the design is a striking structural form, whose powerful rhythm recalls both the legacy of Italian engineering and the intricate craftsmanship of the Duomo di Milano.

Engineered to capture and intensify crowd energy, the stadium's acoustic design ensures supporters remain at the heart of the spectacle, helping create an environment designed to be among the most atmospheric in world football. Enhanced accessibility, modern hospitality concepts and a broad range of seating options, from world-class premium experiences to popular seating areas, will ensure the venue welcomes every generation of fan, while offering new ways to experience the game.

The two teams will continue to share their home stadium, a unique tradition that started in the late '40's of the 20th century, when Inter moved to San Siro as well. Unlike most of the teams around the world of soccer, Inter and AC Milan decided to continue sharing their home stadium after leaving the current arena. After years of failed projects and attempts, the new stadium is now a concrete reality. In 2025, the Milan City Council approved the sale of the city's San Siro stadium to the two clubs Inter and AC Milan. Now, the two Italian teams have decided to move into a new direction and era.

As Italian soccer is facing a crisis also regarding their infrastructures, the Generali Stadium can drastically increase the match revenues of both Inter and AC Milan, putting them at the level of the European rivals. At the same time, seeing the teams leave the legendary San Siro will be hard.

San Siro has been the home of AC Milan and Inter, but its history extends far beyond soccer. The iconic stadium has hosted some of the most memorable sporting and cultural events, including the opening ceremony of the 2026 Winter Olympic Games and legendary concerts by some of the biggest names in music. From Bob Marley's historic performance in 1980, the first-ever concert at San Siro, to unforgettable shows by the Rolling Stones, David Bowie, Michael Jackson, Madonna, Taylor Swift, U2 or Bruce Springsteen, who has famously described San Siro as his second home, the stadium has become a landmark far beyond the world of sport. Now, a new era is about to start but the "old" San Siro won't be forgotten.

Un nuovo simbolo per Milano.Una nuova casa per le future generazioni di tifosi Interisti.​Generali Stadium 🏟️ ‌ pic.twitter.com/9wmNGfrVI9

#1264. Emerging economies are embracing solar power and skipping fossil fuels much faster than Europe or the US

Renewable electricity is cheaper than ever. While the West got rich on coal and oil, some of the world's poorest countries are banking on solar, wind and water instead.

As emerging economies and global living standards rise, is the world in for another fossil fuel boom? The data says not. Countries from Southeast Asia to Sub-Saharan Africa aren't investing in fossil fuels as the West did; they're investing in electricity powered by renewables.

When the US and Europe industrialized in the 19th and 20th centuries, they did so using fossil energy. From coal ovens, gas heating and combustion-engine cars to electricity produced in coal and gas power plants, entire societies relied on polluting fuels.

Yet while burning fossil fuels allowed industrialized countries to boom, it also caused the climate crisis that is linked to extreme weather events around the world today.

Many of the same countries that became economically powerful off the back of fossil fuels are now trying to transition to renewables, but centuries of legacy infrastructure hold them back.

Because a gas boiler won't run on wind power and a diesel truck cannot be solar-powered, societies looking to shift to green energy need to use more electricity and increase their share of renewables.

That is where many middle- and lower-income countries have an advantage. With less existing energy infrastructure built around fossil fuels, they are better placed for a faster rollout of renewable electricity sources.

In many instances, solar power in particular is now cheaper to produce than fossil electricity. And unlike large coal or gas plants, which take years to construct and millions in investments, solar and wind farms can be built quickly and with much less upfront cost.

At the same time, according to an analysis by renewables think tank Ember, electronic devices like refrigerators, electric stoves or air conditioners have all become much cheaper in the last decades, making electricity a more affordable option as an energy source for cooking, heating and more.

While electric cars are still a luxury item in most places, their prices are coming down too. And a UN study found that in India, Indonesia and Vietnam electric scooters and motorbikes already cost the same as petrol models. Yet a lot less to fuel.

All this means that renewable electricity is quickly becoming the best choice for the wallet — not just for the climate. And countries are taking note.

"We're seeing a leapfrog take place right across the emerging markets,” said Kingsmill Bond, energy strategist at Ember. "The whole of Asia is electrifying quickly, and the whole of Europe and the United States is stagnant."

In 2023, only around a quarter of global electricity was generated by renewables. But that figure is rising fast, and almost all new capacity added these days is based on solar or wind power.

Lower-income countries already use less fossil fuels and more renewables than higher-income ones.

And large middle-income economies are outpacing richer ones as well. In 2023, solar power alone made up at least six percent and ten percent of electricity in India and Vietnam, respectively. The global average was five percent.

This boom has meant middle- and lower-income countries are electrifying fast, consuming less energy directly from fossil fuels than richer countries. Vietnam, for instance, is already using more electricity than the US, Europe and even China, and India is following the same path.

But the potential for energy leapfrogging might be particularly high in low-income countries, especially across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia and Namibia are rapidly expanding their energy infrastructure to meet the demands of a growing, young population. But rural areas in many countries are not connected to electricity grids.

Joel Nana, project manager at South African NGO Sustainable Energy Africa says that "even when there is access to power, it's often not reliable."

Until a few years ago, he says, people defaulted to diesel generators to meet their energy needs. That came at a cost because importing fuel is particularly expensive in many African countries, meaning energy crises and oil price fluctuations hit much harder.

These factors make solar power a solution for both energy access and independence. And it has become so cheap that Nana says it's a "no-brainer."

"Some businesses can make back their investment in just two years, so why would you want to deploy anything else?” he said. "Solar has rapidly become the de facto default technology that everyone falls back on.”

And once it is set up, it is very effective. Sub-Saharan Africa is extremely well-suited to solar power. It gets more sun than almost anywhere in the world, and has enough space for solar farms to cover electricity demand hundreds of times over.

"If you add solar plus batteries, you can get cheap electricity about 90 percent of the time from the sun alone”, said Kingsmill Bond.

Countries like Namibia, South Africa, Kenya and Senegal have expanded their solar capacity massively in the past few years.

In a 2026 report for African Tech Futures Lab and Ember, Nana analyzed import data from China and estimated that around 100,000 solar panels were installed across Africa every day in 2026, up 45 percent from just the previous year.

Similar trends are emerging all across the world. In Pakistan, for example, people have been buying solar panels from China en masse in the past few years to avoid steep electricity grid prices and frequent power outages.

Aleksi Lumijärvi, director for knowledge, policy and finance at the International Renewable Energy Association says these decisions can have a major impact on the global economy in the coming decades.

"Industrial companies will find that it will be cheaper to move production to, for example, somewhere in Sub-Saharan Africa, because they have this cheap, clean solar power plus batteries available.”

Kingsmill Bond says where electricity is cheap and abundant, wealth will follow.

"You're going to have faster growth in the emerging markets, you will have fewer financial crises. It will make a material difference to people's quality of lives.”

Nana says the next step for African countries is to establish policies that ensure everyone benefits from the solar boom.

"We are heading towards the most decentralized grid in the whole world within the next five years,” he told DW. His mantra for governments, he says, is: "This is happening, whether you like it or not.” He expects a wave of new energy regulations, many of which are now in the final stages of negotiation, to come into effect across Africa in the coming months and years.

"Countries are realizing it's in their interest to integrate this technology into national strategies, to share the benefits and to make use of this competitive advantage."

All data and code behind this analysis can be found in this Github repository.

#1262. Nobelitis — How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur

After being chosen for one of the world's most prestigious awards, some Nobel laureates lose touch with reality and suddenly start spouting unscientific nonsense. They're afflicted by what some have called "Nobelitis."

Linus Pauling won not one, but two Nobel Prizes — the first, for chemistry, in 1954 for his research into the nature of the chemical bond, and the Peace Prize in 1962 for his work in the anti-nuclear weapons movement.

The American chemist not only won two Nobel Prizes, but won them on his own, a rare feat for any scientist. Such an honor often turns laureates into global superstars overnight, with millions hanging on their every word.

That instant fame can be dangerous, said Nils Hansson, a professor in the Department of History, Theory and Ethics of Medicine at Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf. Especially, he said, when these world-renowned experts "start spreading crazy, unproven scientific theories" — ideas that, when disseminated by Nobel laureates, risk being taken seriously.

That's what happened with Pauling. Beginning in the mid 1960s he began claiming that vitamin C was a universal remedy, a cure for everything from cancer to cardiovascular conditions and degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis or osteoarthritis.

Pauling developed an alternative treatment he called orthomolecular medicine, based on specific doses of vitamins and minerals for each patient. To this day, some 60 years later, evidence for his methods remains inconclusive.

Pauling's case is a classic example of "Nobelitis," or "Nobel disease" — not an official diagnosis, but an informal term used to describe how some laureates begin to suffer delusions of grandeur later in life. It was first coined by Paul Nurse, president of The Royal Society, the UK's national academy of sciences, and himself a winner of the Nobel Prize.

"Be skeptical of everything, including yourself and your own ideas," Nurse said in a 2019 interview with KU Leuven University in Belgium, when asked what made someone a good scientist. In cases of Nobelitis, that self-skepticism is the first to go.

That was also the case with virologist Luc Montagnier, who was jointly honored in 2008 for his discovery of the human immunodeficiency virus, HIV, with colleague Francoise Barre-Sinoussi in the early 1980s.

Montagnier would later go on to support homeopathic medicine, another alternative treatment of disease and claim that HIV transmission in Africa could be diminished through better hygiene and nutrition.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Montagnier said the SARS-CoV-2 virus had been created in a lab with parts of the HIV genetic code. "It's difficult for a practicing virologist to say that a Nobel laureate in virology is spreading nonsense," said German virologist Christian Drosten on NDR's Coronavirus Update podcast in May 2020. "But that is utter nonsense."

James Watson, who was never known for his modesty, also let fame go to his head. In 1962, he was awarded the Nobel Prize along with Maurice Wilkins and Francis Crick for their discovery of the structure of the DNA molecule. But in the early 2000s, Watson repeatedly spread racist theories that Black people were less intelligent than white people.

For medical historian Hansson, Watson is a prime example that the Nobel Prize is not automatically awarded to a person who should be considered as a role model.

"You may have made a fantastic discovery, but that doesn't make you a universal genius," he said.

But the great expectations of an admiring public may also contribute to the development of Nobelitis. Paul Nurse, who won the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine in 2001, soon found himself getting daily requests for interviews on all sorts of topics.

"As if suddenly I was acknowledgeable about all workings of the world and of human beings," he told DW.

Nurse had this advice for researchers: "Be careful quite what you say. Talk about things that you do know something about that would be fine. And if you don't know so much or you're not sure about something, be really clear that you're not sure."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hansson has also noticed that the media eagerly report whatever Nobel laureates say — even when prize winners stray far from their area of expertise.

Nobelitis sufferers are leaders in their fields and rightly honored for their work with the Nobel. But they're also regular individuals, not immune to megalomania and other behavioral problems — meaning that homeopathy, orthomolecular medicine and other pseudosciences don't automatically become credible just because they're backed by a Nobel Prize winner.

This article was originally written in German.

#1261. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Our side to take on Brentford 👊 #BRELIV https://t.co/24Xblf6j3G

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1260. HEARTS 1-2 HIBS - PLAYER RATINGS: Which midfielder ran the show at Hampden? Who missed chances to force extra time?

Published: 12:59 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 13:09 EDT, 1 November 2026

Hibs ripped up the form book to  claim a thrilling victory over city rivals Hearts in  the Premier Sports Cup semi-final at Hampden.

Despite falling behind to an early header by Claudio Braga, the Premiership's bottom-placed side came roaring back with goals from Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

Hearts piled on the second-half pressure, but Marink Reedijk's side held firm to secure a place in the final against Rangers next month.

After a dramatic derby that will be remembered for years to come, Paul Forsyth assesses the individual performances.

Blameless for the two goals, he did his best to repel Hibs with a string of saves. Denied Passlack, Boyle and, in the closing stages, Klidge.

Had his hands full when Boyle threatened to run riot, but stuck to his task. Supported the attack well when Hearts grew desperate.

Caught flat-footed and square when Boyle stole in behind him to net Hibs’ equaliser. Otherwise solid enough when the pressure was on.

Man of the match Joe Newell celebrates with Jamie McGrath after their  team go 2-1 ahead

Bust a gut to cover and thwart Hibs’ explosive breaks. Produced a number of excellent blocks, most notably one that denied Elding.

Stood up well when Hearts needed him. His outstanding sliding block to thwart Passlack late in the game was as good as a goal.

Left the field after just 14 minutes with a horrible head knock, picked up when he nodded Calvin Miller’s cross narrowly wide.

Outnumbered in the first half, he looked lost in midfield. Far more influential when Hearts later got a grip of that department.

Stretched his opponents as Hearts grew into the game, but never really came up with a telling pass or effort on goal.

Caused all sorts of problems with his early crosses, only to become the latest addition to Hearts’ ridiculous injury list. Hobbled off before the interval.

Quiet in the first half, save for a perfect cross that Braga should have converted. Direct, dangerous and back to his best after the interval.

Claudio Braga misses a late chance to force extra time in the Premier Sports Cup semi-final

Opened the scoring from close range, but could and should have done more. Missed two free headers and had a powerful shot saved.

SUBSTITUTES: Wilson (Dhanda 83) (Magnusson 14), Guendouz (Miller 37), Benjaminsen (Kerjota 81)

Unused: Fulton, Williams, Kabore, Findlay, Pollock.

Nowhere to be seen when Braga nodded Hearts ahead from inside the six-yard box, but two saves, denying Braga and Guendouz, were massive.

Aggressive, positive and willing to give Hibs width in attack. Should have scored with an early chance after he was set up by Newell.

Fell asleep for Braga’s early opener, but settled into the game and was a pillar of Hibs’ defence when the pressure mounted.

Switched off to allow Braga a free header that slipped wide. His powerful header at the other end was directed straight at the goalkeeper.

Took full advantage of the early freedom he was given wide on the left. Responded well to later pressure, especially with a brilliant tackle on Kerjota.

Properly exploited Hearts’ depleted midfield with a strong, authoritative first-half display. Less influential after Hearts tweaked their set-up.

His positive, probing work was crucial to Hibs’ first-half dominance. Clipped the top of the crossbar with one shot. Set up his team’s second goal with another.

Strong and tactically aware. By stepping inside, he increased the midfield numbers, allowing McGrath to push forward and Passlack to overlap.

Playing off the front, he supported Elding at every opportunity. Reacted well to snap up the rebound for Hibs’ second.

Martin Boyle equalises for Hibs with a low shot that goes in off the goalkeeper and post

Inspirational talisman in attack. Transformed the game with a timely equaliser, which he stroked in off the goalkeeper and post. Almost scored a second.

Occupied Hearts’ backline without offering a sustained goal threat. His lovely hook over a square defence set up Boyle for the equaliser.

SUBSTITUTES: Klidge (Elding 74), Wright (Newell 74), Cadden (Boyle 85), Hanley (McGrath 85).

Unused: Smith, Iredale, Suto, Matondo, Abdulai.

Failed to cope with the early loss of Tomas Magnusson, which turned the game.

Gave his side numerical superiority in midfield, as well as the resources later  to protect their lead.

On Saturday, AC Milan will host Inter at San Siro for the first Derby della Madonnina of the season. It's a clash between two of the most important teams in Europe and the first derby for Portuguese coach Ruben Amorim, who joined AC Milan in the summer after leaving Manchester United in January. The two clubs will play at the iconic Italian arena, but on Thursday they unveiled plans for the new stadium that will replace San Siro, which both clubs currently share. The new San Siro will be named Generali Stadium after Italian insurer Generali acquired the naming rights in a deal worth €650 million ($725 million) over 20 years.

The project is a "71,500-seat stadium designed around one of football's most iconic atmospheres, setting a new standard for the live fan experience," according to the clubs. A bold architectural vision by Foster + Partners and MANICA, bringing together Lord Norman Foster and David Manica, the two architects who previously worked on the design of London's Wembley Stadium. The new arena will feature a striking X-frame structure and a sweeping double-curved roof, conceived to become Milan's next landmark. The stadium is a "defining investment" by RedBird and Oaktree, the owners of AC Milan and Inter, respectively, to "strengthen sporting competitiveness, unlock future growth and help shape the next era of Italian football." Two seating tiers form a continuous 360-degree bowl, creating exceptional sightlines and an immersive connection between fans and pitch. At either end, the Curvas rise as single, steep walls of support, drawn forward toward the field of play with seating inclinations of up to 37 degrees to amplify both atmosphere and visual impact. At the heart of the design is a distinctive structural form, whose powerful rhythm recalls both the legacy of Italian engineering and the intricate craftsmanship of the Duomo di Milano.

#1258. Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 658, pages 1141–1152 (2026) Cite this article

Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Here we review current advances in our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of these diseases and discuss consequences with respect to emerging targets and treatment strategies, which are increasingly enabling more robust disease control and the first prospects of a cure for previously chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases.

#1257. Ronaldo stays on under cloud as Messi exits internationals

Just hours before Lionel Messi played his last match for Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo posted his latest salvo in a row with Portugal. Ronaldo wants to play on despite the troubles, while Messi bathed in adulation.

They are the two players who have defined the last two decades. As football became ever more popular, commercial and dominant in the cultural and sporting landscape, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi remained its twin peaks.

Along with that has come endless social media posts, stories and discussions about who is better. Does Messi's World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina trump Ronaldo's Euro 2016 win and two Nations League titles? Or does the Portuguese's greater number of goals mean more? How about their club honors?

It is, essentially, a subjective argument and not one that can ever be resolved. It remains to be seen whether that's also true of the public spat between Ronaldo and his Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

On Tuesday, Messi scored a 126th goal in his 208th game for Argentina. Shortly before he did, Ronaldo posted a 2,000-word statement in which he stopped short of quitting the national team but said there was an "absolute breakdown of trust" between him and the coach.

Ronaldo's comments refer to Portugal's recent match against Norway in which he said he was initially to be rested before being asked to warm up as a substitute without ever being brought on. The striker, 41, walked away from the team's camp for the remainder of the international break, but said the story is not over.

"I can promise all my fans, and naturally especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches. There will be time for that," said Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

"Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach's word, as anyone who witnessed these conversations can attest, I should not have done it," Ronaldo said. "The responsibility is entirely mine. I apologize to the Portuguese people once again, but the breaking of one's word has, for me, a defining impact.

"I felt that, from that point on, my staying would only harm the group, and I did what I have always said I would do if I didn't feel useful: I picked up my bags and left," he continued before suggesting he accepted there may be a need for the coach or federation to punish him.

It was a long way from the emotional scenes in Rosario, Argentina. Instead of anger and recrimination, the overriding emotions there were gratitude, nostalgia and sadness.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you," Messi, who now plays his club football for Inter Miami in the US, told the 80,000 fans who had packed in to see him score a penalty in a 3-0 win over Benin.

For some, the contrasting evenings offered a neat synopsis of the pair. Ronaldo, less naturally gifted than his counterpart, has made the most of his talents with a singular focus which many believe often makes him prioritize himself over the team. He has had similar fallouts with managers and head coaches before, including Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, Erik ten Hag at Manchester United and Portugal's 2022 World Cup coach, Fernando Santos.

Ronaldo's much-discussed aim to reach 1,000 career goals is held up by some as further evidence of where his motivations lie.

"You know what my goal is. I want to win trophies, and I want to reach that number (1,000 goals) that you all know. I will reach the number for sure, if no injuries," he said last December. He is currently on 979.

For others, that is simply what is required to be the best. While Messi's quiet character and general refusal to play out his life in public suggest a more humble character focused on helping the team, his genius has undoubtedly changed the teams around him. In the 2026 World Cup, he barely broke into a run but still led an otherwise fairly limited Argentina to the final with eight goals.

There will be no more Messi goals for Argentina and, despite his promises, no absolute assurances that the world will see Ronaldo in a Portugal shirt again. For now, both will head back to their club sides to play out their twilight years away from the intensity of Europe's top leagues. But wherever they go from here, the spotlight will keep following.
