#1240. NWSL Decision Day scores, playoff bracket, takeaways: Gotham FC cement their dynasty, Seattle Reign survive

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 NWSL regular season might be over, but the fun is just getting started after an exciting NWSL Decision Day. All 16 NWSL clubs kicked off at once during a final afternoon of the regular season with plenty of high stakes on the line. This year's edition arrived with the NWSL Shield still up for grabs, awarded to the team with the most points, one final playoff spot in play, and multiple home-field advantages to settle.

When the final whistle sounded, it was Gotham FC that lifted the NWSL Shield, with San Diego Wave finishing just behind in second place, and Seattle Reign grabbing the final playoff spot.

Here are the big takeaways from the chaotic day:

Gotham FC 2, Utah Royals 0 San Diego Wave 1, Bay FC 0Kansas City Current 2, Racing Louisville 0 Washington Spirit 2, Chicago Stars 0 Seattle Reign 1, Orlando Pride 0Angel City 4, Boston Legacy 1 North Carolina Courage 1, Denver Summit 0 Portland Thorns 2, Houston Dash 0

With decision day done and dusted, the final results confirm the 2026 NWSL playoff bracket. More decision-day wins by Washington Spirit, 2-0 over Chicago, and Kansas City Current's 2-0 win against Racing Louisville confirm they get to host at least one home playoff game. First-place Gotham and second-place San Diego will also host, and if they win in the quarters, they will host semifinal fixtures.

San Diego, Angel City, and Kansas City all step into the playoffs on hot streaks. All three clubs are unbeaten in their last five games, with the Current on a five-game win streak.

NWSL playoffs begin Nov. 6, and the 2026 NWSL Championship will be played on Nov. 21. Fans can watch the biggest game of the year on CBS.

THE 2026 @NWSL PLAYOFFS ARE SET 🏆 pic.twitter.com/BtB3Wme9Uh

Friday, Nov. 6San Diego Wave vs. Utah Royals, 10 p.m.Saturday, Nov. 7KC Current vs. Angel City, 12 p.m.Sunday, Nov. 8Gotham FC vs. Seattle Reign, 12:30 p.m.Washington Spirit vs. Portland Thorns, 3 p.m.

Gotham needed only a draw to clinch their first-ever Shield in club history, but they did more than that and won 2-0 at home at Sports Illustrated Stadium. The club heads into the playoffs as the top seed after winning previous NWSL Championships as the lowest-ranked eighth seed.

The East Coast side has been a force to be reckoned with, winning the Shield during the longest season ever, the league's first 30-match schedule. The club had a significant points margin in late summer, but inconsistency and roster rotation due to injuries down the stretch pushed the Shield race to decision day, with Washington Spirit in contention through the penultimate matchweek and San Diego Wave still in contention on decision day.

San Diego did their part to make things interesting with a 1-0 win at Bay FC, but Gotham's early attacking surge set them up for success. Forward Midge Purce created the space for a laser cross in front of goal to Guro Reiten.

Gotham are making their Shield push 🏆Midge Purce sets up Guro Reiten as Gotham strike first on Decision Day 🤩🎥 @NWSL pic.twitter.com/8xLu5xuqKK

The lengthy season has affected all clubs this year, though Gotham's late-season string of injuries was particularly noticeable, with recent season-ending injuries to defender Bruninha and breakout rookie forward Jordynn Dudley. Attacker Jaedyn Shaw recently withdrew from U23 USWNT camps in mid-October due to an injury, and was available for Gotham's penultimate game last week but did not enter the match after warming up.

She's rocking a leg sleeve now and making an impact for the club, and scored the last goal after subbing in.

THAT’S JUST HOW IT’S DONE pic.twitter.com/BEj9KsAu6p

The goal sealed the win, and the return of Shaw and Rose Lavelle, both from injury, was a welcome sight for a team that has leaned on depth all season. Midfielder Jaelin Howell, among the team leaders in minutes played, left the match in the first half with a right ankle injury and will be evaluated closer to the quarterfinals. For now, Gotham capped the race that was theirs to win.

The eighth and final NWSL playoff spot came down to a battle between three clubs. Seattle Reign controlled their own fate, while North Carolina Courage and Denver Summit each needed to take the other out and root for Orlando Pride to win.

Seattle's identity this year has been more about organization and defense than goals, and their 1-0 victory over Orlando to clinch the final playoff spot was about as representative of the 2026 Seattle Reign as you could get. Playing particularly motivated, with playoffs at stake, and honoring longtime Reign veteran Jess Fishlock, Seattle pulled ahead just past the hour mark on a set piece that featured not one, but two flicks, and a clinical finish by center back Jordyn Bugg.

The backheel, the finish, just 🤩 pic.twitter.com/mtMSki9G25

#1238. Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3,4,5,6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100—a known command neuron for walking—as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.

#1237. Derek McInnes will need to do more than 'win ugly' if he is to thrive as Rangers manager

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 13:55 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:39 EDT, 1 November 2026

There have been several Rangers managers over the past ten years or so who never quite seemed to grasp the most basic and fundamental parameters of the job.

You either win matches and win trophies, or you are deemed a failure. If you do not fulfil that remit, there is no mitigation that can be offered. No extra points for artistic merit.

It is a reality which never felt like it sat all that comfortably with the likes of Mark Warburton, Michael Beale, Philippe Clement, Russell Martin or Danny Rohl.

Derek McInnes has spoken repeatedly this season about the fact that winning matches is ultimately what underpins everything else.

Unlike many of his predecessors, McInnes knows what is expected of him, and he knows what will and will not be tolerated by supporters.

Even on days when his team do not play overly well and it turns into a grind, as was the case in this Premier Sports Cup semi-final against Aberdeen at Hampden yesterday, getting the win is all that matters.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes enjoys his team's Premier Sports Cup victory over Aberdeen

Rangers fans have never demanded silky free-flowing football. Even Walter Smith’s nine-in-a-row team would never be mistaken for prime Barcelona. But they were efficient, effective and relentless.

But here’s the rub. Rangers are too often a tough watch at the moment. Winning ugly is a valuable and necessary trait to have for any manager in the Ibrox hotseat, no question.

When it starts to become the default method, however, it becomes more of a concern. This is where McInnes is still searching for the right balance in this Rangers team.

In the early part of the season, he flip-flopped between various different systems: 4-3-3, 4-2-3-1, 3-5-2, before eventually settling on 4-4-2.

Perhaps it was the back-to-back victories over Celtic in September that cemented in his own mind the belief that 4-4-2 would be the way forward.

But there have been times recently when it has looked an awkward fit. It didn’t work at all against Hearts at Tynecastle last week as Rangers scraped a 2-2 draw.

And, despite eventually grinding Aberdeen into submission courtesy of a late winner from Ryan Naderi, it didn’t really work yesterday.

Aberdeen arrived short-handed, with five defenders missing through injury or suspension, and set up to make the evening as awkward as possible for Rangers.

By and large, Stephen Robinson’s side succeeded in doing exactly that. It was a performance which offered some signs of life despite their woeful form in the league.

But the reality for Robinson heading into next weekend’s home clash with Hibs is that he probably needs a win in order to save his job.

Aberdeen will also rue a massive opportunity that was squandered by Kevin Nisbet on 76 minutes when the score was locked at 0-0.

After Stuart Armstrong fed a pass into his path, Nisbet hesitated when the situation demanded that he hit it first time.

Striker Ryan Naderi celebrates with supporters after scoring the only goal of the semi-final

Rangers dominated possession and had 25 shots at goal, although the fact that only five of those were on target was described as ‘embarrassing’ by McInnes.

But it was often slow and disjointed. As was the case at Tynecastle, they completely bypassed midfield and went long to Naderi and his strike partner Kevin Kelsy, looking to then play off second balls.

You wonder what might be possible from this Rangers team if they were to go with three in midfield and really control games properly and play through the lines.

It’s not like they don’t have the personnel. Nico Raskin and Dan Neil are more than capable of getting the ball down and playing football.

But the overall balance of the midfield just doesn’t look right at present. Perhaps this was why McInnes tried to shake things up by dropping Neil and playing James Penrice in the middle of the pitch at Hampden.

RANGERS (4-4-2): Pandur 6.5; Sterling 5, Fernandez 6.5 (Godfrey 89), Makhanya 7.5, Rommens 6 (Neil 65); BOUANANI 7.5 (Curtis 89), Penrice 7, Raskin 6, Min-su 6 (Gassama 65); Naderi 7.5, Kelsy 6.5 (Chukwuani 89).

ABERDEEN (3-5-2): Muller 7; Devlin 6.5 (Marshall 89), Molloy 6.5, Milne 6.5; Gyamfi 3 (Armstrong 14), Ronan 6 (Smith 89), Lyons 6.5, Aremu 7 (Yogane 89), Guinness-Walker 7.5; Nisbet 4, Mouloua 5 (Ntelo 56).

Penrice, a left-back by trade, didn’t have a poor game by any stretch. After eventually reverting to his normal position when Neil came off the bench, he teed up the winner for Naderi.

But, playing him in midfield was a change that never really worked. It was a square peg in a round hole – and actually highlighted the lack of faith that McInnes has in some players.

Tochi Chukwuani and Vanja Dragojevic were signed for a total outlay of almost £9million. Chukwuani hasn’t started a game since the defeat to Jablonec and has been limited to substitute appearances.

Dragojevic also hasn’t featured from the start since the Jablonec game – and has made only one substitute appearance since then.

The word from Rangers is that the 20-year-old midfielder, who captained Partizan Belgrade, is a talent but still very raw. That’s fine. But he is not going to develop if he doesn’t play any football.

Chukwuani and Dragojevic were both signed for good money. The current system has cast them as bystanders. It is incumbent on McInnes as manager to nurture that talent.

All in all, this was an exercise in winning ugly for Rangers. There is, of course, a lot to be said for that. Especially in cup semi-finals, getting the job done is all that matters.

But when winning ugly starts to become the norm rather than a fallback, it is only natural that fans will start to question the style of play.

Badredine Bouanani was Rangers’ best player against Aberdeen. He was a constant menace to them, cutting in from the right on to his left foot.

Aberdeen striker Kevin Nisbet could not come up with the goal his team needed at Hampden

Minsu Kim probably had his poorest game yet in a Rangers jersey. But there’s no doubting his talent and the fact he’s a player around whom things should be built this season.

Ultimately, McInnes is still searching for the right balance. That search is visible in the selections and in the way the team plays.

A midfield that can control the tempo, progress the ball cleanly through pressure, and offer both defensive cover and creative outlets remains a work in progress.

This victory at Hampden demonstrated the progress being made in terms of a team who can grind it out, but also highlighted some of the limitations that remain in this Rangers team.

Winning ugly is a useful habit. Whether it can evolve into something more fluent on a consistent basis remains to be seen.

Whether midfielders purchased at considerable expense can be integrated rather than left on the periphery, and whether the long-ball tendency becomes a Plan B to fall back on or merely the default style of play – these are the issues that will define how this Rangers team develops under McInnes.

#1236. How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited the UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands

Argentina and the UK once fought a war over the Falkland Islands. Now, the multibillion-dollar Sea Lion oil project has reignited old tensions, with Buenos Aires seeking to put a stop to the plans.

Home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.

However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in the North Falkland Basin is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.

Argentina has laid claim to the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, for two centuries. In 1982, the dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.

A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory.

The Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface. Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project was stopped within two weeks.

The oil project is being run by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.

Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."

He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.

"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.

Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."

Howerver, he thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."

Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.

The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.

That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.

"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."

However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.

Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were Milei's legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.

"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.

However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.

"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."

Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."

Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.

In a televised address last month, the Argentine president also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.

Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns, and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with US President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."

Bragger played this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer said it would be "very shocking" if the US came down on the side of Argentina.

While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.

"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.

#1235. Roy Keane shows softer family side in new holiday snaps

Roy Keane is renowned for being a tough character on and off the field â first as a player, then as a pundit â with crunching tackles and even tougher words down the camera.

But while he may be one of footballâs most feared hardmen, away from the game and with his family, heâs just like anyone else â a doting grandfather with a softer side.

Recently, the former Manchester United captain showed that side in full on Instagram, sharing a series of snaps from a family holiday to celebrate his 54th birthday.

Among the photos and videos were moments of Keane splashing around in the pool with his grandchildren, helping them build sandcastles on the beach, and smiling proudly as he held his youngest â and third â grandchild, born earlier this year.

The caption to his birthday post was as warm as the images themselves: "Happy Birthday to me. All the gifts I need."

For a man whose career was built on grit and steel, it was a rare public glimpse of the gentler moments that matter most.

Even the toughest captains, it turns out, have a soft centre.

#1234. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Instead, his scanning of the pitch before receiving the ball had revealed that goalkeeper Walter Benítez was off his line and Brighton’s attacking players were being tightly guarded by defenders. Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.

The Premier League is set to introduce a new LGBTQ+ inclusion campaign after ending its partnership with Stonewall, the charity behind the widely recognised Rainbow Laces initiative.

Stonewallâs Rainbow Laces campaign, launched in 2013, became a fixture across English football, with players from all Premier League clubs wearing rainbow-coloured laces and captains donning rainbow armbands to promote acceptance and equality. After over a decade of collaboration, the league will now lead its own campaign, timed to coincide with LGBTQ+ History Month in February, The Telegraph report.

"Alongside other sporting bodies the FA has been instrumental in advancing LGBTQ+ inclusion at the grassroots level and more recently the Women's Super League has taken up the mantle as the women's game has grown - enabling Rainbow Laces to reach more diverse audiences."

Additionally, Manchester United scrapped plans for LGBTQ+ support jackets after a player refused to participate.

With no openly gay or bisexual players currently in the Premier League, and the surge in discriminatory incidents, some question the timing of the split from Stonewall â an organisation highly respected for its work in LGBTQ+ advocacy.

Details of the Premier Leagueâs new campaign are still under wraps, but as the league presses âreset,â thereâs hope it will introduce a meaningful and effective initiative that advances equality rather than undermines it.

#1231. Early-onset cancer rising worldwide: Causes, risk, prevention

Across Latin America, early-onset cancer rates have risen, especially of bowel, breast and cervical cancers. But it is a worldwide trend.

The numbers are striking. Some cancer rates have doubled in the past 20 years. It's just not yet clear whether we're seeing a rise in actual cases or whether we're seeing more early-stage cases because of better awareness, diagnosis and treatment in hospitals.

Take, for example, colorectal (or bowel) cancer: In 2001, about one in every 26,000 people under 50 in England were diagnosed with it each year. By 2023, the rate of diagnoses was about one in 12,000. Twice what it was at the turn of the century.

That's according to the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), an international network of charities, which analyzed registry data from England, the United States and the Netherlands. It found the number of new cancer cases had risen for seven cancers in England alone.

So, rates have doubled, but the numbers overall are still small, said Amy Berrington de Gonzalez, a professor of clinical epidemiology at the Institute of Cancer Research in London.

"Cancer is still very uncommon among young people," Berrington de Gonzalez told DW. "Three times a small number is still a small number."

But she and other scientists still want to know why this is happening, because it is a worldwide trend. Latin America is a case in point.

A 2025 study analyzed registry data from 50 countries and territories up to 2017. It found early-onset colorectal cancer rising in 27 of those regions.

In Latin America, rates rose in Chile, Argentina, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Puerto Rico. Chile's rise — at almost 4% per year — was among the highest.

In Brazil, the evidence comes directly from hospitals. At the A.C. Camargo Cancer Center in Sao Paulo, the number of colorectal cancer patients under 50 grew by 7.6% per year between 2000 and 2023. That's a five-fold increase.

The number of patients over 50 grew even faster — at 8.1% — or about six-fold.

But since these figures came from a single hospital, they do not show whether cases are rising across Brazil. They may only reflect that this one hospital is treating more patients.

"We need better cancer registration systems," said Berrington de Gonzalez, "especially in countries like Brazil and Mexico, where obesity rates have also been increasing."

Marc Gunter, professor of cancer epidemiology at Imperial College London, said he expected Latin America to follow richer countries as diets there become more Westernized and lifestyles more sedentary. "I think it's already happening," he said.

In another study in 2025, involving 42 countries, Berrington de Gonzalez compared data from two age groups — 20 to 49 years and 50 years and older — between 2003 and 2017.

Six cancers — thyroid, breast, colorectal, kidney, uterine and leukemia — had risen among the younger groups in most countries. All but colorectal cancer were seen to rise in older adults, too.

In fact, colorectal cancer stood out. In about a third of the countries, it rose faster in younger adults than in older ones. "It is the one cancer that seems to be increasing in younger people whilst decreasing in older people," said Berrington de Gonzalez.

This has consequences for research. If cancers are rising in all age groups, the causes are likely to be widespread, so studies looking only at young people risk chasing complicated explanations with too little data to test them, she said.

A US study of pancreatic cancer in adults aged 15 to 39 years found the rise was almost entirely made up of early-stage tumors.

The authors said this suggested that instead of the number of cancer cases going up, it was the number of early diagnoses that had gone up. And that can be explained by better awareness in the community, with people getting checked more often.

But the data for colorectal cancer looks different: Some US studies show it rising in advanced stages of the disease as well, which suggests an increase in the number of cases, not just the number of diagnoses.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Obesity is an established cause of at least 13 cancers, according to the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).

According to a 2021 review of existing studies, young adults with obesity were almost twice as likely to develop colorectal cancer before the age of 50.

Obesity has also spread fastest among the young. The WHO reports that obesity rates have doubled among adults since the 1990s and quadrupled among adolescents.

Some also say ultra-processed foods and microplastics cause cancer. But Gunter said the evidence was inconclusive.

"There's a lot of hype," Gunter said, adding that more research was needed. Berrington de Gonzalez agreed: "Diets have changed, but we don't yet know the role they might play."

Gunter said individuals should not be blamed for living in societies built around convenience foods and desk jobs, and that lasting change needed public health policy.

But he also said that young people could lower their cancer risk by maintaining a healthy weight, moving more, eating more fiber and cutting back on processed meat.

"Going for a walk, being more physically active, eating more fruits and vegetables," he said. "Those things are maybe not so trendy, but they are really important."

For a 30-year-old reading this, Berrington de Gonzalez's message was one of reassurance: Cancer at a young age remains relatively rare.
